human: Stars form from dense cores in turbulent molecular clouds. According to the standard scenario of star formation, dense cores are created by cloud fragmentation. However, the physical mechanisms driving this process are still not fully understood from an observational standpoint.
ai: Stars emerge from the dense cores found within turbulent molecular clouds. Under the conventional model of star formation, these dense cores come into being through the fragmentation of clouds. Nevertheless, the physical processes that propel this fragmentation are not yet completely comprehended through observational data.

human: Molecular clouds fragment into dense, compact cores, with gravitationally bound cores being widely recognized as the primary sites of protostellar formation. The process of gravitational fragmentation is considered key to core creation in molecular clouds (e.g. Larson, 1985; André et al., 2010). Recent observations from the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) appear to have provided empirical support for this concept. These observations show that the core separations within high-mass, cluster-forming molecular clumps are in reasonable agreement with the predictions of thermal Jeans fragmentation (Klaassen et al., 2018; Beuther et al., 2022; Lu et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2022; Ishihara et al., 2024; Sanhueza et al., 2019; Morii et al., 2024).This suggests that thermal gravitational, or thermal Jeans, fragmentation governs core formation in high-mass regions.
ai: Molecular clouds undergo a process of fragmentation, resulting in the formation of dense, compact cores. These cores, particularly those bound by gravity, are widely acknowledged as crucial locations for the emergence of protostars. The phenomenon known as gravitational fragmentation is often cited as a fundamental mechanism behind the formation of these cores within molecular clouds (e.g., Larson, 1985; André et al., 2010). Recent data collected from the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array ALMA seems to lend empirical support to this theoretical framework. These findings reveal that the spacing between cores within high-mass, cluster-forming molecular clumps aligns well with the forecasts made by the thermal Jeans fragmentation model (Klaassen et al., 2018; Beuther et al., 2022; Lu et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2022; Ishihara et al., 2024; Sanhueza et al., 2019; Morii et al., 2024). This indicates that thermal gravitational fragmentation, or thermal Jeans fragmentation, plays a pivotal role in regulating the formation of cores within high-mass regions.

Their investigation successfully identified approximately 10^3 dense cores. The findings reveal that the median distance between these cores is around 7800 astronomical units. This measurement aligns well with the thermal Jeans length typical for the parent clumps. This thermal Jeans length is calculated using the formula ( λ J sim c s sqrt{{π}{G rho}} ), where c s represents the sound speed, G is the gravitational constant, and rho stands for the density. Additionally, the mass of each core, as determined by the Jeans mass equation, is consistent with theoretical expectations.

human: These results suggest that thermal Jeans fragmentation plays a significant role in core formation within dense, cluster-forming regions. However, it remains unclear whether the same dynamics apply in other environments. In several nearby molecular clouds, such as Orion A and ρ -Ophiuchus, most dense cores have been found to be gravitationally unbound and pressure-confined (Maruta et al., 2010; Kirk et al., 2017; Takemura et al., 2023). The mechanisms responsible for the formation of these unbound cores remain uncertain.

Observations from nearby molecular clouds, including Orion A and ρ-Ophiuchus, reveal that many of the dense cores identified are not gravitationally bound but are instead confined by pressure (Maruta et al., 2010; Kirk et al., 2017; Takemura et al., 2023). The processes leading to the emergence of these unbound cores have yet to be fully understood.

human: This paper focuses on nearby low-mass clouds, specifically the Polaris Flare (hereafter Polaris) and Lupus I, where the role of cloud self-gravity is relatively diminished compared to the influence of supersonic turbulence, which may even dominate over self-gravity. To achieve a deeper understanding of core formation in various cloud environments, we apply methods similar to those used by Ishihara et al. (2024) to investigate the physical processes governing core formation in these less dense, low-mass molecular clouds.
ai: This study delves into the characteristics of low-mass clouds in close proximity, with particular attention given to the Polaris Flare, or simply Polaris, alongside Lupus I. In these specific regions, the impact of a cloud’s gravitational pull on itself appears to be less significant when weighed against the formidable influence of supersonic turbulence. In some cases, this turbulence could indeed prevail over gravitational forces. To unravel the complexities of core development within these varied cloud settings, we employ approaches analogous to those utilized by Ishihara et al. 2024. These methods allow us to explore and analyze the physical mechanisms that regulate core formation within these less dense, low-mass molecular clouds.

human: We consider three key fragmentation mechanisms: thermal Jeans fragmentation, turbulent Jeans fragmentation, and turbulent fragmentation. In thermal Jeans fragmentation, the balance between thermal pressure and self-gravity determines how gravitationally bound structures form. The characteristic mass and length scales in this scenario are the Jeans mass ( M J ) and Jeans length ( L J ), which depend on the cloud’s temperature and density (Jeans, 1928; Larson, 1985).
ai: We examine three principal mechanisms that contribute to fragmentation: thermal Jeans fragmentation, turbulent Jeans fragmentation, and turbulent fragmentation. In the context of thermal Jeans fragmentation, it is the interplay between the thermal pressure and the force of self-gravity that dictates the formation of gravitationally stable structures. Within this framework, we define specific mass and length scales known as the Jeans mass M J and Jeans length L J, which are functions of the cloud’s intrinsic temperature and density parameters, as originally conceptualized by Jeans 1928 and further elaborated by Larson 1985.

human: Turbulent Jeans fragmentation is a variation of thermal Jeans fragmentation, whereby turbulent pressure supports the cloud, leading to larger characteristic mass and length scales than in the thermal case. However, this model does not account for the full properties of cloud turbulence and is only applicable to larger structures for which turbulent motions can be approximated as isotropic (e.g. Mac Low & Klessen, 2004; Palau et al., 2015).
ai: Turbulent Jeans fragmentation represents a distinct version of thermal Jeans fragmentation. In this scenario, the presence of turbulent pressure acts to sustain the cloud, resulting in characteristic mass and length scales that are notably larger compared to those found in the purely thermal scenario. Nevertheless, this particular model falls short of addressing all the intricacies associated with cloud turbulence. Its application is limited, being suitable primarily for larger structural formations where turbulent movements can be sufficiently assumed to be isotropic, as discussed in the works of Mac Low and Klessen 2004 and further explored by Palau and colleagues in 2015.

human: In turbulent fragmentation, dense cores form through the dynamical compression of local turbulence (Padoan & Nordlund, 2002). The density probability distribution function (PDF) in turbulent clouds tends to follow a log-normal distribution due to repeated compression (Padoan et al., 2020). In a turbulent medium with a power-law energy spectrum, there are no inherent characteristic mass and length scales. However, in the interstellar medium, the power law breaks at the sonic scale, l S , where turbulent velocity dispersions become comparable to the sound speed (Federrath & Klessen, 2012). For nearby molecular clouds, this scale is typically measured to be 0.1 pc ( au). Therefore, the sonic scale, l S , may represent the characteristic length for turbulent fragmentation, with the corresponding mass ( M S ) estimated as , respectively,where is the average cloud density. Since these three fragmentation mechanisms predict different characteristic mass and length scales, we aim to constrain the dominant fragmentation process in these nearby clouds by deriving core masses and separations from observational data.
ai: In the intricate phenomenon of turbulent fragmentation, dense cores emerge as a result of the dynamic squeezing caused by localized turbulence (Padoan & Nordlund, 2002). Within turbulent clouds, the density probability distribution function PDF typically aligns with a log-normal distribution, attributable to successive compression events (Padoan et al., 2020). A turbulent environment possessing a power-law energy spectrum lacks intrinsic characteristic mass and length dimensions. Nevertheless, in the realm of the interstellar medium, the power-law spectrum deviates at the sonic scale, denoted as l S, where the dispersions in turbulent velocities become analogous to the speed of sound (Federrath & Klessen, 2012). For molecular clouds in close proximity, this sonic scale is generally quantified at approximately 0.1 parsecs au. Hence, the sonic scale, l S, might serve as the fundamental length scale pertinent to turbulent fragmentation, with the associated mass, M S, being computed accordingly based on the average density of the cloud. Considering that these three distinct fragmentation processes propose various characteristic mass and length scales, our objective is to pinpoint the leading fragmentation mechanism within these nearby clouds by extracting core masses and intervals from observational data.

human: Strong stellar magnetic fields and dense winds are predicted to exist in young stars such as V1298 Tau. Despite being very challenging, revealing radio emission from SPI at GHz frequencies would probe the properties of the stellar magnetospheres, providing a measure of the stellar magnetic fields, and potentially allowing for the modelling of the planetary magnetic fields (see e.g. Callingham et al., 2024, and references therein). human: We observed V1298 Tau in C-high band with the SRT on three consecutive days (26-28 June 2024), each time on intervals of about 1 hour. Full-Stokes parameters were acquired with the SARDARA backend (Melis et al., 2018) in the frequency range 6000 - 7200 MHz, at a spectral resolution of 1.46 MHz per channel. With a resolution of 2.9 arcmin at 6.6 GHz, we expect a confusion noise of ∼ 0.4 mJy (e.g. Condon, 2002). We calculated that the known radio source NVSS J040522+200958, which is located at 92 arcsec from our target, contaminates the beam with a flux of 0.15 mJy in C-band. Although the use of a single dish for detecting radio stars is not optimal due to much lower resolution and sensitivity compared to interferometry, the observations with SRT represent a proof of concept for a kind of object such as V1298 Tau, for which non-periodic, irregular peak emission at a mJy level could be expected from very intense and fast bursts (e.g. Bower et al., 2016; Launhardt et al., 2022), and potentially caught by SRT at different epochs than those covered by JVLA and uGMRT. We performed on-off position switching on the target, each observations lasting 1 minute. On 26 June we carried out 12 on-off pointings, while on 27 and 28 June we performed 21 on-off cycles. The on position was centred on V1298 Tau while the off was taken with a 1 degree azimuth offset at the same elevation. The beam FWHM in the considered frequency range is 2.9 arcmin. We recorded the data stream by acquiring 33 full bandwidth spectra per second. Band-pass, flux density, and polarization calibrators were done with at least three cross scans on the source calibrators 3C147, 3C48, 3C138 and 3C84 performed at the beginning of each observing run. The data reduction was done with the Single-dish Spectral-polarimetry Software (SCUBE; Murgia et al., 2016). We applied the gain-elevation curve correction to account for the gain variation with elevation due to the telescope structure gravitational stress change and we corrected for the atmosphere opacity. We eliminated all RFI at specific well-known frequencies and ran an automatic flagging procedure to eliminate all residual RFI. Finally, we averaged the RFI-cleaned spectral channels of all samples together and produced a light curve by subtracting the interpolated intensity of the nearby off positions from the on positions.

In our research, we demonstrate that a streamlined version of graphcodes can effectively output a description of a two-parameter module. This description is tantamount to a presentation of the module itself. Representing the module as a graph facilitates an uncomplicated transition between combinatorial structures and algebraic expressions. Specifically, the connected components of the graphcode are akin to the summands of the module, while isolated paths within the graph are equivalent to intervals. We provide evidence that, in practical scenarios, graphcodes significantly enhance the efficiency of decomposing a module into its indecomposable summands. Furthermore, adopting the graphcode perspective allows the development of a straightforward algorithm aimed at determining whether a persistence module can be decomposed into intervals within a specific timeframe. This presents an improvement over the previously established time complexity bound.

ai: Breaking down a persistence module into its simplest, indivisible parts offers a valuable method for understanding its framework. This process is an extension of the barcode or persistence diagram approach used in one-parameter persistence. Thanks to the Krull-Remak-Schmidt theorem, this breakdown is almost uniquely determined, although the pieces themselves can become quite intricate. Despite this complexity, if the module is concrete, the complete decomposition can be handled efficiently in polynomial time by employing the overarching meataxe algorithm, as noted in [27]. A more rapid algorithm for dealing with persistence modules has been introduced by Dey and Xin [18], who capitalized on the notion that the presentation is distinctly graded. Recently, Dey, Jendrysiak, and Kerber [14] have advanced beyond this requirement by developing an effective implementation that operates without assuming distinct grading, which is available in their library. Although graph codes cannot entirely dissect the module, they nonetheless expose some of its internal configuration and can, for instance, enable a comprehensive decomposition, as we illustrate.

human: Large Language Model (LLM) applications have emerged as a prominent use case for Function-as-a-Service (FaaS) due to their high computational demands and sporadic invocation patterns.However, serving LLM functions within FaaS frameworks faces significant GPU-side cold start.A fundamental approach involves leveraging a template with function state saved on GPUs to bypass the cold start for new invocations.Yet, this approach struggles with the high GPU footprint, dynamic initialization behaviors, and lazy GPU kernel loading inherent in LLM functions, primarily due to a lack of insight into the underlying execution details.In this paper, we introduce T, an optimized FaaS framework for LLM applications that achieves fast startups by tracing fine-grained execution paths.By utilizing the traced execution details, T generates adaptive function templates, effectively breaking startup barriers for LLM functions.Extensive evaluations demonstrate that T reduces cold start latency by and improves the -ile time-to-first-token by , surpassing state-of-the-art methods.
ai: Applications based on large language models LLMs have increasingly become a noteworthy example of Function-as-a-Service FaaS usage, largely due to their demanding computational power needs and irregular invocation patterns. Nonetheless, deploying LLM functions within FaaS environments is hampered by notable delays known as GPU-side cold starts. A basic strategy to tackle this involves creating a template where the function’s state is preserved on GPUs, allowing subsequent invocations to skip the cold start phase. However, this method encounters obstacles such as the substantial GPU resource usage, the variable nature of initialization processes, and the procrastinated loading of GPU kernels specific to LLM functions. These challenges arise chiefly because of an inadequate understanding of the deep execution dynamics. In the present study, we introduce an innovative FaaS framework named T, specifically designed to optimize LLM applications by facilitating rapid startups through tracking detailed execution pathways. By harnessing these meticulously traced execution insights, T develops adaptable function templates which successfully dismantle the startup impediments of LLM functions. Comprehensive evaluations reveal that T effectively diminishes cold start latency and enhances the time-to-first-token performance, bettering current leading methodologies in the process.

human: Function-as-a-Service (FaaS) [1] has emerged as the leading serverless paradigm in cloud platforms [2, 3]. By adopting functions as the basic unit of scheduling, FaaS provides distinct benefits for both application developers and cloud providers.FaaS allows developers to focus on core function logic without caring infrastructure management.Additionally, its pay-as-you-go model lowers costs, particularly for functions with low invocation frequency [4].For cloud providers, FaaS enhances resource utilization by enabling more effective resource management, ensuring efficiency and scalability.

For developers, FaaS enables concentration on essential function logic, freeing them from the complexities of managing underlying infrastructure. Furthermore, its pay-as-you-go pricing structure reduces expenses, especially for functions that are seldom called upon [4]. On the side of cloud providers, FaaS optimizes resource usage by facilitating more efficient management, thereby enhancing overall efficiency and scalability of resources.

human: Large language model (LLM) applications are emerging as a prominent use case for FaaS.These applications require both rapid innovation and significant GPU resources but may encounter low invocation frequencies, particularly during early deployment phases.The high computational demands and unpredictable workloads make FaaS an ideal solution for hosting LLM functions.Recognizing these benefits, many companies, such as Hugging Face and RunPod [5, 6, 7], now offer FaaS services designed for LLM applications.

These sophisticated applications demand swift innovation alongside substantial GPU resources. However, they often face infrequent invocation rates, especially during the initial stages of rollout. The combination of intense computational requirements and the unpredictability of workloads makes FaaS a perfect match for deploying LLM functions efficiently. Many businesses, including Hugging Face and RunPod, have recognized these advantages and now provide FaaS offerings specifically tailored for LLM applications.

human: We observe that the inherent long cold startup problem in FaaS becomes much worse, exacerbated by the complexity of LLM execution environments.From memory stack aspect,executing LLMs requires managing a large footprint across a three-tier memory hierarchy: storage, host memory, and GPU memory.From application aspect,different from traditional FaaS applications, costly dynamic model initialization is often required.For instance, multilingual functions [8] adapt to individual requests by dynamically attaching language-specific LoRA adapters [9] to a shared base LLM [10, 11, 12].The dynamics makes many cache-based optimizations inefficient.From context preparing aspect,inference on GPUs necessitates preparing the execution environment, including creating CUDA contexts [13] and other setup operations.
ai: The intrinsic issue of prolonged cold startup times in Function as a Service FaaS setups becomes notably more severe due to the intricate nature of executing large language models LLMs. Considering the memory stack perspective, running LLMs necessitates the maneuvering of substantial amounts of data within a comprehensive three-layered memory structure: storage, host memory, and GPU memory. From the application standpoint, unlike conventional FaaS applications, there is often a necessity for the costly procedure of dynamically initializing models. For example, multilingual functions adapt to the unique demands of incoming requests by dynamically integrating language-specific LoRA (Layer-specific Optimization and Resource Allocation) adapters with a common foundational LLM. This dynamic integration process renders many cache-based optimization strategies less effective. Regarding the preparation of context, performing inference on GPUs demands meticulous preparation of the execution environment, which includes the creation of CUDA contexts and performing other preparatory operations.

human: illustrates the cold start process of an LLM function: initializing the model on the host (loading the checkpoint into host memory), transferring the model from the host to the GPU, and performing the inference on GPU.The first two steps are the primary contributors to cold start. Recent studies [14, 15] have proposed techniques to mitigate the startup latency associated with host-side initialization.In the upper half of , state-of-the-art frameworks [14] overlap storage-to-host model loading with host-to-GPU data transfer and cache the models in a host-side memory pool.However, even if the storage-to-host transfer (the first step) is optimized to negligible level [14], the time-to-first-token (TTFT) remains greater than inference latency, primarily due to host-to-GPU data transfer (the second step).
ai: The cold start procedure of a large language model LLM function involves several key steps. Initially, the model must be set up on the host, which entails loading the checkpoint into the host’s memory. Subsequently, the model is transferred from the host’s environment to the GPUs, where inference is performed. The major factors contributing to the cold start are largely found in these first two steps. Recent research efforts, documented in studies [14, 15], have put forward methods aimed at reducing the startup lag that occurs during the host-side initialization phase. In the upper portion of , contemporary frameworks [14] have introduced the practice of simultaneously loading the model from storage to host while concurrently transferring data from host to GPU. These frameworks also incorporate the caching of models within a memory pool situated on the host side. Nevertheless, even with the optimization of the initial storage-to-host transfer step to an almost insignificant duration [14], the time required for the first token TTFT continues to exceed the inference latency, mainly because of the time consumed during the host-to-GPU data transfer, which constitutes the second step in the process.

human: To entirely eliminate cold start, a fundamental solution is template-start [16, 17].A template consists of a pre-initialized function state cached in memory.Template-start allows new invocations to launch directly from the template, bypassing all initialization steps.To prevent data conflicts, the template must be request-agnostic, and a copy-on-write mechanism is critical for safe template sharing.As shown in the bottom right of , by saving the initialized LLM in GPU memory as a template, we could directly launch a new invocation, entirely excluding the cold-start latency.Unfortunately, we find that template-start, which blindly reuses an existing function state without understanding the execution details across function invocation, is generally ineffective for LLM functions.
ai: To completely eliminate the issue of cold starts, one fundamental approach is the use of a template-start mechanism, as discussed in sources [16, 17]. A template, in this context, refers to a function state that has been pre-initialized and stored in memory. The template-start method enables new function calls to commence directly from the stored template, thereby bypassing all the typical initialization steps. To avoid any data conflicts, it is essential for the template to be entirely independent of specific requests, and employing a copy-on-write strategy is crucial to ensure the safe sharing of the template. According to the depiction at the bottom right, by caching the initialized large language model LLM within the GPU’s memory as a template, it becomes possible to trigger a new function call instantaneously, effectively eliminating the delays associated with cold starts. However, our findings indicate that the template-start approach, which indiscriminately reutilizes an existing function state without thoroughly considering the execution specifics across various function calls, generally proves ineffective for LLM functions.

human: Firstly, template-start struggles to reconcile the need for fast startup with high template density, due to the substantial footprint of LLMs.E.g., an Nvidia RTX A6000 GPU (48 GB) can accommodate only one template for the function in .With such a low template density, template-start is impractical within a FaaS framework, where multi-tenancy is essential.Based on the fact that model weights in the template are accessed sequentially (kernel by kernel) during inference [18],we identify the opportunity to overlap host-to-GPU data transfers with inference.Such overlap potentially reduces the template footprint and increases template density without impacting latency.However, such overlapping cannot be achieved without knowing the order of weights are accessed in a model during inference.
ai: To begin with, the method known as template-start encounters significant difficulties in balancing the requirement for rapid initialization with the necessity of maintaining a high density of templates. This challenge arises primarily due to the large memory demands of large language models LLMs. For instance, an Nvidia RTX A6000 GPU, which offers a memory capacity of 48 GB, has the ability to hold merely a single template for the intended function. The resulting minimal density of templates renders template-start inefficient in a Function as a Service FaaS environment, where the capacity to support multiple tenants concurrently is crucial. Given that the weights of the model within the template are accessed in a sequential manner-kernel by kernel-during the inference process [18], we have identified a potential strategy to enhance efficiency. This involves overlapping the data transfers from the host to the GPU with the ongoing inference computations. By doing so, it is possible to diminish the memory demands of the template and consequently boost the density of templates without adversely affecting the latency. Nonetheless, implementing such an overlapping strategy is contingent upon having a clear understanding of the sequence in which the model’s weights are accessed during inference operations.

human: Secondly, template-start fails to reduce cold start latency for functions with dynamic initialization.As previously discussed, LoRA adapters, which are dynamically attached to the base model, are request-specific [19, 20, 21].Although these adapters account for less than of the base model, the initialization of such LLM functions does not meet the criteria for being saved in the template.Ideally, it is possible to mitigate cold start for dynamic LLM functions, by creating a template with the most reusable initialization.Such design currently cannot be achieved, lacking a mechanism that identifies and excludes dynamically initialized components.
ai: Secondly, the template-start approach encounters difficulties in lowering the cold start latency for functions that involve dynamic initialization. As previously highlighted, LoRA adapters are appended dynamically to the core model and are tailored to specific requests [19, 20, 21]. Despite these adapters constituting a minimal portion of the base model, initializing these large language model LLM functions does not qualify for preservation within the template structure. Ideally, one could address the issue of cold start delays for dynamic LLM functions by formulating a template that encompasses the most commonly reusable initialization processes. However, achieving such a design is currently hindered by the absence of a framework capable of identifying and excluding components that are initialized in a dynamic fashion.

human: Thirdly, starting new invocations from a template with model initialized still suffers from cold start overhead.Our study in § also reveals that the inference time during a cold start is still higher than that within a fully warm function state, where the model has been loaded and executed once.The key factor is that the code segments for kernel execution are lazily loaded onto GPU during the first inference [22].Such overhead can be eliminatedif these code segments could be proactively loaded when pre-warming processes for new invocations.However, without prior knowledge of the specific GPU kernels launched during inference,such proactive code loading cannot be achieved.
ai: Thirdly, initiating fresh invocations using a template with the model already initialized continues to experience cold start latency issues. Our investigation in § uncovers that inference times remain longer during a cold start compared to when the function is entirely warm, meaning the model has been loaded and executed at least once. The chief reason behind this delay is that the code segments required for kernel execution are only loaded onto the GPU during the initial inference, as noted in reference [22]. To mitigate this overhead, these code segments should ideally be loaded in advance during the pre-warming stages of new invocations. Unfortunately, without prior insight into which specific GPU kernels will be activated during inference, this kind of proactive code loading remains unfeasible.

human: To this end, we introduce T, an efficient FaaS framework tailored for LLM applications with fast cold start.The key insight of T is that a detailed understanding of the fine-grained execution paths of an LLM function-spanning initialization and inference-unlocks new opportunities to optimize cold start.Unfortunately, the fine-grained execution paths required for startup optimizations are implicit within each invocation and cannot be manually exposed by function developers.T integrates a lightweight tracing mechanism to automatically extract these fine-grained execution paths at runtime.Using adaptive function templates generated from traced execution paths, T tackles the cold-start problem for LLM functions by two optimizations: proactive code segment loading and adaptive state forking.While proactive code segment loading ensures a fully pre-warmed GPU context, adaptive state forking efficiently reuses static components and overlaps model loading with inference.
ai: To achieve this objective, we unveil T, a highly efficient Function-as-a-Service FaaS framework specifically designed for large language model LLM applications, boasting a rapid cold start. The central concept behind T is rooted in a comprehensive comprehension of the intricate execution pathways of an LLM function that encompass both initialization and inference. This insight reveals new avenues for optimizing cold starts. Unfortunately, each invocation embeds these meticulous execution paths, which remain obscured and cannot be manually accessed by function developers. To address this, T incorporates a lightweight tracing mechanism, enabling the automated extraction of these detailed execution paths during runtime. By leveraging adaptive function templates derived from these traced execution paths, T addresses the cold-start issue for LLM functions through two primary optimizations: proactive loading of code segments and adaptive state forking. The proactive loading of code segments guarantees a thoroughly pre-warmed GPU context, while adaptive state forking adeptly reutilizes static components, effectively overlapping the model loading phase with the inference process.

human: We implement T by extending PyTorch to serve as the runtime for LLM functions.T transparently supports LLM functions wrapped with a wide range of LLM models.We conducted extensive evaluations of T using representative LLMs [12, 11, 10, 23, 24, 25] of various sizes, both with and without LoRA enabled.Experimental results show that T achieves speedup in cold start latency compared to state-of-the-art solutions.Furthermore, under real-world workloads, T reduces the -ile of TTFT by .The key contributions are as follows:We present a detailed analysis of the cold-start overhead of LLM functions on GPUs and highlight the obstacles of directly applying template-start for optimization.We identify that the primary challenge in optimizing the cold start of LLM functions lies in the unawareness of the fine-grained execution paths underlying invocations.We build up a lightweight, weight-centric tracing mechanism to automatically expose the fine-grained execution paths without manual effort.We consolidate optimizations based on the traced fine-grained execution paths to minimize the startup latency of cold LLM function invocations.

human: Stage-1 in primarily involves loading model checkpoints into host memory.State-of-the-art solutions [14] tailored for LLMs utilize a pinned host memory pool to efficiently load and cache model weights from local storage.With host memory offering significantly greater capacity than GPU memory ( in our testbed), advanced pre-loading policies [32, 27, 26] can further reduce the impact of Stage-1 to a negligible level.Throughout this paper, unless otherwise indicated, we assume that model weights are pre-cached in host memory by existing solutions.

2503.06421.section: Warming of CUDA context on GPU.
human: Stage-2 in involves the creation of the CUDA context, which initializes essential data structures for GPU-enabled processes.While this stage is notoriously time-consuming, it is function-agnostic, meaning it can be pre-warmed independently of the function invocations.As a result, pre-warming the CUDA context with a process pool allows it to be excluded entirely from the cold start of LLM function invocations.

By doing so, employing a process pool to pre-warm the CUDA context effectively removes its involvement in the initial, unoptimized activation of LLM function calls.

However, this particular approach is intrinsically tied to the workload, thereby not effectively resolving the cold start issues associated with model loading via PCIe. Furthermore, as far as we have determined, there appears to be an absence of studies focused on completely removing the inefficiencies encountered in Stage-4.

human: A strawman solution of achieving warm GPU function states for cold invocations is adopting template-start [17, 16], a method proven effective in the traditional CPU-only FaaS to resolve cold start.As shown in -(a), this method saves only request-agnostic initializations in a template and leverages the system call to launch new invocations from the template within 10ms.With data sharing via CUDA inter process communication (CUDA IPC) [35], a similar template for LLM functions can be prepared by first loading the model into GPU.-(b) illustrates this approach and summarizes its limitations, which stem from GPU or LLM-specific factors and are further elaborated below.
ai: One proposed method to tackle the issue of getting GPUs to transition smoothly into active states during infrequent invocations is to employ the template-start strategy, as referenced in works like [17, 16]. This technique, originally successful in addressing cold starts within CPU-exclusive Function-as-a-Service FaaS frameworks, involves maintaining a set of request-independent initializations stored in a template. Through the use of system calls, it can ignite new invocations from this template in less than 10 milliseconds. Depicted in -a, this method provides a foundation for quick activations.Furthermore, by harnessing CUDA inter-process communication (CUDA IPC) [35] for sharing data, a similarly structured template for Large Language Model LLM functions can be formulated. This involves pre-loading the model onto the GPU, facilitating swift operational readiness. Depicted in -b is an illustration of this method along with a discussion of its constraints. These limitations primarily arise from factors specifically related to GPUs or LLMs, and a more detailed analysis of these challenges is available further in the text.

2503.06421.section: Fast startup but low template density.
human: The strawman solution requires warming the entire model.After the warm-up phase, the GPU memory utilized by the template primarily consists of two components: the CUDA context (around 500 MB), and the model weights. compares the memory footprint of traditional small models with that of popular LLMs.While the footprint of small models can be even smaller than the requirement for the CUDA context, the situation becomes significantly worse for LLMs due to their substantial memory demands.As mentioned before, an Nvidia RTX A6000 GPU can support only a single template for Llama2-13B.Such low template density for fast startup is impractical for a FaaS framework, which is designed to accommodate numerous tenants’ functions.
ai: To implement the initial solution, it’s necessary to warm up the entire model beforehand. Once this warm-up is completed, the GPU memory allocation used by the template mainly involves two elements: the CUDA context-occupying roughly 500 MB-and the model’s weights. A comparison is made between the memory usage of conventional small models and that of well-known large language models LLMs. While smaller models may even consume less memory than the CUDA context demands, the scenario becomes drastically more challenging for LLMs due to their hefty memory requirements. Previously mentioned, an Nvidia RTX A6000 GPU can only host a single template for the Llama2-13B model. Such sparse template capacity for achieving a rapid startup is not feasible for a Function as a Service FaaS architecture, which is traditionally intended to efficiently support a multitude of tenants with their distinct functions.

human: Employing the strawman solution requires that the saved function state within the template is request-agnostic.Failure to do so would result in incorrect outputs and undermine the statelessness principle of FaaS[37].Nonetheless, the model initialization for LLM functions inherently exhibits request-specific variability.Application developers may utilize parameter-efficient finetuning techniques [38], like LoRA [9], to better meet individual user needs [19, 20, 21].As shown in , LoRA [9] allows the base model to remain unchanged across invocations while loading user-specific LoRA adapters for each request.Although adapters are significantly smaller than the base model (< ), the initialization of such dynamic LLM functions is not request-agnostic and cannot benefit from template-start.This limitation reduces the general applicability of template-start for resolve cold start.
ai: Implementing the strawman solution mandates that the preceding function state encapsulated within the template must remain free from request-specific dependencies. Failing to uphold this guideline could produce inaccurate results and compromise the fundamental statelessness tenet of Function as a Service FaaS [37]. Nevertheless, initializing models for Large Language Model LLM functions is inherently subject to variation based on individual requests. To better tailor services for unique user requirements [19, 20, 21], application developers might employ parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods [38], such as Low-Rank Adaptation LoRA [9]. As demonstrated in , LoRA [9] allows the base model to stay unchanged during repeated invocations by integrating LoRA adapters that are specific to each user request. Although these adapters are considerably smaller than the base model (< ), the initialization of such dynamic LLM functions does not exist independently of specific requests, and therefore, cannot take advantage of the benefits offered by template-start. This limitation subsequently weakens the broad applicability of the template-start strategy in addressing cold start issues.

human: Not all GPU data are shareable through CUDA IPC, as only memory explicitly allocated by the process is accessible through this mechanism.Code segments used for launching kernels during inference fall into this category. The CUDA runtime implicitly and lazily loads these segments during the first invocation of the related kernels.Thus, the strawman solution still suffers from cold kernel calls (around in ).A straightforward mitigation is to eagerly load all code segments during pre-warming of CUDA context.Our experiments show that this approach incurs an additional 1.12 GB of GPU memory consumption and increases the pre-warm time for a process from 830 ms to 3050 ms.This significant overhead makes it impractical to maintain a process pool for LLM invocations.
ai: Certain types of GPU data cannot be shared via CUDA Inter-Process Communication IPC, primarily because only memory that is explicitly allocated by a specific process is eligible for access through this method. Code segments utilized in the process of launching kernels during inference are categorized under this limited accessibility. The CUDA runtime, in its design, loads these code segments in an implicit and delayed manner, happening only during the initial invocation of the associated kernels. Because of this characteristic, the basic solution still encounters the issue of initial kernel calls being sluggish-evident in performance metrics such as time delays. To address this problem directly, a basic solution involves the proactive, or eager, loading of all necessary code segments during the pre-warming phase of the CUDA context. According to our experimental data, implementing this method results in an increased GPU memory usage by an additional 1.12 gigabytes. It is also associated with a marked increase in the time required for pre-warming a process, lengthening it from 830 milliseconds to a substantial 3050 milliseconds. This notable overhead in both memory usage and time renders it impractical to maintain a process pool for invoking Large Language Models LLMs, thereby posing challenges in optimizing resource efficiency.

human: (a) depicts a fine-grained execution path for a specific model weight.In a framework like PyTorch [39] for building LLM functions, weights are loaded from host to the GPU as tensors during initialization and subsequently utilized by operators through GPU kernel launches during inference.Moreover, model inference is also commonly represented as a data flow graph consisting of interconnected operators.By aligning the execution paths of all weights with the topological order of operators in inference, we derive the intrinsic dependencies of cold-start LLM invocation, as shown in -(b).
ai: a presents a detailed execution sequence for a particular model weight. In environments such as PyTorch [39], which is used for creating large language model LLM functions, weights are initially transferred from the host to the GPU as tensors during the setup phase. They are thereafter used by operators that are triggered via GPU kernel executions during the inference stage. Model inference is also frequently visualized as a data flow graph, where operators are linked together in a network. By synchronizing the execution routes of all weights with the sequential organization of operators during inference, we can uncover the inherent dependencies associated with the initiation of a cold-start LLM, as illustrated in b.

human: (b) reveals three key optimizations to address the limitations. 1) Kernel execution can overlap with weights loading required for subsequent kernels, removing the need to store the entire model in template.Since model loading via PCIe and inference latencies are comparable (hundreds of milliseconds), carefully managed overlapping would avoid extra latency while increasing template density.2) Dynamic elements of model initialization, such as LoRA adapters, can be removed by comparing execution paths across multiple invocations.As these elements constitute only a small fraction, and the base model’s weights are still saved within the template, dynamic LLM functions would benefit from template-start.3) Kernels specific to an LLM function can be profiled during inference and loaded proactively. Since each LLM function typically uses a small subset of kernels from the kernel libraries, these kernels can be pre-warmed with minimal overhead but excluded from cold start.
ai: b delineates three pivotal strategies designed to mitigate existing constraints. First, the execution of kernels can be made concurrent with the loading of weights for ensuing kernels, thus negating the necessity to store the entire model within the template. Given that the durations for model loading through PCIe and inference are both in the range of hundreds of milliseconds, meticulously orchestrating this overlap can circumvent unnecessary latency while simultaneously enhancing the density of the template. Second, dynamic aspects of model initialization, like the LoRA adapters, can be eliminated by conducting a comparison of execution pathways across multiple runs. Even though these dynamic segments make up just a small proportion, and the weights of the base model remain preserved within the template, dynamic large language model functions would gain efficiency from starting with the template. Third, it is possible to profile kernels unique to a large language model function during the inference phase and proactively load them. Typically, each function employs only a minor portion of the kernels available from the kernel libraries, allowing for these kernels to be preemptively warmed up with negligible additional load, all while circumventing the impact of a cold start.

human: There are several challenges in achieving the above optimizations based on fine-grained execution paths. 1) Fine-grained execution paths are implicit, making them difficult to be exposed manually by developers;2) LLM functions have per-invocation dynamic behaviors, requiring runtime extraction of execution paths;3) General support of these optimizations for various customized LLM functions is hard within a FaaS framework.
ai: Several significant obstacles arise when attempting to implement the aforementioned optimizations that rely on detailed execution paths. First, these fine-grained execution paths are inherently implicit, which poses a considerable challenge for developers attempting to manually reveal them; second, functions involving large language models LLM exhibit dynamic behaviors with each invocation, necessitating the real-time extraction of these execution paths; third, providing broad support for these optimizations across a wide range of customized LLM functions proves particularly difficult within a Function-as-a-Service FaaS framework.

human: To address these challenges, we introduce T, an efficient FaaS framework tailored for LLM applications.T first proposes a lightweight mechanism for transparently tracing fine-grained execution paths.By leveraging these paths, T resolves cold start issues across diverse LLM functions, achieving high template density, robust templates, and pre-warmed kernel calls.
ai: To tackle the aforementioned hurdles, we present a novel solution in the form of T, an optimized Function-as-a-Service framework specifically designed for large language model applications. T initially suggests an unobtrusive approach to systematically trace detailed execution routes. By effectively utilizing these routes, T manages to mitigate cold start issues that arise in various LLM functionalities. This process allows for the attainment of high template density and adds to the creation of durable templates. Moreover, T facilitates the execution of pre-warmed kernel calls, enhancing overall system efficiency.

human: Depicts the design of T, along with a streamlined function invocation workflow.T comprises three key modules: a , a , and a .Each function invocation runs atop a runtime tracer that traces the fine-grained execution paths with low overhead (§).It closely interacts with the template server to generate the function templates and launch new invocations.The template server stores the function templates and retrieves model weights from a pinned host memory pool for each invocation.The process pool provides pre-warmed processes for new function invocations.
ai: The text illustrates the architecture of T and details an efficient workflow for function calls within its framework. T is constructed with three primary components: a , a , and a . Every time a function is called, it operates on a runtime tracer that meticulously tracks the precise execution sequences with minimal interference (§). It maintains a close coordination with the template server to fabricate the function templates and to initiate new function calls. This template server is responsible for housing the function templates and acquiring model weights from a dedicated host memory pool that is pinned, tailored for each new function invocation. Furthermore, the process pool contributes by offering pre-prepared processes to facilitate new function executions.

human: For each LLM function, a function template is prepared either offline or online, based on fine-grained execution paths.T can adjust the size of model weights cached on the GPU within the template, while the remaining weights are loaded concurrently with inference.The template is updated by excluding dynamic components at runtime (§).Once the template is ready, T accepts user requests.Using the template, it pre-warms processes by initializing CUDA contexts and loading kernel code segments proactively (§).Upon invocation, T adaptively forks the saved LLM from the function template as follows:CPU operations for static model architectures are skipped,dynamic components are initialized as required,and weights not cached on the GPU are loaded asynchronously.When overlapping model loading with inference, T provides strict correctness guarantees.(§).
ai: For each function executed by a large language model LLM, a dedicated template is formulated either beforehand or in real-time, depending on specific and detailed execution pathways. Within this template, T is capable of adjusting the volume of model weights that are kept in the GPU cache, whereas the additional weights are accessed simultaneously with the inference process. During runtime, dynamic segments are systematically excluded to keep the template current. Once finalized, T is then ready to handle incoming user requests. With this template, processes are prepped ahead of time through the proactive initialization of CUDA contexts and pre-loading of kernel code snippets.When these models are called into action, T adeptly spins off the preserved LLM clone from the function template in a manner that bypasses any CPU activities related to fixed model structures. It only initializes dynamic components as needed and loads any weights not pre-cached on the GPU asynchronously. By effectively overlapping the model’s loading phase with the inference operation, T ensures unequivocal accuracy and correctness at every step.

human: T adheres closely to the programming model of modern FaaS frameworks, as shown in .To express an LLM function in a traceable manner, T imposes minimal requirements on application developers. illustrates an example of defining a function using Llama2-13b with LoRA enabled in T.The most noticeable difference is that model developers need to wrap the function initialization within a method decorated with and explicitly invoke it within the function handler,This requirement arises because an LLM model with dynamics must be initialized for each invocation.The decorator accepts an optional argument, , to indicate whether the initialization is static or dynamic.Without annotation, T defaults to treating it as dynamic.
ai: T closely follows the structure of contemporary FaaS frameworks, as depicted in the figure. To capture an LLM function in a traceable format, T requires developers to meet only minimal conditions. An example illustrating the definition of a function using Llama2-13b with LoRA activated in T is provided here. One of the most marked distinctions is that model developers are required to encapsulate the function initialization within a specifically decorated method and then explicitly call it within the function handler. This step is necessary because for each instance of invocation, an LLM model with dynamic properties needs to be initialized. The decorator can take an argument that is optional, which signifies whether the initialization process is static or dynamic. If there is no annotation present, T assumes by default that the process is dynamic.

human: In this section, we first introduce T’s lightweight tracing mechanism, which transparently extracts fine-grained execution paths.Additionally, we show details of generating function templates for startup optimizations.
ai: In this part of the document, we begin by presenting T’s lightweight tracing framework, which seamlessly captures detailed execution trajectories. Furthermore, we elaborate on the process involved in crafting function templates that enhance startup performance.

human: Fundamentally, LLMs are large-scale deep learning models targeting natural language processing tasks.Therefore, LLMs follows the generic deep learning paradigms, where model inference is abstracted as a data flow graph composed of tensors and operators [40].While prior works [41] have leveraged this property to trace inference, T further extends it to model initialization.This extension is driven by the observation that, once loaded into host memory, a weight is represented as a tensor, and subsequent operations performed on it-such as transferring weights from CPU to GPU-are all implemented as deep learning operators.Fortunately, these traceable operations correspond to the fine-grained execution paths that T needs to optimize the startup process.T leaves other non-traceable CPU operations during initialization to be executed as normal.
ai: At their core, Large Language Models LLMs are substantial deep learning architectures purposefully designed to address tasks in natural language processing. Accordingly, these LLMs adhere to the universal deep learning framework, where the model’s inference is represented as a data flow graph, which is itself composed of tensors and operators, as noted in various studies [40]. Whereas previous research efforts [41] have exploited this inherent aspect to track inference, innovation brought by T takes it a step further by applying it to the model’s initialization phase. This enhancement stems from the realization that once weights are stored in the host memory, they are encapsulated as tensors, with subsequent manipulations-such as shifting weights from the CPU to the GPU-executed through deep learning operators. Thankfully, these traceable operations align with the detailed execution pathways that T aims to enhance for optimizing the initialization sequence. T excludes certain CPU processes, which lack traceability during the initialization phase, allowing them to be carried out in the usual manner.

human: Blindly tracing function invocation involves going through all tensors and operators, even those used for temporary storage or reshaping during inference.This leads to considerable runtime overhead.Our preliminary results show that the overhead can be several times greater than that of a standard cold-start invocation.Since T focuses on optimizing cold starts in LLM function invocations, and model weight loading dominates the initialization, there is no need to treat initialization and inference with the same tracing mechanism.
ai: When undertaking the process of indiscriminately tracking function calls, one inevtiably examines every tensor and operator, including those merely employed for temporary storage or reshaping during inference procedures. This unfocused approach introduces substantial runtime overhead. Our initial findings indicate that this overhead can far exceed several multiples of a typical cold-start function call. Given that T is specifically designed to enhance cold starts in large language model LLM function invocations, and since the loading of model weights is the primary factor in initialization, it is unnecessary to apply a uniform tracing strategy for both initialization and inference phases.

human: Therefore, T adopts a weight-centric two-phase tracing approach, as illustrated in .This method focuses on execution paths related to weights.During model initialization, T employs strict tracing to construct data flow graphs (DFGs) for generating weight tensors. Each weight tensor’s DFG specifies the shape used for initialization, the checkpoint for loading weight data, and other relevant details.Using the DFG, T identifies weights that are dynamically initialized. For example, in an LLM function with LoRA enabled, the adapters are flagged as dynamic because they are sourced from different checkpoints, although their shape remains the same.During inference, T employs lax tracing, capturing only the access patterns of weights, including their order and associated GPU kernels.The decorator in enables T to differentiate between the two phases, activating the appropriate tracing mechanism.
ai: As a result, T utilizes a dual-phase tracing strategy centered around weights, which is elaborated in detail in the illustration found in . This method prioritizes the tracking of execution paths that are specifically associated with weights. At the stage of model initialization, T applies an exacting approach to tracing in order to construct data flow graphs DFGs crucial for the generation of weight tensors. Each weight tensor’s DFG outlines critical specifics such as the shape necessary for its initialization, the particular checkpoint from which weight data is loaded, and other pertinent information. With the aid of the DFG, T singles out weights that are initialized in a dynamic manner. Take, for instance, a function in a large language model LLM where Low-Rank Adaptation LoRA is active; here, the adapters are tagged as dynamic due to being derived from multiple checkpoints, although their dimensions do not change. When it comes to inference, T adopts a more relaxed tracing approach, focusing on capturing merely the access patterns associated with weights, detailing their sequence and the corresponding GPU kernels. The decorator provided in facilitates T’s ability to distinguish between these two distinct phases, enabling the activation of the suitable tracing mechanism.

human: With the traced fine-grained execution paths, T generates the function templates for LLM functions managed by the template server.The function template generated is adaptive in several key aspects:first, it perceives the necessary kernels for proactive code segment loading with minimal overhead;second, it adapts its saved state to accommodate dynamic LLM initialization;third, its GPU memory consumption could be adjusted with loading efficiency guarantee.Such adaptiveness enables T to address cold starts for various LLM functions, regardless of whether models are dynamically initialized, or what workloads are processed (e.g., model sizes, request rates, input lengths, etc.).As shown in , the template for a specific LLM function is generated as follows.
ai: By meticulously tracing the detailed execution paths, T constructs the function templates for LLM functions that are managed by the template server. These generated function templates exhibit adaptability in several significant ways: firstly, they detect the essential kernels required for the preemptive loading of code segments, ensuring minimal overhead; secondly, they adjust their preserved state to facilitate dynamic initialization of LLMs; thirdly, they allow for the modification of GPU memory usage while maintaining the promise of loading efficiency. This flexibility empowers T to effectively handle cold starts across various LLM functions, irrespective of whether models are initialized dynamically or the nature of the workloads being tackled, such as differing model sizes, varying request rates, input lengths, among others. Illustrated in is the method by which a specific LLM function template is formulated.

human: Firstly, information about GPU kernels required for proactive loading of code segments is stored in the template.Since LLM models often consist of multiple identical transformer blocks, T scans all traced operators and filters them by removing duplicates.GPU kernels associated with these operators are then identified as candidates for proactive loading.
ai: To begin with, details regarding GPU kernels, which are essential for the proactive loading of code segments, are documented within the template. Large language models frequently include numerous identical transformer blocks. Consequently, T examines all the operators that have been logged and systematically eliminates any redundancy by filtering out duplicate entries. The GPU kernels linked with these distinct operators are subsequently earmarked as candidates suitable for proactive loading.

human: Secondly, model weights are stored in the template with a re-ordered memory layout. T reorganizes the weights based on the traced access order. Without this reorganization, our evaluation in § reveals that overlapping efficiency can be easily compromised by misordered weight initialization, highlighting the necessity of T’s tracing mechanism. By leveraging the traced access order, T also retains a subset of model weights on the GPU while preserving only the memory layouts of others, thereby optimizing the template size. Weights stored as memory layouts in the template are efficiently loaded into the GPU during inference.
ai: Secondly, within the template, the model weights undergo storage with a reorganized memory structure. T meticulously rearranges these weights following the access order it has tracked. In the absence of this thoughtful reorganization, as our assessment in § demonstrates, the efficiency of overlapping may suffer significantly due to improperly ordered weight initialization. This underlines the crucial role of T’s tracking mechanism. By capitalizing on the access order it has traced, T not only maintains a portion of the model weights on the GPU, but also conserves just the memory layouts of other weights, thus optimizing the overall size of the template. This strategic storage approach ensures the weights, existing in the form of memory layouts within the template, are loaded into the GPU with optimal efficiency during the inference phase.

human: Thirdly, data flow graphs for generating each model’s weights are stored in the template to facilitate the exclusion of dynamic components at runtime. Since T cannot identify all dynamic components of an LLM model in a single tracing pass, its low-overhead tracing mechanism enables the incremental exclusion of these components during runtime.
ai: Furthermore, within the template, the data flow diagrams essential for producing the weights of each model are carefully stored. This organization aids in the removal of dynamic elements when the program is in operation. Given that T is not capable of detecting every dynamic component of a large language model during a solitary tracing attempt, its tracing protocol, which imposes minimal overhead, affords the opportunity to progressively eliminate these components in real-time execution.

human: In this section, we introduce the key startup optimizations in T based on insights from fine-grained tracing: proactive code segment loading, and adaptive state forking.
ai: In this part of our discussion, we delve into the primary optimizations implemented during the startup phase in T, which are informed by detailed tracing analyses. These optimizations include the proactive preloading of code segments and the strategic forking of states in an adaptive manner.

human: Avoiding cold kernel call startup requires knowledge of the kernels to be launched during inference.As discussed in §, template-start incurs a 180-millisecond cold start due to the absence of this information.T addresses it by leveraging traced kernels stored in its template to proactively load the relevant code segments during process pre-warming.As a result, new invocations do not suffer cold kernel calls.
ai: To prevent the latency associated with cold kernel startups, one must have a clear understanding of which kernels will be initiated during the inference process. As highlighted in section §, initiating a template results in a 180-millisecond delay from a cold start because such knowledge is lacking. A solution to this issue is implemented by T, which uses traced kernels that are preserved within its template. By doing so, it strategically loads necessary code segments ahead of time during pre-warming of the process. Consequently, this means that any subsequent invocations are not hindered by the delays typically caused by cold kernel calls.

human: However, this process requires launching the corresponding kernels on the GPU to trigger proactive loading, which also occupies computational resources.To minimize interference with other ongoing invocations, T reduces the input dimensions of the triggering kernels.Additionally, as GPU kernels are already deduplicated during template generation, the kernel code segments are efficiently loaded during pre-warming with minimal computational and memory overhead, as evaluated in §.
ai: Nonetheless, initiating this procedure necessitates deploying the relevant kernels on the GPU to commence pre-emptive loading, inevitably consuming some of the computational resources. To lessen the impact on other simultaneous processes, T strategically reduces the input size of these initiating kernels. Furthermore, since the GPU kernels undergo a deduplication process during the generation of templates, the kernel code components are seamlessly loaded during the pre-warming phase, ensuring minimal computational strain and memory usage, as assessed in section §.

human: Another issue arises from the multi-tenancy of FaaS, where a single GPU instance serves multiple LLM functions.Proactively loading code segments for all deployed functions within a single process may lead to excessive GPU memory usage and increased triggering latency.To address this, T employs a proactive loading policy that aligns with the set of LLM functions currently cached in the host memory of the GPU instance.During the process pool’s pre-warming phase, T triggers the loading of all the deduplicated kernels corresponding to the templates for these cached functions.This policy ensures that the code segments of frequently accessed kernels are readily available.
ai: A further complication emerges from the multi-tenant nature of Function-as-a-Service FaaS, where a solitary GPU instance is tasked with managing numerous large language model LLM operations. If one were to load all pertinent code segments for these deployed functions into a single process preemptively, it might result in an unsustainable increase in GPU memory consumption and heightened activation latency. To mitigate this problem, the strategy used by T involves a proactive loading policy that syncs with the cache of LLM functions currently present in the GPU instance’s memory. During the preparatory pre-warming stage of the process pool, T initiates the loading of all deduplicated kernels that match the templates of these cached functions. This approach guarantees the immediate availability of code segments for kernels that are accessed frequently.

human: With the process pre-warmed with loaded code segment, T employs adaptive state forking to efficiently initialize function states from the template for new invocations.
ai: Prior to executing new calls, and with the code segment already loaded and warmed up, T utilizes adaptive state forking to streamline the initialization of function states. This is achieved by drawing from the established template to cater to any fresh invocations.

human: When an LLM is dynamically initialized based on user requests, the function initialization cannot be saved into the template for fast startup in template-start. As shown in , T maximizes reuse of static elements from the existing state within the template by leveraging its traced fine-grained execution paths. Since dynamic elements typically account for only a small portion of the entire model (barely ), T achieves fast startup by reusing the majority of the initialized LLM.
ai: When an LLM is set up on-the-fly according to user demands, it becomes impossible to store the initialization of the function within the template for quick launching during the template-start process. As is demonstrated, T strategically optimizes the reuse of immutable components by drawing from the pre-existing state within the template, utilizing meticulously mapped execution pathways. Given that dynamic components generally represent a minimal section of the complete model, often insignificantly small, T can remarkably hasten the startup by reutilizing the bulk of the initialized LLM.

human: Specifically, T supports both dynamic initialization and template-based startup through its runtime tracing.Instead of directly reusing function state from template, T executes function initialization atop of runtime tracer.For model weight identified as static initialization, T reuses it from the template server.For model weight identified as dynamic initialization, T initializes it within user code.
ai: In particular, T offers versatility by accommodating both dynamic initialization and template-centric startup processes, utilizing its runtime tracing to achieve this. Rather than directly importing the state of a function from a template, T opts for initializing the function via the runtime tracer method. When it comes to model weights that require static initialization, T efficiently reclaims them from the preexisting template server. Conversely, for model weights marked for dynamic initialization, T takes care of this process directly within the user’s code environment.

human: The left part of presents an example of how T forks a new invocation from its function template.During initialization, T traces the operators involved in GPU weight initialization, generating a data flow graph for comparison with the pre-saved graphs in the function template.For weights (e.g., weight-1, weight-5, weight-4, and weight-3) whose data flow graphs match the template, T skips operator execution and directly initializes the tensors by forking GPU memory pointers from the template.In contrast, weight-2, loaded from a different adapter, has a data flow graph inconsistent with the template.As a result, T replays the operators for weight-2 to dynamically initialize it.
ai: In the illustration on the left, an example is shown where T initiates a new instance based on its function template. During the initialization phase, T meticulously traces the operators involved in initializing GPU weights, constructing a data flow graph that can be compared against the graphs stored in the function template. For certain weights, such as weight-1, weight-5, weight-4, and weight-3, whose data flow graphs align perfectly with the template, T bypasses the execution of operators, opting instead to directly initialize the corresponding tensors by duplicating GPU memory pointers from the existing template. However, weight-2, which is sourced from a different adapter, presents a data flow graph that does not conform to the template. Consequently, T reenacts the operators for weight-2, enabling its dynamic initialization.

human: Dynamic elements, such as LoRA adapters, are handled within user code and can be loaded either from host memory or storage.A function with LoRA enabled may be equipped with thousands of request-specific adapters [21, 20, 19].Due to this specificity, the caching policies of FaaS frameworks often fail to effectively cache checkpoints for these adapters.To ensure a fair comparison in §, T currently loads these dynamically initialized adapters directly from storage.
ai: In user code, dynamic components like LoRA adapters are managed and can be accessed either directly from the host memory or retrieved from storage. Functions that have LoRA capabilities may incorporate numerous adapters tailored for specific requests [21, 20, 19]. This level of customization frequently results in caching challenges, as the caching strategies employed by FaaS frameworks often do not efficiently retain checkpoints for these adapters. For the purpose of ensuring an equitable comparison in §, T is now retrieving these adapters that are initialized on the fly directly from storage.

human: On the left side of , when weights such as weight-3 and weight-4 are forked from the template, only their GPU memory addresses are allocated initially.At this point, their actual data temporarily resides in the host memory pool and T’s template server is loading these weights into the GPU asynchronously in the background.In this case, T is capable of overlapping model loading with inference, thus reducing TTFT of an cold-start LLM invocation to the latency of either loading or inference, whichever is longer.
ai: On the left section, when elements like weight-3 and weight-4 are duplicated from the existing template, only the GPU memory pointers are set up at first. During this time, the actual data for these weights is temporarily stored within the host memory pool. Meanwhile, T’s template server is actively engaged in asynchronously transferring these weights into the GPU in the background. T utilizes this approach to concurrently handle model loading alongside inference, effectively cutting down the time-to-first-task TTFT when initiating a large language model LLM from a cold start. The reduction is equal to the time taken for either loading or inference, depending on which process takes longer.

human: While template server enables overlapping, two key issues remain: efficiency and correctness.The misalignment between the order of weight initialization and their access order reduces overlapping efficiency when weights are loaded arbitrarily.T leverages the traced access order to ensure weights are loaded in the correct sequence.As shown in the right of , although weight-3 is initialized before weight-4, the template server loads weight-4 ahead of weight-3 because weight-4 is consumed by a kernel first during inference, according to the traced access pattern.
ai: Although utilizing a template server facilitates overlapping, there still exist two principal challenges: efficiency and correctness. A notable problem arises from the discrepancy between the sequence in which weights are initialized and the order in which they are accessed. This misalignment can diminish the efficiency of overlapping, particularly when weights are retrieved in a non-sequential manner. To tackle this, T makes use of the recorded access order to ensure that weights are loaded as needed. For instance, as illustrated on the right, despite the fact that weight-3 undergoes initialization before weight-4, the template server opts to load weight-4 prior to weight-3. human: FaaS frameworks typically keep a launched function instance alive for a predefined interval to handle subsequent requests and avoid cold starts.However, for dynamic functions that initialize different models per request, the initialized models cannot be reused for subsequent requests.With adaptive fork, T retains static model weights on the GPU during initialization while only re-initializing dynamic components.This allows dynamic functions in T to benefit from the performance enhancements of keep-alive.To enable adaptive support for keep-alive across all LLM functions, T requires application developers to specify whether a function is dynamically or statically initialized, as mentioned in .During the keep-alive interval, this information allows T to skip initialization for static function invocations and leverage adaptive state forking for dynamic ones.Without this specification, T assumes all functions are dynamic, leading to inefficient keep-alive management for static functions.

2503.06421.section: Tailored memory pool in template server.
human: T’s template server is designed to efficiently transfer model weights from host memory to the GPU. When overlapping host-to-GPU data transfers with kernel execution, a single LLM may require the transfer of numerous weight tensors.Transferring these tensors individually, as stored in the template, could saturate the command queue for memory copy operations [43], leading to significant overhead during function initialization.To address this, T’s template server automatically merges weight tensors into fewer tensors when their total number exceeds a threshold.
ai: Designed for optimal performance, T’s template server enables the seamless transfer of model weights from host memory to the GPU. When coordinating data movement from the host to the GPU simultaneously with kernel execution, a single large language model LLM might necessitate the migration of multiple weight tensors. If these tensors are transferred one by one as organized in the template, it could overwhelm the command queue dedicated to memory copy operations [43], thus creating notable delays when initializing functions. To mitigate this issue, the template server developed by T autonomously consolidates weight tensors into a smaller number of larger tensors whenever their total quantity surpasses a certain limit.
