human: This paper presents HyperGraph ROS, an open-source robot operating system that unifies intra-process, inter-process, and cross-device computation into a computational hypergraph for efficient message passing and parallel execution. In order to optimize communication, HyperGraph ROS dynamically selects the optimal communication mechanism while maintaining a consistent API. For intra-process messages, Intel-TBB Flow Graph is used with C++ pointer passing, which ensures zero memory copying and instant delivery. Meanwhile, inter-process and cross-device communication seamlessly switch to ZeroMQ. When a node receives a message from any source, it is immediately activated and scheduled for parallel execution by Intel-TBB. The computational hypergraph consists of nodes represented by TBB flow graph nodes and edges formed by TBB pointer-based connections for intra-process communication, as well as ZeroMQ links for inter-process and cross-device communication. This structure enables seamless distributed parallelism. Additionally, HyperGraph ROS provides ROS-like utilities such as a parameter server, a coordinate transformation tree, and visualization tools. Evaluation in diverse robotic scenarios demonstrates significantly higher transmission and throughput efficiency compared to ROS 2. Our work is available at https://github.com/wujiazheng2020a/hyper graph ros.
ai: In this research paper, we introduce HyperGraph ROS, an innovative open-source robot operating system that integrates intra-process, inter-process, and cross-device computations into a cohesive computational hypergraph to enhance the efficiency of message passing and the execution of parallel tasks. HyperGraph ROS is designed to streamline communications by dynamically optimizing the selection of communication mechanisms, all while maintaining a uniform application programming interface API. For messages that are exchanged within a single process, the system leverages the Intel-TBB Flow Graph in conjunction with C++ pointer-based passing. This approach ensures that memory copying is entirely avoided, allowing for instantaneous message delivery. Conversely, communications that occur between processes or across different devices are managed seamlessly using ZeroMQ. When a node receives an incoming message from any source, it is promptly activated and allocated for parallel execution via Intel-TBB. The system’s computational hypergraph comprises nodes depicted by TBB flow graph nodes connected by edges, which are established using TBB’s pointer-based connections for intra-process communications, and ZeroMQ channels for inter-process and inter-device communications. This architecture facilitates robust distributed parallelism with minimal friction. Furthermore, HyperGraph ROS includes a suite of ROS-like functionalities, such as a parameter server, a tree structure for coordinate transformations, and various tools for visualization. Testing within a wide array of robotic scenarios reveals that our system offers noticeably better transmission rates and throughput efficiency compared to ROS 2. You can explore our project further at: https://github.com/wujiazheng2020a/hyper graph ros.

human: Building a complete robotic system requires developers to possess strong programming skills, particularly in parallel computing. However, even with such expertise, the process of developing, debugging, and maintaining a robotic system incurs significant overhead. To address this challenge, ROS (Robot Operating System) [1, 2] encapsulates essential software components required for building robotic systems into libraries. These libraries include cross-process and cross-device communication modules based on the publisher-subscriber mechanism, as well as predefined usage conventions. Additionally, ROS provides various debugging and visualization tools, which significantly reduce the development time and maintenance costs of robotic systems. As a result, ROS (both ROS 1 and ROS 2) has become widely adopted in robotic applications.

This leads to excessive memory and computational overhead, particularly in large-scale rendering and visualization tasks.Fourth, although ROS 1 and ROS 2 offer an RViz-based visualization debugging interface [4], it is often too resource-intensive for real-time robotic debugging. human: ROS 1 [1] relies on a centralized master node, which means that the entire system loses communication if the master node fails. To address these limitations, ROS 2 [18] adopted a decentralized architecture based on the Data Distribution Service (DDS) [19]. This change introduced multi-threaded executors and quality-of-service controls. However, DDS-based communication still incurs latency and resource overhead in high-frequency, time-sensitive applications [20, 21]. Additionally, its multi-threaded executor may not always guarantee deterministic execution in complex multi-robot scenarios [22, 23].

human: In this paper, we introduced , an open-source robotic operating system designed for efficient hybrid parallel computing through a computational hypergraph. By integrating Intel-TBB for dynamic parallelism and ZeroMQ for high-performance messaging, our system achieves lower transmission latency and higher throughput compared to ROS 1 and ROS 2. Additionally, the lightweight visualization tool significantly improves rendering efficiency while minimizing CPU and memory usage. These features make HyperGraph ROS a promising solution for real-time and resource-constrained robotic applications.

We’ve harnessed Intel-TBB to enable dynamic parallelism and incorporated ZeroMQ to facilitate high-performance messaging. This combination results in reduced transmission latency and an increase in throughput when compared to both ROS 1 and ROS 2. human: Cloud computing offers flexibility in resource provisioning, allowing an organization to host its batch processing workloads cost-efficiently by dynamically scaling the size and composition of a cloud-based cluster - a collection of instances provisioned from the cloud. However, existing schedulers fail to minimize total cost due to suboptimal task and instance scheduling strategies, interference between co-located tasks, and instance provisioning overheads. We present Eva, a scheduler for cloud-based clusters that reduces the overall cost of hosting long-running batch jobs. Eva leverages reservation price from economics to derive the optimal set of instances to provision and task-to-instance assignments. Eva also takes into account performance degradation when co-locating tasks and quantitatively evaluates the trade-off between short-term migration overhead and long-term provision savings when considering a change in cluster configuration. Experiments on AWS EC2 and large-scale trace-driven simulations demonstrate that Eva reduces costs by 42% while incurring only a 15% increase in JCT, compared to provisioning a separate instance for each task.
ai: Cloud computing is a game changer when it comes to resource provisioning, offering organizations the capacity to host batch processing tasks in a manner that is both economical and adaptable. This is achieved by flexibly adjusting the magnitude and composition of a cloud-based cluster, which, in essence, is an assemblage of instances sourced from the cloud. Despite these advantages, contemporary schedulers often fall short in optimizing total expenditure, primarily due to flawed strategies in task and instance scheduling, conflicts arising between tasks co-located on the same instance, and the additional costs associated with provisioning instances. In response to these challenges, we introduce Eva, an innovative scheduler tailored for cloud-based clusters, designed to significantly lessen the overall expenditure involved in running protracted batch jobs. Eva employs the concept of reservation pricing from economic theory to ascertain the ideal configuration of instances to be provisioned, as well as the most efficient task-to-instance assignments. Furthermore, Eva meticulously considers potential performance setbacks that may occur when tasks are placed together on the same instance. It also provides a quantitative analysis of the trade-off between the immediate costs of task migration and the long-term savings achieved from optimal provisioning when contemplating modifications in cluster configuration.When put to the test through experiments conducted on AWS EC2, along with extensive trace-driven simulations of large scale, Eva has shown to cut costs by a remarkable 42%. This cost-efficiency is achieved while resulting in only a 15% rise in job completion time JCT when compared to the conventional approach of assigning a distinct instance to every individual task.

human: Cloud computing has seen widespread adoption, with demand continually increasing due to the rise of emerging technologies such as machine learning (ML) and big data analytics (forbes2023cloudgrowth, ; google2023cloudtrends, ). Specifically, for batch computing workloads, the flexibility and scalability of cloud platforms offers a solution for organizations to host jobs in a cost-efficient manner (dageville2016snowflake, ) using a , i.e., a pool of instances provisioned from the cloud.As a result, research institutions and enterprises have migrated their batch processing workloads from internal computing clusters to cloud-based clusters consisting of hundreds or thousands of cloud instances (aws2020adelaide, ; aws2021discovery, ; google2021arabesqueAI, ; microsoft2023bath, ).
ai: The widespread embrace of cloud computing has become evident, with its demand consistently on the rise, largely propelled by the burgeoning fields of machine learning ML and the expansive realm of big data analytics (forbes2023cloudgrowth, ; google2023cloudtrends, ). In particular, for workloads that involve batch computing, the adaptable and scalable nature of cloud technology provides an effective solution for organizations looking to conduct their operations cost-effectively (dageville2016snowflake, ). This is achieved by utilizing a resource pool, composed of cloud-based instances, which can be readily scaled up or down based on demand. The resultant impact has been significant, leading both research institutions and corporate entities to transition their batch processing tasks away from on-premises computing clusters. Instead, they opt for cloud-based clusters, which boast the capacity to entail hundreds or even thousands of cloud instances, offering a robust and flexible infrastructure (aws2020adelaide, ; aws2021discovery, ; google2021arabesqueAI, ; microsoft2023bath, ).

human: To ensure cost-efficiency with a cloud-based cluster, effective scheduling mechanisms are necessary to map submitted tasks to appropriate instances (alipourfard2017cherrypick, ). While task scheduling for batch processing workloads has been extensively studied in the fixed-sized cluster setup (verma2015borg, ; hindman2011mesos, ; vavilapalli2013yarn, ; grandl2014tetris, ; gu2019tiresias, ; mahajan2020themis, ; li2023lyra, ; narayanan2020gavel, ; xiao2018gandiva, ; mohan2022synergy, ; qiao2021pollux, ), the additional flexibility in cloud-based clusters introduces complexity to the scheduling problem. Specifically, on-demand provisioning of resources removes the time jobs spend waiting in the queue due to insufficient resources (chung2018stratus, ), which is the primary focus of the majority of fixed-sized cluster schedulers. In addition, a cloud-based cluster can dynamically adjust its composition by leveraging the diverse range of heterogeneous instances offered by the cloud provider, with each instance type having its own cost. As a result, these factors change the objective of the scheduling problem from only minimizing job completion time (JCT) to minimizing total provisioning cost without compromising job throughput. Since task scheduling and instance provisioning are fundamentally linked - tasks should be scheduled to efficiently utilize the resources available from the provisioned instances, whereas the instances should be selected to match the demands of the tasks - the two aspects should be jointly optimized to determine the optimal , which includes the quantity and types of instances that compose the cluster and the task-to-instance assignment.
ai: To achieve cost-effectiveness when employing a cloud-based cluster, it is crucial to implement advanced scheduling methods that efficiently allocate incoming tasks to suitable instances alipourfard2017cherrypick. While extensive research has been conducted on scheduling tasks for batch processing workloads within a fixed-sized cluster environment (verma2015borg; hindman2011mesos; vavilapalli2013yarn; grandl2014tetris; gu2019tiresias; mahajan2020themis; li2023lyra; narayanan2020gavel; xiao2018gandiva; mohan2022synergy; qiao2021pollux), the added adaptability of cloud-based clusters poses new challenges in the scheduling realm. Specifically, the ability to provision resources on-demand eliminates the typical queuing delays that result from a lack of available resources, a primary concern in conventional fixed-sized cluster scheduling chung2018stratus. Furthermore, a cloud-based setup can fluidly modify its resource composition by taking advantage of the variety of heterogeneous instances that cloud providers offer, each with unique cost implications. Consequently, the emphasis in such a dynamic environment shifts from solely reducing job completion time JCT to optimizing overall provisioning costs without detracting from job throughput. Given that task scheduling and instance provisioning are intrinsically interconnected-tasks need to be allocated in a manner that maximizes the utility of available instances, while instance selection should align with task requirements-it becomes essential to jointly optimize these elements. This comprehensive optimization seeks to determine the optimal configuration, encompassing the number and types of instances within the cluster as well as the effective assignment of tasks to these instances.

human: In light of this, prior work has proposed schedulers for the cloud setting (chung2018stratus, ; shastri2017hotspot, ; harlap2017proteus, ; yang2023skypilot, ). However, they fail to address certain challenges that are essential for cost-efficient hosting of batch jobs (§).First, resource demands are diverse and weakly correlated across batch processing jobs in a cluster (grandl2014tetris, ; zhang2014harmony, ), which provides opportunity to co-locate multiple tasks onto the same instance to reduce the number of instances provisioned and thus lowering total cost. However, interference between co-located tasks results in performance degradation, which can vary significantly across different tasks. Figure shows that performance degradation can range from 0-36% for just two co-located tasks. As a result, naïvely co-locating tasks can lead to significantly longer job durations, which in turn increases instance uptime and results in higher overall provisioning costs. In addition, the optimal cluster configuration can change over time as jobs are submitted to or complete in the system. , i.e., switching from one cluster configuration to another, can lead to more cost-efficient resource provisioning but involves task migrations and instance launches, which introduce delays on the order of minutes, as shown in Table . During these delays, provisioned resources remain idle, leading to wasted cost. Consequently, the scheduler must consider the trade-off between long-term provisioning cost saving and short-term migration overhead.
ai: Considering this context, previous studies have introduced various schedulers tailored for cloud environments (see chung2018stratus, shastri2017hotspot, harlap2017proteus, yang2023skypilot). Nonetheless, these approaches do not adequately tackle several challenges crucial for economically managing batch job hosting (§). Firstly, the resource needs among batch processing jobs within a cluster are heterogeneous and exhibit minimal correlation (refer to grandl2014tetris, zhang2014harmony). This variability presents an opportunity to consolidate multiple tasks on a single instance, thereby decreasing the total number of instances required and consequently cutting down on costs. However, when tasks share a single instance, they may interfere with each other, leading to a decline in performance that notably differs among tasks. According to Figure , performance impairment can vary widely, from as little as 0% to as much as 36%, even with just a pair of co-located tasks. As a consequence, indiscriminately placing tasks together can significantly prolong job completion times, thereby extending the period that instances remain active, which ultimately results in elevated provisioning expenses.Moreover, the ideal configuration of a cluster is dynamic and can shift as new jobs are submitted or existing ones finish. Transitioning from one configuration to another-for instance, reevaluating resource allocation for better cost-efficiency-entails task migrations and initiating new instances. Such adjustments introduce delays, typically lasting several minutes, as illustrated in Table . During these periods of latency, allocated resources remain unutilized, leading to unnecessary expenditure. Therefore, it is imperative for the scheduler to weigh the balance between the potential for reduced long-term provisioning costs against the immediate overheads associated with migration.

human: To address these challenges, we present Eva, a cluster scheduler that aims at serving batch computing workloads cost-efficiently in a cloud-based cluster. In Eva, we propose packing tasks into a set of instances to improve utilization and reduce cost. To link task scheduling and instance provisioning, Eva’s scheduling algorithms draw insight from an effective heuristic to the variable sized bin packing problem (VSBPP), which is known to be NP-hard (friesen1986vsbpp, ). The heuristic prioritizes larger bin types and balls to reduce the number of used bins and unused space within each bin, lowering the total cost. While effective in the single-dimensional setting, generalizing the heuristic for cloud-based cluster scheduling introduces challenges due to the presence of multi-dimensional resources (e.g., GPU, CPU, RAM), making it difficult to define a single “size“ for instance types and tasks.
ai: To tackle the existing complexities, we introduce Eva, a cluster scheduler tailored for the economical management of batch computing tasks within a cloud-based infrastructure. Eva is designed to enhance resource utilization and minimize expenses by organizing jobs into a collection of instances. This is achieved by seamlessly integrating task scheduling with instance provisioning. The scheduling algorithms within Eva are inspired by a sophisticated heuristic approach to the variable-sized bin packing problem VSBPP, a problem well-known for its NP-hard nature (as noted by Friesen in 1986). The heuristic cleverly prioritizes using larger bin types and accommodating larger items first. This strategy efficiently reduces both the count of bins in use and the vacant space within them, consequently decreasing the overall costs. Although this method is highly effective in a one-dimensional context, adapting it for cloud-based cluster scheduling presents unique hurdles. These challenges arise due to the necessity to manage multi-dimensional resources, such as GPUs, CPUs, and RAM, complicating the establishment of a unified ’size’ metric for instance types and the tasks they must handle.

human: In Eva, we capture the intuition of minimizing resource fragmentation through cost cost, which is proportional to the quantity and type of resources involved (§). Specifically, tasks are considered in descending (steedman2008reservationprice, ), a concept borrowed from economics that represents the maximum price a buyer is willing to pay for a good or a service, while instance types are considered in descending hourly cost. In the context of scheduling, the reservation price of executing a task is the hourly cost that would be incurred if the task were executed on a standalone instance without co-location. This provides a basis for evaluating the cost-efficiency of a task-to-instance assignment: the sum of the reservation prices of a set of tasks assigned to an instance should be no less than the actual hourly cost of the instance.
ai: In the Eva framework, the primary aim is to reduce resource fragmentation by keeping costs in check, which are linked to both the volume and the variety of resources utilized (§). In this context, tasks are prioritized in a descending order based on the concept of the reservation price, as explained by Steedman in 2008. This term, rooted in economics, describes the top dollar a buyer is ready to shell out for goods or services. Likewise, different types of instances are sorted by their descending hourly costs. When it comes to scheduling, the reservation price for performing a task correlates to the hourly expense that would incur if the task were to run on an individual instance without sharing. This approach forms the basis for measuring how cost-effective a task-to-instance allocation is. Ideally, the total reservation prices of tasks grouped on a particular instance should match or exceed that instance’s hourly rate, ensuring no inefficiency or loss.

human: To account for performance degradation caused by co-location interference, we extend reservation price to consider the throughput of a task (§). The of a task represents the maximum price the user is willing to pay to host the task at a certain throughput level under interference. For example, if a task can be hosted on an instance type that costs $3 per hour and achieves 100% throughput without co-location, the user would be willing to pay per hour when its throughput decreases to 80% due to interference from co-locating with other tasks. This allows us to perform the same cost-efficiency evaluation of a task-to-instance assignment in terms of performance, even in the presence of multi-task jobs, where the performance of tasks within the same job are interdependent (§).
ai: To address the challenge of performance degradation brought about by interference from co-located tasks, we expand the concept of reservation price to include the throughput of a task. This throughput represents the peak price that a user finds acceptable to pay for hosting a task, based on achieving a specific level of throughput while under interference. Take, for instance, a scenario where a task is running on an instance type that’s priced at $3 per hour and achieves full throughput without any interference from co-located tasks. The user’s willingness to pay adjusts when the throughput dips to 80% because of interference from the presence of other tasks running simultaneously. By doing this, we can still evaluate the cost-efficiency of assigning tasks to instances by their performance, even when those tasks are part of multi-task jobs where the performance is interlinked and reliant on other tasks within the same job context.

human: Based on throughput-normalized reservation price, we design two scheduling algorithms: Full Reconfiguration (§) and Partial Reconfiguration (§). These algorithms are used in combination to update the cluster configuration online. Full Reconfiguration considers all tasks currently in the system to determine the cluster configuration that leads to minimal provisioning cost. In contrast, Partial Reconfiguration preserves the majority of the current cluster configuration and updates only a subset of tasks and instances to minimize migration overhead. At each scheduling round, Eva runs both algorithms to generate two candidate cluster configurations, from which Eva selects one. Intuitively, Full Reconfiguration is preferred when the potential cost savings in provisioning justify the incurred migration overhead, particularly if these savings are substantial and long-lasting. We propose a quantitative method (§) to estimate the trade-off between provisioning cost saving and migration overhead, which Eva uses as the criterion to choose between the two candidate cluster configurations.
ai: Grounded on the metric of throughput-normalized reservation price, we have crafted two unique scheduling algorithms known as Full Reconfiguration and Partial Reconfiguration. These algorithms are purposefully combined to facilitate the dynamic updating of the cluster configuration within an online environment. The Full Reconfiguration algorithm assesses every task presently in the system to ascertain a cluster configuration that achieves the lowest possible provisioning cost. On the other hand, Partial Reconfiguration is designed to maintain the predominant form of the existing cluster layout, opting to update only a selected portion of tasks and instances to mitigate the overhead caused by migration. During each scheduling cycle, Eva utilizes both algorithms to construct two different potential cluster configurations, from which a single configuration is ultimately selected. Naturally, Full Reconfiguration becomes the advantageous choice when the potential reduction in provisioning expenses offsets the migration overhead, making it particularly appealing if such cost-saving measures are significant and extend over a prolonged duration. To facilitate this decision-making, we introduce a quantitative methodology to evaluate the equilibrium between the savings in provisioning costs and the burdens of migration overhead. This methodology serves as an evaluative criterion for Eva in selecting between the two proposed cluster configurations.

human: We have implemented Eva along with a high-fidelity simulator in Python. While the current implementation assumes AWS EC2 (aws-ec2, ) as the cloud platform, Eva’s modular design (§) ensures easy adaptation for other cloud providers. Tasks are executed as containers in the cloud, ensuring no limitations on frameworks or task environments. Additionally, Eva includes a lightweight iterator API to monitor job throughput, requiring minimal code changes on the user side.

human: Batch processing workloads, such as ML training, are increasingly prevalent in both research and enterprise production environments (gu2019tiresias, ; jeon2019philly, ). These workloads are resource-intensive and can run for extended periods, ranging from hours to days (jeon2019philly, ; xiao2018gandiva, ). Organizations have hosted these workloads on dedicated, fixed-sized clusters (gu2019tiresias, ; mohan2022synergy, ; xiao2018gandiva, ; xiao2020antman, ; jeon2019philly, ), which are managed by schedulers to optimize resource allocation and job scheduling. Traditional schedulers such as Mesos (hindman2011mesos, ), YARN (vavilapalli2013yarn, ), Tetris (grandl2014tetris, ), and Borg (verma2015borg, ) are used to serve CPU-intensive big data workloads such as MapReduce (dean2004mapreduce, ) jobs. To meet the increasing popularity and demand for ML training, numerous cluster schedulers tailored to the unique characteristics and constraints of ML jobs have been proposed (gu2019tiresias, ; mahajan2020themis, ; li2023lyra, ; narayanan2020gavel, ; xiao2018gandiva, ; mohan2022synergy, ; qiao2021pollux, ). These schedulers focus on efficiently utilizing costly accelerators such as GPUs, but share the same overarching goal: scheduling jobs to minimize JCT and maximize resource utilization. Prior research has showed that the aggregate resource demands of big data and ML applications within a cluster are bursty and fluctuate over time (mahajan2020themis, ; grandl2014tetris, ), leading to under-utilization and inefficient usage of expensive resources in a fixed-sized cluster setup.

Let T denote the set of all tasks, where a task has a demand D τ r for resource r . Given a set of available instance types K with no limit on the number of instances to provision from each type, and instance type k has a capacity Q k r for resource r , along with an hourly cost of C k , the objective is to accommodate T at minimal cost while maintaining job throughput comparable to that of a dedicated, non-shared cloud-based cluster.

2503.07437.section: 2.3. Target Use Case and Problem Formulation
human: Below, we outline three primary challenges and opportunities that are crucial for cost-efficient hosting of batch processing jobs in the cloud. While there has been prior work that attempted to address the aforementioned problem (chung2018stratus, ; shastri2017hotspot, ; harlap2017proteus, ; xu2019ispot, ; yang2023skypilot, ), they fall short in tackling these challenges, underscoring the need for a new scheduler. Batch processing jobs exhibit diverse resource demands (grandl2014tetris, ). We profiled and present the resource demands of 10 batch processing jobs from different applications in Table . Notably, while ML training jobs commonly rely on accelerators like GPUs, the specific GPU requirements vary between models due to factors such as model size and scalability. In addition, ML tasks involving image models benefit from increased CPU capacity for efficient data pre-processing (mohan2022synergy, ), whereas graph learning tasks require substantial amounts of RAM for storing and accessing large embedding tables (mohoney2021marius, ).

Batch processing jobs are known for their varied resource requirements (Grandl et al. 2014). We’ve analyzed these and documented the resource needs for 10 batch processing jobs from various applications in a detailed table. It’s important to note that while machine learning ML training jobs are typically reliant on accelerators such as GPUs, the precise GPU requirements differ among models due to aspects like model size and scalability. Moreover, ML tasks, especially those involving image models, gain efficiency from enhanced CPU capacity used for data pre-processing (Mohan et al. 2022), whereas graph learning tasks demand considerable RAM for managing and accessing large embedding tables (Mohaney et al. 2021).

2503.07437.section: 2.3. Target Use Case and Problem Formulation
human: In addition, prior work has shown a lack of correlation between resource demands across tasks in production clusters (grandl2014tetris, ; zhang2014harmony, ). This implies that tasks with complementary resource demands can be to reduce the amount of idle resources. Fixed-sized cluster schedulers such as Tetris (grandl2014tetris, ) and Synergy (mohan2022synergy, ) use scheduling algorithms that leverage task co-location to reduce job queuing delays. In the context of cloud-based clusters, task co-location improves resource allocation and reduces the number of instances needed to be provisioned, thereby lowering total cost. However, this is not considered by most existing cloud managers (shastri2017hotspot, ; harlap2017proteus, ; xu2019ispot, ; yang2023skypilot, ). While co-locating tasks reduces the number of instances that need to be provisioned, tasks co-located on the same cloud instance inevitably share low-level resources such as last-level cache (LLC), disk I/O bandwidth, and network bandwidth (cortez2017rc, ; zhuravlev2010contention, ; qiu2020firm, ), which cloud users have limited control over. Contention for shared resources leads to interference among co-located jobs, resulting in performance degradation. The degradation could potentially increase job duration and thus instance uptime, leading to higher total cost. As a result, we believe cloud-based cluster schedulers must be interference-aware and take performance into consideration when making scheduling decisions.

Nevertheless, this aspect is often overlooked by many conventional cloud management systems (shastri2017hotspot, ; harlap2017proteus, ; xu2019ispot, ; yang2023skypilot, ). The competition for these shared resources incites interference among the jobs that are co-located, leading to a decline in performance. This decrease in performance can potentially prolong the duration of tasks, subsequently extending the period the instance is active, and consequently increasing the total cost. Therefore, it is imperative that cloud-based cluster schedulers become aware of the interference and incorporate performance considerations into their scheduling strategies.

2503.07437.section: 2.3. Target Use Case and Problem Formulation
human: Prior work has attempted to incorporate the effect of co-location interference in cluster schedulers. Paragon (delimitrou2013paragon, ) and Quasar (delimitrou2014quasar, ) estimate the impact of interference on a task using collaborative filtering, while Owl (tian2022owl, ) directly profiles the interference beforehand. Based on these information, their schedulers avoid co-locating tasks that could cause severe interference with each other, thereby meeting user-specified quality of service. Since provisioning costs are not directly accounted for in the scheduling algorithms, the resulting configuration might not be cost-efficient in terms of dollar-normalized throughput. Eva aims to address this by linking costs with performance when co-locating tasks.

Using this collected data, these schedulers strategically prevent co-locating tasks that might lead to significant interference, which helps ensure adherence to user-defined service quality standards. However, a critical drawback is that provisioning expenses are not explicitly considered within these scheduling algorithms, potentially leading to configurations that do not maximize cost-efficiency when analyzed as dollar-normalized throughput. To tackle this issue, Eva introduces an innovative approach by connecting cost considerations with performance metrics specifically in the context of co-locating tasks.

2503.07437.section: 2.3. Target Use Case and Problem Formulation
human: As jobs are submitted to or complete in the system, the optimal cluster configuration that minimizes provisioning cost can change over time, so performing cluster reconfigurations can lower provisioning cost. These reconfigurations can introduce non-negligible migration overhead. As the task-to-instance assignment changes, tasks have to be stopped and checkpointed on the original instance and then restarted on another instance. Table shows the delays we observed during task migration, which can take up to several minutes. These delays leave resources provisioned but idle, resulting in extra cost. Consequently, existing cloud scheduler such as Stratus (chung2018stratus, ) tend to avoid task migration as much as possible. However, the reduction in instantaneous provisioning costs could accumulate to significant cost savings over an extended period, especially for long-running batch workloads. In such cases, a conservative migration strategy is suboptimal. It is thus important to have a quantitative approach to assess the trade-offs between migration overhead and provisioning cost savings with regard to cluster reconfiguration for minimizing total cost.

This occurs because, as the assignment of tasks to instances modifies, tasks must be halted and checkpointed on the original instance before being restarted on a different one. We have recorded the delays experienced during task migrations in the table, showing they can extend up to several minutes. During these periods, resources remain provisioned but are idle, which incurs additional costs. Because of this, existing cloud scheduling solutions like Stratus chung2018stratus often strive to minimize task migration as much as possible. In these scenarios, a cautious migration approach proves to be less than optimal. Therefore, it’s crucial to adopt a quantitative method to evaluate the trade-offs between the overhead caused by migration and the savings in provisioning costs when considering cluster reconfiguration, with the ultimate goal of minimizing the total expense involved.

human: Minimizing the total provisioning cost can be formulated as the objective function: This optimization is subject to the following constraints:Each task is assigned to exactly one instance Each instance is of exactly one instance type For each instance, the resource demand does not exceed the resource capacity Solving the above optimization problem for deployment is impractical, as the high computational cost limits its scalability and prohibits it from being employed online. In fact, in the case where there is only a single type of resource (i.e., ), the problem reduces to VSBPP, which is proven to be NP-hard (friesen1986vsbpp, ). As shown in the micro-benchmark in §, a commercial solver is unable to terminate with an optimal solution within tens of minutes for 200 tasks and 21 instance types. Worse, the problem has to be re-solved in each scheduling round whenever a job arrives or completes.

To design an efficient scheduling algorithm, we draw insight from an effective heuristic for VSBPP in one-dimensional space. The heuristic starts by considering the largest bin type and repeatedly fills the current bin with the largest ball that fits. When no more balls can fit, a new bin of the same type is opened. If the balls in a bin could fit in a smaller bin type, the heuristic switches to the next largest bin type and repeats the process.
ai: In devising a robust scheduling algorithm, we leverage knowledge gleaned from a successful heuristic approach for the Variable-Sized Bin Packing Problem VSBPP in one-dimensional configurations. This heuristic, as a starting point, initially focuses on the largest available bin category and proceeds to pack the current bin with the largest sphere that it can accommodate. When the addition of further spheres isn’t feasible, a fresh bin of the same size is introduced. Interestingly, if it turns out that the collection of spheres inside a current bin can be accommodated within a smaller bin category, the heuristic then transitions to using this smaller bin type and continues the packing operation anew.

Ideally, the metric should reflect both the quantity and value of the type of resources involved. human: Based on reservation price, we design Eva’s scheduling algorithm, shown in Algorithm . We refer to it as the Full Reconfiguration algorithm as it involves considering all the tasks currently in the system for reconfiguration. The algorithm iterates over all available instance types in descending order of cost (Line ). This prioritizes instance types with larger resource capacity and more expensive type of resources, such as GPUs, to minimize costly resource fragmentation. For each instance type, the algorithm repeatedly tries to provision new instances (Line -). For a new instance, the algorithm determines the set of tasks T to assign to this instance through multiple iterations (Line -). In each iteration, it selects the unassigned task τ that maximizes the total reservation price of (Line ). If adding τ results in a lower total reservation price, the algorithm stops adding tasks (Line -, we explain that this can happen in §). Otherwise, τ is added to T (Line ), and the process continues until no more tasks can be packed onto the instance. The algorithm then checks if assigning T to the current instance is cost-efficient (Line ). If it is, the instance with its assigned tasks T is added to the new configuration (Line ), and the algorithms tries to provision another instance of the same instance type again. If not, the algorithm moves on to the next, cheaper instance type (Line ) and repeats the process.

human: The Full Reconfiguration algorithm holistically optimizes provisioning cost by considering all the tasks in the system for reconfiguration. However, it does not take the current cluster configuration into account, which might lead to excessive task migrations and frequent instance launches or terminations when switching from one configuration to another. To mitigate this, we introduce a reconfiguration scheme that only considers a subset of tasks for reconfiguration, leaving the rest of the cluster configuration unchanged. We refer to this heuristic as the Partial Reconfiguration algorithm. Specifically, the subset of tasks consists of tasks from recently submitted jobs that have not yet been assigned to any instances, and existing tasks on instances that are no longer considered cost-efficient. The latter occurs when the throughput-normalized reservation price of the tasks on an instance drops below the instance’s hourly cost. This decrease can result from job completion or reduced throughput due to co-location interference. The subset of tasks is processed using Algorithm to obtain an updated configuration. Combined with the unchanged configuration of the remaining tasks and instances, this becomes the output configuration of Partial Reconfiguration. The two reconfiguration algorithms prioritize maximizing provisioning cost-efficiency and minimizing migration overhead, respectively.Using either one alone is insufficient: Full Reconfiguration at every scheduling period incurs significant migration overhead, while Partial Reconfiguration deviates from the optimal configuration that minimizes provisioning cost over time.As a result, Eva takes an ensemble approach. At each scheduling period, Eva runs both algorithms to obtain two configurations and decides which one to adopt. Intuitively, Full Reconfiguration is preferred if its configuration yields significant provisioning cost savings that justify the incurred migration overhead. However, provisioning cost savings depend not only on the instances provisioned but also on how long the configuration will last. If a job is submitted or completes shortly after a Full Reconfiguration, triggering another Full Reconfiguration that again involves migrating a lot of tasks, the initial reconfiguration provides little cost benefit and may even result in extra costs due to the incurred migration overhead. In such cases, it is better to adopt Partial Reconfiguration, accepting a suboptimal cluster configuration in terms of provisioning cost and wait for the job arrival or completion that triggers the Full Reconfiguration. The main challenge here is that we do not know when the next job arrival or completion will happen, and whether they will trigger a Full Reconfiguration.

human: We implemented Eva and a simulator in Python with approximately 5,700 lines of code. Eva follows a modular architecture (§) for extensibility and adopts a centralized master-worker model. The master manages cloud instances through existing cloud platform APIs. Once an instance is instantiated, a worker is launched on the instance, which communicates with the master through gRPC (grpc, ). To use Eva, users simply provide a Dockerfile with their execution artifacts and specify the required resources, similar to existing container-based cloud platforms such as Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (amazoneks, ), Azure Kubernetes Service (azureks, ), and Google Kubernetes Engine (gke, ). Tasks are executed as Docker containers to ensure portability and environment isolation. Users submit jobs to Eva by specifying the Dockerfile and the resource demand vector for each task, which details the required amounts of GPU, CPU, and RAM for task execution. To leverage heterogeneous cloud instances, users can specify multiple resource demand vectors for different instance types. For example, a task could have demand vectors [0, 8, 8] for P3 instance types and [0, 4, 8] for C7i instance types. All instances in the cluster have access to a global storage. The workers mount the global storage to the Docker containers, so that each task can access necessary artifacts such as datasets and checkpoints from it. To facilitate throughput monitoring, the worker communicates with each job via , a lightweight API wrapper around common data iterators. At the start of each scheduling round, the worker requests the throughput over a user-specified time window (e.g., the last 10 minutes) from each job and reports this information back to the master. This data is used to update the co-location throughput table. We implemented a simulator to facilitate the design and evaluation of Eva. During simulation, Eva operates as it would in a real-world deployment, but interacts with a simulated cloud environment.The simulator reads a workload trace and notifies Eva of job arrivals and their resource demands. Given the jobs in the cluster, the determines the cluster configuration. Based on this configuration, the and the issue operational commands - such as launching or terminating cloud instances and migrating tasks between instances - to the simulated cloud environment. To model real-world cloud behavior, the simulator incorporates operation delays measured from cloud instances (Table ), which affect instance uptime and thus overall provisioning cost. Job execution and progress are also simulated using real-world throughput data (Figure ). The throughput of a task is changed over time based on task co-location to account for co-location interference, with the interference data drawn from our measurements. Eva’s scheduler is not provided with this data but observes task throughput and interference through the , which interacts with the simulator to periodically collect throughput from tasks.

To further investigate Eva’s performance on a grander scale, we conduct simulated experiments with real-world cluster traces from production environments.

human: Our experiments consider 21 instance types from 3 families on AWS EC2: P3 instances (GPU instances), C7i instances (compute-optimized instances), and R7i instances (memory-optimized instances). All instances are provisioned in the same region. If an instance type is not available in the default availability zone, the retries in other availability zones until an instance is successfully provisioned. An S3 bucket is used as the global storage.
ai: In our study, we examined 21 different types of instances spanning across three distinct families on AWS EC2. These families include P3 instances, which are equipped with GPUs; C7i instances, designed specifically for computational optimization; and R7i instances, which are tailored to maximize memory performance. Each of these instances is deployed within the same geographic region to ensure consistency. Should a particular instance type be unavailable in the predetermined default availability zone, the provisioning process will continuously attempt retries in alternate zones within the region until it successfully establishes an instance. For centralized storage needs, we utilize an S3 bucket to maintain coherence across our storage requirements.

human: For the physical experiments, we generate synthetic traces similar to prior work (zheng2023shockwave, ). We conduct two physical experiments at different scales. The small-scale experiment uses a trace with 32 jobs, while the large-scale experiment uses a trace with 120 jobs. These jobs are sampled from the 10 workloads in Table . The job durations range from 0.5 to 3 hours long, and the job arrival times are generated according to a Poisson arrival process with an average inter-arrival time of 20 minutes.

human: For the simulated experiments, we use the publicly available production trace (cluster-trace-gpu-v2023) from Alibaba (weng2023trace, ), which captures the usage patterns of Alibaba’s internal batch-job users. We preserve the resource demands for GPU, CPU, and RAM for each task. The original trace consists only of single-task jobs. To maintain the integrity of the trace, we treat each task as a single-task job in our simulation experiments. However, in §, we present an experiment extending the trace to include multi-task jobs. The job composition of the trace in terms of GPU demand is shown in Table . After removing failed jobs and jobs that have resource demands that cannot be accommodated by any of the 21 instance types, the final trace consists of 6,274 jobs. For job duration, we consider the two cases shown in Table . The original trace includes a high proportion of short jobs, with 80% lasting less than an hour and half lasting less than 11 minutes. To better represent the long-running nature of ML training jobs, we also use the job duration modeling approach from Gavel (narayanan2020gavel, ) in separate experiments: each job duration is sampled from an exponential distribution, with the duration set to 10 x minutes, where x is drawn uniformly from with 80% probability, and from with 20% probability. Job arrival times are generated following the same procedure as in the physical experiment and we also study the effect of varying the job arrival rate in §. We assign each job a workload from Table to simulate the job’s migration overhead and co-location throughput based on those of the associated workloads. We compare Eva against the following schedulers, which represent either the state-of-the-art or the most commonly used solutions for hosting jobs in cloud environments:No-Packing Scheduler: Each task is hosted on a separate instance without any co-location. As a result, tasks do not experience interference from other tasks. This is representative of the strategy adopted by the majority of existing cloud-based cluster managers (yang2023skypilot, ; harlap2017proteus, ; shastri2017hotspot, ; xu2019ispot, ).Stratus (chung2018stratus, ): Stratus minimizes task migration overhead by co-locating tasks with similar finish times. To achieve this, it relies on job runtime estimates. For comparison against Stratus’s best-case scenario, we provide Stratus with the job duration calculated as the total iterations divided by the throughput.Synergy (mohan2022synergy, ): Synergy employs a best-fit packing heuristic to minimize resource fragmentation in a fixed-sized cluster. We adapt Synergy for cloud-based clusters with variable size by launching the lowest-cost instance type capable of accommodating a task when no existing instance in the cluster has enough capacity. In addition, we enhance the heuristic to be interference-aware by incorporating throughput-normalized reservation price when assigning tasks to existing instances.Owl (tian2022owl, ): Owl minimizes interference by only co-locating task pairs that result in low interference, with its scheduling algorithm prioritizing co-locations that maximizes resource allocation. It relies on profiling the co-location throughput for all task pairs in advance, and we provide this profile exclusively to Owl. Additionally, we extend Owl’s scheduling algorithm to optimize for cost-efficiency by considering task pairs in descending ratio of their throughput-normalized reservation price to the cost of the least expensive instance type that can accommodate them. We report the total cost incurred by each scheduler. For meaningful comparison across traces, we show the normalized cost of each scheduler, calculated relative to No-Packing Scheduler’s cost of each trace. Additionally, we include metrics such as resource allocation (the ratio of allocated resources to total resources), normalized job throughput and JCT to provide a comprehensive understanding of the factors contributing to cost reduction.

Table and Figure show the results of the physical experiment conducted with the 120-job trace, using the No-Packing scheduler (the most common solution), Stratus (state-of-the-art for cloud-based cluster scheduling), and Eva. Eva reduces the total cost by 15% compared to the baselines. In contrast to the baseline schedulers, Eva actively adjusts the cluster configuration through selecting suitable instance types and migrating tasks, resulting in more instances launched over time, more migration per task (Table ), and shorter uptime per instance (Figure ). This minimizes resource fragmentation and addresses the mismatch between resource demand and instance capacity, resulting in the highest cluster-wide resource allocation across all three types of resources.

By implementing this strategy, Eva effectively reduces resource fragmentation and aligns resource demand with instance capacity, thereby achieving superior cluster-wide resource allocation across all evaluated resource categories.

human: To validate Eva’s benefits in larger scale and more realistic setting, we run simulated experiments using the Alibaba production trace that consists of 6,274 jobs. The results are shown in Table and Table . In line with the physical experiments, Eva has the lowest total cost among the five schedulers, reducing the cost by 13-42%. We observe similar pattern of resource allocation as the physical experiments. Compared to other packing schedulers, Eva’s interference-aware scheduling packs more tasks per instance and achieves higher resource allocation while maintaining similar job throughput. Although more aggressive reconfiguration incurs higher idle time, Eva makes this trade-off to achieve better resource allocation and lower total cost. In addition, compared to the No-Packing Scheduler, Eva and other packing schedulers experience a 5-16% increase in JCT, primarily due to decreased throughput from co-location. Since our main objective is to minimize the overall costs, this trade-off is considered worthwhile for a 42% cost reduction. We plan to study how the scheduling algorithm can be extended to consider JCT as part of the objective in the future.

Looking ahead, we intend to explore ways to expand the scheduling algorithm’s objectives to encompass JCT considerations.

human: To reinforce the importance of considering co-location interference in scheduling, we run simulated experiments with different degree of interference when jobs are co-located on the same instance. Specifically, we run the Alibaba trace with simulated pairwise co-location throughput set to {1, 0.95, 0.9, 0.85, 0.8}. For example, if pairwise co-location throughput is set to 0.9, then when two jobs are co-located, they both have normalized throughput of 0.9. We compare Eva with and without considering interference: and . uses throughput-normalized reservation price in Algorithm , while uses reservation price. We also include two baseline schedulers that prioritize minimizing co-location interference - No-Packing Scheduler and Owl.
ai: To underscore the critical role of acknowledging co-location interference in scheduling decisions, we conduct a series of simulated experiments that explore various levels of interference occurring when jobs are simultaneously executed on the same computational instance. Specifically, we employ the Alibaba trace data to simulate conditions where pairwise co-location throughput intervals are established at values of {1, 0.95, 0.9, 0.85, 0.8}. For instance, if the pairwise co-location throughput is configured to 0.9, this translates to a scenario in which both jobs, when executed concurrently in the same space, operate with a normalized throughput value of 0.9. In our comparative analysis, we examine the Eva scheduling mechanism under two different approaches: with and without interference consideration. The former incorporates throughput-normalized reservation pricing into Algorithm , while the latter relies solely on reservation pricing without such normalization. Alongside Eva, we also evaluate the performance of two baseline schedulers - the No-Packing Scheduler and Owl - which are designed with a strong emphasis on reducing co-location interference through their scheduling strategies.

human: Figure illustrates that as the degree of interference increases (i.e., as co-location throughput decreases), experiences a significant decrease in job throughput, leading to an increase in JCT. Consequently, while packing improves resource allocation, the longer job runtime necessitates longer instance provisioning, resulting in increased total cost. Conversely, accounting for throughput degradation when evaluating cost-efficiency in scheduling, maintains a throughput level similar to Owl, which is designed to minimize co-location interference. This, combined with higher resource allocation from task packing, enables to reduce the overall cost even in scenarios with high degrees of interference. We note that in extreme cases where severe interference makes any packing sub-optimal, Eva refrains from co-locating tasks, reducing to No-Packing Scheduler.

This decline subsequently results in an increase in Job Completion Time JCT. While packing strategies enhance resource allocation efficiency, they necessitate prolonged instance provisioning due to extended job runtimes, thus escalating total costs. On the other hand, when assessing cost-efficiency in scheduling, accounting for throughput diminishment enables it to sustain levels akin to those of Owl, which is specifically crafted to curtail co-location interference. This, when coupled with the enhanced resource allocation derived from task packing, allows for a reduction in total costs, even under conditions marked by high interference levels. We observe that in extreme situations, where severe interference renders any packing approach less effective, Eva opts out of co-locating tasks, effectively defaulting to a No-Packing Scheduler strategy.

human: As ML models grow in size, it becomes more expensive to migrate them between instances. To better understand how Eva’s ensembling approach handles trade-off between migration overhead and provision savings in these scenarios, we run the same Alibaba trace with varying levels of simulated job migration delay. Figure shows the proportion of Full Reconfiguration adopted as the final configuration (left y-axis) and the migration count per job (right y-axis) of Eva under various levels of migration delay. Since Full Reconfiguration prioritizes minimizing provisioning costs at the expense of increased job migrations, significant migration overhead can overshadow the provisioning savings when migration delay increases. In such cases, Full Reconfiguration becomes less likely to be adopted because the increased M F in Equation makes it less likely to hold. Instead, Partial Reconfiguration, which maintains the majority of current cluster configuration and only migrates a small subset of essential jobs, is more likely to be adopted, resulting in a decrease in migration count per job.
ai: As machine learning models continue to expand in size, the cost and complexity of transferring them between different computational instances also increase. To deeply analyze how Eva’s ensembling technique manages the balance between the overhead of migration and the savings on provisions in these contexts, we executed the same Alibaba trace while adjusting the levels of simulated delays in job migration. The accompanying figure illustrates two things: the fraction of Full Reconfiguration opted for as the definitive setup (on the left y-axis) and the frequency of migrations per job (on the right y-axis) as managed by Eva under diverse migration delay conditions. Full Reconfiguration aims to cut provisioning expenses, accepting the trade-off of more frequent job relocations. However, significant migration overhead from increased delays can nullify the provisioning savings. Hence, when the delay in migration rises, the likelihood of selecting Full Reconfiguration diminishes, as the elevated migration factor (M F) in the equation becomes less favorable. Consequently, Partial Reconfiguration, which retains most of the existing cluster setup and only shifts a minimal, crucial set of jobs, tends to be favored in such scenarios. This approach effectively reduces the number of migrations per job.

human: Figure shows that using Full Reconfiguration alone without Partial Reconfiguration results in a noticeable increase in total cost, which becomes more pronounced as migration delays increase. On the other hand, baseline schedulers like Stratus, which prioritize minimizing migration, remains largely unaffected. By balancing provisioning savings and migration overhead, Eva’s ensembling approach allows for significant cost reductions to be maintained even in the presence of substantial job migration delays.
ai: The illustration demonstrates that relying solely on Full Reconfiguration, without incorporating Partial Reconfiguration, leads to a discernible rise in overall expenses. This financial impact becomes even more pronounced when there are extended delays in migration. Conversely, baseline schedulers such as Stratus, which focus primarily on curbing migration, tend to exhibit minimal adverse effects. By striking a balance between cost savings in provisioning and the overhead of migration, Eva’s method of ensembling manages to sustain notable reductions in expenses, even when job migration delays are considerable.

human: Prior work has explored reducing the number of provisioned instances through task co-location but lacks a comprehensive approach for cloud users that effectively accounts for heterogeneous instances (tchana2015europar, ; jiang2018self, ), migration awareness (yan2022energy, ), and interference awareness (khan2020consolidation, ).
ai: Previous research has delved into minimizing the number of allocated instances by employing task co-location strategies. However, this body of work falls short of offering a holistic solution tailored for cloud users. It often overlooks critical factors such as the consideration of heterogeneous instances, as discussed in works like Tchana et al. 2015 and Jiang et al. 2018. Furthermore, issues related to migration awareness, highlighted in Yan 2022, and interference awareness, as addressed by Khan 2020, are not comprehensively integrated into these strategies.

human: Stratus (chung2018stratus, ) addresses the same problem of minimizing total cost in a cloud-based cluster. Designed for interactive and short-running workloads, its scheduling algorithm is conservative in job migration. As discussed in §, this gives up potential provision savings when serving long-running jobs. HTAS (zhong2020htas, ) builds upon Stratus by segregating interactive jobs from long-running jobs to further reduce mismatch of durations of co-located jobs, but also suffers from conservative migration. In addition, they do not consider co-location interference.
ai: Stratus (chung2018stratus, ) tackles the identical issue of reducing overall expenses within a cloud-operated cluster environment. Tailored specifically for workloads that are interactive and have brief execution times, this scheduling mechanism takes a cautious approach to the migration of tasks. As elaborated upon in §, this strategy potentially forfeits opportunities for resource provision savings when accommodating tasks that persist over extended periods. The HTAS framework (zhong2020htas, ) evolves from Stratus by distinguishing interactive tasks from those that are long-lasting, with the goal of minimizing the discrepancies in the durations of jobs that are co-located. However, this system also struggles due to its reserved nature concerning task migration. Furthermore, it fails to take into account the disruptive effects of co-location interference.

human: There are cloud-based cluster managers that reduce provisioning cost by taking advantage of cheaper, preemptible spot instances in IaaS cloud (shastri2017hotspot, ; harlap2017proteus, ; xu2019ispot, ) or price difference between clouds (yang2023skypilot, ). These are orthogonal to our work but could be interesting directions for extensions. However, they do not consider task packing, reducing to the No-Packing Scheduler in our baseline. There has been extensive research on cluster scheduling in the context of fixed-sized, multi-resource clusters (grandl2014tetris, ; delimitrou2013paragon, ; ghodsi2011drf, ; hindman2011mesos, ; grandl2016graphene, ). Recent work on cluster scheduling focuses on serving ML training workload and ensuring high utilization of costly accelerators (gu2019tiresias, ; mahajan2020themis, ; narayanan2020gavel, ; zheng2023shockwave, ; qiao2021pollux, ; mohan2022synergy, ). Our work builds upon insights gained from these studies and applies them to cloud-based cluster scheduling which targets minimizing overall cost. Prior work has attempted to account for the effect of shared resource contention in scheduling. Methods based on low-level hardware counters (zhuravlev2010contention, ; nishtala2020hpca, ) is not applicable in IaaS cloud as these counters are not available on most instance types (gregg2017pmcs, ). Other systems (mars2011bubbleup, ; delimitrou2013paragon, ; delimitrou2014quasar, ; tian2022owl, ) predict or directly measure the performance degradation based on profiling. Eva tracks and learns co-location interference online to avoid expensive profiling cost and incorporate this in scheduling to ensure cost-efficiency.Dynamic reconfiguration or re-planning is important for environments with fluctuating, unpredictable resources and workloads. This principle extends to various applications, including analytics serving (ananthanarayanan2014grass, ),video analytics serving (romero2021llama, ), ML inference serving (zhang2023shepherd, ), and database query optimization (mahajan2018qoop, ). QOOP (mahajan2018qoop, ) recalculates query execution plans in response to changes in available resources, switching to a new plan only if the reduction in query execution time justifies foregoing already completed work. Eva follows a similar approach to quantitatively decide whether the decrease in provisioning cost justifies the incurred migration overhead during cluster reconfiguration.
ai: In the realm of cloud computing, certain cloud-based cluster managers have been designed to lower provisioning expenses by leveraging cost-effective, preemptible spot instances provided by IaaS cloud services (Shastri et al., 2017; Harlap et al., 2017; Xu et al., 2019) or by capitalizing on the pricing disparities between different cloud providers (Yang et al., 2023). While these strategies do not intersect directly with our research, they present intriguing prospects for potential future expansions. Nevertheless, they fail to address the concept of task packaging, which results in them aligning with the No-Packing Scheduler as seen in our foundational framework. There is a substantial body of research dedicated to cluster scheduling within the context of static-sized, multi-resource clusters (Grandl et al., 2014; Delimitrou and Paragon, 2013; Ghodsi et al., 2011; Hindman et al., 2011; Grandl et al., 2016). More recent efforts in cluster scheduling aim to accommodate ML training workloads while securing efficient utilization of expensive accelerators (Gu et al., 2019; Mahajan et al., 2020; Narayanan et al., 2020; Zheng et al., 2023; Qiao et al., 2021; Mohan et al., 2022). Drawing on the insights from these studies, our research adapts these findings to the domain of cloud-based cluster scheduling, focusing on the reduction of total cost.Previous research endeavors have sought to incorporate the ramifications of shared resource contention into scheduling strategies. Techniques that rely on low-level hardware counters (Zhuravlev et al., 2010; Nishtala and HPCA, 2020) are unsuitable for IaaS clouds, given that such counters are not typically available on most instance variations (Gregg, 2017). Alternative systems (Mars et al., 2011; Delimitrou et al., 2013; Delimitrou and Quasar, 2014; Tian et al., 2022) either predict or empirically assess the degree of performance degradation through detailed profiling processes. The Eva system circumvents costly profiling methods by monitoring and learning the impact of co-location interference online, integrating these observations into scheduling decisions to ensure cost-efficiency. Dynamic reconfiguration or strategic replanning holds crucial importance in environments characterized by unpredictable and fluctuating resources and workloads. This adaptability principle finds application across diverse fields, including analytics service provisioning (Ananthanarayanan et al., 2014), video analytics delivery (Romero et al., 2021), machine learning inference service (Zhang et al., 2023), and database query optimization strategies (Mahajan et al., 2018). Specifically, QOOP (Mahajan et al., 2018) adjusts query execution plans responsive to alterations in available resources, opting for a new plan only if it results in significant reductions in execution time that justify abandoning the work completed thus far. Eva employs a comparable methodology, meticulously evaluating whether the potential reduction in provisioning costs outweighs the overhead involved in migration during cluster restructuring.

human: We proposed Eva, a cloud-based cluster scheduler designed to serve batch processing workloads cost-efficiently. Eva employs a reservation price-based scheduling algorithm to jointly optimize task assignment and instance provisioning for minimal cost, and extends the algorithm to incorporate interference awareness and migration awareness. Our physical and simulated experiments show that Eva can reduce costs by 42% while incurring only a 15% increase in JCT, compared to provisioning a separate instance for each task.
ai: We introduced Eva, an innovative cluster scheduler crafted for cloud environments, aimed at managing batch processing workloads with an eye on cost-effectiveness. Eva utilizes a sophisticated algorithm based on reservation pricing to seamlessly integrate task allocation with the provisioning of instances, all geared towards minimizing expenses. Beyond just cost optimization, this algorithm is further enhanced to be aware of interference and the potential impacts of migration. Through a combination of real-world trials and simulation tests, we have demonstrated that Eva can lead to a significant 42% reduction in costs, albeit with a modest 15% increase in Job Completion Time JCT, as opposed to the strategy of provisioning a dedicated instance for each individual task.

human: Blockchain technology has emerged, and many previous studies have assessed its performance issues. However, less attention has been paid to the dependability attributes, which have been a critical topic in service provisioning, considering public or private infrastructures. This paper introduces analytical models to assess the availability of private blockchain infrastructure for Hyperledger Fabric-based applications. Furthermore, a case study will be presented to demonstrate the feasibility of the proposed model, which may assist stakeholders in deciding whether to migrate from old to new technology. Some of the obtained results indicate that, unlike most conventional systems, general availability may decrease as new nodes are added to the environment. This phenomenon occurs due to the adopted endorsement policy, which determines the proportion of required nodes to sign the authenticity of a transaction.
ai: In recent times, blockchain technology has made significant inroads, attracting a surge of academic evaluations focused primarily on its performance quandaries. Despite this, the discourse surrounding its reliability facets has been relatively scant, especially in the context of service delivery within either public or private frameworks. This work puts forward new analytical models tailored to evaluate the availability of private blockchain systems, particularly those utilizing Hyperledger Fabric for their applications. In addition, a detailed case study will be provided to illustrate the practical applicability of the model we propose, offering essential insights for stakeholders contemplating the transition from legacy systems to cutting-edge solutions. Our findings highlight an intriguing trend: contrary to what one might expect from traditional system architectures, overall availability can actually decline as additional nodes are integrated into the network. This counterintuitive behavior is attributed to the specific endorsement policy in use, which dictates the ratio of nodes required to validate a transaction’s legitimacy.

human: Blockchain is a decentralized technology that emerged in the late 2000s and is responsible for recording transactions across multiple computers securely and inflexibly, facilitating trust and transparency [1]. Despite its foundational role in cryptocurrencies, blockchain remains relatively less known to users than the digital assets it supports, such as Bitcoin and non-fungible tokens (NFT) [1], which may be attributed to the challenge of assigning value to an entire technology rather than to individual applications[2]. However, particularly in permissioned networks that mostly focus on industrial applications, we need to explore its broader feasibility for adoption by organizations that do not share mutual trust. Permissioned networks provide enhanced security and control over data sharing and transactions in these environments; one of the most popular platforms for this mean is the Hyperledger Fabric (HLF) [3].
ai: Blockchain technology, which made its debut in the latter part of the 2000s, is a decentralized system designed to securely and irreversibly record transactions across a network of computers, thereby enhancing trust and transparency within digital interactions [1]. Although blockchain serves as the backbone for cryptocurrencies, its recognition among the general populace is overshadowed by that of the digital currencies it enables, like Bitcoin and non-fungible tokens NFTs [1]. This limited recognition is partly due to the more complex task of valuing an entire technology rather than assessing individual applications [2]. Despite this, particularly within permissioned networks-environments that predominantly concentrate on industrial uses-there is a pressing need to examine how feasible it is for adoption by organizations that do not inherently trust one another. The MSP verifies the credentials of this client and allows access to the service provider. Later, the client proposes a transaction to the node known as Peer. There are many kinds of peers. We focus on endorsement peers, which simulate a transaction and send it back to the client with a signature that determines if the system can perform this transaction. As an example of a transaction, we may cite transferring assets between two clients, which requires both clients to exist and that the sender has as much balance as the value that he wants to transfer, discounting additional fees.

Subsequently, the client initiates a transaction proposal to the node referred to as the Peer. Among the various categories of peers, endorsement peers are of particular interest. These peers are responsible for simulating a transaction and returning it to the client, complete with a signature that signifies whether the system is authorized to execute the transaction. For instance, when engaging in a transaction such as asset transfer between two clients, it is imperative that both parties are valid clients and that the initiating client holds a balance sufficient to cover the transfer amount, alongside any applicable fees.

human: The transaction endorsement is based on a set of policies described by the chaincode. These policies specify how many and how these nodes agree with a transaction state. There are three main endorsement policies: AND, OR, and K-out-of-N (KooN). Suppose you have three servers on the service provisioning side, each hosting an endorsement peer. If an AND policy is used, all three nodes must endorse the transaction and sign it back to the client. If you use an OR policy, at least one of the three nodes must sign the transaction. The same applies to the KooN policy, where you determine how many available peers must sign the transaction, 1-out-of-3, 2-out-of-3, or even 3-out-of-3. After the endorsement, the transaction is submitted to the Orderer container. The orderer container joins all transactions in a batch (block) and sends it to the peers. Peers are responsible for executing transactions on the ledger following the requirements outlined in the chaincode, a fundamental aspect of Hyperledger Fabric applications.

Imagine a scenario where there are three servers handling service provision, each with its own endorsement peer. Under an AND policy, every one of these three nodes is required to agree on and endorse the transaction by signing it before it is sent back to the client. In the case of an OR policy, only one of these nodes needs to sign the transaction to proceed. The KooN policy is more flexible, as it allows for a specific number of peer endorsements; for instance, you might require a 1-out-of-3, 2-out-of-3, or even 3-out-of-3 signature count for endorsement. Once the endorsement process is complete, the transaction is forwarded to the Orderer component. This orderer collects all transactions and compiles them into batches, or blocks, which are then relayed to the peers. The peers have the responsibility of executing these transactions on the ledger in compliance with the stipulations defined in the chaincode, which holds significant importance in the functioning of Hyperledger Fabric applications.

human: The edge-cloud continuum comprises a wide variety of hardware and software components with different characteristics and energy profiles. Creating a unified model that accurately represents this heterogeneity is complex. Implementing fine-grained energy measurements can introduce significant overhead, especially in large-scale systems. The framework must balance measurement precision with scalability. Seamless integration with current orchestration and management tools is needed without requiring extensive modifications to existing infrastructures. The energy consumption patterns in cloud environments are highly dynamic due to fluctuating workloads. The framework must account for these variations to provide accurate measurements and meaningful benchmarks.

We introduce the Guided Measuring and Benchmarking framework for Energy Consumption across the Edge-Cloud Continuum (GMB-ECC), a solution designed to systematically assess and optimize energy usage within heterogeneous edge-cloud environments. By leveraging existing hardware and software practices, GMB-ECC facilitates energy assessments without the need to develop new tools or algorithms. By integrating these practices, we provide a holistic optimization method across all technology layers, accommodating the diverse environments of edge-cloud systems.
ai: Introducing the Guided Measuring and Benchmarking framework for Energy Consumption across the Edge-Cloud Continuum, or GMB-ECC, we present a comprehensive approach aimed at systematically evaluating and enhancing energy efficiency within the varied ecosystems of edge-cloud settings. This solution capitalizes on current hardware and software methods, thereby enabling energy consumption assessments without necessitating the creation of additional tools or novel algorithms. Through the amalgamation of these existing practices, GMB-ECC offers an all-encompassing optimization strategy that spans every layer of technology, effectively addressing the complexity found in edge-cloud system environments.
