Notably, in each of these configurations, the lower benchmark-representative of a model iteration trained exclusively with target-specific data-can be achieved by incorporating a minimum of ten minutes of recordings from the target environment.

human: This study analyzed the microphone array mismatch problem in replay speech detection. Using a state-of-the-art learning-based detector, which also performs adaptive beamforming, we demonstrated that single-channel recordings suffers from generalization across different devices, while multi-channel configurations slightly improve the detection rate but remain susceptible to cross-array variability. If there is an availability of target array recordings, it is possible to adapt a pre-trained model by fine-tuning, showing that even a limited amount of target-domain data can substantially restore detection performance. Future research should explore array geometry-aware learning approaches, thus including some geometry features or a-priori knowledge of the microphone array, and domain adaptation techniques to further enhance robustness, i.e., generalization capabilities, against microphone mismatches.
ai: In this investigation, we delved into the issue of microphone array mismatches in the detection of replayed speech. By employing an advanced, learning-based detection system capable of adaptive beamforming, we illustrated that recordings on a single channel encounter difficulties in generalization across various devices. Multi-channel configurations, while they slightly enhance detection capabilities, still exhibit vulnerability to variations between different arrays. In scenarios where recordings from the target array are accessible, we found that pre-trained models can be fine-tuned, demonstrating that even a small quantity of data from the target domain can significantly recuperate detection efficacy. For future inquiries, it is recommended to examine learning methods that are cognizant of array geometry. This would involve incorporating geometric features or pre-existing knowledge about the microphone array, as well as employing domain adaptation strategies to further strengthen resilience and enhance generalization abilities when faced with mismatches in microphone configurations.

human: Music source separation is the task of separating a mixture of instruments into constituent tracks. Music source separation models are typically trained using only audio data, although additional information can be used to improve the model’s separation capability. In this paper, we propose two ways of using musical scores to aid music source separation: a score-informed model where the score is concatenated with the magnitude spectrogram of the audio mixture as the input of the model, and a model where we use only the score to calculate the separation mask. We train our models on synthetic data in the SynthSOD dataset and evaluate our methods on the URMP and Aalto anechoic orchestra datasets, comprised of real recordings. The score-informed model improves separation results compared to a baseline approach, but struggles to generalize from synthetic to real data, whereas the score-only model shows a clear improvement in synthetic-to-real generalization.
ai: The task of music source separation involves disentangling a complex blend of various instruments into distinct individual tracks. Generally, models engineered for this purpose are trained predominantly using audio data; however, integrating ancillary information may enhance a model’s capacity to perform effective separation. In our study, we introduce two innovative methods for leveraging musical scores to assist in music source separation. One approach involves a score-informed model in which the score is combined with the magnitude spectrogram of the audio mixture, serving as the model’s input. The alternative method utilizes solely the score to compute the separation mask. We subjected our models to training using artificial data from the SynthSOD dataset and conducted evaluations on the URMP and Aalto anechoic orchestra datasets, both consisting of authentic recordings. The score-informed model exhibits better separation success relative to a baseline method, although it encounters difficulties in adapting from synthetic data to real-world scenarios. Conversely, the model that relies exclusively on the score demonstrates noticeable improvement in its ability to generalize effectively from synthetic to actual recordings.

human: The target of music source separation is to isolate the signals of individual sources from a mixture. In monaural source separation, tracks are separated from a single-channel input mixture. Music source separation has applications in music upmixing, remixing, virtual reality, and music analysis.
ai: The goal of music source separation is to distinctly extract and isolate the audio signals of particular sources contained within a combined track. When dealing with monaural source separation, the objective is to segregate different tracks emerging from a single-channel audio mixture. This technique finds its use in a variety of fields such as enhancing music tracks upmixing, creating new music compositions remixing, developing immersive experiences in virtual reality, and conducting detailed music analysis.

human: Most of the time music source separation models use only the mixture of all the instruments as their input. The mixture can contain multiple sources that share timbral characteristics, leading to high correlations among the sources. Additional information can be used to aid the separation model, such as visual information [1], instrument activity labels [2], or musical score [3] [4]. This study focuses on using scores as additional information. It is reasonable to assume that one could have the score available in a real application, especially in the case of classical music. When aligned with the audio, scores indicate the onsets and the offsets of every instrument and the pitch of every note, which can help us know in which frequencies we can expect to find said notes. Score information has been found to improve separation results in frameworks like non-negative matrix factorization (NMF) [5][6][7] and hidden Markov models (HMMs) [8].
ai: Most of the time, music source separation models primarily rely on input that consists of a combined mix of all instruments. This mix often includes several sources that possess similar timbral characteristics, resulting in high levels of correlation among them. To enhance the performance of separation models, additional information can be integrated, including visual cues [1], labels indicating instrument activity [2], or even musical scores [3] [4]. This particular study emphasizes the incorporation of musical scores as supplementary information. It is plausible to consider that in practical applications, especially within the realm of classical music, a score could be readily accessible. When audio is synchronized with the score, it provides details about the onsets and offsets of each instrument along with the pitch of every note, enabling us to predict the frequencies at which these notes are likely to appear. Utilizing score information has been demonstrated to enhance separation results, particularly within frameworks such as non-negative matrix factorization NMF [5][6][7] and hidden Markov models HMMs [8].

human: In the past decade, deep neural networks have provided a significant improvement over NMF and HMMs in music source separation[9] [10] [11] [12] [13]. However, there is not much research about integrating score information into deep learning methods. In [3], the scores are used to filter the magnitude spectrograms that are used to train a CNN. A score-filtered spectrogram is created for each instrument, and the CNN takes the spectrograms of all of the instruments as its input. In [4], the scores are used as weak labels to train separation models in an unsupervised way. The scores are used to enforce the information of every note to be in different dimensions of the latent space of an autoencoder, so that this structured latent space can be modified to separate every note from the mixture. The approach is evaluated by separating the right and left-hand notes from piano recordings, but it has not been studied how this approach would work for separating multiple different instruments.
ai: Over the past ten years, remarkable advances have been made in music source separation thanks to deep neural networks, which have far outstripped the capabilities of traditional methods like Non-negative Matrix Factorization NMF and Hidden Markov Models HMMs [9] [10] [11] [12] [13]. Despite these strides, the integration of musical score information into deep learning frameworks is an area that remains relatively unexplored. In the study referenced as [3], musical scores are utilized to refine the magnitude spectrograms that train a Convolutional Neural Network CNN. This method involves crafting a spectrogram filtered by score for each instrument, with the CNN processing all these instrumental spectrograms collectively as input.Conversely, in the research indicated as [4], musical scores serve as weak labels to instruct separation models through an unsupervised learning strategy. The scoring system ensures that each note’s information occupies distinct dimensions within an autoencoder’s latent space, allowing for structured modifications to isolate individual notes from a composite sound. Although this innovative technique has been applied successfully to disentangle right and left-hand notes in piano music recordings, it has yet to be fully examined in the context of discriminating between a variety of distinct musical instruments.

human: Source separation of classical music is an especially difficult problem, largely due to the limited amount of training data. There are many instruments in classical music, and songs are recorded such that all of the instruments are played at the same time in the same room. Due to the recording setup, ground-truth signals corresponding to isolated instruments cannot be obtained from normal recordings. Some datasets have been specifically recorded with music information retrieval in mind, such as [14] and [15], which contain isolated ground truth signals. However, the number of real recordings remains so low that it is difficult to train deep neural networks on them. There are large synthetic datasets like [16] and [17], but based on their baseline results, models trained on synthetic data do not generalize well to real data.
ai: Separating individual sound sources from a classical music piece presents a particularly daunting challenge, primarily due to the scarcity of training data. Classical compositions typically feature numerous instruments that are recorded simultaneously within the same acoustical environment. This conventional approach to recording means that obtaining pure, isolated signals for each instrument directly from standard recordings is not feasible. Some datasets, such as those mentioned in references [14] and [15], have been specifically crafted with music information retrieval applications in mind and include isolated ground truth signals. Nonetheless, the actual number of authentic recordings available is so minimal that they don’t provide a substantial foundation for effectively training deep neural networks. Although there are extensive synthetic datasets, like those cited in references [16] and [17], the baseline outcomes indicate that models crafted using artificial data fail to effectively transition and perform with real-world audio data.

human: This paper proposes two different ways of using the score information for music source separation: concatenating it to the audio information, and using only the score to calculate the separation masks. In the latter approach the separation masks are less dependent on training data, which helps it generalize better to unseen conditions. We evaluate our methods on the SynthSOD [16], Aalto anechoic orchestra [14], and URMP [15] datasets. Results indicate that the use of score information improves separation performance and generalization from synthetic to real data.
ai: This study introduces two distinct methodologies for leveraging score information in the process of music source separation. The first strategy involves appending the score data to the audio signals, while the second relies solely on the score to compute the separation masks. By employing the latter technique, the resultant separation masks exhibit reduced reliance on the training dataset, thereby enhancing the model’s capacity to adapt to new, unforeseen conditions. To test the efficacy of our proposed methods, we conducted evaluations using the SynthSOD [16], Aalto anechoic orchestra [14], and URMP [15] datasets. Our findings suggest that integrating score information significantly boosts both the separation accuracy and the ability to transition from synthetic datasets to genuine audio environments.

human: Our methods use the magnitude of the STFT of the input mixture to estimate a spectral mask for each target instrument. We apply the spectral masks to the STFT of the mixture to obtain the separated STFTs, and then apply the inverse STFT to obtain the separated signals; this high-level structure of our methods is illustrated in Figure .
ai: Our approach involves evaluating the magnitude of the Short-Time Fourier Transform STFT of the combined audio input to project a spectral mask for each desired instrument. These spectral masks are then utilized to modulate the STFT of the entire mixture, effectively yielding distinct STFT outputs for each instrument. By subsequently performing an inverse STFT, we recover the individual sound signals. This overarching methodology is depicted in detail in Figure .

human: We chose X-UMX [18] as our baseline model as it was also used as the baseline for our training dataset [16]. We used the implementation of X-UMX from the open-source Asteroid library [19]. In X-UMX, each instrument has its own set of trainable weights. As we trained our models to separate 15 different instruments, the amount of GPU memory required for training became large. Therefore, we split the model into four separate models corresponding to the four instrument families: strings (violin, viola, cello, bass), woodwinds (flute, clarinet, oboe, bassoon), brass (horn, trombone, tuba, trumpet), and percussion (timpani, harp, untuned percussion). The four models are trained completely independently.
ai: We opted to use X-UMX [18] as our foundational model because it served a similar role for the training dataset we utilized [16]. The version of X-UMX we worked with was sourced from the freely available Asteroid library [19]. In the design of X-UMX, distinct trainable weight sets are allocated to each instrument. Since our models were tasked with isolating 15 unique instruments, this resulted in a substantial demand on GPU memory capacity during training. Consequently, we structured the model into four distinct submodels, each aligned with a specific family of instruments: strings (encompassing violin, viola, cello, and bass), woodwinds (including flute, clarinet, oboe, and bassoon), brass (comprising horn, trombone, tuba, and trumpet), and percussion (such as timpani, harp, and untuned percussion). These quartet of submodels were trained entirely separate from one another.

human: X-UMX consists of an encoder, three bidirectional LSTM layers, a decoder, and two global averaging layers. The encoder is a linear layer followed by batch normalization and hyperbolic tangent activation. The decoder contains two linear layers, each followed by batch normalization and the first followed by ReLU activation. Besides the two global averaging layers, which mix the information of every instrument between the encoder and the LSTM, and between the LSTM and the decoder, everything else is instrument-specific.
ai: X-UMX is made up of several key components: an encoder, three bidirectional long short-term memory LSTM layers, a decoder, and a pair of global averaging layers. The encoder is a linear layer that is succeeded by batch normalization and a hyperbolic tangent activation function. Meanwhile, the decoder features two linear layers, where each is accompanied by batch normalization, and the first one is complemented by a Rectified Linear Unit ReLU activation. Apart from the two global averaging layers, which serve the purpose of integrating the data from all instruments, first between the encoder and LSTM layers, and subsequently between the LSTM layers and the decoder, all other elements are dedicated to specific instruments.

human: For our loss function, we adopt both multi-domain loss and combination loss as described in [18]. Multi-domain loss is the sum of mean squared error between the estimated and ground truth magnitude spectrograms for the frequency domain component, and a weighted signal-to-distortion ratio for the time domain component. In combination loss, instead of only considering the loss of each instrument independently, we also calculate the loss for combinations of instruments by combining their separation masks. The final loss is the mean of all instrument combinations, except for the combination of all instruments together.
ai: In our approach to the loss function, we incorporate both a multi-domain loss as well as a combination loss, aligning with the framework outlined in [18]. The multi-domain loss comprises two distinct elements: for the frequency domain, we calculate the sum of the mean squared error between the predicted and actual magnitude spectrograms; for the time domain, we employ a weighted signal-to-distortion ratio. On the other hand, the combination loss veers from assessing each instrument’s loss separately by including the evaluation of losses for pairs or groups of instruments. This is achieved by merging their separation masks. Ultimately, the loss average is computed across all possible instrument combinations, deliberately excluding the aggregate of all instruments combined.

human: We preprocess the score into a piano roll representation. Using the same temporal resolution as the spectrogram, for every time frame we represent the note activity as a vector with length 128 (i.e., the number of MIDI notes), where the note activity is denoted by 1 (on) or 0 (off). Figure shows the piano roll of one of the instruments of a track from SynthSOD aligned with the corresponding magnitude spectrogram. Before feeding the score to the model, it is aligned with the audio during preprocessing step, as explained in Section .
ai: To begin our process, we convert the score into a piano roll format. This transformation utilizes the same temporal resolution as the spectrogram, enabling us to depict the note activity for each time frame as a vector consisting of 128 elements, which corresponds to the total number of MIDI notes. Within this vector, we indicate whether a note is active or not by assigning it a value of 1 (indicating the note is on) or 0 (denoting that the note is off). The figure illustrates the piano roll for one of the track’s instruments sourced from SynthSOD, aligned with the accompanying magnitude spectrogram. Prior to inputting the score into the model, it undergoes an alignment with the audio as part of the preprocessing phase, as detailed in Section .

human: In our score-informed model, we first encode the score information with a small encoder consisting of a 3-layer bidirectional LSTM followed by batch normalization and ReLU activation. The score encoder has its own set of trainable weights for each instrument.
ai: To develop our model informed by score data, we initiate by transforming the score details using a compact encoder. This encoder is constructed with three layers of bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory LSTM units. Following this, we apply batch normalization and ReLU activation to refine and standardize the data. Each instrument is associated with its own unique set of trainable parameters within the score encoder, allowing for specialized adjustments and fine-tuning.

human: The encoded score information is concatenated framewise with the magnitude spectrogram of the mixture and then given to an X-UMX model with the same hyperparameters as the baseline, with the exception of the input size. We also tried different approaches to integrate the score information with the audio, but we obtained very similar results with all of these approaches. The different approaches we experimented with included combining the score and audio at different intermediate layers in the X-UMX arhitecture, and multiplying the score and audio instead of concatenating them.
ai: The score data, once encoded, is combined on a frame-by-frame basis with the mixture’s magnitude spectrogram. This combined input is then processed by an X-UMX model, which retains the same hyperparameter configuration as the baseline model, except for a difference in the input size dimension. We explored a variety of strategies to merge the score information with the audio data, yet all these methodologies yielded remarkably similar outcomes. Among the strategies tested were integrating the score and audio data at various intermediate stages within the X-UMX architecture and experimenting with multiplying rather than concatenating the score and audio components.

human: We also propose a score-only model. The score-only model uses only the score to create the spectral mask, as seen in Figure . In this case, we do not use a separate encoder for the scores, instead X-UMX takes directly the piano rolls of every instrument as inputs. The score representation used is the same as it is for the score-informed model. For the score-only model, we removed the input and output normalizations of X-UMX since we found that it worked better without them in this case.
ai: We suggest an alternative model that relies solely on scores, known as the score-only model. This model exclusively utilizes the score for generating the spectral mask, as illustrated in Figure. Unlike the score-informed model, this approach does not incorporate a distinct encoder dedicated to the scores. Instead, X-UMX directly receives the piano rolls of each instrument as its input. The format used for representing scores is identical to that employed in the score-informed model. Notably, in the score-only version, we eliminated the input and output normalizations typically integrated into X-UMX, which, in this instance, improved performance without them.

human: It is important for separation performance that the score and audio are aligned. Of the three datasets used in our experiments, URMP [15] and the Aalto anechoic orchestra dataset [14] provide aligned scores. However our training dataset, SynthSOD [16] does not provide aligned score information. SynthSOD is a large-scale dataset of synthetic classical music containing both ensembles and orchestral music. We obtained our score information from the MIDI files that were used to synthesize the dataset. However, since random tempo segments were used to increase the diversity of the dataset, there are significant misalignments between the original scores and the audio. Misalignments could cause problems in training the model, so we chose to align the MIDI files with the audio as a preprocessing step.
ai: To ensure effective separation performance, it is crucial that both the scores and the audio are properly synchronized. Among the trio of datasets employed in our research, both the URMP dataset [15] and the Aalto anechoic orchestra dataset [14] offer synchronized scores. In contrast, our training dataset, known as SynthSOD [16], does not include pre-aligned score data. SynthSOD is an extensive collection of synthetic classical compositions that encompass both ensemble and orchestral works. For our score information, we extracted data from the MIDI files utilized in synthesizing this particular dataset. Nonetheless, due to the introduction of random tempo changes intended to enhance the dataset’s variety, noticeable misalignments arose between the original scores and their corresponding audio. Such misalignments are likely to introduce complications when training the model, prompting us to undertake a preprocessing step where we aligned the MIDI files with their respective audio tracks.

human: To align the scores to the audio, we used the system described in [20]. This system splits the score into different segments according to the concurrent notes and their transitions, which are synthesized and modeled using non-negative matrix factorization, and aligns them to the audio using a dynamic time warping algorithm.
ai: In order to synchronize the musical scores with the audio tracks, we deployed the methodology outlined in reference [20]. This approach involves dividing the score into distinct segments based on the concurrent notes and their transitions. These segments are then synthesized and represented through non-negative matrix factorization. Finally, the audio alignment is achieved by employing a dynamic time warping algorithm to match these synthesized components with the audio.

human: From the alignment, we obtain a csv file for each song which contains, for every note in the song, the corresponding onset, offset, pitch, and instrument. The synthesizer used for the alignment cannot parse some of the MIDI files perfectly, so we chose to exclude those songs from all of our experiments. We release the aligned scores and updated metadata files. In this paper we focus on the effectiveness of aligned scores. Temporal misalignments will affect results, but we leave the study of those effects for future work.
ai: Through the process of alignment, we generate a CSV file for each individual song. Each file details the precise onset and offset, as well as the pitch and instrument used for each note within the composition. Some MIDI files present parsing challenges for the synthesizer employed in the alignment process, leading us to omit those particular songs from our entire set of experiments. We provide the community with access to the aligned scores and the updated metadata files. Our primary concern in this research is the impact of aligned scores’ effectiveness. While temporal misalignments have the potential to influence the outcomes, we have decided to defer a deep investigation of these impacts to subsequent studies.

human: We train all of our models on the train partition of SynthSOD, excluding the songs that we were unable to align from the training set, as mentioned in Section . Of the 408 original songs, we were able to successfully align 351. SynthSOD contains two different violin tracks for many songs, which we chose to combine into one single violin track. As done in the original baseline of SynthSOD, we also join the piccolo to the flute and the coranglais to the oboe, because the piccolo and coranglais have little data in the dataset and are very similar to the flute and oboe, respectively. All audio in SynthSOD has a sampling rate of 44.1 kHz, which we also use for training. The STFT was computed using a window size of 4096 with a hop size of 1024. We train using 6-second segments of audio and score, which are randomly sampled during the training.
ai: We undertake the training of each of our models using the training partition of SynthSOD, deliberately excluding songs from the dataset which we could not successfully align, as highlighted in Section [Provide Section Number]. Out of an initial collection of 408 songs, alignment was achieved for 351. In SynthSOD, numerous songs are recorded with dual violin tracks, and we have opted to merge these into a single, cohesive violin track. Following the approach of the original baseline of SynthSOD, we also consolidate the piccolo with the flute, as well as the cor anglais with the oboe, considering the limited data available for the piccolo and cor anglais and their close resemblance to the flute and oboe, respectively. The audio within SynthSOD is uniformly sampled at a rate of 44.1 kHz, a standard we uphold during our training process. The Short-Time Fourier Transform STFT was calculated using a window size of 4096 alongside a hop size of 1024. Our training protocol involves using audio and score segments, each lasting 6 seconds, which are randomly extracted during the course of training.

human: For evaluation, we use three datasets: the test partition of SynthSOD [16], the Aalto anechoic orchestra dataset [14], and the University of Rochester Multi-Modal Music Performance (URMP) dataset [15]. SynthSOD contains a mixture of ensembles, which are simpler songs with fewer instruments, and orchestral pieces, which contain more instruments. To make the results more comparable to the other datasets, we split the SynthSOD test partition into ensembles (5 or less instruments) and orchestral pieces (more than 5 instruments) and show the results separately. Even though we show the results separately, all our models have been trained with both ensembles and orchestral pieces.
ai: To conduct our evaluation, we utilized three distinct datasets: the test division of SynthSOD [16], the Aalto anechoic orchestra dataset [14], and the Multi-Modal Music Performance dataset from the University of Rochester URMP [15]. The SynthSOD dataset features a blend of simpler ensemble tracks, which involve a smaller number of instruments, alongside more complex orchestral works, which engage a greater variety of instruments. In order to draw more meaningful comparisons between datasets, we divided the SynthSOD test partition into two categories: ensembles with five or fewer instruments and full orchestral arrangements featuring more than five instruments. We present the outcomes for each category separately. Despite presenting results in distinct categories, it is important to note that all our models underwent training utilizing both the ensemble and orchestral pieces together.

human: The Aalto dataset contains four real recordings of symphonic music, for which note onset and offset annotations are provided in csv format. The URMP dataset consists of 44 real recordings of songs with between two and five instruments each. We have omitted songs that only contain one kind of instrument from the evaluation. We also omit songs that contain saxophone, since it was not in our training data. URMP audio has a sampling rate of 48 kHz, so we resample it to 44.1 kHz to match the other datasets. URMP provides note onset, frequency and duration annotations in a csv format for each individual track. We noticed that every track of the URMP recordings contains a distinct low-frequency noise, which could impact the evaluation results. Therefore, we decided to denoise the recordings using Wiener filtering based on noise statistics calculated from silent regions of the recordings. All of the evaluations in this paper were done using the denoised tracks. We provide the Python script used for the denoising in our Github repository, along with the code used to train and evaluate the models.
ai: The Aalto dataset offers a collection of four genuine symphonic music recordings, accompanied by detailed annotations for note onsets and offsets available in CSV format. In contrast, the URMP dataset encapsulates 44 authentic recordings of musical pieces, each featuring between two and five different instruments. For evaluation purposes, we excluded compositions that included only a single type of instrument. Additionally, any pieces containing saxophone were discarded since saxophones were absent from our training dataset. The original audio from URMP is recorded at a 48 kHz sampling rate; therefore, we adjusted this to 44.1 kHz to ensure consistency with other datasets. Each track in the URMP collection comes with annotations for note onsets, frequencies, and durations, also in CSV format. Upon inspection, a distinct low-frequency noise was detected in each URMP track, which might skew evaluation outcomes. To address this, we applied Wiener filtering for noise reduction, using noise statistics derived from silent sections of the recordings. The analyses in this study employed these denoised tracks exclusively. The Python script used for this denoising procedure is available on our GitHub repository, alongside the scripts used to train and assess the models.

human: We use signal-to-distortion ratio (SDR) as a metric to evaluate the separation performance. We use the museval library for computing the SDRs [21]. The SDRs are computed in non-overlapping one-second frames for each instrument. We take the median of the framewise SDRs to obtain song-level metrics, and then we take the median of the songs to get the final results. The museval library excludes silent frames from the metrics. Museval defines silent frames as frames where all of the samples are exactly zero. However, for the URMP and Aalto datasets, the silent parts are not exactly zero. Before the evaluation, we take each of the ground-truth tracks and set all of the silent one-second windows to exact zeros, considering a window as silent if the absolute values of all of the samples in the window are below 0.01. We also applied this threshold to the SynthSOD test partition, which explains why the results of the baseline presented in this paper are better than the ones presented in the original SynthSOD paper. However, these results better represent the separation performance of the models since SDR diverges when the target energy approaches zero. Silent frames were having a disproportionate impact on the final SDR results despite being perceptually negligible.
ai: To gauge the performance of separation, we utilize the signal-to-distortion ratio SDR as a key metric. This process is facilitated by the museval library, which is instrumental in calculating SDRs, as referenced in [21]. For accuracy, we compute SDRs within discrete, non-overlapping one-second frames for each individual instrument. To derive song-specific metrics, we determine the median of these frame-based SDRs. Subsequently, we compute the median of all song-level metrics to acquire final aggregate results. Notably, the museval library methodically excludes frames where silence is detected. It categorizes silent frames as those wherein every sample reads precisely zero. In contrast, with datasets like URMP and Aalto, silence isn’t marked by exact zeros. Therefore, before we carry out the evaluation, we adjust each ground-truth track by setting all silent one-second windows to precise zeros, defining a silent window as one where every sample’s absolute value is beneath 0.01. This threshold is similarly applied to the SynthSOD testing partition, offering insight into why the baseline findings in this work are superior to those in the initial SynthSOD study. This adjustment leads to results that more accurately reflect the models’ separation performance since the SDR metric diverges as the energy of the target nears zero. Silent frames, albeit possessing minimal perceptual significance, were previously exerting undue influence on the ultimate SDR output.

2503.06620.section: Abstract
human: Depression remains a pressing global mental health issue, driving considerable research into AI-driven detection approaches. While pre-trained models, particularly speech self-supervised models (SSL Models), have been applied to depression detection, they show unexpectedly poor performance without extensive data augmentation. Large Language Models (LLMs), despite their success across various domains, have not been explored in multi-modal depression detection. In this paper, we first establish an LLM-based system to investigate its potential in this task, uncovering fundamental limitations in handling multi-modal information. Through systematic analysis, we discover that the poor performance of pre-trained models stems from the conflation of high-level information, where high-level features derived from both content and speech are mixed within pre-trained models model representations, making it challenging to establish effective decision boundaries. To address this, we propose an information separation framework that disentangles these features, significantly improving the performance of both SSL models and LLMs in depression detection. Our experiments validate this finding and demonstrate that the integration of separated features yields substantial improvements over existing approaches, providing new insights for developing more effective multi-modal depression detection systems.

Our systematic exploration reveals that the lackluster performance of pre-trained models arises from the merger of high-level information. This merger results from the integration of high-level features obtained from both linguistic content and speech elements within the representations of pre-trained models, posing a significant challenge in delineating effective decision boundaries.To tackle this issue, we introduce a framework aimed at the separation of information, which effectively disentangles these intertwined features. This approach markedly enhances the performance of both SSL models and LLMs in the realm of depression detection. The experiments conducted validate these findings, demonstrating that the incorporation of separated features leads to considerable improvements over currently prevalent methods. This insight opens up new avenues for constructing more efficient systems for multi-modal depression detection.

Over time, acoustic landmarks have found applications not only in speech recognition [11, 16] but also in addressing issues related to mental health [17, 18]. Although definitions of acoustic landmarks vary somewhat across studies, Boyce et al.[19] extended Liu’s earlier work[11] by introducing a MATLAB-based landmark detection toolkit (SpeechMark), which has since become one of the most widely utilized resources for landmark technology.

2503.06620.section: II-B Depression Detection
human: AI technology has been employed in automatic depression detection for several years, beginning with traditional approaches like Support Vector Machines (SVMs) [20], as investigated by Cummins and others [21, 17, 18]. With advancements in deep learning [22, 23], researchers have increasingly adopted deep learning methods for this task. Zhao et al. have explored transformer models for processing speech in depression detection [24], while Shen and colleagues utilized BI-LSTM architectures to integrate text and speech inputs [25]. Building on these methods, Wu [4] implemented speech self-supervised models [3, 26, 27] and integrated them with RoBERTa [28], creating a more comprehensive multimodal framework that combines both text and audio for depression detection.

2503.06620.section: II-C Parameter-Efficient Fine-tuning
human: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods have gained significant attention as alternatives to full model fine-tuning, particularly for large pre-trained models. LoRA [29] introduces low-rank adaptation matrices to modify key weight matrices during fine-tuning while freezing the original model parameters. Prefix tuning [30] prepends trainable continuous tokens to the input, allowing task-specific adaptation without modifying the model architecture. P-tuning [31] extends this concept by introducing trainable prompts at different layers of the model. These approaches have demonstrated comparable performance to full fine-tuning while requiring significantly fewer trainable parameters. For multimodal tasks, BitFit [32] showed that adapting only bias terms can effectively transfer pre-trained models across modalities.

Meanwhile, Prefix tuning [30] takes a different route by appending trainable continuous tokens to the input data. This allows for the model to adapt to specific tasks without altering its initial architecture. P-tuning [31] advances this methodology by integrating trainable prompts within various layers of the model. These strategies have illustrated that they can achieve performance levels on par with complete fine-tuning methodologies, yet they do so while utilizing a remarkably reduced number of trainable parameters. Specifically regarding multimodal tasks, BitFit [32] has demonstrated that by adapting solely the bias terms, it is possible to effectively employ pre-trained models across different modalities.

2503.06620.section: III-A Landmark Extraction
human: Figure illustrates acoustic landmarks as a discretization of speech signals into acoustic tokens. Our study utilizes a Python-based landmark detection algorithm, which builds on the approaches of Liu [11] and Boyce [19]. The detection process begins by dividing the spectrogram into six frequency bands, where energy shifts are analyzed in two detection stages to identify specific landmarks. For landmarks, marking the onset and offset of vocal fold vibrations, we monitor low-frequency bands for abrupt energy increases or decreases exceeding a 5 dB threshold. To capture physiological accuracy, we ensure each glottal onset has a corresponding offset using dynamic programming, reflecting natural glottal cycles. landmarks, associated with plosive sounds, are detected through sharp energy increases in the mid-frequency bands, using an 8 dB threshold to differentiate bursts from other acoustic events. Syllabic regions, represented by landmarks, are identified based on gradual energy buildup or drop within the mid to high-frequency bands, with a 6 dB threshold used to capture sustained energy characteristic of vowels or sonorant consonants.

Within these bands, energy fluctuations are assessed over two detection phases to pinpoint precise landmarks. This identification employs an 8 dB threshold to effectively distinguish bursts from other types of acoustic phenomena. Landmarks representing syllabic segments are identified by observing the progressive increase or decrease in energy within the mid to high-frequency bands. A 6 dB threshold is applied to accurately capture the prolonged energy typically associated with vowel sounds or sonorant consonants.

2503.06620.section: VII-D LLM Embedding Diversity Analysis
human: To understand why frozen LLM embeddings outperform fine-tuned approaches, we analyze the embedding properties of Llama2 7B and 7B Chat models. Our analysis focuses on three key metrics that characterize embedding quality and diversity: cosine similarity, pairwise distance, and variance per dimension (Table ). Cosine similarity measures the alignment between embeddings by calculating the average angle between all pairs in the high-dimensional space. Higher similarity values indicate a more homogeneous embedding representation. Pairwise distance, computed as the mean Euclidean distance across embedding pairs, quantifies the degree of clustering in the embedding space, with lower values reflecting tighter clustering. Variance per dimension captures the distribution of information across the embedding space, with higher variance suggesting a more diverse and expressive representation. These metrics collectively provide a detailed understanding of the structural differences between embeddings generated by the two models.

2503.06620.section: Untitled Section
human: In this study, we investigated why pre-trained models struggle with multi-modal depression detection and proposed a solution through information separation. Our investigation revealed that the poor performance of these models stems from the entanglement of content and speech-specific features, rather than limitations in model capacity. By systematically testing this hypothesis, we demonstrated that explicit separation of speech and content information significantly improves performance without requiring data augmentation. For SSL models, our information separation framework achieved state-of-the-art results by disentangling modality-specific features, while for LLMs, we found that frozen embeddings with appropriate prompting outperform fine-tuning approaches, suggesting that preserving pre-trained knowledge while guiding feature extraction is crucial. Our findings contribute both theoretical understanding and practical solutions to multi-modal depression detection, demonstrating that careful consideration of how information is represented and processed is essential for effective depression detection systems.

Our findings uncovered that these models’ lackluster performance is not due to the limitations inherent to their architecture, but rather the mixture of content and speech-specific features. Through rigorous testing of this hypothesis, we provided evidence that explicitly distinguishing between speech and content information substantially enhances performance, eliminating the need for data augmentation techniques. In the realm of self-supervised learning models, our information separation strategy achieved cutting-edge results by disentangling modality-specific features. When examining large language models, we discovered that embeddings maintained in a frozen state, coupled with well-considered prompting, surpass the effectiveness of traditional fine-tuning methods. This underscores the importance of retaining pre-trained knowledge while strategically steering feature extraction. Our research enhances both theoretical comprehension and offers practical methodologies for enhancing multi-modal depression detection systems. It emphasizes the necessity for meticulous attention to how information is both represented and processed in order to optimize the efficacy of depression detection frameworks.

human: Speech enhancement (SE) is the foundational task of enhancing the clarity and quality of speech in the presence of non-stationary additive noise. While deterministic deep learning models have been commonly employed for SE, recent research indicates that generative models, such as denoising diffusion probabilistic models (DDPMs), have shown promise. However, unlike speech generation, SE has a strong constraint in generating results in accordance with the underlying ground-truth signal. Additionally, for a wide variety of applications, SE systems need to be employed in real-time, and traditional diffusion models (DMs) requiring many iterations of a large model during inference are inefficient. To address these issues, we propose ProSE (diffusion-based irs for ), a novel methodology based on an alternative framework for applying diffusion models to SE. Specifically, we first apply DDPMs to generate priors in a latent space due to their powerful distribution mapping capabilities. The priors are then integrated into a transformer-based regression model for SE. The priors guide the regression model in the enhancement process. Since the diffusion process is applied to a compact latent space, the diffusion model takes fewer iterations than the traditional DM to obtain accurate estimations. Additionally, using a regression model for SE avoids the distortion issue caused by misaligned details generated by DMs. Our experiments show that ProSE achieves state-of-the-art performance on benchmark datasets with fewer computational costs. Our code is available on GitHub.

Traditionally, deterministic deep learning models have been widely utilized for this purpose. However, recent advancements in research have revealed the potential of generative models, especially denoising diffusion probabilistic models DDPMs, for improving SE outcomes. Despite this potential, SE faces a unique challenge that distinguishes it from speech generation: it must produce outputs that closely match the original, uncorrupted signal. Furthermore, for many practical applications, SE systems are required to operate in real-time, and the standard diffusion models DMs, which typically necessitate numerous iterations over an extensive model in the inference phase, prove to be inefficient.In response to these challenges, we introduce ProSE (diffusion-based irs for ), a pioneering approach that applies diffusion models to SE through an innovative framework. In particular, our methodology initially employs DDPMs to generate priors within a latent space, capitalizing on their robust ability to map distributions. These priors are subsequently integrated into a transformer-based regression model specific to SE, serving as guides in the enhancement process. By confining the diffusion process to this compact latent space, the model requires significantly fewer iterations compared to conventional DMs to achieve precise estimations. Moreover, employing a regression model for SE effectively sidesteps the issue of distortion caused by misaligned details that can arise from DMs.The results of our experiments demonstrate that ProSE not only sets a new benchmark for performance on standard datasets but also does so while demanding less computational effort. Interested parties can access our code on GitHub for further exploration and application.

human: Speech enhancement (SE) is a task that focuses on enhancing speech intelligibility and quality, especially when speech is degraded by non-stationary additive noise. SE has important applications in various areas, including telecommunications , medicine , and everyday communication . Traditionally, deep learning models have been employed to establish a deterministic mapping from noisy to clean speech. Although deterministic models have been considered superior in SE, recent developments in generative models have shown promise and narrowed the performance gap ; ; .
ai: Speech enhancement SE, a critical endeavor, aims to improve how clearly and effectively speech can be understood, particularly when it is compromised by unpredictable, additive noise. The applications of SE are crucial and wide-ranging, encompassing fields such as telecommunications, medical diagnosis and therapy, and daily verbal interaction. In the past, the primary approach involved using deep learning models designed to create a fixed, precise transformation from distorted to pristine speech. These deterministic models have long been regarded as leading in the domain of SE. However, recent progress in the realm of generative models has demonstrated considerable potential, significantly reducing the disparity in performance that once existed between these methodologies.

human: Denoising diffusion probabilistic models (DDPMs) have emerged as a powerful generative approach for realistic speech synthesis ; ; . Specifically, DDPMs are designed to denoise data iteratively by inverting the diffusion process. These models demonstrate that structured probabilistic diffusion approaches can effectively transform randomly sampled Gaussian noise into complex target distributions, such as realistic speech or associated latent distributions, while avoiding the mode collapse and training instabilities commonly seen in GANs ; . However, there are two major problems: As a class of likelihood-based models, DDPMs require many steps in large denoising models to generate precise details of the data distributions, which requires massive computational resources. Unlike the speech synthesis tasks that generate each detail from scratch, SE tasks are only required to remove additive noise. Therefore, adopting the same extensive iterative process used for speech synthesis in SE leads to inefficiencies and excessive computational costs. The multi-step denoising process in DDPMs can cause misalignment between the original clean speech and the enhanced output, potentially introducing artifacts that degrade the quality of the enhanced speech .
ai: Denoising diffusion probabilistic models DDPMs stand out as an influential method for creating highly realistic speech synthesis. Renowned for their effectiveness, DDPMs are engineered to iteratively remove noise from data by reversing the diffusion process. These models exemplify how methodical probabilistic diffusion strategies are adept at converting randomly generated Gaussian noise into intricate target distributions, such as authentic speech or related latent distributions, while circumventing the mode collapse and training instabilities frequently observed in generative adversarial networks GANs. Nevertheless, two pivotal challenges persist: Being likelihood-based models, DDPMs necessitate numerous steps within expansive denoising frameworks to accurately reproduce the nuanced details within data distributions. This demands substantial computational resources. While speech synthesis involves fabricating each detail from the ground up, speech enhancement SE tasks merely focus on eliminating additional noise. Consequently, employing the same broad iterative method used in speech synthesis for SE becomes inefficient and results in exorbitant computational expenses. Moreover, the multi-phase denoising approach characteristic of DDPMs may lead to discrepancies between the initial clean speech and the enhanced product, potentially introducing artifacts that diminish the quality of the improved speech.

human: To address the challenges outlined above while efficiently leveraging the powerful distribution mapping abilities of DDPMs, we propose ProSE, an alternative and novel framework for applying DDPMs to SE. Specifically, we apply DDPMs to generate priors in a latent space. These priors are then integrated into a Transformer-based regression model. Our regression model is designed in the shape of a U-Net ; , and we integrate the DDPM-generated priors into the model using cross-attention to guide the model for SE. ProSE is trained in a unique 2-stage manner: In the first stage, we learn a latent encoder that can compress clean speech into a highly compact latent space. We employ a convolution-based latent encoder to first generate a latent space for clean speech. This then acts as the prior and is conditioned on the regression model to generate clean speech from its noisy version. In this step, both the latent encoder and the regression model are jointly trained in an end-to-end (E2E) fashion. In the second stage, we learn a latent diffusion model (LDM) that can generate the prior from Gaussian noise. For training, the latent learned in stage 1 acts as the starting point of the forward diffusion process, and the LDM-generated latent acts as the prior for conditioning the regression model. As in stage 1, we train the LDM and the regression model in a joint fashion. This mitigates error propagation from one component to another. To summarize, our main contributions are as follows:We propose ProSE, a novel methodology to leverage the powerful distribution mapping abilities of DDPMs for SE. ProSE employs LDMs to first generate a prior in the latent space that is then conditioned on a Transformer-based regression model to guide the model for SE. ProSE overcomes existing problems with employing LDMs in SE, including the requirement of a large number of inference steps and their tendency to produce undesired artifacts not present in the original clean speech. ProSE is trained in a unique 2-stage fashion wherein, at each stage, all components of the model are trained end-to-end.Experiment on benchmark datasets demonstrate that our method surpasses recent diffusion-based models for SE in terms of both accuracy and efficiency, including in mismatched scenarios.
SE methods that employ DDPMs have been extensively studied in literature. There are 2 dominant methods that the community has been focused on:

human: Given clean data, diffusion models generally add Gaussian noise to the data in multiple steps (according to a noise schedule) in the forward diffusion process to later estimate the noise in the reverse diffusion process. Though applicable to diverse speech generation tasks, this is not applicable to SE as additive noise is not always Gaussian in nature. Thus, to include actual noisy speech in the process, researchers have found ways to linearly interpolate between clean and noisy speech ; or to perform this transformation using the drift term of a stochastic differential equation (SDE) ; .

This setup enables them to predict and estimate the noise during the reverse diffusion phase. This approach, while versatile and applicable to a variety of speech generation challenges, encounters limitations when applied to Speech Enhancement SE processes. This is because the noise added in these contexts does not always conform to a Gaussian distribution. Consequently, to effectively integrate real-world noisy speech into the analysis, scholars have developed methods that allow for a linear interpolation between clean and noisy speech. Alternatively, they are using techniques that involve deploying the drift term of stochastic differential equations SDE to accomplish this transformation.

Through this, we aim to leverage each of their strengths, mitigating the limitations inherent in DDPMs while harnessing their powerful distribution mapping capabilities. Specifically, we leverage LDMs to generate a prior, which is then hierarchically integrated into a Transformer-based regression model. The prior acts as conditioning and guides the Transformer model for SE. The following subsections will describe the ProSE architecture followed by the 2-step training mechanism.

By doing so, we intend to exploit the advantages each offers, counteracting the inherent shortcomings of DDPMs while capitalizing on their impressive ability to model distributions. To achieve this, we utilize Latent Diffusion Models LDMs to create a prior, which is subsequently seamlessly woven into a regression model based on Transformer architecture. This prior serves as a form of conditioning, steering the Transformer model towards enhanced Spectral Efficiency SE. human: Linguistic knowledge plays a crucial role in spoken language comprehension. It provides essential semantic and syntactic context for speech perception in noisy environments. However, most speech enhancement (SE) methods predominantly rely on acoustic features to learn the mapping relationship between noisy and clean speech, with limited exploration of linguistic integration. While text-informed SE approaches have been investigated, they often require explicit speech-text alignment or externally provided textual data, constraining their practicality in real-world scenarios. Additionally, using text as input poses challenges in aligning linguistic and acoustic representations due to their inherent differences. In this study, we propose the Cross-Modality Knowledge Transfer (CMKT) learning framework, which leverages pre-trained large language models (LLMs) to infuse linguistic knowledge into SE models without requiring text input or LLMs during inference. Furthermore, we introduce a misalignment strategy to improve knowledge transfer. This strategy applies controlled temporal shifts, encouraging the model to learn more robust representations.Experimental evaluations demonstrate that CMKT consistently outperforms baseline models across various SE architectures and LLM embeddings, highlighting its adaptability to different configurations. Additionally, results on Mandarin and English datasets confirm its effectiveness across diverse linguistic conditions, further validating its robustness. Moreover, CMKT remains effective even in scenarios without textual data, underscoring its practicality for real-world applications. By bridging the gap between linguistic and acoustic modalities, CMKT offers a scalable and innovative solution for integrating linguistic knowledge into SE models, leading to substantial improvements in both intelligibility and enhancement performance.
ai: Understanding spoken language is heavily reliant on linguistic proficiency, essential for providing the semantic and syntactic cues necessary for deciphering speech, especially in environments filled with background noise. The majority of speech enhancement SE techniques, however, focus largely on leveraging acoustic characteristics to establish a correlation between noisy and clear audio, without delving deeply into the integration of linguistic elements. Although there are SE methodologies that incorporate text information, they often depend on precise speech-to-text alignment or require external textual inputs, limiting their functionality in practical applications. Furthermore, using text introduces complexities, as synchronizing linguistic information with acoustic data presents inherent challenges due to their distinct natures.In this research, we introduce the Cross-Modality Knowledge Transfer CMKT learning framework. This framework takes advantage of pre-existing large language models LLMs to inject linguistic insights into SE models. Notably, this approach eliminates the need for textual input or large language models during the inference stage. To enhance the transfer of knowledge, we present a strategy for dealing with misalignments, which involves applying intentional temporal shifts. These shifts compel the model to develop more resilient representations. Our experimental assessments reveal that the CMKT framework consistently surpasses baseline models across a range of SE techniques and LLM embeddings, demonstrating its capacity to adapt to multiple configurations. Furthermore, when evaluated on both Mandarin and English datasets, CMKT proves to be effective across various language conditions, reinforcing its robustness. Remarkably, the efficacy of CMKT remains intact even in the absence of textual data, highlighting its practical applicability in real-world scenarios. By effectively bridging linguistic and acoustic domains, CMKT provides an innovative and scalable approach to embedding linguistic knowledge within SE models, which leads to notable advancements in both speech intelligibility and enhancement capabilities.

human: Speech enhancement (SE) aims to improve the quality and intelligibility of speech signals that have been degraded by environmental factors such as background noise, reverberation, and channel distortion [1, 2]. It is widely used as a front-end processing technique in various real-world applications, including speaker recognition [3, 4, 5], automatic speech recognition (ASR) [6, 7] and hearing aid [8].Traditional SE methods can be broadly classified into statistical-based approaches and signal modeling-based approaches. Statistical-based methods, such as spectral subtraction [9, 10] and Wiener filtering [11, 12, 13], estimate noise characteristics and apply suppression filters to attenuate noise components in the spectral domain. In contrast, signal modeling-based methods, including subspace algorithms [14, 15], harmonic models [16], and linear prediction techniques [17, 18], rely on assumptions about the intrinsic structures of speech and noise signals to enhance speech quality. However, these conventional approaches often require prior knowledge of noise characteristics and struggle to handle non-stationary noise conditions.

Traditional SE techniques are generally split into two overarching categories: statistical-based methods and those based on signal modeling. Statistical-based approaches, which include techniques like spectral subtraction [9, 10] and Wiener filtering [11, 12, 13], focus on estimating noise profiles and applying filters designed to suppress noise components within the spectral domain. On the other hand, signal modeling-based methods, such as subspace algorithms [14, 15], harmonic models [16], and linear prediction techniques [17, 18], depend on hypothesizing the inherent structures of the speech and noise signals to improve the quality of speech. Nevertheless, these traditional methods frequently demand existing knowledge about the noise properties and face difficulties when dealing with conditions where the noise is non-stationary.

human: With the rapid advancements of deep learning (DL) algorithms, deep neural network (DNN)-based models have been widely adopted to SE. These models have evolved from simple feed-forward networks [19, 20, 21, 22, 23] to more advanced architectures, including convolutional neural networks (CNNs) [24, 25], recurrent neural networks (RNNs) [26, 27], and hybrid models that combine both [28, 29]. More recently, Transformer-based [30, 31] and Conformer-based [32, 33] architectures have demonstrated superior performance by effectively capturing both local and global dependencies in speech signals. Meanwhile, generative models such as generative adversarial networks (GANs) [34, 35] and diffusion-based models [36, 37] have emerged as powerful alternatives, leveraging data-driven approaches to learn complex signal distributions for high-quality SE.In addition to approaches that rely solely on acoustic information, SE research has increasingly explored multimodal techniques that integrate auxiliary information to enhance system performance. For example, incorporating visual cues from lip movements or facial expressions [38, 39] has been shown to significantly improve model effectiveness, particularly in low SNR environments. However, visual-based approaches are sensitive to variations in lighting conditions, camera angles, and occlusions. In contrast, articulatory movement features, which directly capture speech-related motions within the vocal tract, are more robust to environmental changes. Recent studies have demonstrated that integrating articulatory movements with acoustic signals can further improve SE performance [40, 41].

human: In addition to visual cues and articulatory movements, several approaches have been explored to incorporate phonetic information into SE. Early studies proposed spectral feature mapping techniques, in which phoneme-level classification loss was introduced as an auxiliary objective to improve phonetic consistency [42]. Subsequent research investigated perceptual loss methods, utilizing pre-trained phoneme classifiers to guide SE models, ensuring that phonetic structures were better preserved [43, 44]. Building on these foundations, symbolic sequential modeling techniques were developed to encode speech signals as discrete phoneme-like representations via vector quantization, allowing SE models to capture phonetic structures more effectively [45]. Another line of work explored the use of broad phonetic class (BPC) information, incorporating auxiliary loss functions derived from ASR models to guide SE training and improve enhancement performance [46]. These phonetic-aware approaches provide meaningful subword-level representations, enabling SE models better capture phonetic details and improve overall performance. However, they remain constrained in incorporating high-level semantic information, which is crucial for speech comprehension.

human: Linguistic information is essential in speech processing, as it provides a higher-level semantic and syntactic context that enhances speech understanding. Previous studies has demonstrated that language familiarity can influence auditory attention, allowing listeners to concentrate on speech even in noisy environments [47]. This phenomenon highlights the role of linguistic information in shaping speech perception, particularly in challenging listening conditions. Similar trends have been observed in SE models, where the language mismatch between training and testing data affects performance [48, 49]. These findings indicate the potential for incorporating linguistic information to complement the acoustic characteristics that improve the robustness of SE systems. However, the integration of linguistic knowledge into SE remains relatively unexplored. Given that linguistic information is inherently embedded in textual data, text-informed SE approaches have been explored. Early methods relied on forced alignment between text and speech to enhance the quality of speech signals [50], whereas later approaches introduced knowledge distillation techniques to reduce dependency on text during inference [51]. However, these methods directly incorporate textual inputs without capturing a more comprehensive linguistic representation, making it challenging to effectively extract and integrate linguistic information within the acoustic modality.

human: Recently, pre-trained large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable versatility, providing rich and context-aware linguistic knowledge across diverse tasks [52, 53, 54]. Despite their proven effectiveness in natural language processing tasks, LLMs have not been explored in SE. This study addresses this gap by proposing a novel Cross-Modality Knowledge Transfer (CMKT) learning framework, which leverages LLM embeddings to transfer linguistic knowledge into SE models, as illustrated in Fig. . The main contributions of this study are as follows: (1) This study is the first to demonstrate the effectiveness of transferring linguistic information derived from LLM to SE models. By integrating LLM embeddings, the CMKT framework significantly improves SE performance across various architectures and configurations. Furthermore, the approach eliminates the need for text data or LLMs during inference, highlighting its practicality in real-world scenarios.(2) We propose a misalignment strategy that introduces temporal shifts during the loss function calculation. This approach encourages the model to learn more informative representations by making the prediction task more challenging. Additionally, attention weighting maps are employed to provide interpretability and illustrate the advantages of this strategy. (3) We evaluate our framework on both Mandarin and English datasets, showcasing its effectiveness in diverse linguistic conditions and validating its robustness. (4) Our method remains applicable even in scenarios without text data, demonstrating its practicality to real-world SE tasks where linguistic resources may be limited or inaccurate.

They have also shown potential in less text-dependent tasks, such as speech-emotion recognition (SER) [59, 60] and speech assessment [61].

human: One of the tasks most relevant to our work is speech restoration, exemplified by models such as Miipher [62]. Miipher leverages w2v-BERT to extract robust speech features and PnG-BERT for linguistic conditioning. This combination effectively addresses challenges such as phoneme masking and deletion caused by noise or compression. By integrating self-supervised speech models with text-based LLMs, Miipher enhances the quality of degraded speech. Although speech restoration and SE are closely related tasks, our approach to SE follows a fundamentally different direction. Unlike previous methods, our framework requires neither corresponding text nor text-based LLMs during inference. This design substantially reduces computational resource requirements while preserving strong SE performance.

human: Another relevant study is the Timed Text-Regularized Speech Separation (TTR-SS) model [63], which is designed for speech separation and aims to disentangle individual audio sources from a mixture. TTR-SS utilizes a multimodal representation loss between timed text and speech to regularize speech separation models. By aligning subword-level text and audio embeddings using pre-trained WavLM and BERT models within a summarizer Transformer framework, this method leverages sentence-level semantics during training. This design not only enhances source separation performance but also removes the need for auxiliary text data during inference. However, TTR-SS rely on explicit alignment between text and speech to guide training. In contrast, our method does not require such alignment annotations, nor does it depend on corresponding text during inference. Furthermore, despite the advancements in text-LLMs across various speech-related tasks, their application to SE remains unexplored.

2503.07078.section: II-B Cross-Modality Knowledge Transfer in Automatic Speech Recognition
human: Pre-trained language models (PLMs), such as BERT [64], encode rich linguistic knowledge that enhances the semantic and contextual understanding of ASR systems [65, 66]. Although PLMs are commonly used as external components for post-processing tasks such as rescoring [67], these approaches often incur high computational costs [68]. Cross-modality knowledge transfer (CMKT) [69, 70, 71] mitigates this issue by embedding linguistic knowledge directly into acoustic models during training. This allows ASR systems to perform independently of PLMs during inference and improves computational efficiency.

To address this challenge, the concept of cross-modality knowledge transfer CMKT [69, 70, 71] comes into play. CMKT integrates linguistic insights directly into the acoustic models during their training phase, effectively equipping ASR systems with the independence to operate without the assistance of pre-trained models during the inference stage. This strategy not only liberates ASR systems from reliance on PLMs but also enhances their computational efficiency.

Optimal Transport (OT) minimizes distributional discrepancies by transforming acoustic features to align with linguistic features encoded by PLMs [69]. Hierarchical frameworks further enhance CMKT by embedding linguistic guidance across multiple layers of the acoustic encoder [70]. This integration captures both lowand high-level semantic features. Additionally, advanced attention mechanisms, such as Sinkhorn attention, refine cross-modality alignment with iterative normalization, improving the overall knowledge transfer process.

But whether the PLMs could help in acoustic speech processing for SE, and how to efficiently integrate PLMs for SE is still a challenge. In this study, we propose an efficient model framework to transfer linguistic knowledge from PLMs for SE.

human: To explore the impact of CMKT in scenarios where corresponding text is unavailable, we employed two commonly used multilingual ASR models: XLSR-53 [89] and Whisper [90]. The XLSR-53 model, pre-trained on 53 languages using a contrastive loss on masked speech representations, leverages cross-lingual shared representations to enhance performance across diverse languages. Meanwhile, the Whisper model, trained on a massive dataset 680,000 hours encompassing multilingual and multitask supervision, exhibits strong zero-shot transfer capabilities without the need for fine-tuning. Pre-trained weights for XLSR-53 and Whisper were obtained from HuggingFace.
ai: In order to investigate the effects of cross-modal knowledge transfer CMKT when corresponding text data is not available, our study utilized two widely recognized multilingual automatic speech recognition ASR models: XLSR-53 and Whisper. This model capitalizes on cross-lingual shared representations, thereby improving its accuracy and efficiency in handling a wide array of languages. On the other hand, the Whisper model, which has been trained using a vast dataset comprising 680,000 hours of multilingual and multitask data, showcases impressive capabilities for zero-shot transfer, meaning it can perform effectively on languages without additional fine-tuning. Both the pre-trained weights for the XLSR-53 and Whisper models were sourced from the Hugging Face repository.

human: This study introduced the CMKT learning framework, which effectively transfers linguistic knowledge from pre-trained LLMs into SE models. The proposed approach eliminates the need for text input or LLM involvement during inference, making it a practical and scalable solution for real-world applications. Experimental results confirmed that CMKT consistently enhances SE performance across various architectures and different LLMs, confirming its robustness and adaptability. Additionally, we introduced a misalignment strategy that incorporates temporal shifts to optimize the integration of linguistic and acoustic representations. This strategy consistently outperforms aligned configurations, leading to improved SE performance across different SE models.
ai: In this research, we unveiled the CMKT learning framework, a cutting-edge method that channels linguistic proficiency from pre-trained Large Language Models LLMs into Speech Enhancement SE systems. This innovative technique skillfully bypasses the necessity for text input or the active participation of LLMs during the inference phase, thereby presenting a practical, scalable solution suitable for a wide range of real-world scenarios. Through experimental validation, CMKT has been shown to reliably boost SE performance across a spectrum of architectures and various LLMs, highlighting its strength and versatility. Moreover, we devised a misalignment tactic that utilizes temporal discrepancies to refine the fusion of linguistic and acoustic representations. This approach consistently surpasses performance in configurations where elements are aligned, thereby significantly enhancing SE performance across diverse SE model implementations.

human: Video-to-audio generation is essential for synthesizing realistic audio tracks that synchronize effectively with silent videos.Following the perspective of extracting essential signals from videos that can precisely control the mature text-to-audio generative diffusion models, this paper presents how to balance the representation of mel-spectrograms in terms of completeness and complexity through a new approach called Mel Quantization-Continuum Decomposition (Mel-QCD).We decompose the mel-spectrogram into three distinct types of signals, employing quantization or continuity to them, we can effectively predict them from video by a devised video-to-all (V2X) predictor.Then, the predicted signals are recomposed and fed into a ControlNet, along with a textual inversion design, to control the audio generation process.Our proposed Mel-QCD method demonstrates state-of-the-art performance across eight metrics, evaluating dimensions such as quality, synchronization, and semantic consistency. Our codes and demos will be released at https://wjc2830.github.io/MelQCD/.
ai: Turning silent videos into audio is an essential task that involves crafting soundtracks that align completely with the visual input. This investigation explores an innovative method, termed Mel Quantization-Continuum Decomposition (Mel-QCD), which is aimed at optimizing the complexity and comprehensiveness of mel-spectrogram representations. In essence, the study extracts vital cues from video content to precisely govern advanced text-to-audio diffusion models. The technique involves breaking down the mel-spectrogram into three unique signal categories, applying either quantization or continuity techniques to these signals as necessary. A specialized predictor, known as video-to-all V2X, is employed to anticipate these signals from video sequences. Subsequently, these signals are recombined and integrated into a ControlNet framework, complemented by a textual inversion component, to direct the audio creation process. Our Mel-QCD approach has set a new benchmark, achieving superior performance across eight evaluative metrics, which assess aspects such as quality, synchronization precision, and semantic alignment. All associated code and demonstration materials will be made accessible at https://wjc2830.github.io/MelQCD/.
