ai: In this study, we introduce Mel Quantization-Continuum Decomposition (Mel-QCD) Control as a means to strike a balance between simplicity and precision. Our methodology addresses the challenge by finding an equilibrium between the representation of the mel-spectrogram in terms of its completeness and the intricacy involved. We commence by breaking down the mel-spectrogram into three distinct components: semantic, energy, and standard deviation vectors. To enable accurate signal prediction derived from video inputs, we propose the quantization of semantic vectors into distinct codes. These are used to build a semantic vector quantization SVQ codebook, where each codebook index stands for a specific semantic component. This quantization process significantly reduces complexity without resulting in a significant loss of information. Furthermore, when it comes to the energy and standard deviation vectors, which are inherently low-dimensional data, we delve into their significant reliance on maintaining continuous distributions to assure completeness. Consequently, we strongly recommend preserving their original forms, ensuring that their representations remain intact.

This enhancement ensures a more consistent alignment of the generated audio with the video, thereby preserving the fundamental semantic integrity.

human: The primary driver of success in audio generation tasks is the use of Text-to-Audio (TTA) models. Previous efforts adopt GANs [, ], normalizing flows [, ], and VAEs [] in this task. Recently, diffusion models [] have demonstrated significant generative potential in visual domains and have subsequently been extended to audio generation. DiffSound [] employs a discrete diffusion model to generate sounds from text prompts. Make-An-Audio [] and AudioLDM [] excel in generation quality by leveraging advanced latent diffusion models (LDMs) []. The following works further incorporates several enhancing designs. Make-An-Audio2 [] introduces structured text encoding to improve semantic alignment. AudioLDM2 [] unifies any audio signal into a universal representation, thus supporting various audio generation. Tango [] utilizes Flan-T5 [] as the text encoder to precisely convey complex textual concepts. Auffusion [] reduces the demand for data and computational resources while maintaining excellent text-audio alignment. In this paper, our method is built upon Auffusion, inheriting its excellent text-conditioned generation capabilities while extending it to understand visual semantics.
ai: The key to achieving success in generating audio through textual input lies primarily in the deployment of Text-to-Audio TTA models. Historically, different approaches utilizing Generative Adversarial Networks GANs, normalizing flows, and Variational Autoencoders VAEs have been explored for this purpose. More recently, diffusion models have shown remarkable generative capacities in the realm of visual media and have since been adapted for audio creation. For instance, the DiffSound model employs a discrete diffusion process to craft sounds based on given text descriptions. Models like Make-An-Audio and AudioLDM stand out in terms of quality by harnessing advanced latent diffusion models LDMs. Moreover, subsequent research has integrated additional enhancements to push the boundaries further. Make-An-Audio2, for example, implements structured text encoding, thereby augmenting the alignment of semantic content. Similarly, AudioLDM2 standardizes audio signals into a universal format, thus enabling support for diverse audio generation tasks. In the Tango model, the use of Flan-T5 as a text encoder allows for the precise articulation of intricate textual ideas. Meanwhile, Auffusion succeeds in curtailing the need for extensive data and computational power without compromising the quality of text-audio alignment.In our study, we base our methodology on the Auffusion model, building upon its remarkable capacity for text-conditioned generation. Additionally, we extend its functionality to include an understanding of visual semantics, thereby broadening its application scope.

human: Another popular research, Video-to-Audio (VTA), aims to generate audio that is semantically aligned and temporally synchronized with the video content. Based on how they connect visual and audio, we categorize the current work into two types. The first category involves training video-to-audio models from scratch. SpecVQGAN [] and Im2wav [] design an autoregressive network to generate audio tokens based on the input visual tokens. DiffFoley [] employs a diffusion model while introducing contrastive learning to unify the video-audio features. VTA-LDM [] is based on the LDMs and directly combine the visual embeddings through cross attention. However, they require a large-scale high-quality visual-audio aligned data for training, hence another category of methods has emerged, resorting to the foundational TTA models. Seeing-and-hearing [] and VTA-Mapper [] both project audio to the text embedding space, which is then processed by a pretrained TTA generator. However, the shared video-text space struggles to maintain the fine-grained temporal cues. Concurrent FoleyCrafter [] and ReWaS [], inspired by the structural control of ControlNet [] in text-to-image tasks, utilize onset or energy inferred from visuals as mel-spectrogram hints to explicitly control audio generation. Apparently, these representations lose a lot of visual details, leading to unsatisfactory results. An intuitive solution is to increase signal information, but the difficulty of signal prediction also increases accordingly. Consequently, we delve into the properties of mel-spectrograms and propose several designs to make them easier to predict from visual features,achieving a balance between completeness and complexity.
ai: A noteworthy area of study gaining traction is Video-to-Audio VTA synthesis, which seeks to produce audio tracks that not only align semantically but also synchronize precisely with video content in a temporal manner. The field’s projects are generally divided into two main approaches based on how they couple visual data with audio output. One approach involves building video-to-audio models completely from square one. Techniques like SpecVQGAN and Im2wav create an autoregressive framework aimed at generating audio tokens from given visual tokens. Meanwhile, DiffFoley uses a diffusion model combined with contrastive learning to bring together audio and video features in a unified form. VTA-LDM employs latent diffusion models by merging visual embeddings using cross-attention mechanisms. Nonetheless, these approaches demand large-scale, high-quality datasets with superb visual-audio alignment for effective training, prompting a different category of methods that utilize foundational Text-to-Audio TTA models. For instance, Seeing-and-hearing and VTA-Mapper convert audio into a text embedding space, which is subsequently processed by a pretrained TTA generator. Yet, the shared video-text space poses challenges in capturing the intricate temporal nuances. Simultaneously, FoleyCrafter and ReWaS, drawing inspiration from the structured control pioneered by ControlNet in text-to-image conversions, utilize visual cues such as onset or energy to guide audio generation through mel-spectrogram hints. Unfortunately, these methods often strip away crucial visual information, leading to less satisfactory outcomes. To counter this, an obvious approach might be to enrich signal information, which invariably complicates signal prediction. Therefore, our focus shifts to exploring the properties of mel-spectrograms, through which we introduce several novel design strategies. These strategies are crafted to enhance predictability from visual cues, striking a balance between the fidelity of the audio and the modeling complexity.

human: In this paper, we introduced a novel method for generating audio that aligns closely with conditional videos using Mel Quantization-Continuum Decomposition (Mel-QCD). We emphasized that representing the mel-spectrogram with predictable and comprehensive information enables effective control over text-to-audio diffusion models, facilitating seamless audio synthesis that corresponds to the video. Mel-QCD aims to optimize the trade-off between completeness and complexity in mel representation, further enhanced by our video-to-all (V2X) predictor for precise audio generation control.Extensive experiments and ablation studies demonstrate that our approach produces high-quality audio with superior temporal synchronization and semantic consistency when conditioned on video input.
ai: In this research paper, we unveil an innovative approach to generating audio that meticulously aligns with conditional video inputs, utilizing a technique we refer to as Mel Quantization-Continuum Decomposition (Mel-QCD). A key aspect of our methodology is the representation of the mel-spectrogram in a manner that encompasses both predictability and comprehensive data. This enables precise manipulation of text-to-audio diffusion models, ultimately facilitating the smooth creation of audio that matches the video context. The primary objective of Mel-QCD is to achieve an optimal balance between the completeness of the mel representation and its inherent complexity. This balance is further refined by our implementation of a video-to-all V2X predictor, which offers enhanced control over audio generation specifics. ai: In this study, we conduct an in-depth analysis of a Gaussian Process Regression GPR-based approach for estimating background, carrying out a range of tests utilizing a background spectrum that has been documented in a CMS investigation [30]. This particular background presents notable challenges, as it encompasses regions that precede the smoothly declining segment. The CMS study methodically categorizes the background into three distinct sections, each modeled by a separate mathematical function. However, due to GPR’s inherent adaptability, this intricate spectrum can be managed with greater simplicity. We highlight that employing the commonly used Radial Basis Function RBF kernel, with appropriately fine-tuned L2 regularization, can deliver outstanding results. Consequently, the hyperparameter suite for a GPR-based method includes not only the constraints for kernel parameters but also the components of the regularization matrix. The discovery potential of this methodology is assessed using a specific algorithm [34]. Upon deploying a minimally optimized set of hyperparameters, we discern a promising level of sensitivity to potential narrow resonances. Moreover, we extend the background prediction to the High-Luminosity Large Hadron Collider (HL-LHC) to evaluate GPR’s durability in the context of increasing luminosity. Unlike the conventional functional fitting techniques that faced significant scrutiny during Run 2, the GPR-based strategy maintains impressive stability even in scenarios relevant to HL-LHC. We also experiment with the signal extraction protocol, albeit without fine-tuning for this particular objective. Although the initial results are favorable, there is room for enhancement. A systematic and automated approach to fine-tuning a GPR-based model to accommodate broad use cases is immensely beneficial and represents a fascinating avenue for prospective research.

human: Since its first observation in the 1970s, neutrino-induced neutral-current single positive pion production (NC1 π + ) has remained an elusive and poorly understood interaction channel. This process is a significant background in neutrino oscillation experiments and studying it further is critical for the physics program of next-generation accelerator-based neutrino oscillation experiments. In this Letter we present the first double-differential cross-section measurement of NC1 π + interactions using data from the ND280 detector of the T2K experiment collected in ν -beam mode. We compare the results on a hydrocarbon target to the predictions of several neutrino interaction generators and final-state interaction models. While model predictions agree with the differential results, the data shows a weak preference for a cross-section normalization approximately 30% higher than predicted by most models studied in this Letter.
ai: Since it was first detected back in the 1970s, the phenomenon of neutrino-induced neutral-current single positive pion production, often abbreviated as NC1 π+, has baffled scientists and remained a challenging interaction channel to fully comprehend. This process serves as a major source of background noise in neutrino oscillation experiments, making its study essential for the advancement of next-generation neutrino oscillation research, especially those reliant on accelerator-based experiments. In this publication, we report on the pioneering measurement of the double-differential cross-section for NC1 π+ interactions, accomplished using data collected from the ND280 detector, which is part of the T2K experiment’s operations in ν-beam mode. Our findings on a hydrocarbon target are juxtaposed against the theoretical predictions issued by various neutrino interaction simulation tools and models of final-state interactions. Although these models are largely consistent with the differential results we obtained, the empirical data reveals a slight inclination towards a cross-section normalization that is roughly 30% higher than what the majority of the models analyzed in this publication predict.

human: This article presents a study of single π + production in neutrino neutral-current interactions (NC1 π + ) using the ND280 detector of the T2K experiment. We report the largest sample of such events selected by any experiment, providing the first new data for this channel in over four decades and the first using a sub-GeV neutrino flux. The signal selection strategy and its performance are detailed together with validations of a robust cross section extraction methodology. The measured flux-averaged integrated cross-section is , 1.3 σ above the NEUT v5.4.0 expectation.

The report elaborates on the strategy for selecting the signal and assesses its effectiveness, alongside thorough validations of a comprehensive methodology for extracting the cross section. The determined flux-averaged integrated cross-section results 1.3 standard deviations above the predictions made by NEUT version 5.4.0.

() and searches for exotic physics. Better understanding neutrino interactions has become a priority, particularly at energies of GeV, where nuclear effects involved in neutrino-nucleus interactions pose a significant experimental challenge et al. et al. (). Despite an increasing abundance of inclusive and exclusive cross section results, some channels still remain largely unexplored experimentally. A prime example of this is single π + production in neutrino-nucleus neutral-current interactions, in which a neutrino scattering off a proton is able to transform it into a neutron while additionally producing a positive pion. Existing data for this channel consists of observations in bubble chamber experiments built in the 1970s to test the validity of the Standard Model, which predicted the existence of this process. In particular, the Gargamelle propane freon bubble chamber et al. et al. () and the ANL deuteron bubble chamber et al. et al. () reported the observation of tens of interactions associated to this channel over the expected background. The data from Gargamelle, at an average neutrino energy of 2 GeV, was later re-analyzed and presented at the NuInt 2002 conference, leading to the only existing cross-section value for this channel ().

human: In this article, we address this situation using data of the near detector ND280 of the T2K experiment. We report the strategy and selection algorithm performances used to identify the largest existing sample of events for this channel, consisting of more than two hundred selected signal events. We present the observed event distributions in angle and momentum for the selected π + track, and compare them to simulation predictions. We describe the signal cross section extraction methodology and tests performed in the analysis to validate the robustness of the measurement and its statistical interpretation. Lastly, we report the measured double-differential signal cross section and compare it to T2K’s simulation. Comparisons to alternative models are presented in [] .

human: T2K et al. et al. () is a second generation accelerator-based long-baseline neutrino oscillation experiment in Japan, using a highly pure ν μ or ν ̄ μ neutrino beam et al. et al. () generated using facilities at the Japan Proton Accelerator Research Complex (J-PARC). The beam, described in more detail in Sec. , is measured twice: once before and once after neutrino oscillations have occurred. Firstly, measurements are taken at a near detector facility at J-PARC located 280 m downstream from the neutrino production target. This facility consists of INGRID et al. et al. () located on-axis, Wagasci-BabyMIND () at 1.5∘ off-axis, and ND280 at 2.5∘ off-axis, which is used in this study and described further in Sec. . Secondly, measurements are taken at Super-Kamiokande et al. et al. (), a 50 kt water Cherenkov detector. Super-Kamiokande is located 295 km further downstream and placed at 2.5∘ off-axis. In this article, beam data measured by the ND280 detector is used.

In this experimental setup, neutrino oscillations are probed by evaluating the beam at two distinct stages: initially, the beam is assessed prior to any oscillations occurring, and subsequently, after oscillations have taken place.The preliminary assessment takes place at a proximal detector facility situated 280 meters downstream from the site where the neutrino beam is initially produced. Located 295 kilometers further along the trajectory of the beam, Super-Kamiokande is also situated 2.5 degrees off-axis. The focus of this article is on the data captured by the ND280 detector, which provides crucial insights into the subtleties of neutrino oscillations.

human: The T2K experiment uses a beam of neutrinos generated through the bombardment of a monolithic graphite target with a 30 GeV proton beam at the J-PARC facilities. The integrated data collection is measured in Protons on Target (POT), which quantifies the total exposure. The proton beam interactions with the target produce a secondary beam composed primarily of pions and kaons, which are focused using a set of three magnetic horns. T2K can run in either ν or ν ̄ beam mode by focusing positive or negative mesons respectively. Mesons decay in a 96 m long helium-filled decay volume ending in a beam dump at the downstream end. High momentum muons crossing it are monitored using the MUMON detector (). The meson decays result in the final beam of neutrinos, with a flux prediction at the ND280 detector site presented in Figure . This study utilizes a total of POT collected in ν -beam mode. Because most neutrinos arise from pion decays via , the neutrino energy spectra are strongly dependent on the beam off-axis angle et al. et al. (). T2K exploits this feature by positioning ND280 and Super-Kamiokande, its main detectors for the oscillation analysis, at 2.5∘ off-axis, utilizing a narrow energy neutrino beam peaking at around 0.6 GeV. T2K’s neutrino beamline has been recently upgraded et al. et al. (); nevertheless, all of the data in this study corresponds to runs prior to the beam upgrade.

human: The T2K Near Detector at 280 meters (ND280), presented in Figure , is a magnetized particle detector. It consists of sub-detector modules located inside the refurbished UA1/NOMAD magnet, providing a 0.2 T field used to bend charged particles moving inside ND280. The UA1 magnet yoke is instrumented with plastic scintillator slabs working as a Side Muon Range Detector (SMRD) et al. et al. (), and surrounding an electromagnetic calorimeter (ECal) et al. et al. () that nearly hermetically encapsulates its inner elements that are mounted on a steel frame. Inside it, going from upstream to downstream, the beam passes through the π 0 detector et al. et al. (), and the inner ND280 tracker consisting of three gaseous Time Projection Chambers (TPC1, 2, 3) et al. et al. (), interleaved with two Fine-Grained Detectors (FGD1, 2) et al. et al. (). FGD1 is a plastic scintillator detector, consisting of 15 planes of two layers. Every layer is made up of 192 parallel bars, with consecutive layers using bars with alternate orientations along the two axes perpendicular to the neutrino beam. FGD2 follows a similar layout to that of FGD1, but alternating seven plastic scintillator planes with six inactive water bags.The FGDs provide a total active target mass close to two tons, while the TPCs are used to identify different types of particles and their kinematics by measuring their curvature and . In the measurement reported in this article, interactions starting in the FGD1 are selected. To increase the signal purity, the fiducial volume of FGD1 excludes 6 bars at each side of the detector as well as the first and the last planes.

The cut on true proton momentum is discussed in the following section (Sec. ). All events that would be signal (NC1 π + 0p) but don’t satisfy the true proton momentum condition. ν and ν ̄ interactions without charged leptons and at least one neutral pion in the final state. Due to its low cross section, NC1 π + events are expected to make up only 1.3% of all interactions in FGD1. A selection algorithm was developed to identify a subset of events enriched in signal, contained in a signal sample, complemented by background-enriched samples. The logic of the selection algorithm, associated with Figure , is as follows: The main track in the event, i.e. the only track that exits FGD1, must reach at least one ND280 TPC, creating a reconstructed track segment of sufficient length to ensure good TPC information. Events with multiple tracks that escape the FGD1 volume are rejected, as for signal events only one track is expected. Events with one additional track contained in FGD1 are retained separately, in a dedicated sample, that will be referred to as the Additional Track Sample (). The track trajectory in the TPC must show curvature matching a forward-moving, positively charged particle according to ND280’s magnetic field. To reduce background from events outside the FGD1 target, called out-of-fiducial volume (OOFV) events, any events with tracks reconstructed upstream of FGD1 are rejected. Three sequential vetos are applied based on the presence of reconstructed tracks in the most upstream TPC, the pi-zero detector, and the upstream part of the ECal. No Michel Electron (ME) signatures are identified in FGD1. ME are produced in μ decays and are identified looking for delayed hits. For FGD1, their detection efficiency is %. The TPC particle identification (PID) information -based on the measured with respect to the particle momentum measured by curvaturemust be compatible with that of a Minimum Ionizing Particle (MIP). Tracks rejected by this cut are retained separately in the TPC PID Sample (). For those tracks reaching the ECal, their PID information must be compatible with a hadron. The ECal offers excellent capabilities in separating μ vs charged π , and in consequence, rejected events are collected in a separate control sample, named the ECal PID Sample (). Lastly, the main track in FGD1 must be compatible with a MIP. This cut disentangles the cases where a π + exits FGD1 and the cases where a negatively charged particle travels backwards and stops in the FGD1.

human: Low momentum protons, arising from nuclear effects including FSI, are often merged during the reconstruction to the other reconstructed tracks modifying their observed light yield. In consequence, the FGD1 PID cut, which depends on the observed light yield, is sensitive to low momentum protons below the tracking threshold. The efficiency to select NC1 π + events with protons is presented in Fig. .NC1 π + events with proton momentum below 200 MeV/ c are sometimes selected and are therefore included in the signal definition to be robust against model prediction discrepancies. Events with protons above 200 MeV/ c are rarely selected, with much lower selection efficiency than other NC1 π + events. Therefore, they are treated as background. To validate this choice, fake data studies modifying the number of background NC1 π + events with protons were performed, and as later reported in Sec. , no measurement bias was observed.

Consequently, the particle identification PID cut applied to the Fine-Grained Detector 1 FGD1, which relies on this observed light yield, demonstrates particular sensitivity to low momentum protons that fall below the tracking threshold. The effectiveness in selecting neutral current single π+ (NC1 π+) events that include protons is visualized in Figure    . NC1 π+ events where the proton momentum is measured under 200 MeV/c are occasionally selected. Therefore, they are incorporated into the definition of the signal to ensure robustness against any discrepancies that might arise in model predictions. However, events featuring protons with momenta exceeding 200 MeV/c are seldomly selected and exhibit a significantly reduced selection efficiency compared to other NC1 π+ events. As a result, these are categorized as background. To support this decision, investigations using simulated data in which the number of background NC1 π+ events containing protons was varied were conducted. According to subsequent findings presented in Section   , no bias was detected in the measurement results.

human: The selection algorithm requires that all events have TPC information for the main track. A veto is applied to those events with activity in the most upstream TPC, and accordingly, only NC1 π + events with a forward-going π + can be selected. The selection efficiency is highest for small angles with respect to the beam, as the probability of reaching TPC2 decreases with increasing angle.The probability of a track entering the TPC2 from FGD1 also increases with momentum. However, even in the most favorable case, when the π + is forward-going and the interaction vertex is in the downstream region of FGD1, π + tracks below 200 MeV/ c are unlikely to be successfully reconstructed in the TPC. These effects can be clearly observed in the selection efficiency, presented in Fig. . NC1 π + events have three particles in the final state, whereas most of the competing backgrounds have only two. Therefore, for the same neutrino energy, the main track in NC1 π + is expected to have lower momentum than that of most background events and consequently the purity is best for low track momenta. Accordingly, we focus on studying and measuring the NC1 π + cross section defined by 0.5 and GeV/ c , which will hereafter be referred to as the Region of Interest (RoI).

human: T2K has identified the largest sample of data associated to NC1 π + interactions, and used it to perform the first differential cross-section measurement of this process. The unique design of T2K’s near detector ND280, utilizing a 0.2 T magnetic field and diverse sub-detector technologies, has proved essential in realizing this study. ND280’s magnet and the TPCs were crucial to separate μ - from π + and to precisely measure the track kinematics. FGD1 distinguished forwardfrom backward-going single π + -like tracks, while the ECal separated μ + from π + . Thanks to these combined performances and the large amount of data collected by ND280, the signal selection criteria presented in this article were capable of identifying over two hundred expected signal events. In the RoI of the signal sample, an efficiency of about 30% and a purity of 50% was achieved.

The ND280’s magnet, alongside the Time Projection Chambers TPCs, played a pivotal role in distinctly separating μfrom π+ and in accurately determining the track kinematics. This ensemble of high-performance technologies, along with the substantial volume of data amassed by ND280, enabled the signal selection criteria outlined in this article to successfully pinpoint over two hundred anticipated signal occurrences. Within the Region of Interest RoI of the signal sample, an efficiency nearing 30% as well as a purity rate of 50% was attained.

human: The Precision Reactor Oscillation and Spectrum Experiment, PROSPECT, was a segmented antineutrino detector that successfully operated at the High Flux Isotope Reactor in Oak Ridge, TN, during its 2018 run.Despite challenges with photomultiplier tube base failures affecting some segments, innovative machine learning approaches were employed to perform position and energy reconstruction, and particle classification. This work highlights the effectiveness of convolutional neural networks and graph convolutional networks in enhancing data analysis. By leveraging these techniques, a 3.3% increase in effective statistics was achieved compared to traditional methods, showcasing their potential to improve performance. Furthermore, these machine learning methodologies offer promising applications for other segmented particle detectors, underscoring their versatility and impact.

By capitalizing on these advanced techniques, the team achieved a notable 3.3% enhancement in effective statistics in comparison to traditional analytical methods, highlighting their ability to boost performance. Additionally, the adaptability and significant impact of these machine learning approaches suggest promising applications in various other segmented particle detectors, illustrating their considerable versatility.

human: The PROSPECT experiment measured the ν ̄ e emitted by the High Flux Isotope Reactor in 2018 to measure possible oscillation effects due to sterile neutrinos [1, 2, 3]. Reactor ν ̄ e were detected through the inverse β-decay reaction (IBD), where the outgoing positron carries the kinetic energy of the ν ̄ e and the delayed-neutron capture provides a tag to distinguish IBD from numerous reactor and cosmogenic backgrounds. Measuring possible ν ̄ e oscillations requires sufficient position resolution and suppression of backgrounds. PROSPECT accomplished this with a detector consisting of an 11 × 14 array of liquid scintillator segments outfitted with PMTs at either end of the segment, allowing cm-scale precision in the localization of energy deposits. The position along the length of the segment (henceforth z ) was estimated utilizing the timing difference and relative amplitude of the light detected by the two PMTs.
ai: In 2018, the PROSPECT experiment set out to investigate potential oscillation effects involving sterile neutrinos by examining the antineutrinos, or ν̄e, emitted by the High Flux Isotope Reactor [1, 2, 3]. The experiment detected these reactor-born antineutrinos through the inverse β-decay reaction IBD. This process is characterized by the outgoing positron, which carries away the kinetic energy of the ν̄e, while a delayed neutron capture offers a distinct signature to effectively differentiate IBD signals from the myriad backgrounds stemming from both the reactor and cosmic sources. To observe any oscillations of ν̄e, the experiment necessitated a high degree of positional resolution along with robust background suppression. PROSPECT achieved this objective using a sophisticated detection system comprising an array of liquid scintillator segments arranged in an 11 × 14 grid, equipped with photomultiplier tubes PMTs on both ends of each segment. This configuration enabled the experimenters to determine the precise location of energy deposits with centimeter-level accuracy. By analyzing the timing differences and relative light intensities detected by the two PMTs, estimations were made regarding the position along the z-axis, which refers to the lengthwise dimension of the segment.

human: Neutron detection and background suppression were enhanced by doping the liquid scintillator with Li 6 that allowed neutron identification through the Li 6 (n, α ) H 3 reaction. The liquid scintillator was based on Eljen-309 which produces a larger amount of scintillation light in the tail of the measured PMT pulse for nuclear recoils versus electron-like recoils [4]. This allows ’Pulse Shape Discrimination’ (PSD) to be used to distinguish different classes of events. For PROSPECT, PSD is constructed using the tail area of the PMT pulse shape, divided by the total pulse shape area. When combined with energy information from the amount of light collected, the PSD provides a clear separation of neutron capture events from positron interactions.

This upgrade facilitated the identification of neutrons as they interact via the Li-6 (n, α) H-3 reaction. The formulation of the liquid scintillator was based on Eljen-309, which has the capability of generating more scintillation light towards the end of the photon multiplier tube PMT pulse in cases of nuclear recoils as opposed to electron-like recoils [4]. This characteristic enables the use of ’Pulse Shape Discrimination’ PSD to differentiate between various event types. In the case of PROSPECT, PSD is formulated by taking the area of the tail portion of the PMT pulse shape and dividing it by the total area of the pulse shape. This, together with energy data obtained from the collected light, enables a clear distinction between neutron capture occurrences and positron interactions.

human: During the course of the experiment, a subset of the PMT bases failed because of the ingress of liquid scintillator into the PMT housings, which caused damage to the voltage divider circuitry. Segments with one or both PMTs failed were ignored for the initial IBD analysis [3]. Approximately a third of the segments were affected by the end of the run. This naturally led to the question of whether it is possible to utilize information from single-ended (SE) segments, i.e those containing only one active PMT, for the purpose of position, energy and pulse shape (PSD) determination as opposed to double-ended (DE) segments. Detailed studies of SE event reconstruction (SEER) were performed and a large improvement in background rejection achieved by extracting additional particle identification information [5, 6]. This paper explores the possibility of reconstructing these quantities in SE segments using machine learning (ML) techniques. The reconstructed quantities are then used for the purpose of background rejection. A performance comparison is made between the ML-based analysis and a simpler approach based on the pulse shape of a single PMT. Additionally, a comparison between the performance of different ML algorithms will also be shown. We find that utilizing ML improves the accuracy of the position, energy, and particle type reconstruction for single-ended events. Finally, the impact of applying ML-based SE event reconstruction (SEER) to the IBD selection is evaluated.

By the conclusion of the run, nearly one-third of the segments were compromised. This situation naturally raised the inquiry of whether information from single-ended SE segments-those comprising only a single operational PMT-could be leveraged for determining position, energy, and pulse shape discrimination PSD, in contrast to the typically double-ended DE segments. Comprehensive investigations into single-ended event reconstruction SEER were conducted, resulting in a significant enhancement in background rejection by extracting additional insights into particle identification [5, 6]. This paper delves into the feasibility of reconstructing these parameters within SE segments employing machine learning ML methodologies. These reconstructed parameters are subsequently utilized for background discrimination. A comparative analysis of the performance between ML-based approaches and a more straightforward technique, which relies on the pulse shape data from a single PMT, is presented. Furthermore, the study provides a comparison of the efficacy of various ML algorithms. Our findings indicate that employing ML leads to a more precise reconstruction of position, energy, and particle classification in single-ended events. Lastly, an evaluation of the impact of incorporating ML-based SE event reconstruction SEER on the IBD selection process is presented.

human: In this Section we describe the methodology for reconstructing quantities of interest for an IBD analysis for SE segments. First, a general description of the problem along with the conventional method for event reconstruction is given. This is followed by a discussion on the utilization of machine learning techniques to improve upon the SE event reconstruction. Finally, we demonstrate an improvement in our ability to reconstruct the position, energy, and particle type of the SE event.

We begin by laying out a broad overview of the problem, including a description of the traditional approach employed in event reconstruction. Afterward, we delve into a discussion that highlights the application of machine learning techniques in enhancing the reconstruction processes for SE events. Concluding this section, we showcase how these improvements significantly enhance our capacity to determine with greater precision the position, energy, and type of particle involved in SE events.

On the other hand, the z impact on the PSD is significantly smaller than its impact on energy, making the SE PSD a useful quantity for determining electron-like vs heavier recoiling particles. The average of the means is stored in the calibration database for each segment. A two parameter function is fit to the σ distribution as a function of energy, . human: For IBD event selection, a prompt candidate must contain only ionization-like pulses in all SE and DE segments using their respective SE or DE PSD distributions. With a better energy estimate from ML, one can more accurately reject backgrounds where the neighboring energy depositions are too large to actually be annihilation gammas.

human: We also use ML to create a classifier that gives a class score for each segment that detected energy during an event. The score represents the likelihood that signal came from an event of the given class. This information can be used for particle identification (PID). These are labelled electron-like (ionization), proton-like (recoil), neutron capture on Li 6 (ncap), muon, and ingress. The events are classified using DE information in the manner described in the previous section for ncap, ionization, and recoil. Muons are any event with a total energy above 15 MeV.Events above the recoil-like PSD are considered ’ingress’ events, which occurred within scintillator that leaked into the PMT housings. human: Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) as first introduced by [7] are deep neural networks that are ideal for learning translationally invariant features of spatial data. CNNs consist of several convolutional layers chained together.Each convolutional layer applies a set of filters (also called kernels) to process the input data. Each filter is a small matrix of trainable weights. During the convolution operation, these filters systematically slide across the input data, segment by segment. At each position, the filter performs an element-wise multiplication between its weights and the corresponding section of the input data it’s currently positioned over. The sum of these multiplications becomes a single value in the output feature map.The output of the series of convolutional layers can then be fed into a linear network in order to output a classification score or some other metric. For a mathematical review of convolutional network layers, we refer readers to Reference [8].
ai: Convolutional neural networks, often abbreviated as CNNs, were initially presented by [7] and are sophisticated deep learning models that excel at identifying translationally invariant features in spatial datasets. These networks are structured from multiple convolutional layers interconnected in a sequence. Within each layer, a collection of filters, sometimes known as kernels, is employed to transform the input data. These filters are essentially compact matrices consisting of adjustable weights that undergo training. As part of the convolution process, each filter methodically sweeps over the input data in a segment-by-segment fashion. Positioned meticulously, the filter conducts an element-wise multiplication between its weights and the specific segment of the input it overlayed. The resultant feature map includes individual entries derived by summing these element-wise multiplications to produce a single output value per segment position. The cumulative output from these convolutional layers can subsequently be introduced into a linear network, aiming to generate a classification score or an alternative evaluative metric. For an in-depth exploration of the mathematical foundation underlying these convolutional network layers, interested readers should consult Reference [8].

human: The convolution operation combines information across all input channels to produce each output channel (feature map). Each output channel is produced by convolving all input channels with a separate set of trainable kernels and summing the results. In the case of PROSPECT data, the input channels are the two PMT waveforms concatenated together, or the extracted features in the feature-based models.

human: In this work, the output of each convolutional layer is passed through a batch normalization layer, followed by an activation layer. A batch is a subset of the training data that is evaluated together for one forward and backwards pass where gradients of all parameters are calculated then adjusted based on the learning parameters used. The batch normalization layer [9] transforms the value at each channel in the output of the convolutional layer, x ^ k , into the signed mean variance for that channel, x ̄ k :

Within this context, a batch refers to a segment of the training dataset that undergoes evaluation simultaneously during a single forward and backward pass. This process involves calculating the gradients for all parameters and subsequently modifying them according to the specified learning parameters. The batch normalization layer, as described in reference [9], alters the value present in each channel of the convolutional layer’s output, denoted as x^k, converting it into the signed mean variance for that specific channel, represented as x ̄^k.

The variable ε is a small number used to avoid division by zero, and γ k and β k are free parameters designed to scale and shift the output of the normalization. Batch normalization layers are widely used in CNNs for the purpose of speeding up training of the network parameters.The activation layer used is a rectified linear unit (ReLU) layer which sets negative values of the input to 0.

human: To apply CNNs on PROSPECT data, one must choose how to map the PMT data to the inputs of the CNN. The natural choice given the spatial arrangement of the detector segments is to assign the features of each of the 14x11 segments to a spatial input. In this scenario, the features fed into the model are either the waveforms of each of the two PMTs concatenated as described in Section or the extracted features as described in Section . Signals are clustered in time with a 20 ns window [3], and each segment containing PMTs with signals above threshold corresponds to the inputs to the CNN. All segments that did not detect pulses above threshold in a given cluster are ignored.Note that this 20 ns clustering window defines an ’event’ for CNN input purposes, with all pulses within this window processed together as a single input instance.Because the typical event occurring in the PROSPECT detector only contains 2 - 4 segments with signals above threshold, the input to the neural network is very sparse. This makes the PROSPECT data ideal for sparse convolutional networks utilizing sparse matrix algebra to calculate the output of each convolutional layer. For this reason, the sparse CNN library spconv [10] was chosen. The spconv library allows one to use submanifold sparse convolutional layers [11] which only transfers information from nonzero segments to the next layer. This technique significantly reduces the computational burden of the network without any loss of information relevant for segment level predictions. All CNN networks used for SE reconstruction utilize these submanifold convolutions for every convolutional layer.

In this setup, the input features that are submitted to the model can either be the concatenated waveforms from each of the two PMTs, as discussed in Section    , or the features derived and detailed in Section    . Time-based clustering of signals is performed using a 20 nanosecond window [3], where each segment comprising PMTs with signals that surpass a predefined threshold is linked as input for the CNN. Segments that do not register pulses exceeding this threshold within a cluster are disregarded entirely. It is important to highlight that this 20 nanosecond window functions as a definitional boundary for what constitutes an ’event’ in the context of CNN input, with all detected pulses within this time frame being processed as a singular input instance. This sparsity makes PROSPECT data exceptionally suitable for sparse convolutional networks that leverage sparse matrix algebra to compute outputs for each convolutional layer. Consequently, the spconv library [10] was selected for this purpose, as it effectively employs submanifold sparse convolutional layers [11], which only propagate information from active, nonzero segments to subsequent layers. This method dramatically lowers the computational demands on the network while ensuring no loss of critical information needed for predictions at the segment level. Every CNN employed for SE (single event) reconstruction integrates these submanifold convolutions throughout every convolutional layer.

human: There are two types of inputs for the CNN models: (1) PMT waveforms after baseline subtraction, time alignment and value normalization is applied, and (2) extracted features from the waveforms and DE reconstruction when applicable. Henceforth when referring to “waveform“ models or “extracted feature“ models, we are referring to models that either utilize the full waveform from the PMT or the extracted features. The preparation of these inputs are described in detail below. Analog waveforms from each PMT are digitized by a CAEN V1725 250 MHz 14-bit waveform digitizer. We will refer to each value of the digitized signal as a sample which represents the average voltage over a 4 ns sampling interval.

An additional 5 samples were used for the purposes of this study and 6 samples were added for potential offsets between detectors in a given cluster. The first pulse that arrived is set so that the eighth sample contains the arrival time. All other pulses are offset such that their arrival sample is at sample n, where , t i is the arrival time of the waveform in the cluster and t 0 is the arrival time of the first waveform. The round function selects the nearest integer, rounding down for midpoint values.

human: Position reconstruction is a difficult problem for SE segments due to the fact that the nominal position reconstruction algorithm relies on both the light ratio between PMTs and the differential timing between PMTs. Any SE segment reconstruction method must rely solely on the timing distribution of the light collected for each pulse within the cluster. Without any knowledge beforehand of the type of CNN architecture that would best suit this problem, an experimental approach was taken to determine what works. Both full waveforms and extracted quantities were used as inputs to the CNN. The results were benchmarked against a simple “nearest neighbors average“ approach in which we simply average the z position reconstructed from neighboring double-ended segments.

This involved utilizing both complete waveforms and selectively extracted data points as input for the CNN. The efficacy of this method was evaluated by comparing it to a straightforward “nearest neighbors average“ technique, where the z positions reconstructed from adjacent double-ended segments are averaged to derive a value.

Generic convolutional layers will typically shrink the feature space, but when a padding of is used, the output size will remain the same as the input. Here F is the spacial size of the filter, each filter being a square grid of parameters. Note that F must be an odd number for this to work. For this reason, convolutional layers were varied with filter sizes of 1, 3, 5, and 7. The total number of layers were varied up to 12 and a parameter representing the number of layers where F is set to 1, also called pointwise convolutional layers was also used. Finally, a parameter representing the expansion (or contraction) of features is used to set the number of output features, and thus the number of filters used at each layer. Since the output needs to be one feature, the number of output channels at each layer is calculated by a linear change in features from the previous layer, with the number of expansion layers being another tunable hyperparameter. The remaining layers linearly shrink the outputs to 1. These hyperparameters, or parameters describing the architecture of the network, were varied using a gradient-free optimization method as described in Section . Through experimentation it was found that layers with larger numbers of intermediate layers outperformed smaller numbers up to around 10 layers, beyond which there was no improvement. human: Training is split into epochs. An epoch consists of one full pass of the training dataset in which the gradients of each batch are computed and model weights are updated until all batches in the dataset have been exhausted. At this point the model is tested on the validation dataset. This sequence constitutes a single epoch. The loss for the validation dataset in a given epoch is compared to the current best loss of all epochs. If the loss fails to improve by a certain amount for a number of epochs in a row, the training is automatically ended. This criterion varies from problem to problem, but typical values used in this work were five epochs failing to improve the loss by 0.01 resulted in cancellation of the training run. Model weights for the best validation loss are saved for later use. Splitting into separate training and validation datasets in this manner prevents over-training in which the model finds patterns in the training dataset that don’t generalize to other data.
ai: Training is organized into several cycles known as epochs. An epoch involves processing the entire training dataset whereby, through each complete pass, gradients for every batch are calculated, and the model’s weights are revised accordingly. This continues until every batch within the dataset has been processed. Once this loop ends, the model undergoes evaluation using the validation dataset. This entire sequence defines a single epoch. During each epoch, the loss observed for the validation dataset is monitored and compared with the lowest loss recorded across all epochs. Should the loss not exhibit improvement beyond a specified threshold over a series of consecutive epochs, the training process is halted automatically. This stopping criterion can differ based on the specific problem at hand, but in the context of this study, training was discontinued if, after five consecutive epochs, the loss did not decrease by 0.01. The model weights associated with the best validation loss are preserved for future application. By segregating the training and validation datasets in this manner, the model is shielded from overfitting, which is the inclination to identify patterns in the training dataset that do not translate to new, unseen data.

human: Optimization is performed using a gradient-free optimization library Optuna [15]. Hyperparameters of the model are chosen and varied within bounds that are allowed given the memory constraints and CPU resources available. A typical set up for the hyperparameter search would be to set the number of trials to 100, vary between three and five hyperparameters, and set a flag to prune unpromising trials. It was found that the default hyperparameter sampler and trial pruner was sufficient for our needs. The default sampling algorithm is the Tree-structured Parzen Estimator algorithm [16]. The default pruner is the median pruner, which will prune the trial if the trial’s best intermediate result is worse than median for previous trials at the same epoch.
ai: The process of optimization utilizes the gradient-free optimization library known as Optuna [15]. When selecting the model’s hyperparameters, they are adjusted and varied within pre-defined limits, which are dictated by the available memory and CPU capabilities. In a standard scenario for hyperparameter exploration, one might configure the system to conduct 100 trials, adjusting between three to five hyperparameters, and activate a flag to discard any trials that appear unpromising. Through our experimentation, we discovered that the library’s default settings for both hyperparameter sampling and trial pruning adequately met our requirements. The Tree-structured Parzen Estimator algorithm [16] serves as the default mechanism for sampling. Additionally, the default pruning mechanism employs the median pruner, which is designed to terminate a trial if its best performance at any intermediate stage falls below the median result of previous trials conducted at the same epoch.

human: A sqlite [17] database was used to store trial results. This allowed for easy parallelization of the hyperparameter optimization process. Multiple hyperparameter runs were set off on a process utilizing two threads, one thread reserved for data computations and one for data loading. Each run would be allocated approximately two days of processing time. Each thread references the same database for determining loss values for previous trials used for the next parameter selection and as a reference for when to prune unpromising trials. We found that when utilizing a CPU cluster for hyperparameter optimization, only using one thread for computations and one for data loading was by far the most efficient choice, as increasing this number only gave marginal gains in terms of computational efficiency. For example, utilizing two threads for computations sped up the time for a single epoch in one test by 30% at the cost of double the resources. With only two threads in use for training, we could run many more models simultaneously with the available CPU resources.

human: GCNs have already been shown to be useful in particle physics experiments [18] and various neutrino physics experiments, including IceCube [19], liquid argon-based time projection chambers such as DUNE [20] [21], and scintillator-based neutrino experiments [22].GCNs are ideal for PROSPECT data due to their effectiveness at representing sparse datasets. Graphs can be arbitrarily large and therefore code written for training on graphs implements sparse matrix algebra [23]. Implementation of the GCN on PROSPECT data follows the architecture modeled by the CNNs as described in Section . This general architecture is shown in Figure . Graphs are composed of nodes and edges. Similar to the CNN construction, we utilize event clusters as individual graphs. The ’nodes’ of the graph are segments that had one or more PMTs above threshold. The features of each node are then either the two PMT waveforms concatenated together or the extracted waveform features. The ’edges’ of the graph are defined using a k -nearest neighbors approach. Here k is a parameter of the network that represents the maximum number of connections a segment can have. If an event contains more segments above threshold then the segment will be connected to the segments in closest proximity. Through experimentation, it was found that a k value of 4 or greater was optimal. Since most of the events contain a multiplicity of 5 or less, this means that for most events each segment is connected to every other segment.
ai: Graph Convolutional Networks GCNs have already demonstrated their value in the domain of particle physics investigations [18] and have proven beneficial across numerous neutrino physics studies, such as IceCube [19], DUNE’s liquid argon time projection chambers [20] [21], and experiments utilizing scintillators for neutrinos [22]. GCNs are particularly well-suited for analyzing PROSPECT data due to their proficiency in handling sparse datasets. Since graphs can be of infinite size, the algorithms devised for their training incorporate algebra related to sparse matrices [23]. When applying the GCN framework to PROSPECT data, the architecture is inspired by the convolutional neural networks CNNs as elaborated in Section . Figure depicts this broad architecture. Within these graphs, nodes and edges are the fundamental components. Drawing a parallel with the CNN architecture, we treat event clusters as discrete graphs. The ’nodes’ represent segments where one or more photomultiplier tubes PMTs have surpassed a set threshold. Node features are then configured as either the two PMT waveforms merged together or the extracted characteristics of the waveform. Employing a k-nearest neighbors method, the ’edges’ are created. In this context, k denotes a network parameter that signifies the upper limit on the number of connections a segment is allowed. In cases where an event features multiple segments exceeding the threshold, connectivity is established with the nearest segments. After thorough experimentation, it emerged that a k value set to 4 or higher yielded the best results. Given that most events have a segment multiplicity of five or fewer, this configuration implies that, generally, each segment is interlinked with all the other segments in an event.

human: While equation shows the basic idea behind a graph convolutional layer, there are a number of ways this can be implemented and a number of variations on the idea can be used to enhance training speed and model performance. The python package pytorch geometric [23] is utilized for the implementation and as of this writing has 42 different graph neural network (GNN) layer operators implemented. Rather than completing a detailed study of each one of these operators to choose one that best fits our use case, a brute force approach was used where the easiest ones to implement were tested in a hyperparameter search. human: The primary difference between the graph architecture and the equivalent CNN architecture is the choice of adjacency matrix which determines which segment features are convolved together. The k -nearest-neighbors ( k -NN) approach was also utilized for PID classification. This means that for each segment in the cluster, the k -nearest segments above threshold in the cluster are connected to it. Self-loops can also be included, meaning the segment’s own features can be convolved with the layer weights for that segment’s output. The choice to use self loops along with the parameter k were varied in the hyperparameter search, and it was found that self loops are not necessary along with k values of greater than or equal to 6. Because most events have a multiplicity of 4 or fewer, it was optimal to connect all of the segment features with each other segment in the event.
ai: The main distinguishing factor between graph-based and convolutional neural network CNN architectures lies in their use of the adjacency matrix. This matrix determines which features of segments are subjected to convolutional operations. To classify using PID, the k-nearest-neighbors (k-NN) method was employed. Here, each segment within a cluster is linked to its k-nearest peers, surpassing a set threshold within the same cluster. Additionally, self-loops-which allow a segment’s features to be convolved with its layer weights to produce that segment’s output-can be included. During hyperparameter tuning, both the inclusion of self-loops and the k parameter were adjusted. The results indicated that self-loops were not essential when k equaled or exceeded 6. Given that the majority of events consist of 4 or fewer multiplicities, the most effective approach involved connecting each segment’s features to every other segment within the event.

human: In addition to GCNs and CNNs, other architectures were attempted. The simplest type of neural network, a fully-connected neural network (FCNN) was applied to the waveforms prepared as described in Section . A fully connected neural network (FCNN) is one in which each input is connected to every output.Each layer in this type of network can be described as a linear transformation, Here y is the output of the layer, x is the input, A is a matrix of trainable weights and b is a trainable constant. These will be referred to as linear layers. It was found through experimentation that the best models were those in which a number of linear layers are chained together, first expanding the input waveform into a size roughly twice that of the number of samples fed into the network. This is followed by a number of layers that shrink the number of outputs to a single output which is the prediction. FCNN were approximately as successful at predicting the z position for events that have a multiplicity of one as GCNs and CNNs. For higher multiplicity events, CNNs and GCNs that take in all data from neighboring segments to predict the single segment perform better than FCNN models.
ai: Beyond the use of Graph Convolutional Networks GCNs and Convolutional Neural Networks CNNs, exploration of alternative neural network architectures was conducted. Among these, the Fully-Connected Neural Network FCNN, known for its simplicity among neural network types, was applied to analyze waveforms as previously outlined in Section   . An FCNN is characterized by each input neuron being connected to every output neuron, creating a web of connections. Each layer within this architecture executes a linear transformation where the layer’s output, y, arises from applying a matrix of adaptable weights, A, to the input, x, on top of a modifiable constant, b. This type of layer is commonly referred to as a linear layer. Experiments revealed that the most effective models consisted of a sequence of linear layers: initially, these layers expand the input waveform to a dimension approximately double that of the initial sample size. Subsequently, additional layers are tasked with reducing the number of outputs down to a singular prediction output. When it came to forecasting the z position for events with a single multiplicity, FCNNs demonstrated a level of accuracy akin to that of the GCN and CNN models. However, for events with multiple multiplicities, the CNN and GCN models, which incorporate comprehensive data from adjacent segments to extrapolate predictions for a single segment, surpassed the FCNNs in performance.

human: Other, more complex architectures were attempted. Because the waveform is a time series, it was initially thought that utilizing architectures designed for processing time series data could help capture additional information to improve upon the naive approach used in the GCNs or CNNs, which was to simply feed each sample of the waveform as feature layers of the network. To this end, recurrent neural networks (RNNs) and temporal convolutional networks [30] (TCNs) were used to process the waveforms before feeding them into a CNN architecture. In the case of the TCN, the outcome was identical to no TCN being applied. In the case of the RNN, the gradient descent algorithm was unable to converge and no useful predictions were able to be made.
ai: Researchers explored using more sophisticated architectures. Considering that the waveform is a manifestation of sequential data, a hypothesis emerged that leveraging architectures specifically tailored for time series analysis might extract richer details, surpassing the simplistic method employed by Graph Convolutional Networks GCNs or Convolutional Neural Networks CNNs. The initial naive approach involved inserting each waveform sample into the network as distinct feature layers. To explore potential enhancements, both recurrent neural networks RNNs and temporal convolutional networks TCNs were employed to pre-process the waveforms prior to their incorporation into a CNN framework. Interestingly, with the implementation of TCNs, the results mirrored those achieved without their usage. When RNNs were employed, a significant obstacle arose; the gradient descent algorithm encountered difficulties in reaching convergence, rendering it ineffective in generating any beneficial predictions or insights.

human: Another architecture tried in the same vein was 3D convolutional networks where the 3rd axis used is the temporal axis of the waveform. In this construction we use the two samples from both PMTs as the two features fed into the newtork at each time and spatial location. The difficulty with this approach was the enormous amount of time it takes to perform 3D convolutional layers. To decrease the computational complexity, we factorized the time and spatial dimensions by first performing pointwise convolutions in space and length N convolutions in time to reduce the size of the temporal dimension before performing spatial convolutions with a filter of length 1 in the time dimension. This still resulted in a factor of 6 increase in CPU time per epoch relative to 2D convolutions so we did not perform detailed tests of the algorithm.
ai: In a related line of investigation, researchers explored the implementation of 3D convolutional networks, where the additional third dimension serves as the temporal axis encompassing the waveform. For this framework, the input at each point in time and space utilizes data from the two photomultiplier tubes PMTs as distinct features, which the network processes. A significant challenge that emerged with this methodology was the considerable processing time required to execute the 3D convolutional layers. To address this, and reduce the complexity that skyrockets with these computations, an approach was devised to factorize both the temporal and spatial dimensions. Initially, pointwise convolutions are applied across the spatial aspect, coupled with convolutions of length N targeting the temporal dimension to curtail its extent before applying spatial convolutions that use a filter of temporal length 1. However, despite these efforts to streamline efficiency, this strategy still escalated the computational time per epoch by a factor of six compared to 2D convolutions. As a result, we decided against conducting extensive tests of the algorithm due to these impractical processing demands.

A critical aspect to consider is the balancing act involved in increasing the reactor-on data statistics. While boosting these statistics enhances the effective data collection, it simultaneously raises the total reactor-off statistics. This increment introduces further uncertainty tied to the background estimation, which consequently diminishes the effectiveness of statistical measurements. Furthermore, since both reactor-on and reactor-off signals have accidental events subtracted, implementing more rigorous criteria for cuts diminishes these accidental events, thereby reducing their associated uncertainties and ultimately boosting the reliability and effectiveness of the statistical analysis.

human: Convolutional neural networks and graph convolutional networks were applied to the PROSPECT data for the purpose of recovering information from SE segments. It was found that utilizing the full waveform information from the digitized PMT signals were required to provide the best performance for SE reconstruction.CNNs were found to excel at reconstructing the position of the event in SE segments while GCNs performed best at classifying energy depositions in SE segments. With a position reconstruction one can better estimate the amount of energy deposited in a segment and use this to more powerfully reject IBD backgrounds.Similarly, the classification reconstruction can also help determine heavier recoiling particles in SE segments which allows further background rejection. It was shown that the GCN outperformed the tail fraction method of PSD classification for SE segments. This resulted in a larger overall signal to background, which allowed us to relax veto window lengths so as to maximize the effective statistics of the dataset using ML. A 3.3% improvement in effective statistics was achieved over the traditional tail fraction method of particle identification. The demonstrated effectiveness of ML techniques to improve event reconstruction on PROSPECT opens up promising avenues for its application for similar segmented particle detectors, such as PROSPECT-II.
ai: To extract insights from SE segments in the PROSPECT data, convolutional neural networks CNNs and graph convolutional networks GCNs were employed. Comprehensive examination revealed that leveraging the entirety of the waveform data from the digitized photomultiplier tube PMT signals was essential for optimizing single-event SE reconstruction performance. Upon analysis, CNNs were particularly adept at pinpointing the precise position of events within SE segments, whereas GCNs excelled in categorizing energy depositions within those same segments. Understanding the precise location of an event enables more accurate estimations of energy deposited within a segment, thereby enhancing the capability to exclude inverse β decay IBD backgrounds. In a parallel manner, effective classification facilitates the identification of more significant recoiling particles within SE segments, which in turn aids in further background discrimination. It was determined that GCNs surpassed the traditional tail fraction method used in pulse shape discrimination PSD classification for SE segments. This advancement yielded a stronger signal-to-background ratio, allowing for the relaxation of veto window durations, thereby maximizing the dataset’s effective statistics through machine learning techniques. An improvement of 3.3% in effective statistics was realized over the conventional tail fraction approach for particle identification. The proven efficacy of machine learning approaches in enhancing event reconstruction in the PROSPECT project paves the way for their future implementation in analogous segmented particle detectors, including PROSPECT-II.

human: The Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment currently under construction in the US will be a long-baseline neutrino oscillation experiment dedicated to determining the neutrino mass ordering and to measure the CP violation phase in the lepton sector. DUNE will also perform studies of non-beam physics such as atmospheric neutrinos, bursts from supernovae and nucleon decays in which photon detection systems will play a major role in triggering and also provide calorimetric measurements. For the second phase of DUNE, two additional detector modules will be added in the far detector complex in the Sanford Underground Research Facility. We present the Aluminum Profiles with Embedded X-ARAPUCA (APEX) concept as an advanced proposal for the photon detector system of the third DUNE far detector module. This system aims to have an optical coverage of approximately 60% made viable by the technology advancement achieved by the DUNE collaboration on the use of non-conductive optical fibers for power and signal readout of the photon detector units. Such large coverage will provide enhanced light collection capabilities at MeV-scale energy deposit level per interaction and optimal energy reconstruction resolution up to the GeV scale. The attained electrical isolation of the detector units with low noise levels allows for a complete instrumentation of the field cage walls with satisfactory segmentation as the readout scheme envisages a much larger than typical number of channels to be adopted. We discuss the main features of the system, first estimates on its expected performances, potential for physics measurements and prototyping plans for R&D.

Beyond these objectives, DUNE is set to explore various aspects of non-beam physics. This encompasses the study of atmospheric neutrinos, supernova burst signals, and nucleon decays, all of which will heavily rely on photon detection systems. These systems are crucial for initiating triggers and providing calorimetric measurements. As part of DUNE’s second phase, plans are in place to install two additional detector modules at the far detector site located within the Sanford Underground Research Facility. We are introducing the Aluminum Profiles with Embedded X-ARAPUCA APEX, a sophisticated proposition for the photon detector system in the third DUNE far detector module. This proposal aspires to achieve an optical coverage of nearly 60%, a feat made feasible by breakthroughs in technology by the DUNE collaboration, specifically leveraging non-conductive optical fibers for power supply and signal extraction from the photon detection units. This significant coverage enhancement promises improved light collection at energy deposit levels around the MeV scale and achieves superior energy reconstruction precision up to the GeV scale. Thanks to the effective electrical isolation of the detector units alongside minimal noise levels, comprehensive instrumentation of the field cage walls becomes achievable with adequate segmentation. The readout strategy is designed to implement a considerably larger number of channels than usual. We provide an overview of the system’s primary attributes, initial estimates of its performance predictions, its potential impact on physics measurements, and prototyping strategies for upcoming research and development initiatives.

human: The Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment is a next-generation neutrino detector dedicated to the study of the oscillation phenomena using a powerful neutrino beam, atmospheric neutrinos, neutrinos from astrophysical sources as well as being capable of performing physics beyond the standard matter searches [1]. DUNE has a two-phase implementation plan. Phase I will be composed of two 17 kton far detectors (FD) liquid argon time projection chambers (LArTPCs), a near detector (ND) with a LArTPC module (ND-LAr), a muon spectrometer (TMS), with the addition of an on-axis solenoid magnet plus electromagnetic calorimeter (SAND), and a beam line capable of providing (anti-)neutrinos with a 1.2 MW power. Phase II aims at expanding DUNE capabilities by limiting systematics with a more capable ND and greatly increasing statistics with the construction of another two FDs in addition to boosting beam power to 2.1 MW [2].

This includes a highly potent neutrino beam, atmospheric neutrinos, and those from astrophysical origins, while also venturing into searches that extend beyond the traditional boundaries of standard matter physics [1]. DUNE’s ambitious agenda unfolds in two distinct phases. The first phase involves the integration of two large-scale 17-kiloton far detectors equipped with advanced liquid argon time projection chambers LArTPCs. Alongside these, a near detector will incorporate a LArTPC module (ND-LAr) and a muon spectrometer TMS. Additional components include an on-axis solenoid magnet coupled with an electromagnetic calorimeter, known as SAND, and a beam line engineered to generate (anti-)neutrinos powered up to 1.2 MW. The second phase sets its sights on enhancing DUNE’s capabilities by reducing systematic uncertainties through a more sophisticated near detector, while dramatically bolstering statistical power. This involves the ambitious construction of two additional far detectors and an upgraded beam power reaching 2.1 MW [2].

human: In phase I, there will be one module with anode plane assemblies (APAs) composed of thin copper wires for charge collection displaced vertically so that the ionization electrons will drift horizontally, therefore receiving the name of the Horizontal Drift (HD) module. The scintillation light collecting system will have bar-shaped X-Arapucas placed in between the APAs [3]. The other module will have its anodes composed of perforated PCB layers with conductive strips that will be disposed vertically in the cryostat so that the electron field will be applied vertically, this being called the Vertical Drift (VD) module [4]. Its Photon Detection System (PDS) will have rectangular X-Arapucas positioned along the cryostat walls (outside the active volume) and also on the cathode, in a high voltage environment. A substantial R&D was developed by the collaboration in order to have the photon detectors working using signal-over-fiber and power-over-fiber in a cryogenic environment [5].

In addition, it could improve the determination of the second oscillation peak maximum at ∼ 0.8GeV (which presents a lower interaction count due to the dependence of the cross section on neutrino energy and DUNE beam energy spread in comparison with the first oscillation peak around 2.5GeV). The Aluminum Profiles with Embedded X-ARAPUCA (APEX) concept aligns well with this.

Building on the expertise developed for the cathode PD modules in VD, this concept presents a simplified, lightweight, and low(er)-cost photodetectors, combined with bulk materials of low-radioactive content.

human: The valence quark parton distribution functions (PDFs) of all ground state heavy mesons composed of b or c quarks, are discussed; namely, the pseudoscalar , and B c , together with the corresponding vector ones, , and B c ∗ .We use a QCD-inspired constituent quark model, which has been applied with success to conventional heavy mesons, so that one advantage here is that all parameters have already been fixed by previous studies.The wave functions of the heavy mesons in the rest frame are obtained by solving the Schrödinger equation, then boosted to its light-front based on Susskind’s Lorentz transformation. The PDFs at the hadron scale, are then obtained by integrating out the transverse momenta of the modulus square of the light-front wave function.Our study shows how the valence quark distributions differ between pseudoscalar and vector mesons, as well as among charmonia, bottomonia and bottom-charmed mesons. Comparisons with other theoretical calculations demonstrate that the PDFs obtained herein are in general narrower but align well with the expected patterns. Moreover, each PDF’s point-wise behavior is squeezed with respect to the scale-free parton-like PDF.

The PDFs at the hadron scale are obtained by integrating the transverse momenta from the square of the light-front wave functions. Our investigation reveals the distinctive variations in valence quark distributions between pseudoscalar and vector mesons and among different categories such as charmonia, bottomonia, and bottom-charmed mesons. Upon comparing these findings with other theoretical calculations, we find that these PDFs are generally more constrained but still align effectively with theoretical expectations. In another fascinating domain, quarkonia represent unique entities; these are bound systems of a quark Q and its corresponding antiquark Q̅. This diversity in energy scales lends quarkonia a significant role across various scientific inquiries, including understanding the essence of confinement, testing the Standard Model SM of particle physics, and elucidating the emergence of exotic states like X, Y, and Z.
