Modern PC and workstation GPUs have substantial computing resources allocated for single-precision computations, much more than the resources allocated for double-precision. For instance, the workstation GPU used in this work (Nvidia RTX 4000 Ada) has 48 streaming multiprocessors (SMs), each SM is equipped with 128 CUDA cores that could be used in single precision (FP32) computations, while each SM is also equipped with only 2 CUDA cores that could be used in double precision (FP64) computations. Hence, the FP64 computations rate in Tera floating point operations (TFLOP) is 1/64th of the TFLOP rate of FP32 operations. The small number of FP64 Cores is included only to ensure that programs with FP64 code operate correctly on the GPU.Since LBM is a memory-bound computational method, it is preferred to work with single-precision to optimize the use of the GPU memory bandwidth. The (float) datatype needs 4 bytes to store each number, while the (double) datatype needs 8 bytes to store each number. Hence, the GPU memory bandwidth could be used to transfer twice the amount of (float) numbers than the amount of (double) numbers. This has a major impact on the computational speed of the LBM.In previous work, liquid crystal simulations were only possible in double precision as the single precision computations resulted in non-physical results. The small changes in the velocity field were not captured properly with single precision accuracy. That resulted in a major slowdown in the computational speed of the simulations due to the limited double-precision computational resources in the available GPUs. Therefore, the simulations were carried out for relatively small domains and a limited number of cases to obtain results in a timely manner. To alleviate those limitations, single precision computations were necessary to better utilize the available computational resources. However, the simulation accuracy was of great concern due to the limits of single-precision computations. In this work, we utilize the distribution functions shifting technique reported in Ref. [28] to increase the computational accuracy of the LBM, as shown in Sec. .

To mitigate such constraints, the adoption of single-precision computations became essential to fully exploit the existing computational capacity. human: We have presented an optimized algorithm based on the Ericksen-Leslie model to simulate the hydrodynamics of liquid crystals. Our method combines the lattice Boltzmann method (for the velocity field) with finite differences (for the director field). We introduce two key improvements to enhance precision and enable efficient single-precision computations.

In our work, we unveil two principal innovations designed to boost accuracy and facilitate streamlined single-precision calculations.

human: The first improvement is the shifted distribution function in the lattice Boltzmann method. Since typical velocities in these simulations are extremely low ( ), standard lattice Boltzmann implementations suffer significant precision loss. The shifting technique mitigates this issue, substantially improving accuracy. However, this enhancement alone is insufficient for reliable single-precision simulations because the director field updates are too small in each lattice Boltzmann time step, leading to further precision errors.

Despite this advancement, it remains inadequate for conducting reliable simulations using only single-precision. The reason behind this is that the updates to the director field within each lattice Boltzmann time step are minuscule, resulting in additional precision errors.

human: The second improvement is decoupling the time steps of the lattice Boltzmann and finite-difference methods. By using larger time steps for finite differences, we reduce precision errors and enable the entire simulation to run in single precision without sacrificing accuracy.

Adopting more extensive time intervals for finite differences helps minimize precision errors and makes it possible for the whole simulation to be executed using single precision, all while maintaining the desired level of accuracy.

human: Our results show that, in double precision, accuracy decreases monotonically as the finite-difference time step increases. However, in single precision, accuracy follows a non-monotonic trend: initially, the error decreases as the time step increases due to larger director field updates, reaches a minimum, and then grows due to method-induced errors. This behaviour reveals an optimal time step that maximizes accuracy. In our test case, the error was remarkably low ( %) compared to double-precision simulations, with a speedup of 26.5 times. We illustrate the possibilities opened by this technique by simulations of a large domain with many flowing skyrmions.

human: Predicting particle-laden flows requires accurate fluid force models. However, a reliable particle force model for finite-size particles in turbulent flows remains lacking.In the present work, a fluid force model for a finite-size spherical particle in turbulence is developed by simulating turbulent flow past a fixed spherical particle using particle-resolved direct numerical simulation (PRDNS).Our simulation demonstrates that turbulence increases the mean drag force of the particle, which is consistent with previous studies. By correlating the DNS data as functions of the Reynolds number of particles, the ratio of the particle-to-turbulence scale, and the intensity ratio of the turbulence, an empirical correlation for the mean drag force is obtained.Furthermore, we find that the fluctuations of both the drag and lateral forces follow the Gaussian distribution. Consequently, the temporal variations of the fluctuating drag and lateral forces are modeled using a stochastic Langevin equation.Empirical correlations of the fluctuation intensities and time scales involved in the stochastic model are also determined from the DNS data.Finally, we simulate the movement of a finite-size particle in turbulence and the dispersion of particles in a turbulent channel flow to validate the proposed model.The proposed fluid force model requires the mean flow velocity, the kinetic energy of the turbulence, and the dissipation rate of the turbulence as inputs, which makes it well suited for combination with the Reynolds-averaged Navier-Stokes (RANS) approach.
ai: Forecasting flows that contain particles necessitates precise models of fluid forces. Currently, there is a gap in dependable particle force models suitable for finite-size particles within turbulent flows. This paper introduces a fluid force model designed for a finite-size spherical particle immersed in turbulence. We achieve this by simulating turbulent flow around a stationary spherical particle, leveraging particle-resolved direct numerical simulation PRDNS. The results from our simulations reveal that turbulence enhances the average drag force on the particle, aligning with findings from earlier research. By correlating our direct numerical simulation DNS results with various parameters such as the particle Reynolds number, the ratio of particle size to turbulence scale, and the intensity ratio of the turbulence, we derive an empirical formula for the mean drag force. Moreover, our research shows that the variations in both drag and lateral forces adhere to a Gaussian distribution. As a result, we model the fluctuations in drag and lateral forces over time using a stochastic Langevin equation. We extract empirical correlations for fluctuation intensities and the time scales involved in the stochastic model from the DNS data. Ultimately, we apply the model to simulate the movement of a finite-size particle in turbulence and analyze particle dispersion in a turbulent channel flow to verify its effectiveness. The recommended fluid force model requires the mean flow velocity, turbulence kinetic energy, and the rate of turbulence dissipation as inputs, making it particularly suitable for integration with the Reynolds-averaged Navier-Stokes RANS methodology.

human: Particle-laden flows are ubiquitous in nature and engineering applications, such as sediment transport, dust storms, fluidized bed reactor flow, and the spread of haze pollutants in cities.For decades, numerical methods for particle-laden flows have been greatly developed, and numerical simulation has become a powerful tool in both fundamental research and practical processes.Depending on the different levels of assumptions, the numerical methods for particle-laden flows can be roughly classified as the Eulerian two-fluid method, the Lagrangian particle method, and the fully resolved method (Drew, 1983; Elghobashi, 1994; Crowe et al., 1996; Loth, 2000; Eaton, 2009; Wang, 2009; Balachandar and Eaton, 2010; Yu and Shao, 2010; Fox, 2012; Subramaniam, 2013; Tenneti and Subramaniam, 2014; Kuerten, 2016; Maxey, 2017; Elghobashi, 2019; Brandt and Coletti, 2022; Fox, 2024; Schneiderbauer, 2024).The prediction accuracy of particle-laden flows is critically dependent on the fluid force models used in numerical simulations (Michaelides, 1997, 2003; Loth and Dorgan, 2009).
ai: Particle-laden flows are a common phenomenon encountered in both natural settings and engineering applications. They are crucial in areas such as sediment transport, dust storms, the operation of fluidized bed reactors, and the dispersal of haze pollutants within urban environments. Over the years, impressive advancements have been made in numerical methods for simulating particle-laden flows, establishing numerical simulations as a vital tool in both theoretical research and the execution of practical processes. These numerical methodologies vary based on the assumptions they incorporate and can be broadly categorized into the Eulerian two-fluid approach, the Lagrangian particle technique, and the fully resolved method. These categorizations can trace their origins back to seminal works by researchers such as Drew 1983, Elghobashi 1994, Crowe et al. 1996, Loth 2000, Eaton 2009, Wang 2009, Balachandar and Eaton 2010, Yu and Shao 2010, Fox 2012, Subramaniam 2013, Tenneti and Subramaniam 2014, Kuerten 2016, Maxey 2017, Elghobashi 2019, Brandt and Coletti 2022, and both Fox and Schneiderbauer anticipated for 2024. The fidelity of predictions concerning particle-laden flows largely hinges on the models of fluid forces that are employed in these simulations, as outlined in the works by Michaelides (1997, 2003) and Loth and Dorgan 2009.

human: The point-particle method is a widely used approach based on the Lagrangian framework, which has a long history in particle-laden flow simulations (McLaughlin, 1994; Balachandar, 2009; Eaton, 2009; Soldati and Marchioli, 2009; Kuerten, 2016).In this method, particles are modeled as infinitesimal points with finite mass and momentum, and there exists an exact theory for particle motion in the Stokes flow regime at very small particle Reynolds numbers (Tsai, 1957; Gatignol, 1983; Maxey and Riley, 1983; Tsai, 2022).The fluid forces exerted on a spherical particle include the Stokes drag force, the Basset history force, the added mass force, and the pressure gradient force.With a large particle-to-fluid density ratio, it is usually assumed that the drag force is the most dominant and other force terms can be neglected (Armenio and Fiorotto, 2001).At a finite particle Reynolds number,empirical correlation for the drag force is commonly leveraged, e.g. e.g. the Schiller-Naumann (S-N) drag correlation (Schiller and Naumann, 1933).The point-particle method requires that the particle size is generally much smaller than the smallest scale of turbulence, i.e. i.e., the Kolmogorov length scale.However, for a finite-size particle whose size is larger than the Kolmogorov length scale, the effect of small-scale turbulent motions around the particle may lead to an unreasonable prediction of the particle force with the point-particle method.
ai: The method known as the point-particle approach is a prevalent technique grounded in the Lagrangian framework, boasting a storied tradition in the simulation of flows laden with particles (refer to McLaughlin, 1994; Balachandar, 2009; Eaton, 2009; Soldati and Marchioli, 2009; Kuerten, 2016 for more on this). This approach represents particles as point-like entities possessing definite mass and momentum. For the specific scenario where particles move within the Stokes flow regime, characterized by exceedingly low particle Reynolds numbers, a precise theoretical framework exists to describe their motion (see Tsai, 1957; Gatignol, 1983; Maxey and Riley, 1983; Tsai, 2022). The forces exerted by the fluid on a spherical particle encompass several components: the Stokes drag force, the Basset history force, the added mass force, and the pressure gradient force. In scenarios where the ratio of particle to fluid density is significantly high, it is commonly assumed that the drag force overwhelmingly dominates, allowing other force components to be disregarded (as discussed by Armenio and Fiorotto, 2001). When dealing with finite particle Reynolds numbers, practitioners frequently turn to empirical correlations to estimate the drag force, such as the well-known Schiller-Naumann (S-N) drag correlation (Schiller and Naumann, 1933). A crucial requirement of the point-particle method is that the particle size must remain considerably smaller than the smallest turbulence scale, specifically the Kolmogorov length scale. However, if the particle is of finite size and larger than the Kolmogorov scale, the influence of small-scale turbulence surrounding the particle can lead to inaccurate force predictions when employing the point-particle method.

human: In the last three decades, particle-resolved or fully resolved direct numerical simulation has become a vital approach to resolving the flow around particles directly and accurately predicting particle-laden flows. Several different particle-resolved direct numerical simulation (PRDNS) approaches have been developed, such as the immersed boundary (IB) method (Mittal and Iaccarino, 2005; Uhlmann, 2005; Luo et al., 2007; Breugem, 2012; Kempe and Fröhlich, 2012; Zhou and Fan, 2014; Tao et al., 2018; Huang and Tian, 2019; Wang et al., 2019; Verzicco, 2023; Mittal and Seo, 2023), the distributed Lagrange multiplier (DLM)/fictitious domain approach Glowinski et al. (1999, 2001); Yu and Shao (2007, 2010), and others.PRDNS have been widely used to obtain high-fidelity simulation data, which is greatly helpful in studying particle transport in turbulent flows (Uhlmann, 2008; Shao et al., 2012; Kidanemariam et al., 2013; Picano et al., 2015; Luo et al., 2017; Vowinckel et al., 2019; Costa et al., 2020; Vowinckel et al., 2023; Peng et al., 2024), sediment transport (Ji et al., 2013, 2014; Kidanemariam and Uhlmann, 2014a, b; Vowinckel et al., 2016; Kidanemariam and Uhlmann, 2017; Mazzuoli et al., 2020; Scherer et al., 2022; Zhu et al., 2022; Schwarzmeier et al., 2023), turbulence modulation by particles (Pan and Banerjee, 1996; Vowinckel et al., 2014; Vreman, 2016; Peng et al., 2019, 2020; Costa et al., 2021; Yu et al., 2021; Oka and Goto, 2022; Peng et al., 2023; Balachandar et al., 2024), and developing particle force models (Hill et al., 2001; Van der Hoef et al., 2005; Cate and Sundaresan, 2006; Beetstra et al., 2007; Zeng et al., 2009; Tenneti et al., 2011; Homann et al., 2013; Tang et al., 2015; Zhou and Fan, 2015a, b; Akiki et al., 2017a, b; Balachandar et al., 2020; Seyed-Ahmadi and Wachs, 2020; Zhang et al., 2020; Tavanashad et al., 2021; Seyed-Ahmadi and Wachs, 2022; Xia et al., 2022; Cheng and Wachs, 2023a, b; Peng and Wang, 2023; van Wachem et al., 2024; Xia et al., 2024).

Notable among these are the immersed boundary IB technique as explored by researchers such as Mittal and Iaccarino 2005, Uhlmann 2005, and others extending to Verzicco 2023 and Mittal and Seo 2023. human: Despite its high accuracy, conducting large-scale simulations of particle-laden flows with PRDNS remains prohibitively costly. Therefore, it is necessary to develop reliable particle force models that can be integrated with cost-effective Reynolds-averaged Navier-Stokes (RANS) or large-eddy simulation (LES) techniques for turbulent flows. Various studies have been conducted on particle force models utilizing PRDNS data.However, a considerable proportion of these models focus on laminar flows rather than turbulent flows, which substantially limits their applicability in numerous practical situations. Studies have been conducted on the impact of turbulence on the mean particle drag force, while models for the instantaneous drag force are significantly deficient.In the following, we will review the current progress of the turbulence effects on the drag force of a finite-size particle and the prediction models.
ai: Although the level of accuracy achieved with PRDNS in simulating particle-laden flows is remarkably high, the financial and computational demands associated with conducting simulations on a large scale remain unfeasible. This challenges the need for the formulation of dependable particle force models that are compatible with the more economically feasible methodologies such as Reynolds-averaged Navier-Stokes RANS or large-eddy simulation LES for turbulent flows. A significant body of research has explored particle force models based on the expansive datasets derived from PRDNS. Nevertheless, a substantial number of these models have predominantly concentrated on laminar flows rather than turbulent ones, thus greatly restricting their relevance and usability in a wide range of practical scenarios. While there are studies focusing on the influence of turbulence on the average particle drag force, the development of models that accurately describe the instantaneous drag force remains notably inadequate. In the subsequent sections, we aim to delve into the advancements made regarding the effects of turbulence on the drag force experienced by finite-size particles and explore the predictive models developed in this context.

2503.06541.section: 1.1 Effects of turbulence on the drag force of a finite-size particle and models
human: Some studies investigated the influence of turbulence on particle drag.Bagchi and Balachandar (2003) investigated the influence of freestream isotropic turbulent flow on the drag and lift forces exerted on a spherical particle by PRDNS. Their findings indicated that freestream turbulence does not have a significant or systematic influence on the time-averaged mean drag, and the standard empirical drag formula, based on the instantaneous or mean relative velocity, may accurately predict the mean drag with reasonable accuracy. The prediction accuracy of instantaneous drag reduces as the particle size increases. For smaller particles, the standard drag law effectively captures low-frequency oscillations of particle drag; however, for larger particles, a notable discrepancy arises even in the low-frequency component.Burton and Eaton (2005) studied the interaction between a fixed particle and the decaying homogeneous isotropic turbulence by PRDNS. They found that the Lagrangian point-particle equation of motion underpredicts the particle root mean square (RMS) force, and the RMS force errors between the PRDNS results and those predicted by the Lagrangian particle equation of motion are between 15% and 30%.Zeng et al. (2008) conducted a PRDNS investigation on the force of a single fixed finite-size particle in turbulent channel flow, with the particle positioned at various wall-normal locations. It was found that when the particle is away from the viscous sublayer, the instantaneous drag is accurately captured by the standard drag law; in contrast, the particle drag is underestimated when the particle is in the buffer layer.Kim and Balachandar (2012) performed PRDNS of a particle in freestream turbulence. They stated that the standard drag law defined with uniform flow simulation can accurately predict particle drag when turbulent intensity is sufficiently low (below 5%), while flow non-uniformity substantially influences the forces acting on a finite-size particle as turbulent intensity increases, a factor often overlooked in the context of small particles. They suggested that both deterministic and stochastic components must be incorporated into the particle force model to accurately predict the motion of finite-size particles in turbulent flows.

human: Employing PRDNS to deal with practical particle-laden flows remains impossible due to the enormous computational cost.RANS or LES are more practical alternatives for computing fluid flows in actual applications.Nevertheless, throughout the averaging and filtering procedures in RANS and LES, subgrid-scale (SGS) flow information is filtered out and absent, necessitating modeling its effects on the particle.The existing particle SGS models can be classified into two groups, i.e. i.e. structural models and stochastic models (Marchioli, 2017; Pozorski, 2017).The structural models aim to reconstruct the entire SGS flow velocity field (Kuerten, 2006; Shotorban and Mashayek, 2006a; Marchioli et al., 2008a, b; Ray and Collins, 2014; Park et al., 2017; Zhou et al., 2018; Bassenne et al., 2019; Zhou et al., 2020; Hausmann et al., 2023a, b). The stochastic models try to retrieve some stochastic characteristics of the SGS flow field using stochastic methods (Wang and Squires, 1996; Fede and Simonin, 2006; Shotorban and Mashayek, 2006b; Berrouk et al., 2007; Pozorski and Apte, 2009; Jin et al., 2010; Cernick et al., 2015; Minier, 2015; Innocenti et al., 2016; Taniére and Arcen, 2016; Tenneti et al., 2016; Innocenti et al., 2019; Sabelnikov et al., 2019; Lattanzi et al., 2020; Knorps and Pozorski, 2021; Lo et al., 2022; Rousta et al., 2024).In this work, we focus on the stochastic method due to its capability in particle force modeling.
ai: Harnessing PRDNS for managing flows riddled with particles remains unfeasible because of the dauntingly high computational demands it incurs. When addressing fluid dynamics in real-world scenarios, approaches like RANS or LES represent more viable options. However, during the process of averaging in RANS and filtering in LES, critical subgrid-scale SGS information within the flow is inevitably discarded, requiring subsequent modeling to assess its impact on particles. Existing particle SGS models are categorized predominantly into two distinct types: structural models and stochastic models (Marchioli, 2017; Pozorski, 2017). Structural models work towards reconstructing the entire velocity field of the SGS flow (Kuerten, 2006; Shotorban and Mashayek, 2006a; Marchioli et al., 2008a, b; Ray and Collins, 2014; Park et al., 2017; Zhou et al., 2018; Bassenne et al., 2019; Zhou et al., 2020; Hausmann et al., 2023a, b). On the other hand, stochastic models focus on deducing certain stochastic attributes of the SGS flow field using probabilistic techniques (Wang and Squires, 1996; Fede and Simonin, 2006; Shotorban and Mashayek, 2006b; Berrouk et al., 2007; Pozorski and Apte, 2009; Jin et al., 2010; Cernick et al., 2015; Minier, 2015; Innocenti et al., 2016; Taniére and Arcen, 2016; Tenneti et al., 2016; Innocenti et al., 2019; Sabelnikov et al., 2019; Lattanzi et al., 2020; Knorps and Pozorski, 2021; Lo et al., 2022; Rousta et al., 2024). In the present study, we place emphasis on the stochastic method, recognizing its effectiveness and utility in the modeling of particle forces.

human: Two distinct stochastic modeling approaches have emerged to achieve this purpose. The first approach used the Lagrange stochastic technique to simulate the velocity of the unresolved flow experienced by particles, grounded in the point-particle framework and referred to as the flow Lagrangian stochastic model.This method utilizes statistical flow characteristics obtained from RANS or LES to generate instantaneous flow velocities encountered by particles via a stochastic model in the Lagrangian framework.The flow Lagrange stochastic methods can be classified into discontinuous random walk models (DRW) and continuous random walk models (CRW).The DRW model posits that when a particle traverses an eddy during a specific duration, the fluctuating velocity of the flow within that eddy remains constant. Upon moving to the subsequent eddy, a new fluctuating velocity is established, independent of the prior period (Gosman and Ioannides, 1983; Bocksell and Loth, 2001; Dehbi, 2008; Mofakham and Ahmadi, 2020).The CRW model connects the current velocity fluctuation of the flow field to that of the preceding time step through a Markov chain constructed from the Langevin equation (Wang and Stock, 1992; Bocksell and Loth, 2006), offering a continuous variation of the fluid velocity fluctuation and thus deemed more realistic than the DRW model.The CRW model has been widely used in simulating particle dispersion in turbulent flows (Bocksell and Loth, 2006; Dehbi, 2008, 2010; Mofakham and Ahmadi, 2019, 2020; Jaiswal et al., 2022; Li et al., 2023).
ai: Two unique approaches in stochastic modeling have emerged to address this purpose effectively. The initial approach involves employing the Lagrange stochastic technique, which is geared towards simulating the velocity of the flow that particles encounter, although this flow is not resolved. This is done within the point-particle framework, aptly termed the flow Lagrangian stochastic model. In essence, this method relies on the statistical characteristics of the flow derived from RANS or LES to produce instantaneous velocities that particles experience, integrating a stochastic model into the Lagrangian framework. The flow Lagrangian stochastic models can be categorized into two types: discontinuous random walk models DRW and continuous random walk models CRW.The DRW model operates under the premise that as a particle progresses through an eddy over a given time span, the fluctuating velocity within that eddy remains unchanged. However, once the particle transitions to a subsequent eddy, a new fluctuating velocity is introduced, which is entirely independent of the previous one (Gosman and Ioannides, 1983; Bocksell and Loth, 2001; Dehbi, 2008; Mofakham and Ahmadi, 2020). On the other hand, the CRW model draws a connection between the current velocity fluctuation of the flow and the previous time step’s fluctuation using a Markov chain, which is developed from the Langevin equation (Wang and Stock, 1992; Bocksell and Loth, 2006). This approach allows for a continuous variation in the fluid’s velocity fluctuation, providing a more realistic representation than the DRW model. Due to its realistic simulation capabilities, the CRW model has found widespread application in modeling particle dispersion within turbulent flows (Bocksell and Loth, 2006; Dehbi, 2008, 2010; Mofakham and Ahmadi, 2019, 2020; Jaiswal et al., 2022; Li et al., 2023).

ai: An alternative method for examining the effects of unresolved flow originates from the particle-scale perspective and involves incorporating stochastic models. At this level, these models address particle position, velocity, or acceleration through the Langevin equation, collectively known as the particle Lagrangian stochastic model. For instance, Garzó and colleagues 2012 devised a model focusing on particle acceleration by employing a Langevin model to represent particle velocity fluctuations, thereby accounting for the stochastic impact of neighboring particles in the Stokes flow regime. Later, Tenneti and associates 2016 refined the acceleration Langevin model initially introduced by Garzó et al. 2012 to encompass moderate particle Reynolds numbers using the PRDNS approach. Esteghamatian et al. 2018 proposed a stochastic approach for modeling particle drag, incorporating the ramifications of the filtered microstructure of turbulence via the PRDNS methodology. In 2020, Lattanzi and co-researchers offered a comprehensive depiction of stochastic techniques applicable in Eulerian-Lagrangian simulations. These techniques are used to address the oscillations in the drag force induced by neighboring particles, incorporating the Langevin equation to describe the particles’ position, velocity, and fluctuating drag force. By 2022, Lattanzi and his team advanced the development of a Langevin-based drag force model. This model interprets the neighbor-induced drag variability as a stochastic force within the Eulerian-Lagrangian structure. They completed the model with the integral timescale of the hydrodynamic force fluctuations and the drag’s standard deviation.

human: The studies mentioned above indicate that while there are some correlations for the mean particle drag considering the effects of turbulence, no model for instantaneous particle force is available for direct application to simulate the motion of finite-size particles in turbulence.To fill this gap, we perform PRDNS of a finite-size particle in turbulence across a wide range of turbulence and particle parameters and offer a stochastic model for the instantaneous particle drag and lateral force, accounting for the effects of turbulence.
ai: The aforementioned research suggests that although there are several connections regarding the average drag on particles when the influence of turbulence is taken into account, there is currently no existing model for directly applying instantaneous particle force to simulate the movement of finite-sized particles in a turbulent environment. To address this deficiency, we conduct PRDNS (Particle-Resolved Direct Numerical Simulations) on a finite-sized particle navigating through turbulence, testing it across a broad spectrum of turbulence and particle parameters. We introduce a stochastic model designed to represent the instantaneous drag and lateral forces experienced by particles, fully incorporating the impact of turbulence into its framework.

If traditional inlet and outlet boundary conditions are applied in the streamwise direction, the turbulent flow will decay along the streamwise direction, leading to a nonuniform turbulent flow field around the particle. To address this issue, we employ periodic boundary conditions in the streamwise direction. However, the limited extent of the computational domain will inevitably lead to a reduction in the upstream flow velocity experienced by the particle due to the particle wake.Figure illustrates that the mean streamwise flow velocity at the inlet is below U 0 (where U 0 is the desired mean inflow velocity), and the mean streamwise flow velocity all over the domain decreases over time if the influence of the particle wake is not adequately removed.

ai: In this segment, we introduce a stochastic framework to describe the instantaneous lateral force exerted by fluids, anchoring it on the Langevin equation akin to the fluctuating drag force. The lateral components of the fluid force, which are orthogonal to the prevalent slip velocity direction, are among the three forces impacting the particle. When the incoming flow is even at , the particle’s average lift is null due to the symmetrical nature of the wake formed behind the particle. However, once the flow reaches , an asymmetric particle wake arises, causing the mean lift to deviate from zero; specifically, the mean lift coefficient hovers around 0.06 at (Johnson and Patel, 1999; Kim et al., 2001; Ploumhans et al., 2002; Kim and Choi, 2002; Constantinescu and Squires, 2003; Niazmand and Renksizbulut, 2003; Wang and Zhang, 2011; Liska and Colonius, 2017). Additionally, under uniform inflow, it is observed that the average particle lift is roughly two orders of magnitude less than the average particle drag. In scenarios involving turbulent inflow at , the mean lateral force experienced by the particle is markedly lower than what is observed under uniform flow at an equivalent particle Reynolds number. This phenomenon may be attributed to the turbulence, which disrupts and statistically equalizes the asymmetry of particle wakes. Hence, we hypothesize that the average lateral force impacting the particle is approximately zero, choosing instead to concentrate on modeling the fluctuating segment of the particle’s lateral force.

human: This study conducts a series of direct numerical simulations to accurately compute the drag and lateral fluid forces on a fixed particle in homogeneous and isotropic turbulence superimposed with a uniform flow over a wide range of parameters: the particle Reynolds number is 0.1 ∼ 300, the scale ratio between the particle size and the Kolmogorov scale of turbulence is 0.22 ∼ 76.9, and the turbulence intensity ratio is 0.1 ∼ 20.The background turbulence is kept in a statistically steady state, and the particle wake effect is eliminated by a concurrent precursor technique.Stochastic models based on the Langevin equation for the drag and lateral fluid forces were proposed with the high-fidelity PRDNS data.The proposed models were validated in two problems: the motion of a finite-sized particle in turbulence and the dispersion of small inertial particles in a turbulent channel flow. The predictions of the proposed stochastic models exhibit remarkable consistency with the DNS results in both cases.The inputs of the current model consist of the distributions of the mean flow velocity, the mean kinetic energy of the turbulence, and the mean turbulent dissipation rate, which can be effectively provided by various RANS turbulence closures. Consequently, it can be utilized for numerous particle-laden flow problems while maintaining an acceptable computational cost.

Importantly, the ambient turbulence was consistently maintained in a statistically steady state, and the particle’s wake impact was nullified using a concurrent precursor approach. Two problems were used to validate these models: the movement of a finite-sized particle within turbulent conditions and the dispersion of small inertial particles in turbulent channel flow. Remarkably, the forecasts made by these stochastic models showed excellent agreement with the DNS outcomes in both scenarios. The current model utilizes inputs such as the distributions of mean flow velocity, mean kinetic energy of turbulence, and mean turbulent dissipation rate, which can be efficiently generated by various RANS turbulence closures. Hence, it proves valuable for a wide array of particle-laden flow challenges while keeping computational demands within practical limits.

human: Several issues need further discussion. First, the particle is fixed in our PRDNS, indicating that the particle has an infinite response time τ p . Therefore, the proposed force model can only be reliably applied for highly inertial particles with and ( ρ p and ρ f are the densities of particle and fluid, respectively). In other words, the model cannot be used for particles whose density is close to or smaller than that of the fluid, e.g. e.g. tracer particles. It is also outside the scope of some specific theories for idealized inertialess particles, such as the Tchen-Hinze theory (Hinze, 1975).Second, if we assume that there is a high particle-to-fluid density ratio, then the drag force is the most important, and other forces, such as the added mass and Basset history forces, can be neglected. To relieve the limits of the large density ratio assumption, one can simulate freely evolving particle suspensions in turbulent flows and develop new drag correlations (Tang et al., 2016; Tavanashad et al., 2019, 2021), which are left for future studies.Third, we only consider one-way coupling in the applications of the model, as the disperse phase is dilute. An extension to two-way coupling should be straightforward, and we will consider it in future works. The wake removal method is not responsible for the fluid-particle coupling, which should be essentially determined by the volume fraction or mass loading of the disperse phase.

Such simulations can aid in crafting novel drag correlations, as indicated in the works of Tang et al. 2016 and Tavanashad et al. (2019, 2021). Addressing this is deferred to forthcoming investigations.Lastly, our model, when applied, assumes one-way coupling due to the dilute nature of the disperse phase. human: In this work, we introduce a novel variant of the multivariate quadratic problem, which is at the core of one of the most promising post-quantum alternatives: multivariate cryptography. In this variant, the solution of a given multivariate quadratic system must also be regular, i.e. if it is split into multiple blocks of consecutive entries with the same fixed length, then each block has only one nonzero entry. We prove the NP-completeness of this variant and show similarities and differences with other computational problems used in cryptography. Then we analyze its hardness by reviewing the most common solvers for polynomial systems over finite fields, derive asymptotic formulas for the corresponding complexities and compare the different approaches.

We establish the NP-completeness of this variant, delineating both its similarities and distinctions compared to other computational challenges employed within cryptographic contexts. Following this, we delve into an analysis of its complexity by examining the most widely-used solvers for polynomial systems over finite fields. We further develop asymptotic expressions for the complexities associated with these systems and engage in a comparative assessment of the various methodological approaches.

human: The problem of solving a multivariate quadratic system over a finite field takes the name of Multivariate Quadratic (MQ) problem and is known to be NP-complete. It also seems to be hard on average for a wide range of parameters, but despite its evident difficulty, numerous algorithms have been developed to solve it.The MQ problem is fundamental in cryptography, especially in the post-quantum realm. It serves as the foundation for designing multivariate public key cryptosystems, which form one of the most promising quantum-resistant alternatives. In particular, it has emerged over the years as being remarkably well-suited to the construction of digital signatures. It is even more pervasive in algebraic cryptanalysis, which has a crucial impact on many different families of primitives. Indeed, algebraic attacks aim at solving a polynomial system that models a cryptographic problem.

human: We present here a new variant of the MQ problem. Concretely, if the solution is a vector of variables split into w blocks each of length l , then it must have exactly one nonzero entry for each block. The NP-completeness of the multivariate quadratic problem is preserved when adding the regular condition to the solution.

human: The same regular constraint was originally introduced in the context of code-based cryptography in [AFS05]. Indeed, [AFS05] proposed a family of cryptographic hash functions based on the provably secure regular syndrome decoding (RSD) problem. More recently, the same problem received new attention thanks to its introduction in secure computation to design MPC-protocols [HOSSV22], pseudorandom correlation generators [BCGI18] and digital signatures from MPC-in-the-head [CCJ23, BCC24] or VOLE-in-the-head [CLY24].These works suggest that also the RMQ problem could be used for similar constructions. On the other hand, there have been attempts at improving the cryptanalysis, either with combinatorial techniques [CCJ23, ES24] or with algebraic modelings [BØ23].In continuity with its code-based predecessor, the new variant has been named the Regular Multivariate Quadratic (RMQ) problem.

human: After introducing the computational problem and overviewing its main features, we mainly focus on the study of the asymptotic complexity of the average RMQ instance in the setting of the uniqueness bound. We analyzed the most important families of techniques for solving boolean systems and adapted them to take advantage of the regularity of the solution. On one side, we explore the algebraic algorithms related to Gröbner basis computation [CKPS00, BFSS13] by modeling the regular constraint as additional equations to be satisfied, reviewing different ways of hybridization and estimating the solving degree, in a similar fashion to what has been done for the code-based counterpart in [BØ23]. On the other hand, we investigate how the research line of probabilistic polynomial methods initiated with [LPT17] applies and can be optimized to our context. We also show how an RMQ instance can be transformed into a standard MQ one with fewer variables and analyze the complexity of solving the new system. Finally, we provide comparisons among all the approaches examined. Despite the improvements presented, we conclude that the problem remains difficult in practice in the average case for a large range of parameters and therefore it is potentially suitable for cryptographic purposes.

There is an interesting conjecture-often referred to as the Fröberg conjecture, introduced by Fröberg in 1985-which posits that a majority of polynomial systems exhibit this behavior. In more colloquial terms, when a random polynomial system is chosen, it is likely to appear regular, or in the context of this discussion, semi-regular, with minimal chance of deviation. Conversely, if a polynomial system has any form of predictable organization or patterned structure, the typical results relating to the Hilbert series might no longer apply. This is evident in the specific systems under scrutiny in this study, where the constraints imposed can be converted into quadratic monomial equations, characteristic of their non-random nature. To navigate this complexity, one can partition the system into two distinct segments, akin to the approach taken in a previous study by BØ23. The first segment is treated as generic, and the second is scrutinized separately to address the regularity constraints. Hence, we operate under an assumption designed to encapsulate the essence of semi-regularity in our particular setting, enabling us to extrapolate the Hilbert series pertinent to the resulting ideal.

human: The decision problem of determining whether a boolean multivariate polynomial systems has solutions over F 2 (respectively over its closure) is NP-complete (respectively NP-hard). This result has been proved in [FY79] by reducing the 3-SAT problem to it. The result can be easily adapted to polynomials of degree 2, i.e. the decision MQ problem is NP-complete as well.In the same work where it has been first introduced [AFS05], the regular syndrome decoding problem was also shown to be NP-complete. The polynomial-time reduction is an adaptation of the classic one from the Three Dimensional Matching problem [BMVT78].
ai: Determining whether a system of multivariate Boolean polynomials has a solution over the finite field F2, or over its algebraic closure, poses a significant computational challenge. The complexity of this problem classifies it as NP-complete when considering solutions over F2, and as NP-hard for its closure. This conclusion was first demonstrated in [FY79] through a technique known as reduction, specifically converting the well-known 3-Satisfiability (3-SAT) problem into this polynomial framework. Moreover, this conclusion is not limited to polynomials of higher degrees; it holds true even for polynomials of degree 2, thereby classifying the decision problem regarding quadratic polynomials, known as the MQ problem, as NP-complete as well.In another progressive advancement in combinatorial optimization, the Regular Syndrome Decoding problem also earned the NP-complete classification in the foundational work where it was initially articulated [AFS05]. This classification was achieved by employing a polynomial-time reduction strategy, adapting the classical reduction method from the renowned Three Dimensional Matching problem, as detailed in [BMVT78]. Such reductions serve as fundamental techniques that demonstrate the equivalency of complexities across different computational problems, solidifying their classifications in computational complexity theory.

Network-centric Compositional Testing methodology (NCT)NCT, a specialized approach within Model-Based Testing (MBT), is specifically designed for network protocols. It provides a structured method for creating formal specifications of Internet protocols and subsequently testing them [45]. The NCT principle is demonstrated in Figure using Ivy. The process begins with converting the RFC into an Ivy formal model a. Once the Ivy code is parsed, a generator is used to create concrete and randomized testers b. When a requirement fails, the resulting traces c can be analyzed to identify any potential errors or vulnerabilities.The NCT principle is based on compositional testing, which views formal specifications as a set of interconnected components/processes with their corresponding inputs and outputs. We present a framework for verifying Memoryful Neural Multi-Agent Systems (MN-MAS) against full Linear Temporal Logic (LTL) specifications. In MN-MAS, agents interact with a non-deterministic, partially observable environment. Examples of MN-MAS include multi-agent systems based on feed-forward and recurrent neural networks or state-space models. Different from previous approaches, we support the verification of both bounded and unbounded LTL specifications. We leverage well-established bounded model checking techniques, including lasso search and invariant synthesis, to reduce the verification problem to that of constraint solving. To solve these constraints, we develop efficient methods based on bound propagation, mixed-integer linear programming, and adaptive splitting. We evaluate the effectiveness of our algorithms in single and multi-agent environments from the Gymnasium and PettingZoo libraries, verifying unbounded specifications for the first time and improving the verification time for bounded specifications by an order of magnitude compared to the SoA.
ai: We introduce a comprehensive methodology for assessing Memoryful Neural Multi-Agent Systems (MN-MAS) in relation to comprehensive Linear Temporal Logic LTL criteria. In MN-MAS environments, agents engage with a world that is both non-deterministic and only partially observable. Systems of this nature can include, for instance, multi-agent frameworks built on architectures like feed-forward and recurrent neural networks, as well as those using state-space models. Contrasting with prior methodologies, our approach uniquely offers the capability to validate both bounded and unbounded LTL criteria. We exploit established bounded model checking strategies, such as lasso search and invariant synthesis, to distill the verification challenge into one that revolves around constraint solving. To tackle these constraints, we have innovated efficient techniques that incorporate bound propagation, mixed-integer linear programming, and adaptive splitting strategies. Our methods are rigorously tested in diverse single and multi-agent scenarios derived from the Gymnasium and PettingZoo libraries. Remarkably, this is the first occasion in which unbounded specifications have been verified, with a marked improvement in the verification speed for bounded specifications, outpacing the current state-of-the-art by a whole order of magnitude.

human: Deep generative models have recently been proposed for sampling protein conformations from the Boltzmann distribution, as an alternative to often prohibitively expensive Molecular Dynamics simulations.However, current state-of-the-art approaches rely on fine-tuning pre-trained folding models and evolutionary sequence information, limiting their applicability and efficiency, and introducing potential biases.In this work, we propose a flow matching model for sampling protein conformations based solely on backbone geometry.We introduce a geometric encoding of the backbone equilibrium structure as input and propose to condition not only the flow but also the prior distribution on the respective equilibrium structure, eliminating the need for evolutionary information.The resulting model is orders of magnitudes faster than current state-of-the-art approaches at comparable accuracy and can be trained from scratch in a few GPU days.In our experiments, we demonstrate that the proposed model achieves competitive performance with reduced inference time, across not only an established benchmark of naturally occurring proteins but also proteins, for which evolutionary information is scarce.
ai: In recent advancements, deep generative models have emerged as a promising technique for generating protein conformations aligned with the Boltzmann distribution. This offers a cost-effective alternative to the traditionally resource-intensive Molecular Dynamics simulations. Contemporary leading methods, however, frequently necessitate fine-tuning pre-existing folding models and integrating evolutionary sequence data. This reliance constrains their usability and efficiency, while simultaneously posing the risk of introducing biases. In our research, we put forward an innovative flow matching model to sample protein conformations, using only the geometry of the protein backbone. Our approach utilizes a geometric encoding of the equilibrium structure of the backbone as input, allowing us to condition not only the flow but also the initial prior distribution on this equilibrium configuration instead of depending on evolutionary data. This methodology dramatically accelerates the process, being exponentially faster compared to existing top-tier techniques while maintaining comparable levels of precision. Remarkably, the model can be trained from the ground up using just a few days of GPU processing.Through our experiments, we have shown that this model can deliver competitive performance with significantly decreased inference times. It excels not only on a well-established benchmark comprised of naturally occurring proteins but also on those proteins for which evolutionary data is limited or non-existent.

(2021) introduced AlphaFold 2, which predicts a protein’s structure using patterns found in naturally occurring protein sequences, so-called , upon inference.On the other hand, advancements in generative modeling such as diffusion (Song et al., 2020) and flow-matching (Lipman et al., 2023; Albergo & Vanden-Eijnden, 2022; Tong et al., 2024) have propelled the field of protein design, where several approaches for the generation of novel protein structures have been proposed (Watson et al., 2023; Yim et al., 2023b; Bose et al., 2024).Plausible protein structures conditioned on symmetry or a motif can be designed by these models, without requiring an input sequence (Ingraham et al., 2023; Yim et al., 2024).
ai: Over the past few years, there has been a transformative shift in the domain of protein structure prediction, largely driven by the emergence of geometric deep learning methods (Jumper et al., 2021; Dauparas et al., 2021; Lin et al., 2023). Jumper and colleagues 2021 introduced AlphaFold 2, a breakthrough that enables predicting the three-dimensional form of proteins by leveraging the recurring motifs found in naturally occurring protein sequences, specifically during the inference process. Additionally, cutting-edge advancements in generative modeling techniques such as diffusion models (Song et al., 2020) and flow-matching methodologies (Lipman et al., 2023; Albergo & Vanden-Eijnden, 2022; Tong et al., 2024) have significantly advanced the field of protein design. Here, several innovative strategies for creating new protein structures have been put forward (Watson et al., 2023; Yim et al., 2023b; Bose et al., 2024). These sophisticated models are capable of designing potential protein structures that conform to specific symmetries or motifs, and remarkably, this process does not necessitate a predetermined sequence as input (Ingraham et al., 2023; Yim et al., 2024).

In contrast, protein function depends on structural dynamics (Pacesa et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2024; Benkovic et al., 2008), that is, the protein’s conformational ensemble as given by the Boltzmann distribution, assuming equilibrium.To sample from the Boltzmann distribution, Molecular Dynamics (MD) simulations are an established method in the field (Adcock & McCammon, 2006).However, covering the state space extensively with MD requires long simulation times in order to satisfy ergodicity by overcoming local free energy minima, making conformational sampling often prohibitively expensive.Recently, generative models have been suggested for emulating the sampling of MD conformations, offering inference times that are orders of magnitudes faster than MD (Noé et al., 2019).
ai: The generation of a singular protein structure is achieved by both of these approaches. However, the functioning of proteins is intricately linked to their structural dynamics (Pacesa et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2024; Benkovic et al., 2008), which encompasses the protein’s array of conformations as delineated by the Boltzmann distribution under equilibrium conditions. To explore the Boltzmann distribution adequately, Molecular Dynamics MD simulations have become a cornerstone approach in this discipline (Adcock & McCammon, 2006). Nonetheless, for MD to achieve a comprehensive exploration of the state space, and thereby adhere to ergodicity through the surmounting of local free energy minima, it demands protracted simulation durations, rendering the process of conformational sampling frequently cost-prohibitive. In recent advancements, the deployment of generative models has been proposed for replicating the sampling of MD conformations, which dramatically reduces inference times compared to traditional MD methodologies (Noé et al., 2019).

human: For proteins, current state-of-the-art approaches for such generative models rely on modifications of AlphaFold 2, where noise is introduced into the MSA (Wayment-Steele et al., 2024), the pre-trained folding model is fine-tuned on ensemble data (Jing et al., 2024), or the structure block is replaced by a diffusion model (Lewis et al., 2024).While these approaches are capable of generating realistic conformational ensembles with high distributional accuracy, their efficiency is limited since the sampling of each state requires to predict the overall fold of the protein from the sequence.Consequently, the models rely on processing of evolutionary information such as MSA or weights from protein language models like ESM (Lin et al., 2022). This renders the models not only expensive, but can in addition introduce artifacts for sequences where evolutionary information is scarce or, as for proteins, absent (Lin et al., 2023).
ai: In the realm of protein research, the latest advancements in generative modeling hinge on innovative adaptations of AlphaFold 2. One such method involves incorporating noise into the multiple sequence alignments MSA, as outlined by Wayment-Steele et al. in their 2024 study. Another approach refines the pre-trained folding model by calibrating it using ensemble data, a technique demonstrated by Jing et al. in the same year. Additionally, there is a strategy of replacing the structural component with a diffusion model, as suggested by Lewis et al. 2024. Although these methodologies are adept at generating conformational ensembles that exhibit a high degree of distributional precision, their overall efficiency suffers. This is primarily due to the necessity of predicting the complete protein fold from its original sequence for each state sampled.As a result, these models must process evolutionary data such as MSA or employ weights derived from protein language models like ESM (according to Lin et al., 2022). While this approach can be effective, it leads to models that are not just costly to operate but also prone to generating artifacts. This issue becomes particularly acute when dealing with sequences for which evolutionary data is inadequate or, as in some proteins, entirely absent, as further discussed by Lin et al. in 2023.

human: In this work, we introduce BBFlow, a generative model for protein conformational ensembles based on backbone geometry that is an order of magnitude faster than the current state-of-the-art model AlphaFlow (Jing et al., 2024), at similar accuracy.BBFlow relies on two key innovations. We formulate conformational ensemble prediction as protein structure generation task, conditioned on a distance encoding of the equilibrium structure and propose a conditional prior distribution for flow matching based on geodesic interpolation (Figure ).Notably, our work shows that neither pre-trained weights from a folding model nor evolutionary sequence information is required to generate highly accurate conformational ensembles.Instead, we find that ensembles can even be generated purely geometry-based, without any sequence information.
ai: In this study, we present BBFlow, a novel generative model designed to produce protein conformational ensembles by leveraging backbone geometry. BBFlow distinguishes itself by being significantly faster-by an entire order of magnitude-than the existing leading-edge model, AlphaFlow (developed by Jing et al. in 2024), while maintaining a similar level of accuracy. This innovation is built upon two foundational advancements. First, we frame the task of predicting conformational ensembles as a problem of protein structure generation, which is conditioned on a distance-based encoding of the protein’s equilibrium form. Second, we introduce a conditional prior distribution for flow matching, utilizing geodesic interpolation as a method (illustrated in Figure ). Importantly, our research demonstrates that generating highly accurate conformational ensembles does not require pre-existing model weights from protein folding models or evolutionary sequence data. We discovered that it is feasible to generate these ensembles solely based on geometric data, omitting the necessity for any sequence information entirely.

human: For benchmarking BBFlow, we train and test the model on the ATLAS dataset (Vander Meersche et al., 2024), which contains Molecular Dynamics trajectories of 1390 proteins - the same dataset used for training AlphaFlow.We also test BBFlow on MD trajectories of proteins, where we find similar performance as for naturally occurring proteins while AlphaFlow fails if the equilibrium structure is not provided as template.
ai: To evaluate the performance of BBFlow, we conducted training and testing on the ATLAS dataset, as detailed in the work by Vander Meersche et al. from 2024. This dataset encompasses Molecular Dynamics MD trajectories of 1390 distinct proteins and was also utilized in the development phase of AlphaFlow. In addition, we carried out tests on MD trajectories from proteins, observing that BBFlow achieved performance levels comparable to those seen with naturally occurring proteins. In scenarios where the equilibrium structure was not supplied as a template, AlphaFlow did not perform effectively.

human: Previous deep learning approaches for sampling conformational ensembles such as (Noé et al., 2019), where invertible neural networks are employed, or equivariant flow matching (Klein et al., 2023) usually require training on the specific system of interest.For proteins, a transferable model, AlphaFlow, which relies on fine-tuning the pre-trained folding model AlphaFold 2 (Jumper et al., 2021), has been recently proposed (Jing et al., 2024).While Jing et al. (2024) also introduce a model trained on ensembles deposited in the Protein Data Bank (PDB), the scope of this work is to generate Boltzmann-sampled states and we thus focus on the AlphaFlow models trained on MD.Wang et al. (2024) propose ConfDiff, a diffusion model that relies on a pre-trained sequence representation of AlphaFold 2 and is trained on both the PDB and MD conformations.(Lewis et al., 2024) propose the generative model Bio-Emu with an architecture similar to AlphaFold 2 with the difference that a diffusion module is used for protein structure generation.Bio-Emu is trained on a large custom MD dataset, making it not directly comparable to AlphaFlow and BBFlow.Conformational ensemble prediction was also suggested as transfer application of the recent structure design model FoldFlow++ (Huguet et al., 2024).However, FoldFlow++ underperforms AlphaFlow, which is to be expected since it is not trained on MD data, and is thus not considered in this work.
ai: In recent endeavors involving deep learning methodologies for sampling conformational ensembles, techniques such as those developed by Noé et al. in 2019, which utilize invertible neural networks, or the more recent equivariant flow matching approach by Klein et al. in 2023, typically necessitate specific training tailored to the systems they examine. Within the realm of protein studies, there’s a novel, adaptable model termed AlphaFlow. This model hinges on fine-tuning the extensively-trained folding model known as AlphaFold 2, introduced by Jumper et al. in 2021, and was recently proposed by Jing et al. in 2024. Additionally, Jing et al. 2024 explore a structure shaped by ensembles cataloged in the Protein Data Bank PDB. However, their primary objective pivots on simulating Boltzmann-sampled states; thus, the emphasis is placed on AlphaFlow models specifically trained using molecular dynamics MD data. In a related advancement, Wang et al. 2024 introduce ConfDiff, a diffusion model that is built upon a pre-trained sequence representation from AlphaFold 2 and is educated on a blend of PDB and MD conformations. A different approach by Lewis et al. 2024 presents the generative model Bio-Emu, mirroring the architecture of AlphaFold 2 but incorporating a diffusion module for the creation of protein structures. This Bio-Emu is trained using an extensive, bespoke molecular dynamics dataset, which means it isn’t directly comparable with both AlphaFlow and BBFlow. Predicting conformational ensembles was further explored by proposing it as a transferable application for the new structure design model FoldFlow++ introduced by Huguet et al. in 2024. Nevertheless, FoldFlow++ lags behind AlphaFlow’s performance, likely due to its lack of training on MD data, and is thus excluded from further consideration in the present analysis.

(2023) have proposed flow matching as generalization of diffusion models (Song et al., 2020).A learned flow is used to transform samples from a simple prior distribution p 0 to samples from the target distribution p 1 .The key idea is to learn a time-dependent flow vector field where is the tangent space at point x .The flow is then defined by v t via integration of the flow ODE, The vector field v t can be learned by sampling and , connecting them by a particle-wise flow and regressing on the time derivative of ψ (Lipman et al., 2023).On Riemannian manifolds, ψ is usually chosen as geodesic (Chen & Lipman, 2024).
ai: To draw samples from a specific target distribution within the data domain M, Lipman et al. 2023 introduced the technique of flow matching, which builds upon the foundational work of diffusion models originally described by Song et al. 2020. In this approach, a learned flow mechanism is employed to convert samples originating from a basic prior distribution, denoted as p0, into samples that align with the intended target distribution, referred to as p1. The central concept revolves around the development of a time-dependent flow vector field within the tangent space at any given point x. This flow is then articulated through the vector field vt, which is determined by integrating the flow ordinary differential equation ODE. The process of learning the vector field vt involves sampling initial and target distributions, linking them through a particle-wise flow, and then undertaking regression on the time derivative of the function ψ, as elaborated by Lipman et al. in 2023. When operating within the context of Riemannian manifolds, the function ψ is often selected as the geodesic, following the insights provided by Chen & Lipman in 2024.

ai: A protein’s backbone can be depicted as a sequence of Euclidean frames, as described by Jumper and colleagues in 2021. Each frame is characterized by a rotation and a translation. Consequently, a flow matching process pertinent to protein structures can be articulated on a Riemannian manifold. According to the choice of metric, as detailed by Yim and co-authors in 2023a, the geodesic trajectories for each residue may be decomposed into separate components for rotation and translation. It is customary to parameterize both the observed and anticipated vector fields using a current protein structure, denoted as x t, and an ultimate structure, denoted as x 1. As illustrated in studies by Yim et al., 2023a, alongside Bose et al., 2024, the constituents of the vector field are determined accordingly. A prevalent assumption for the prior distribution p 0 is to employ independent Gaussian distributions for translations and uniform distributions for rotations, as identified in Yim and colleagues’ 2023a work.

human: In order to determine the structure of a protein, the challenging task of mapping from a one-dimensional sequence representation to a three-dimensional backbone geometry has to be solved.Jumper et al. (2021) propose the Evoformer architecture, which predicts a two-dimensional representation for encoding pairwise relationships of sequence elements such as spatial contact.To achieve this, the Evoformer relies on Multiple Sequence Alignment (MSA) - an algorithm that aligns the input sequence with related, naturally occurring protein sequences from a database during inference and training.Since patterns in naturally occurring sequences are often due to proteins from different organisms being related via specific mutations over the course of evolution, such relationships are referred to as .Evolutionary information can encode properties of the structure a sequence is folded into.For example, co-evolving pairs of residues indicate proximity of the respective residues in three-dimensional space (Morcos et al., 2011).While the calculation of an MSA during inference is computationally expensive, a more efficient strategy is to encode evolutionary information by extracting weights from a protein language model (Lin et al., 2023; Rives et al., 2021).
ai: To uncover the architecture of a protein, a complex challenge must be addressed: converting a sequence from its one-dimensional form to a three-dimensional spatial structure. In a study by Jumper and colleagues 2021, they introduce the Evoformer architecture, a novel approach that predicts a two-dimensional framework for capturing pairwise relationships within sequence components, such as spatial contacts. This innovative method leverages Multiple Sequence Alignment MSA, an algorithm used to align an input sequence with related protein sequences found in nature during both the training and inference phases. Due to the fact that the variations seen in naturally occurring sequences often arise from proteins across various organisms being linked through specific evolutionary mutations, such relationships are described in terms of evolution. Evolutionary data can offer clues about the properties of the folded structure of a sequence. For instance, pairs of residues that co-evolve tend to indicate closeness in their spatial arrangement (Morcos et al., 2011). Although determining an MSA during inference involves significant computational resources, a more effective approach involves encoding evolutionary data by deriving weights from a protein language model as illustrated by Lin et al. 2023 and Rives et al. 2021.

human: For training the structure prediction model AlphaFold 2, Jumper et al. (2021) introduce a distance measure d for all-atom protein structures x and x ′ , the Frame Aligned Prediction Error (FAPE).For calculating FAPE for a protein of size N , the structure x is rotated and translated N times, such that each residue is aligned to the respective target residue exactly once.FAPE is then defined as the mean of the N Root Mean Square Deviations (RMSD) of the structure x to the target structure x ′ .
ai: In their work on training the AlphaFold 2 structure prediction model, Jumper and colleagues 2021 presented a method for quantifying distance between complete atomic protein structures, designated as x and x′. This metric, known as the Frame Aligned Prediction Error FAPE, plays a crucial role. To compute the FAPE for a protein comprising N residues, the structure x undergoes a series of N distinct rotations and translations. This process ensures that each residue perfectly aligns with its corresponding target residue just once throughout the procedure. Consequently, FAPE is characterized as the mean value derived from the N calculated Root Mean Square Deviations RMSDs, which measure deviations of the structure x from the target configuration x′.

human: The folding model AlphaFold 2 (Jumper et al., 2021) predicts the structure of a protein from its sequence using evolutionary sequence information in the form of an MSA and a loss that relies on FAPE.While its prediction is deterministic, (Jing et al., 2024) have shown that AlphaFold 2 can be fine-tuned as a flow matching model for conformational ensemble generation by training it to predict structures sampled in Molecular Dynamics (MD) simulation.(Jing et al., 2024) propose to use a harmonic prior, which samples chain-like noisy states, and show that the flow matching vector field can be approximated by applying the squared FAPE loss of AlphaFold 2 to the predicted and target structures.The resulting model, AlphaFlow, achieves outstanding performance at capturing ensemble properties like flexibility and principal components obtained from MD simulation.While AlphaFlow is orders of magnitude faster than MD for sampling a set of representative conformations, its efficiency is limited since it relies on the expensive MSA and the large, pre-trained folding model AlphaFold 2.
ai: AlphaFold 2, a protein folding model introduced by Jumper et al. in 2021, is designed to predict a protein’s structure based on its sequence. It utilizes evolutionary sequence data encapsulated in a multiple sequence alignment MSA along with a loss function known as FAPE. Although the predictions made by AlphaFold 2 are deterministic, Jing et al. in 2024 demonstrated that this model can be adapted into a flow matching model aimed at generating conformational ensembles. This is achieved by training AlphaFold 2 to anticipate structures sampled during Molecular Dynamics MD simulations. The approach proposed by Jing et al. utilizes a harmonic prior, which samples chain-like noisy states, subsequently showing that the flow matching vector field can be approximated by applying AlphaFold 2’s squared FAPE loss to both predicted and target structures. This novel model, named AlphaFlow, excels remarkably in capturing ensemble characteristics such as flexibility and principal components derived from MD simulations. While AlphaFlow significantly outpaces MD in generating a set of representative conformations by being orders of magnitude faster, its efficiency is somewhat restricted due to its dependence on the resource-intensive MSA and the massive, pre-trained AlphaFold 2 model for folding.

human: In this work, we propose to decouple protein conformational ensemble generation from the structure prediction task and introduce a generative model based purely on backbone geometry that does not rely on evolutionary sequence information.We achieve this by conditioning both the flow and the prior on the equilibrium structure of the protein.
ai: In this study, we advance a novel approach that separates the generation of protein conformational ensembles from the task of predicting structures. We present a generative model that focuses solely on backbone geometry, deliberately setting aside any dependence on evolutionary sequence data. Our methodology is characterized by conditioning both the flow model and the prior distribution upon the protein’s stable, or equilibrium, structural configuration.

2503.05738.section: Conditional flow matching for ensemble generation
human: Inspired by FrameFlow (Yim et al., 2023a), a flow matching model for protein structure design, we formulate the task of protein ensemble generation as structure generation task, conditioned on the equilibrium state of the respective protein.In particular, we express the Boltzmann distribution of a given protein as probability distribution of conformations x , conditioned on the equilibrium state x eq of the respective protein.In order to sample from , we learn a flow vector field, that receives protein equilibrium states as additional input.This defines a conditional flow φ t by
ai: Drawing inspiration from FrameFlow (Yim et al., 2023a), a flow-based model for crafting protein structures, we have conceptualized the task of generating protein ensembles as one centered on the generation of structural configurations, contingent upon the protein’s equilibrium state. Specifically, we capture the essence of the Boltzmann distribution related to a particular protein as a probability distribution of various conformations denoted as x, with a condition based on the equilibrium conformation x eq of the given protein. To facilitate sampling from this distribution, we train a flow vector field that incorporates protein equilibrium states as an additional input parameter. This approach effectively delineates a conditional flow phi t through its structure.

human: Crucially, by conditioning the generation not on the sequence but the equilibrium structure, we eliminate the need for evolutionary information and pre-trained folding model weights.We note that assuming the availability of an equilibrium structure is a fair assumption because the main use-case of the model is to offer an alternative to Moleculer Dynamics simulation, which also requires an initial structure.If only a sequence is available, both MD and BBFlow require a structure prediction first, for example with AlphaFold 2.
ai: Importantly, by basing the generation process on the equilibrium structure rather than on the sequence, we remove the necessity for evolutionary data and pre-existing folding model weights. It’s significant to point out that presuming the availability of an equilibrium structure is reasonable. This is because the model’s primary function is to provide an alternative to Molecular Dynamics MD simulation, which similarly demands an initial structure. In situations where only a sequence is present, both Molecular Dynamics and BBFlow necessitate a preliminary structure prediction, such as that provided by AlphaFold 2.

human: In order to learn the conditional flow vector field v t , we use the same model architecture as the recent protein design model GAFL (Wagner et al., 2024), which is an extension of the FrameDiff architecture proposed by Yim et al. (2023b).The input features includethe frames x t at time t , their pairwise spatial distances, positional encodings of absolute and relative sequence positions, and the flow matching time t .The neural network is an equivariant graph neural network, which uses invariant point attention (IPA) (Jumper et al., 2021) as core element.In GAFL, IPA is extended to Clifford frame attention (CFA), where geometric features are represented in the projective geometric algebra and messages are constructed using the bilinear products of the algebra.Frames are consecutively updated along with node and edge features in a series of 6 message passing blocks to predict the target frames x 1 .Compared to Alphafold 2 (Jumper et al., 2021), this architecture is much more shallow and operates only on structural data, hence a sequence-processing module like the Evoformer of AlphaFold 2 is not required.
ai: To master the conditional flow vector field v t, we leverage the same model architecture employed in the recent development of the protein design model known as GAFL (Wagner et al., 2024). This model acts as an enhancement of the FrameDiff architecture introduced by Yim et al. 2023b. The input features encompass frames x t at a given time t, alongside their pairwise spatial distances, the positional encodings that reveal both absolute and relative sequence positions, and the flow matching time t. The neural network deployed is an equivariant graph neural network with invariant point attention IPA employed as a vital element (Jumper et al., 2021). Within GAFL, IPA is augmented to Clifford frame attention CFA, wherein geometric characteristics are encapsulated within projective geometric algebra, and messages are formulated through the bilinear operations of this algebra. Frames undergo successive updates, alongside node and edge features, within a sequence of six message passing blocks aimed at predicting the target frames x 1. This architectural design exhibits a more shallow structure in comparison to AlphaFold 2 (Jumper et al., 2021) as it exclusively engages with structural data. Consequently, the presence of a sequence-processing module akin to the Evoformer within AlphaFold 2 becomes redundant, eliminating the need for such a component in this particular configuration.
