ai: To condition the flow vector field in accordance with Equation , we have adjusted the architecture so that the equilibrium backbone structure of the protein functions as an input feature. Drawing motivation from the concept that views evolutionary data as a contact map (Lin et al., 2023), we’ve opted to encode the pairwise distances of the equilibrium state x eq as the initial edge feature. In this encoding, the distances, ranging from 0 to 20Å, are binned with a dimension of 22 (Yim et al., 2023a). Furthermore, we put forward a method to encode the equilibrium structure in a manner that is rich in geometric significance. Influenced by tensor-based equivariant networks (Schütt et al., 2021) and their representation through local frames (Lippmann et al., 2025), we incorporate equivariant pairwise directions represented as unit vectors, translated into the coordinate frame specific to residue i. By transforming these into a co-rotating coordinate system, the feature components achieve invariance, allowing them to be utilized alongside s as the initial edge feature. Although these directional features e do not contribute to the final model, their impact is scrutinized in our ablation studies.

human: We use amino acid identities as additional node features, by transforming a one-hot encoding via a linear layer to a 128-dimensional embedding.The reasoning behind encoding the amino acid type is that it carries information about the local effective degrees of freedom of the backbone,however, in an ablation we find that also without encoding the amino acid identity, the model performs remarkably well.
ai: Incorporating amino acid identities as supplementary features for nodes involves converting a one-hot encoded representation through a linear transformation into an embedding of 128 dimensions. The rationale for encoding the type of amino acid lies in the valuable information it provides about the local effective degrees of freedom characteristic of the backbone structure. Interestingly, even when we conducted an ablation study that excluded the encoding of amino acid identities, we discovered that the model maintained impressive performance, which was a noteworthy observation.

human: Unlike diffusion models (Song et al., 2020), where Gaussianity of the prior p 0 is a strict theoretical requirement, flow matching, in principle, allows the use of general prior distributions (Lipman et al., 2023).Non-Gaussian, unconditional prior distributions for proteins have been proposed by Ingraham et al. (2023) and Jing et al. (2024).We take this idea a step further and propose a prior distribution for flow matching.Samples are generated by interpolating between samples from an unconditional prior p uncond and the equilibrium structure x eq , where γ is the geodesic between x uncond and x eq , and is a hyperparameter between 0 and 1 that quantifies how close the noise sampled from the prior is to the equilibrium structure (see Figure ).In our experiments, we set .For the unconditional prior distribution p uncond , we use the prior from FrameFlow (Yim et al., 2023a) - the normal distribution for translations and the uniform distribution for rotations.
ai: In contrast to diffusion models such as those discussed by Song et al. in 2020, which necessitate a Gaussian prior, designated as p0, due to strict theoretical conditions, flow matching theoretically supports the employment of more general prior distributions, as noted by Lipman et al. in 2023. This adaptability enables the use of non-Gaussian, unconditional priors in the context of proteins, a concept explored by Ingraham et al. in 2023 and further developed by Jing et al. in 2024. Building on these foundational ideas, we introduce an innovative approach for a prior distribution tailored to flow matching. This is executed by generating samples that interpolate between an unconditional prior, denoted as p uncond, and a structure at equilibrium, referred to as x eq. The interpolation is controlled through γ, which represents the geodesic connecting x uncond and x eq, serving as a hyperparameter fluctuating from 0 to 1. This parameter essentially calibrates the degree to which the noise from the prior resembles the equilibrium structure. This process is illustrated in a corresponding figure. In our experimental setup, we utilized a specified value. As for the unconditional prior distribution, p uncond, we selected the FrameFlow prior, initially proposed by Yim et al. in 2023a, which utilizes a normal distribution for modeling translations and a uniform distribution for managing rotations.

Our approach involves formulating the flow matching process within the manifold of the given data. To achieve this, we develop a conditional flow vector field-articulated by Equation-within the tangent space of our data domain. The parameters are specified by Equation. When conducting regression on this vector field, we compute the ground truth, denoted as v, as a tangent vector along the geodesic path γ FM. (2024) select 1265 for training, 39 for validation and 82 for testing.We train the model, and variants where we leave out key features for an ablation study, for 3 days on two NVIDIA A100-40GB GPUs from scratch, i.e. without initial weights from a pre-trained folding model.For all experiments, we use the same hyperparameters as in FrameFlow (Yim et al., 2023a) and GAFL (Wagner et al., 2024), except for the number of timesteps, which we set to 20.Also the respective feature dimensions are increased by 128 for embedding the amino acid identity as node feature and by 22 or 25, respectively, for embedding the equilibrium structure encoding with or without direction as edge feature.
ai: To carry out a direct comparison between the newly proposed model and the latest leading-edge conformational ensemble generator used for proteins, AlphaFlow (Jing et al., 2024), we undertook the training of BBFlow using the ATLAS dataset (Vander Meersche et al., 2024). This dataset is partitioned into sets for training, validation, and testing, aligning exactly with the way it was handled in previous studies. The ATLAS dataset is comprised of triple trajectories, each extending to 100 nanoseconds of all-atom Molecular Dynamics MD simulations for a total of 1,390 proteins, diverse in terms of their structures. Jing et al. 2024 specifically chose 1,265 proteins for training purposes, 39 for validation, and another 82 for the testing phase. We undertook the training of the model, as well as several variant models wherein certain pivotal features were systematically excluded to conduct an ablation study. This process lasted for three days and utilized two NVIDIA A100-40GB GPUs, commencing with no prior weights from any pre-trained folding model. This means we began training entirely from a fresh start. Furthermore, the dimensions of the respective features were each expanded by 128 to incorporate the amino acid identity as a node feature, while the embedding of the equilibrium structure was adjusted with an additional 22 or 25 for edge features, contingent on whether the direction was encoded or not.

(2024), which quantify how well statistical properties of the generated ensembles - listed below - agree with those obtained by MD.In all experiments, we generate 250 conformations per protein, as in AlphaFlow, and bootstrap the set of MD conformations 100 times in order to estimate the error caused by sampling finitely many states.All metrics are calculated using the C α atoms of the protein structures.
ai: To assess the efficacy of the models being compared, we use a series of critical metrics as outlined by Jing and colleagues in 2024. These metrics are designed to measure the extent to which the statistical characteristics of the generated ensemble conform to those derived from molecular dynamics MD simulations. Consistently across all experiments, we produce 250 conformations for each protein, akin to the approach adopted in AlphaFlow. To gauge the variability introduced by the finite sampling of states, we perform bootstrapping on the MD conformation set 100 times. Every metric is computed utilizing the C α atoms present in the protein structures.

human: The Root Mean Square Fluctuation (RMSF) of C α atoms measures the magnitude of positional deviations of individual residues across the set of conformations.For a given residue, these fluctuations are calculated in a reference frame that is defined by aligning the entire protein to the equilibrium structure and thus implicitly depend on the positions of all other residues.Consequently, RMSF can be interpreted as measure for flexibility, but also encodes global collective behaviour.As in AlphaFlow, we calculate the Pearson correlation between RMSF profiles (for an example see Figure ) obtained from MD and generated ensembles in order to quantify how well the shapes of the profiles match. We also include the Mean Absolute Error (MAE) of per-residue RMSF to measure how well RMSF amplitudes are reproduced, and compare the median over all residues with the ground truth in order to quantify systematic overor understabilization.
ai: The Root Mean Square Fluctuation RMSF of Cα atoms serves as a metric for assessing the extent of positional shifts experienced by individual residues across a collection of conformations. The RMSF calculation for each residue is performed within a reference framework established by aligning the entire protein to its equilibrium structure, meaning the deviations are implicitly connected to the spatial arrangement of all other residues. Therefore, RMSF not only provides insights into the flexibility of residues but also encapsulates overarching collective dynamics of the protein. In alignment with the methodology used in AlphaFlow, we determine the Pearson correlation between RMSF profiles derived from molecular dynamics MD simulations and model-generated ensembles to evaluate the degree to which the profile geometries correspond. Moreover, we look at the Mean Absolute Error MAE of per-residue RMSF values to evaluate the accuracy of RMSF amplitude reproduction, and we compare the median RMSF values across residues to the true reference data to measure the degree of systematic over-stabilization or under-stabilization.

human: For each protein, we calculate the average C α RMSD between any two conformations x as This quantifies the magnitude of conformational changes without requiring a specified reference state.We report the MAE of pairwise RMSD across all proteins and the median pairwise RMSD, the latter of which also quantifies systematic overor understabilization.
ai: To determine the extent of conformational transformation for each protein, we compute the average root-mean-square deviation RMSD of the α carbon (Cα) between every possible pair of conformations labeled as x. This measurement provides a sense of the extent of structural variability inherent in each protein, independent of any predetermined reference state. Additionally, we present the mean absolute error MAE of the pairwise RMSD values across all proteins analyzed, alongside the median value of these pairwise RMSD computations. The median RMSD gives additional insight by highlighting any underlying trends of systematic over-stabilization or under-stabilization within the dataset.

human: A metric that explicitly accounts for conformational changes, and quantifies how well the respective conformations are captured, relies on the Principal Component Analysis of the C α positions across the sampled conformations.We project the generated states on the first two principal components obtained from MD, thus receiving a two-dimensional PCA-projection of each conformation (for examples see Figure ).We report the Wasserstein-2-distance between the distributions of PCA-projections.

By projecting the generated states onto the first two principal components derived from Molecular Dynamics, we acquire a two-dimensional PCA representation of each conformation (refer to examples in Figure ). We then present the Wasserstein-2 distance between the distributions of these PCA-projections.

human: Inference time is, even if orders of magnitude smaller than MD, a critical factor for applications of conformational ensemble generators such as large-scale annotation of datasets or screening of proteins for a target motion.As in (Huguet et al., 2024), we evaluate the inference time per generated conformation of the 302-residue protein 7c45A using an NVIDIA A100-40GB GPU.
ai: While inference time may significantly surpass molecular dynamics in terms of speed by several orders of magnitude, it remains a crucial element when applying conformational ensemble generators, especially for tasks like annotating extensive datasets or assessing proteins for specific target motions. Following the methodology outlined by Huguet et al. 2024, we assess the inference time required for generating conformations of the 302-residue protein 7c45A. This evaluation is performed utilizing the NVIDIA A100-40GB GPU.

(2024), BBFlow is competitive (Table ).Additionally, we investigate the performance of BBFlow, AlphaFlow-T and AlphaFlow-T 12L,dist for different protein lengths (Figure , Figure ) and find that the trends described above hold true for all lengths considered, while the over-stabilization of AlphaFlow-T is particularly prominent for large proteins.

Evidence of this includes small median RMSF and pairwise RMSD values suggesting that AlphaFlow-T and AlphaFlow-T 12L,dist tend to systematically over-stabilize proteins. human: We hypothesize that BBFlow’s greatly reduced inference time for generating high-quality conformational ensembles makes the method interesting for application in protein design pipelines.Efficient generation of conformational ensembles would allow to screen for dynamical properties.However, since proteins often have scarce evolutionary information available, the applicability of models that rely on said evolutionary information is unclear.

By swiftly generating conformational ensembles, it’s possible to evaluate dynamical properties effectively. human: The results show that BBFlow achieves a favorable trade-off between speed and quality of the generated ensembles.At comparable accuracy, it is more than an order of magnitude faster than the current state-of-the-art model AlphaFlow-T and also faster than the distilled model AlphaFlow-T 12L,dist .Crucially, BBFlow does not suffer from the over-stabilization observed in AlphaFlow-T and AlphaFlow-T 12L,dist , which seems to be caused by using templates with AlphaFlow models, impeding the exploration of conformational space.

Importantly, BBFlow circumvents the issue of over-stabilization that plagues AlphaFlow-T and its distilled counterpart, AlphaFlow-T 12L,dist. This over-stabilization appears to stem from the reliance on templates with the AlphaFlow models, which hampers the ability to explore the conformational space effectively.

human: The generation of high-quality conformational ensembles of proteins is a key task in many protein-related fields.Inspired by generative models for protein design, we propose BBFlow, a method for sampling high-quality ensembles with state-of-the-art efficiency while, at the same time, also avoiding problems with proteins and over-stabilization observed in current state-of-the-art models.We achieve this by introducing a conditional prior distribution and encoding the protein’s equilibrium backbone structure as condition in a flow-matching model that is based on backbone geometry, decoupling the structure prediction task from conformational sampling.This eliminates the need for evolutionary information and enables to train the model from scratch, without requiring pre-trained weights from a folding model that is trained on a much larger dataset.We expect that both of these ideas - using a conditional prior in flow-matching and replacing evolutionary information by structure-conditioning - can also be applied to other problems in generative modeling and structural biology.
ai: Creating accurate ensembles of protein conformations is a crucial task across various domains involving proteins. Drawing inspiration from generative models used in protein design, we introduce BBFlow. This innovative approach allows us to sample high-quality ensembles with cutting-edge efficiency while simultaneously mitigating issues related to protein over-stabilization that are evident in state-of-the-art models presently available. Our method achieves this by employing a conditional prior distribution and encoding the equilibrium backbone structure of proteins as a condition. This is implemented within a flow-matching framework that focuses on backbone geometry, thereby separating the tasks of structure prediction from conformational sampling. By employing this strategy, we eliminate the necessity for evolutionary information, which allows us to train the model from the ground up. This approach negates the dependency on pre-existing weights from folding models trained on extensive datasets. We anticipate that both utilizing a conditional prior in the context of flow-matching and substituting evolutionary data with structure-conditioning have broader applications beyond this study and can be extended to other challenges within generative modeling and the field of structural biology.

human: AlphaFlow (Jing et al., 2024) is widely used by practitioners for sampling protein conformational ensembles without MD - it goes well beyond a proof-of-concept.We also see BBFlow as highly relevant in practice, given its significantly increased efficiency at accuracy comparable with AlphaFlow, allowing accurate conformational ensemble generation on a much larger scale.In particular, BBFlow can be applied in pipelines for protein design, where it could enable the screening of generated structures for desired dynamics - a property that is challenging to incorporate into designed proteins so far.
ai: AlphaFlow, as described by Jing and colleagues in 2024, has become an essential tool for professionals seeking to sample protein conformational ensembles without relying on molecular dynamics MD. This technology has moved well past the theoretical stages into practical application. Similarly, BBFlow stands out in real-world scenarios due to its notably enhanced efficiency, which achieves accuracy levels on par with those of AlphaFlow. This efficiency facilitates the generation of conformational ensembles on a much grander scale. BBFlow is especially pertinent for integration into protein design workflows, where it has the potential to allow researchers to screen structures for specific dynamic properties-a challenge that has been difficult to address in the creation of designed proteins up until now.

human: VTX is an open-source molecular visualization software designed to overcome the scaling limitations of existing real-time molecular visualization software when handling massive molecular datasets. VTX employs a meshless molecular graphics engine utilizing impostor-based techniques and adaptive level-of-detail (LOD) rendering. This approach significantly reduces memory usage and enables real-time visualization and manipulation of large molecular systems. Performance benchmarks against VMD, PyMOL, and ChimeraX using a 114-million-bead Martini minimal whole-cell model demonstrate VTX’s efficiency, maintaining consistent frame rates even under interactive manipulation on standard computer hardware. VTX incorporates features such as screen-space ambient occlusion (SSAO) for enhanced depth perception and free-fly navigation for intuitive exploration of large molecular systems. VTX is open-source and free for non commercial use. Binaries for Windows and Ubuntu Linux are available at http://vtx.drugdesign.fr. VTX source code is available at https://github.com/VTX-Molecular-Visualization.
ai: VTX represents a groundbreaking advancement in the realm of molecular visualization software. As an open-source tool, it aims to address the challenges associated with processing vast molecular datasets, surpassing the limitations faced by contemporary real-time molecular visualization programs. Unlike traditional approaches, VTX employs a pioneering meshless molecular graphics engine that leverages impostor-based methodologies alongside adaptive level-of-detail LOD rendering. This innovative approach results in a drastic reduction in memory consumption, thereby allowing users to visualize and manipulate expansive molecular systems in real time. When tested against other popular molecular visualization tools such as VMD, PyMOL, and ChimeraX, using a formidable 114-million-bead Martini minimal whole-cell model, VTX showcased exceptional efficiency by maintaining stable frame rates, even amidst interactive manipulations, on commonly used computer systems. The software is equipped with advanced features like screen-space ambient occlusion SSAO, which substantially enhances depth perception, and includes free-fly navigation to facilitate an intuitive exploration experience of extensive molecular structures. For anyone interested, VTX is completely open-source and free for non-commercial endeavours. Those interested can find the binaries available for Windows and Ubuntu Linux at http://vtx.drugdesign.fr, while the source code can be accessed and explored at https://github.com/VTX-Molecular-Visualization.

human: Recent advances in the determination of atomic resolution molecular structures and assemblies using CryoEM [1], in protein structure prediction methods like AlphaFold [2, 3], and the growing availability of molecular dynamics simulations [4, 5], have significantly increased the volume of molecular structural biology data.Additionally, modern high-performance computing hardware has enabled the simulation of larger molecular systems [6, 7, 8], further amplifying data production. This massive molecular data poses a challenge for existing software solutions in terms of data processing, visualization, and storage.

Furthermore, breakthroughs in computational methods for predicting protein structures, such as those developed with AlphaFold [2, 3], have markedly contributed to this data influx. Alongside these developments, there is a burgeoning accessibility to molecular dynamics simulations [4, 5], which has also played a crucial role in this expansion. Concurrent advancements in high-performance computing infrastructure have facilitated the simulation of increasingly larger molecular assemblies [6, 7, 8], thereby exponentially increasing the amount of data generated. However, this voluminous production of molecular data presents a significant challenge to existing computational tools in terms of managing data processing, visualization, and storage.

human: In this work, we demonstrate the performance of VTX [9] on large molecular datasets by visualizing a 114 million Martini-beads minimal whole cell model published in 2023 [7], which pre-figures future massive molecular systems for molecular dynamics simulation. This serves as a valuable benchmark for future applications of massive molecular dynamics simulation visualization, where memory management and high-quality rendering remain key challenges.

Subsequently, ray-casting is employed to resolve the implicit equation corresponding to the primitive, thus shaping the final form. This method supports rapid and flawless pixel-level rendering (refer to figure ) while significantly reducing bandwidth and memory consumption, a vital consideration when working with extensive molecular structures or dynamic datasets.

human: Cartoon representations in VTX use an adaptive level-of-detail (LOD) approach with tessellation shaders [11]. This allows updates at each trajectory step with minimal computational cost.

human: Instancing is a widely used technique for rendering multiple copies of the same object in a scene simultaneously, significantly improving performance when dealing with many identical objects. By reducing the number of draw calls, it saves both CPU and GPU resource usage. Massive static molecular scenes, containing up to billion atoms, as displayed with YASARA [13] or Mol* [14, 15] effectively leverage instancing. However, instancing assumes that all copies share the same conformation, making it unsuitable for molecular dynamics trajectories where structures evolve independently. In this work, which pre-figures future applications for visualizing molecular dynamics trajectories of massive molecular systems, no instancing is used to display the 2023 Martini minimal whole cell model [7].
ai: Rendering multiple identical objects simultaneously in a scene is efficiently accomplished through a technique known as instancing. This approach is particularly advantageous for enhancing performance when numerous duplicates of an object are involved. By minimizing the need for multiple draw calls, instancing conserves valuable computing resources on both the CPU and GPU fronts. This method is adeptly utilized in vast static molecular scenes, where possibly billions of atoms can be depicted, as seen with applications like YASARA [13] and Mol* [14, 15]. Nevertheless, instancing relies on the presumption that all duplicated objects maintain identical conformation, which makes it unsuitable for scenarios involving molecular dynamics trajectories. In these cases, structures continuously evolve in unique ways. In the present study, which sets the stage for future applications aimed at depicting molecular dynamics trajectories within extensive molecular systems, we deliberately choose not to employ instancing for visualizing the 2023 Martini minimal whole cell model [7].

human: Depth perception is essential for localizing and distinguishing molecular entities in a complex scene. For this purpose, VTX uses a Screen-Space Ambient Occlusion (SSAO) [16] to enhance the perception of structural details and emphasize the burriedness of atoms, improving the understanding of molecular architectures (see figure ).

To achieve this, VTX implements a technique known as Screen-Space Ambient Occlusion SSAO [16]. This method is pivotal in heightening the visualization of detailed structures and accentuating how deeply atoms are buried, thereby enriching one’s comprehension of molecular arrangements (refer to figure).

human: Navigating through large systems composed by multiple proteins, lipids and other heavy molecules poses a new challenge compared to single-protein scale visualization.Traditional trackball navigation, which rotates the camera around a fixed point, can be restrictive for large systems, making it difficult to explore surrounding regions.

human: We develop ProtComposer to generate protein structures conditioned on spatial protein layouts that are specified via a set of 3D ellipsoids capturing substructure shapes and semantics. At inference time, we condition on ellipsoids that are hand-constructed, extracted from existing proteins, or from a statistical model, with each option unlocking new capabilities. Hand-specifying ellipsoids enables users to control control the location, size, orientation, secondary structure, and approximate shape of protein substructures. Conditioning on ellipsoids of existing proteins enables redesigning their substructure’s connectivity or editing editing substructure properties. By conditioning on novel and diverse ellipsoid layouts from a simple statistical model, we improve protein generation with expanded Pareto frontiers between designability, novelty, and diversity. Further, this enables sampling designable proteins with a helix-fraction that matches PDB proteins, unlike existing generative models that commonly oversample conceptually simple helix bundles. Code is available at https://github.com/NVlabs/protcomposer.

human: Proteins are intricate macromolecular machines that carry out a wide variety of biological and chemical processes. A grand vision of rational protein design is to be able to design complex and modular functions akin to those found in nature, where different spatial parts of the protein possess different properties that act in a coordinated fashion (Chu et al., 2024; Kortemme, 2024). However, current paradigms of ML-based protein structure generation are largely limited to unconditional generation (Watson et al., 2023; Yim et al., 2023b), or to inpainting of scaffolds and binders conditioned on known parts of the structure (Watson et al., 2023; Trippe et al., 2022), with no ability to control the higher-level spatial placement or layout of the generated protein. This leads to limited diversity and control of the generated samples and distinguishes protein generation from image generation, where such levels of control are commonplace and lead to new capabilities in the hands of human users (Li et al., 2023a; Rombach et al., 2022; Nie et al., 2024; Zheng et al., 2023a; Zhang et al., 2023a).

The ambitious goal of rational protein design is to engineer sophisticated and modular functionalities similar to those found in nature. In these natural systems, distinct spatial regions of a protein exhibit varied properties, working together harmoniously (Chu et al., 2024; Kortemme, 2024). Nonetheless, present models for machine learning-driven protein structure generation primarily focus on unconditional generation (Watson et al., 2023; Yim et al., 2023b) or on the inpainting of scaffolds and binders while being conditioned on pre-existing structure components (Watson et al., 2023; Trippe et al., 2022). These models lack the capability to manage the overarching spatial arrangements or layouts of the synthesized proteins. This limitation results in a reduced diversity and restricted control over the produced protein samples, setting protein generation apart from image generation. In the realm of image creation, such controls are widespread and empower human operators with novel potentialities (Li et al., 2023a; Rombach et al., 2022; Nie et al., 2024; Zheng et al., 2023a; Zhang et al., 2023a).

human: To bridge this gap in the protein design toolbox, we develop ProtComposer as a means of controlling protein structure generative models with the protein’s layout in 3D space. Specifically, we describe modular protein layouts via 3D ellipsoids 3D ellipsoids augmented with annotations to provide a rough “sketch“ of the protein (Figure ). Similar to blob or bounding box representations in image generation (Nie et al., 2024; Li et al., 2023a), these ellipsoids provide a level of abstraction intermediate between data-level (i.e., voxels) constraints and global conditioning. They are informative enough to control the generation of diverse proteins, but are human-interpretable, easy-to-construct, and do not constrain the low-level details of protein structures. Hence, 3D ellipsoids facilitate a two-stage paradigm in which complex protein designs are expressed as spatial sketches by hand or via heuristic algorithms, and deep learning models “fill in“ these sketches with high-quality, designable backbones.

These ellipsoids function similarly to blob or bounding box visual representations employed in image creation (Nie et al., 2024; Li et al., 2023a), providing a midway level of abstraction that strikes a balance between direct data-level restrictions (such as voxels) and broader overarching conditioning. These ellipsoids are sufficiently detailed to guide the generation of a variety of protein structures. At the same time, they remain easily interpretable by humans and are straightforward to construct, without imposing limitations on the intricate specifics of protein architecture. Consequently, the use of 3D ellipsoids supports a dual-stage approach, whereby intricate protein designs can initially be articulated as spatial outlines, either manually or by employing heuristic algorithms. Following this, deep learning models can then “complete“ these outlines, crafting backbones that are not only of high quality but also amenable to design modifications.

human: In this work, we apply our philosophy to controlling Multiflow (Campbell et al., 2024), a joint sequence-structure flow-matching model with state-of-the-art designability, with 3D ellipsoid layouts annotated with . Multiflow represents protein structures as a cloud of residue frames in and parameterizes the flow network with Invariant Point Attention (Jumper et al., 2021; Yim et al., 2023b). To inject ellipsoid conditioning into this network, we develop an equivariant mechanism for message passing between ellipsoids in 3D space and residue frames, which we call Invariant Cross Attention Invariant Cross Attention. We then fine-tune Multiflow with this cross attention into a conditional model of protein structure and sequence, conditioned on ellipsoid layouts. We develop a classifier-free guidance mechanism with Multiflow, enabling interpolation between ellipsoid-conditioned and unconditional generation. Empirically, we find this family of conditional generative distributions advances the state of the art in protein generation along three axes:

The primary aim of protein structure generative models (Yim et al., 2023b; Ingraham et al., 2023; Bose et al., 2024; Campbell et al., 2024) is aiding computational design of novel novel proteins (Watson et al., 2023; Lauko et al., 2024). Thus, we often desire to generate beyond already existing beyond already existing folds or secondary structure compositions, and to control control generations to satisfy design specifications. To address controllability, there are two main explored avenues beyond scaffolding existing structural motifs (Yim et al., 2024a). First, conditioning on block contact maps and sequential secondary structure specifications (Anand & Achim, 2022; Watson et al., 2023). Second, inference time inference time conditioning, as in Chroma (Ingraham et al., 2023), via projections onto a manifold or via forces from an arbitrary differentiable energy function. Such inference time control enjoys high generality while ProtComposer is trained for a single type of shape and semantic conditioning, but, therefore, enjoys improved adherence to the control (Table ).

human: For image generative models, controllable generation has enabled new applications that make up a significant portion of their utility beyond generating impressive images. To unlock similar new capabilities for protein generation, we follow the transferrable concepts that have crystallized out as crucial. On a technical and architectural level, this includes fine-tuning strong existing generative models with the principle of minimally perturbing the original model’s output in the initialized conditional model (Li et al., 2023a; Zhang et al., 2023b). On a conceptual level, this implies finding the right input specification: for different tasks, different levels of granularity are appropriate. In the image domain, this ranges from pixel-level specifications such as semantic segmentation maps or sketches to more coarse-grained specifications such as bounding-boxes (Li et al., 2023b; Zhang et al., 2023b), or “blobs“ (Nie et al., 2024), akin to our aims for proteins.

human: Flow matching (Liu et al., 2022; Lipman et al., 2022; Albergo & Vanden-Eijnden, 2022; Albergo et al., 2023) aims to learn a time-dependent vector field v that, when integrated from a start time to , transports samples from a noise distribution to a data distribution .To train v , we sample partially noised data from a conditional probability path conditional probability path satisfying and . A common choice is a Dirac that traces out a straight line between x 0 and x 1 or a geodesic for flow matching on manifolds (Chen & Lipman, 2024). At the sampled noisy datapoints x t , we evaluate the vector field and regress it against the conditional vector field conditional vector field that corresponds to the conditional probability path through the continuity equation . At convergence, v approximates the marginal vector field marginal vector field (since the gradients are equivalent to regressing against ) that evolves the prior p 0 to the data distribution p 1 through the marginal probability path marginal probability path .
ai: Flow matching, as discussed in the works of Liu et al. 2022, Lipman et al. 2022, and Albergo & Vanden-Eijnden 2022, as well as Albergo et al. 2023, focuses on the development of a vector field, denoted as vt, that is dependent on time. The objective of this vector field is to facilitate the transition of samples from an initial noisy distribution to a desired data distribution by integrating it over time from the initial point to the end. In the process of training v, data samples that have been partially subjected to noise are taken from a probabilistic path that is conditioned on certain criteria and satisfies designated properties. Typically, a Dirac measure is chosen to represent a linear trajectory between two points x 0 and x 1, or alternatively, one might use a geodesic path when performing flow matching on manifolds, as elaborated by Chen & Lipman 2024. At each of the selected noisy data points x t, the vector field is calculated and then compared to the conditional vector field that aligns with the specified probabilistic path, in accordance with the continuity equation. When the system reaches convergence, the vector field v serves as an approximation of the marginal vector field. This is because the gradient regresses onto this field, thereby allowing the initial distribution p 0 to transform into the target data distribution p 1 via a path defined by marginal probabilities.

human: Proteins are compositional objects-different regions have different properties, and we seek a language in which to succinctly describe this information to control the sampling of a generative model. To do so, we propose to represent a protein’s spatial layout using a set of K ellipsoids, each corresponding to a semantically coherent region of the protein. Each ellipsoid records the number number of residues in the associated region, a categorical semantic feature semantic feature, its position position, and its shape shape in terms of the covariance matrix of the C α coordinates in the region. We argue that this representation of protein spatial layouts finds a favorable tradeoff between a single global annotation, such as a text prompt or protein family, and more complex shape descriptors, such as meshes or voxel grids. A global annotation may be insufficient to provide the desired control over the spatial layout, and a more complex annotation could be difficult to generate or specify without training an additional model. Meanwhile, 3D ellipsoids are expressive and precise, yet easy to generate and manipulate.
ai: Proteins can be thought of as composite structures where various regions exhibit distinct characteristics. We are driven to develop a way of articulating this diverse information succinctly to manage the sampling process in a generative model effectively. Our approach involves characterizing a protein’s three-dimensional configuration by utilizing a collection of K ellipsoids. Each ellipsoid represents a semantically unified segment of the protein. Within each ellipsoid, several attributes are recorded: the count of residues in the pertinent region, a semantic indicator from a categorical set, as well as its spatial coordinates and geometric form, delineated by the covariance matrix derived from the C α coordinates of that region. We advocate for this portrayal of protein spatial arrangements as it deftly balances between overly broad global annotations, like merely a text prompt or protein family classification, and overly intricate shape encoders, such as mesh representations or voxel grids. While global annotations might not suffice for achieving the nuanced control of the spatial layout one might desire, a highly detailed annotation could necessitate the development of another model for generation or specification, which is often cumbersome. In contrast, 3D ellipsoids are able to capture complexity and precision effectively, while remaining straightforward to create and modify.

human: Provided a protein structure, obtaining its ellipsoid representation (e.g., for training purposes) consists of two steps: segmentation segmentation of the protein into semantically coherent regions, and extraction extraction of ellipsoid descriptions for each region. To segment the protein, we consider a simple, non-learned segmentation algorithm that places two residues in the same region if and only if they are both spatially spatially proximal and semantically semantically similar. We construct a segmentation graph by drawing an edge for each such pair of residues and return the list of connected components of this segmentation graph. For each segmented region, we aggregate the residue features to obtain f k and compute the mean and covariance of the C α positions. These steps are illustrated in Figure and further detailed in Appendix Algorithm . We found this to be more reliable than more sophisticated variants using, e.g., K -means or spectral clustering.

The first stage entails slicing the protein into regions that are semantically cohesive, and the second stage involves extracting ellipsoid descriptions that correspond to each identified region. In order to divide the protein into segments, we adopt a straightforward, rule-based segmentation strategy, which does not rely on learning mechanisms. According to this method, two residues are placed within the same region only if they are both physically close to each other and exhibit semantic similarity. To achieve this segmentation, we construct a graph where an edge connects any pair of residues that fulfill the criteria of proximity and similarity, thereby resulting in a segmentation graph. The subsequent task is to identify and return the connected components within this graph. For every segment delineated in this manner, we compile the relevant residue features to derive f k, and calculate the average and covariance of the C {α} locations. These methods are illustrated in the accompanying figure and elaborated upon in the appendix, specifically in Algorithm. Through experimentation, we discovered that this method proved to be more dependable compared to more complex techniques, such as those employing K-means clustering or spectral clustering approaches.

In designing the ellipsoid conditioning mechanism, we have so far made no assumptions about the sources sources of ellipsoids provided during inference. Next to using manually specified manually specified ellipsoids, there is also an opportunity in sampling synthetic ellipsoids synthetic ellipsoids from an additional generative model to sample an unconditional distribution of protein structures factorized as . While it may be tempting to use a deep learning solution for , we purposefully avoid this and argue that the factorization is best leveraged with a simple statistical model over ellipsoid layouts. Instead of a deep learned that may produce layouts that are similar to the training data, a simple statistical model for guarantees sampling diverse and novel novel layouts, which lead to more diverse and novel protein structures from - properties that are crucial for protein design where the aim is commonly to produce novel designs.
ai: In the process of crafting the ellipsoid conditioning mechanism, no preliminary assumptions have been made regarding the origins of the ellipsoids utilized during the inference phase. While one option is to rely on ellipsoids that are manually specified, another intriguing possibility involves drawing synthetic ellipsoids from an additional generative model. This approach allows for sampling from an unconditional distribution of protein structures, which is factorized in a specific manner. Although employing a deep learning approach to handle might sound appealing, we consciously decide against this. We advocate that the factorization method reaches its full potential through the application of a simple statistical model that oversees the arrangement of ellipsoids. A deep learning model may tend to generate layouts that closely emulate the training data, whereas a basic statistical model guarantees the generation of diverse and innovative layouts. These distinct and unprecedented layouts are critical as they yield more varied and novel protein structures derived from - a quality that is immensely important in the field of protein design, where a primary goal often involves creating entirely new designs.

human: To generate novel ellipsoid layouts, we first sample means and covariances for K ellipsoids and then assign secondary structure and residue count annotations. The model over means and covariances is That is, the ellipsoid means and covariances are drawn i.i.d. from isotropic Gaussian and Wishart distributions, respectively, and multiplied with the Boltzmann factor of an energy function that penalizes ellipsoid overlaps. Intuitively, σ controls the ellipsoid’s spread spread, ψ controls their volume volume, ν controls their anisotropy or “roundness“ “roundness“, and U prevents overlaps. The energy U is a simple inverse square repulsion based on pairwise Mahalanobis distances. We sample this via rejection sampling, i.e., by sampling , evaluating their energy U , and rejecting with probability e .
ai: To craft innovative configurations of ellipsoids, we initiate the process by randomly selecting means and covariances for K distinct ellipsoids. Subsequently, we allocate designations related to secondary structure and annotate the quantity of residues. In detail, the framework for these means and covariances involves drawing them independently and identically distributed (i.i.d.) from isotropic Gaussian distributions for the means and Wishart distributions for the covariances. These selections are then scaled by the Boltzmann factor of a specific energy function designed to discourage any overlapping of ellipsoids.In essence, the parameter σ dictates the extent of the ellipsoid’s spatial distribution, ψ regulates their overall volume, ν defines their degree of anisotropy or their deviation from being perfectly spherical, and the energy function U serves to inhibit overlaps among them. This energy function U employs a rudimentary inverse-square repulsion mechanism that relies on the pairwise Mahalanobis distances between the ellipsoids. The sampling of this configuration is achieved through rejection sampling, which involves drawing samples, calculating the corresponding energy U, and subsequently discarding samples with a probability proportional to e.

human: We now show that conditioning on ellipsoid layouts can improve the diversity (and related metrics) of Multiflow generations. Without conditioning, Multiflow and related methods generate highly designable proteins, but exhibit limited secondary structure diversity (73% helices instead of the 42% of PDB proteins) and low complexity by visual inspection (Figure ). Conceptually, this can be thought of as manually controlling the “ellipsoid marginal“ of the generated distribution, where the ellipsoids amount to incomplete, compressed observations of the full state space (i.e., backbone structure).

Here, the ellipsoids serve as partial and compressed indications of the entire state space, effectively representing the protein’s backbone structure.

human: We developed ProtComposer for conditioning protein structure generative models on 3D ellipsoid layouts. We implemented it for Multiflow and secondary structure annotated ellipsoids, using novel architectural components such as Invariant Cross Attention Invariant Cross Attention. We quantitatively ascertained that generations tightly adhere to the input ellipsoid layouts and provided a range of examples to demonstrate how this enables reliably generating proteins with desired layouts via hand-specified ellipsoids and editing existing proteins. To generate unconditionally, we condition on novel and diverse ellipsoid layouts drawn from a newly developed statistical model. This produced a family of protein structure distributions that far surpasses the Pareto frontiers of designability to novelty and diversity achieved by Multiflow. ProtComposer generates more compositional proteins with a helicity close to that of PDB proteins while maintaining designability. We anticipate expanding the annotation types of our ellipsoids to function specifications to further push the frontier of controllable protein design.
ai: ProtComposer was created by our team to facilitate the conditioning of protein structure generative models on three-dimensional ellipsoid configurations. Our application targeted its use for the Multiflow method and ellipsoids annotated with secondary structures, utilizing innovative architectural components such as the Invariant Cross Attention mechanism. Through rigorous quantitative analysis, we established that our generated structures closely mirror the input ellipsoid designs. We showcased various examples to illustrate our method’s capacity for consistently crafting proteins with precise layouts through ellipsoids specified manually and for modifying pre-existing proteins. For scenarios necessitating unconditional generation, our approach involves conditioning on new and varied ellipsoid configurations obtained from a statistical model we have recently devised. This innovation yields a spectrum of protein structure distributions that significantly surpass the previously established Pareto frontiers related to designability, novelty, and diversity, as reached by Multiflow. ProtComposer produces more compositionally intricate proteins, achieving a helicity comparable to that found in PDB proteins, all while maintaining their designability. Looking ahead, we plan to broaden the range of annotation types for our ellipsoids to encompass functional specifications, aiming to push the boundaries of controllable protein design even further.

human: We present a general method for protein structure generation that may be used to aid protein design. Proteins are versatile tools that carry out biological functions. Depending on the purpose our tool is used for-depending on which protein design it is employed to aid-its use is either ethical or unethical. The vast majority of current use cases of similar technology are with the intent of achieving positive outcomes for humanity via, e.g., developing drugs, biomolecules that accelerate industrial processes, or proteins used as tools to improve our understanding of biology itself. Thus, we estimate that the ethical use cases with potential for positive impact on humanity will far outweigh any negative impacts from unethical uses.

The ethical implications of utilizing our method inherently depend on the objectives it serves-specifically, which aspects of protein design it seeks to support. In most instances currently, technologies akin to ours are wielded with the aim of benefiting humanity. Consequently, we posit that the ethical applications, those with the potential to bring about positive human advancements, will substantially overshadow any adverse impacts that might arise from unethical exploitation.

human: Small interfering RNA (siRNA) is a promising therapeutic agent due to its ability to silence disease-related genes via RNA interference. While traditional machine learning and early deep learning methods have made progress in predicting siRNA efficacy, there remains significant room for improvement. Advanced deep learning techniques can enhance prediction accuracy, reducing the reliance on extensive wet-lab experiments and accelerating the identification of effective siRNA sequences. This approach also provides deeper insights into the mechanisms of siRNA efficacy, facilitating more targeted and efficient therapeutic strategies.

The application of cutting-edge deep learning approaches can significantly improve prediction precision, thereby lessening the dependency on labor-intensive laboratory experiments and speeding up the discovery of potent siRNA sequences. Moreover, this methodology affords a more profound understanding of the underlying mechanisms influencing siRNA efficacy, paving the way for more precise and effective therapeutic interventions.

human: RNA interference (RNAi) technology has emerged as a promising therapeutic approach by enabling the sequence-specific silencing of disease-related genes. Small interfering RNA (siRNA) is central to this process, being incorporated into the RNA-induced silencing complex (RISC), which includes proteins such as Argonaute-2 (Ago-2), Dicer, and TRBP[1], [2] and [3]. The antisense strand of siRNA guides RISC to the target mRNA, where Ago-2 mediates cleavage, resulting in gene knockdown[4]. This mechanism allows siRNA to target traditionally undruggable genes, significantly expanding potential therapeutic targets.
ai: RNA interference RNAi technology has gained traction as an innovative therapeutic strategy, allowing for the precise silencing of genes associated with various diseases. This method primarily revolves around the use of small interfering RNA siRNA, which plays a critical role by being integrated into the RNA-induced silencing complex RISC. This complex comprises essential proteins such as Argonaute-2 (Ago-2), Dicer, and TRBP[1], [2], and [3]. Through its antisense strand, siRNA steers RISC to the specific mRNA target, where Ago-2 facilitates the cleavage, leading to the downregulation of the gene[4]. Such a mechanism empowers siRNA with the capability to target genes that were previously considered untreatable, thereby broadening the scope of possible therapeutic interventions significantly.

human: Designing highly efficient siRNAs remains challenging. Effective siRNAs must avoid triggering the innate immune system, achieve high specificity in target cleavage, and minimize off-target effects. Consequently, designing effective siRNA is crucial for RNAi therapeutics, prompting the development of various computational tools. Tools like OligoWalk, siRNAPred, and i-score have limitations due to dataset biases, prediction methods, and off-target effects[5], [6] and [7].

The creation of effective siRNAs requires careful consideration: they must steer clear of activating the body’s innate immune response, exhibit precise specificity for cleaving the intended target, and significantly reduce unintended off-target interactions. As a result, designing siRNAs that perform effectively is a pivotal step in the field of RNA interference therapeutics, leading to the emergence of a variety of computational tools aimed at this challenge. However, tools such as OligoWalk, siRNAPred, and i-score face inherent limitations due to biases present in datasets, the methodologies used for predictions, and potential off-target effects, as documented in references [5], [6], and [7].

human: Early machine learning methods, such as LASSO regression, support vector machines (SVM), and linear regression, improved prediction accuracy but were limited by their simple structures, which failed to capture complex features[8], [9]. With the advent of deep learning, researchers began leveraging advanced models for better understanding siRNA sequences.

These methodologies struggled to encapsulate intricate characteristics. human: Deep learning brought significant improvements. CNNs and DNNs automatically extracted features from siRNA sequences, enhancing accuracy[10]. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) modeled siRNA-mRNA interactions, incorporating thermodynamic parameters[11]. Transformer-based models have excelled in natural language processing and genomics due to their ability to handle sequential data through attention mechanisms[12]. Models like BERT-siRNA leverage pre-training on extensive human genomic sequences to enhance siRNA efficacy prediction[13], [14]. OligoFormer combines Transformers with LSTM and convolutional layers to capture deep sequence features and complex siRNA-mRNA interaction patterns[15], [16] and [17].

Transformer-based architectures have shown exceptional performance in both natural language processing and the field of genomics, largely due to their proficiency in managing sequential data through the use of attention mechanisms [12]. For instance, models like BERT-siRNA capitalize on pre-training using vast datasets of human genomic sequences to enhance the prediction of siRNA efficacy [13], [14]. Furthermore, the OligoFormer model innovatively integrates Transformers with LSTM and convolutional layers to adeptly capture deep-seated sequence features and the complex interaction patterns characteristic of siRNA-mRNA relationships [15], [16], and [17].

human: Despite these advancements, existing models face limitations in interpretability, usability, robustness, and data utilization. In response, we propose DeepSilencer, a deep learning model specifically designed for predicting siRNA knockdown efficiency. Our contributions include:

human: We have implemented a series of innovative approaches to improve the accuracy and robustness of siRNA silencing efficiency prediction. Initially, in response to the limited quantity of siRNA data, we introduced a novel dynamic random data pairing mechanism, namely Selective Pair Sampling, to fully exploit the potential of the available data. Subsequently, given the challenge of aligning different publicly available datasets on siRNA silencing efficiency, we designed a novel multi-task system named Tri-Task Learning Framework. To further refine this framework, we crafted an improved loss function that significantly boosts the model’s accuracy and robustness. Finally, we designed DeepSilencer, a model specifically tailored for RNA sequence analysis. By integrating Transformer and Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) architectures, DeepSilencer effectively captures the intricate features of siRNA sequences, thereby improving prediction accuracy and robustness without the need for pre-training. Detailed introductions of these components will be presented in the following sections.

Enhancements were made to this framework by developing an improved loss function, which substantially elevates both the model’s precision and durability. Ultimately, we created a specialized model for RNA sequence analysis named DeepSilencer. This model skillfully combines the Transformer and Convolutional Neural Network CNN frameworks, enabling it to adeptly capture the complex characteristics of siRNA sequences. As a result, it achieves enhanced prediction accuracy and robustness, bypassing the need for pre-training. Comprehensive explanations of these components will be elaborated upon in the sections that follow.

human: We utilized the datasets summarized by OligoFormer, which aggregated nine studies, resulting in a total of 3,714 siRNAs and 75 mRNAs[18], [19], [20], [21],[22], [23], [24] and [25]. These datasets were organized into three categories: the Huesken dataset, the Takayuki dataset, and a mixed set (Mixset) comprising the remaining data. The inhibition efficacy of siRNAs was normalized to a range of 0 to 100%, with a 70% inhibition threshold distinguishing positive from negative siRNAs.

human: Existing publicly available data on siRNA silencing efficiency are derived from various experimental measurements. However, due to differences in experimental methodologies and measurement techniques, aligning the values across different datasets can be challenging. In the OligoFormer study, the authors addressed this issue by converting continuous values into categorical labels. Specifically, the inhibition efficacy or activity of siRNAs in all datasets was normalized to a range from 0 to 100%, and a threshold of 70% maximum inhibition was used to classify siRNAs as positive or negative.

Nevertheless, due to variances in the experimental approaches and methods of measurement used, it can be difficult to harmonize and reconcile the values across these disparate datasets. In the research conducted by OligoFormer, the researchers tackled this complication by transforming continuous numerical values into categorical labels. They approached this by normalizing the inhibition efficacy or activity of siRNAs across all datasets to a standardized scale spanning from 0 to 100%. They then applied a critical threshold of 70% maximum inhibition to determine whether siRNAs were classified as positive or negative.

human: Our model, , integrates both Transformer and Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) architectures, specifically designed for RNA sequence analysis. The structure of the model is shown in Fig . The Transformer, through its self-attention mechanism, excels at capturing global dependencies within sequences, demonstrating strong modeling capabilities in both natural language processing and bioinformatics. However, siRNA sequences are typically short, and the available data is limited. Additionally, RNA molecular interactions frequently exhibit highly localized characteristics, making it challenging for a Transformer alone to sufficiently capture these local dependencies.
ai: Our proposed model effectively amalgamates the architectures of Transformer and Convolutional Neural Networks CNNs, meticulously tailored for dissecting RNA sequences. The detailed model architecture is illustrated in Fig . The Transformer component, endowed with its self-attention mechanism, is particularly adept at grasping extensive dependencies across sequences. This proficiency is well-recognized in the realms of natural language processing and bioinformatics. Nevertheless, typical siRNA sequences are relatively brief, and the dataset size poses a constraint. Furthermore, interactions at the molecular level within RNA often demonstrate pronounced localized characteristics, thereby complicating the transformative task of capturing such local dependencies using only a Transformer.

human: For instance, the self-attention mechanism of the Transformer performs exceptionally well when handling long sequences because it can simultaneously attend to all positions within the sequence at each layer. However, for short sequences like siRNA, an over-reliance on global information may lead to the model overlooking critical local features. Moreover, Transformer models generally require large datasets to effectively learn the complex relationships between sequences, and the limited size of siRNA datasets might hinder the model’s generalization capabilities.
ai: For example, the self-attention mechanism embedded within the Transformer architecture excels at managing lengthy sequences due to its ability to concurrently focus on every position throughout the sequence in each processing layer. Yet, in the context of short sequences such as those found in small interfering RNA siRNA, there exists a risk of the model overemphasizing global data, which might result in neglecting essential local characteristics. Furthermore, Transformer models typically demand substantial datasets to adeptly capture the intricate interconnections between sequences. The relatively small scale of siRNA data collections could, therefore, impede the model’s ability to generalize effectively.

human: In contrast, Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), with their local receptive fields and weight-sharing mechanisms, are adept at extracting local features and possess a strong inductive bias. Studies have shown that CNNs exhibit robust performance when dealing with small-scale datasets. For example, CoAtNet combines convolutional and Transformer modules to achieve significant performance improvements on large-scale image datasets like ImageNet[30]. Similarly, Astroformer demonstrates that combining convolutional and Transformer structures and training from scratch can achieve excellent results on small-scale datasets[31].
ai: On the other hand, Convolutional Neural Networks CNNs are distinguished by their localized receptive fields and ability to share weights, making them proficient at isolating and identifying local features, which gives them a considerable inductive bias. Research has indicated that CNNs perform exceptionally well with datasets of a smaller scale. For instance, CoAtNet integrates convolutional elements with Transformer modules to deliver remarkable enhancements in performance on extensive image datasets such as ImageNet[30]. In a comparable manner, Astroformer illustrates that integrating convolutional and Transformer frameworks and initiating training from the ground up can lead to outstanding outcomes on smaller-scale datasets[31].

human: The latter part of the model comprises several one-dimensional ConvNeXtBlocks, which further enhance the integration of local information. ConvNeXt is an enhanced convolutional neural network architecture that improves performance through various innovations. ConvNeXtBlocks primarily consist of downsampling layers, depth-wise convolutions, LayerNorm, multilayer perceptrons (MLPs, equivalent to Feed Forward Layers in this context), and residual connections. In our implementation, we made a slight modification by substituting the original 2D convolutions with 1D convolutions. We incorporated multiple ConvNeXtBlocks to progressively extract and integrate local features:The convolutional operations are divided into three stages, with downsampling achieved by setting the convolutional stride to 2 at the end of the first two stages.The first convolutional stage reduces the hidden layer dimension from 128 to 64, followed by a stride-2 convolutional layer for further downsampling. This stage contains 2 ConvNeXtBlocks.The second convolutional stage reduces the hidden layer dimension from 64 to 32, employing multiple stride-1 and stride-2 convolutional layers to gradually extract features. This stage comprises 3 ConvNeXtBlocks.The final convolutional stage maintains the dimension at 32 and includes 1 ConvNeXtBlock.After the convolutional stages, a flattening operation merges the hidden and sequence dimensions before passing the features to the task-specific layers.

human: The dynamic nature of proteins, influenced by ligand interactions, is essential for comprehending protein function and progressing drug discovery. Traditional structure-based drug design (SBDD) approaches typically target binding sites with rigid structures, limiting their practical application in drug development. While molecular dynamics simulation can theoretically capture all the biologically relevant conformations, the transition rate is dictated by the intrinsic energy barrier between them, making the sampling process computationally expensive. To overcome the aforementioned challenges, we propose to use generative modeling for SBDD considering conformational changes of protein pockets. We curate a dataset of apo and multiple holo states of protein-ligand complexes, simulated by molecular dynamics, and propose a full-atom flow model (and a stochastic version), named DynamicFlow, that learns to transform apo pockets and noisy ligands into holo pockets and corresponding 3D ligand molecules. Our method uncovers promising ligand molecules and corresponding holo conformations of pockets. Additionally, the resultant holo-like states provide superior inputs for traditional SBDD approaches, playing a significant role in practical drug discovery.
ai: Understanding the ever-changing behaviors of proteins, especially how they interact with various ligands, is fundamental to grasping how these biological molecules function and advancing new strategies in drug discovery. Conventional methods in structure-based drug design SBDD generally focus on targeting binding sites that are perceived as immovable, which can impede their effectiveness in practical drug development scenarios. Although in theory, molecular dynamics simulations have the potential to reveal all biologically significant conformations, the rate at which these transitions occur depends on the inherent energy barriers between different states. This limitation renders the exhaustive sampling process highly resource-intensive in terms of computation. To navigate these hurdles, we are advocating for the use of generative modeling within SBDD, emphasizing the conformational transformations of protein pockets over time. We have compiled a comprehensive collection of data that includes both apo states and multiple holo states of protein-ligand complexes, achieved through molecular dynamics simulations. Building on this, we introduce a full-atom flow model, along with a stochastic variant, which we call DynamicFlow. This model is designed to effectively transform apo pockets and perturbed ligands into their holo counterparts along with the associated three-dimensional ligand structures. Our approach is pivotal in identifying potential ligand molecules and their corresponding holo conformations. Furthermore, the holo-like states derived from our method offer enhanced starting points for traditional SBDD techniques, thus significantly contributing to the practical processes involved in drug discovery.

human: Modern deep learning is advancing several areas within drug discovery. Notably, among these, structure-based drug design (SBDD) (Anderson, 2003) emerges as a particularly significant and challenging domain. SBDD aims to discover drug-like ligand molecules specifically tailored to target binding sites. However, the complexity of chemical space and the dynamic nature of molecule conformations make traditional methods such as high throughput and virtual screenings inefficient. Additionally, relying on compound databases limits the diversity of identified molecules. Thus, deep generative models, such as autoregressive models (Luo et al., 2021; Peng et al., 2022) and diffusion models (Guan et al., 2023; Schneuing et al., 2022), have been introduced as a tool for 3D ligand molecule design based on binding pockets, significantly transforming research paradigms.

Moreover, the dependence on existing compound libraries constrains the variety of molecules that can be identified. To address these limitations, cutting-edge deep generative models, including autoregressive models (Luo et al., 2021; Peng et al., 2022) and diffusion models (Guan et al., 2023; Schneuing et al., 2022), have been employed. These models facilitate the design of 3D ligand molecules based on the architecture of binding pockets, thus bringing a transformative shift in research methodologies.

This binding can affect the protein’s function by inhibiting the biological signaling pathway associated with a disease.

Nevertheless, the dynamic nature of proteins plays a pivotal role in effective drug discovery processes (Karelina et al., 2023; Boehr et al., 2009). Due to thermodynamic fluctuations, proteins do not maintain a single shape but exist as a collection of diverse conformational states, each capable of interacting uniquely with different drug compounds. The shift among these conformational states frequently results in the emergence of hidden pockets, which are intimately linked to the protein’s biological functions. When a drug binds to a protein, the protein’s configuration can be subtly adjusted, enabling it to adopt varying shapes to enhance its interaction with the drug in a process known as induced fit (Sherman et al., 2006). This interaction has the potential to modulate the protein’s function by disrupting the disease-related biological signaling pathways.

As illustrated in , the Abl kinase exists in both active and inactive apo states (6XR6, 6XR7), which differ in their DFG conformations. Type I kinase inhibitors, such as Dasatinib (2GQG), bind and stabilize the DFG-in conformation. In contrast, type II inhibitors like Imatinib (2HYY) stabilize the inactive conformation by occupying the ATP-binding pocket. Considering these dynamic conformational shifts is crucial for designing compounds that precisely target this kinase, as such structural nuances directly influence binding and efficacy.

human: We take a step towards integrating protein dynamics into structure-based drug design. First, we curate a dataset based on a large collection of molecular dynamics traces of protein-ligand complexes.Our dataset comprises both apo and multiple holo states of each protein-ligand complex. We propose an SE(3)-equivariant full-atom flow model, named , that simultaneously transforms the apo state of protein pockets and noisy ligands into holo states and their corresponding binding ligand molecules. Our method integrates insights from both machine learning and biology, utilizing the flow model’s ability to transport one arbitrary distribution to another. We employ apo and holo state pairs as a natural coupling for conditional flow matching to train our flow model, making it learn the dynamics of both backbone frames and side-chain torsions of protein pockets. Simultaneously, we use continuous and discrete flow matching to model the distribution of atom positions, atom types, and bond types of ligand molecules. Additionally, we propose a stochastic version of our flow to further promote the robustness. Notably, to comprehensively capture the protein-ligand interaction, we meticulously design a full-atom model that incorporates both SE(3)-equivariant geometrical message passing layers and residue-level Transformer layers.The experimental results demonstrate the ability of our method to discover biologically meaningful protein conformation and promising ligand molecules.Interestingly, we find that the conformation states of protein pockets discovered by our method can serve as improved input for SBDD methods that treat proteins as rigid entities. We highlight our main contributions as follows:We present a meticulously curated dataset consisting of both apo and multiple holo states of protein-ligand complexes derived from molecular dynamics simulation, offering new opportunities for AI-driven drug discovery.We propose a full-atom flow model and a stochastic version that transform apo states of protein pockets to holo states and generates the corresponding 3D ligand molecules simultaneously.We design a full-atom model with both atom-level SE(3)-equivariant geometrical message passing layers and residue-level Transformer layers, which captures comprehensive protein-ligand interactions and flexibly models protein backbone frames and side-chain torsions.Our method generates meaningful protein conformation shifts and promising ligand molecules with high binding affinity. The discovered conformations also further enhance SBDD methods with rigid pockets as input.

Structure-based drug design (SBDD) aims to develop ligand molecules capable of binding to specific protein targets. The advent of deep generative models has revolutionized the field, producing significant results.Luo et al. (2021); Peng et al. (2022); Liu et al. (2022a) and Zhang et al. (2022) employed an autoregressive model to generate atoms (and bonds) or fragments of a ligand molecule given a specific binding site with 3D structure.Guan et al. (2023); Schneuing et al. (2022); Lin et al. (2022) integrated diffusion models (Ho et al., 2020) into SBDD. These models initially generate the types and positions of atoms through iterative denoising, followed by determining bond types through post-processing.Some recent studies have sought to enhance these methods by incorporating biochemical prior knowledge.Huang et al. (2023) integrated protein-ligand interaction priors into both the forward and reverse processes to refine the diffusion models.While these studies have shown promising results in evaluations, their disregard for protein dynamics limits their applicability in practical drug development.

With the emergence of deep generative models, the landscape of this field has been transformed, yielding remarkable outcomes. For instance, the studies by Luo et al. 2021, Peng et al. 2022, Liu et al. 2022a, and Zhang et al. 2022 utilized an autoregressive approach to generate the atoms and bonds or even fragments of ligand molecules for a particular 3D binding site. Furthermore, Guan et al. 2023, Schneuing et al. 2022, and Lin et al. 2022 incorporated diffusion models as introduced by Ho et al. 2020 into the SBDD framework. These diffusion models commence by iteratively generating the positions and types of atoms through a denoising process, subsequently determining bond types via post-processing techniques. Certain researchers have embarked on advancing these approaches by infusing them with biochemical priors. For example, Huang et al. 2023 integrated protein-ligand interaction priors throughout both the forward and reverse stages to enhance the diffusion models’ precision. Although these investigations have demonstrated encouraging outcomes during evaluations, a significant limitation arises from their neglect of protein dynamics, which ultimately constrains their usability in real-world drug development scenarios.

human: This paper addresses the problem of efficiently classifying high-dimensional data over decentralized networks. Penalized support vector machines (SVMs) are widely used for high-dimensional classification tasks. However, the nonsmoothness of the objective function poses significant challenges in developing efficient decentralized learning methods. Many existing procedures suffer from slow, sublinear convergence rates. To overcome this limitation, we consider a convolution-based smoothing technique for the nonsmooth hinge loss function. The resulting loss function remains convex and smooth. We then develop an efficient generalized alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) algorithm for solving penalized SVM over decentralized networks.Our theoretical contributions are twofold. First, we establish that our generalized ADMM algorithm achieves provable linear convergence with a simple implementation. Second, after a sufficient number of ADMM iterations, the final sparse estimator attains near-optimal statistical convergence and accurately recovers the true support of the underlying parameters. Extensive numerical experiments on both simulated and real-world datasets validate our theoretical findings.

human: Penalized support vector machines (SVMs) have been enduringly powerful tools for high-dimensional classification tasks, building on the seminal contributions of Boseret al. (1992) and Vapnik (2000). The standard objective function for penalized SVMs combines the hinge loss with a penalty term. Commonly used penalties include the l 2 penalty (as in the classical SVM), the l 1 penalty, SCAD (Parket al., 2012; Penget al., 2016), and nuclear norm penalties (Xuet al., 2024). Among these, the l 1 and elastic-net penalized SVMs, introduced by Wanget al. (2006) and Zhuet al. (2003), are particularly notable for their ability to perform both classification and variable selection. Sparse decision rules enhance interpretability and stability-features highly desirable to practitioners such as physicians. Furthermore, Penget al. (2016) rigorously analyzed the convergence behavior and error bounds of the l 1 penalized SVM, providing additional theoretical support for its utility.
