human: We address this question affirmatively by proposing a novel method, called . Our main contributions are outlined below: To mitigate the challenges posed by the nonsmooth hinge loss, we first consider a convolution-based smoothing technique (Wanget al., 2022; Chen andChen, 2024). This approach constructs a new loss function that is both smooth and convex, facilitating the development of efficient optimization algorithms for penalized SVMs. To derive sparse classification rules in decentralized networks, we present a generalized ADMM algorithm tailored to the penalized CSVM. This algorithm incorporates a quadratic majorization of the smoothed loss function, allowing all updates to have closed forms via efficient matrix-vector multiplications. In high-dimensional settings, the lack of strong convexity in the objective function often limits the convergence guarantees of classical ADMM. Existing theory typically establishes only sublinear convergence rates or convergence to a limiting point. By leveraging the strong convexity of the newly introduced smoothed loss function, however, we prove that the proposed algorithm enjoys fast convergence. This notable improvement ensures that the number of communication rounds required scales logarithmically with the desired accuracy, significantly enhancing computation and communication efficiency in decentralized settings. We establish optimal statistical guarantees on both estimation accuracy and support recovery for our decentralized estimation process. After a sufficient number of ADMM iterations, the proposed estimator attains the optimal statistical convergence rate, matching that of an equivalent in-memory penalized SVMs where all data are pooled. Moreover, we prove that the method achieves exact support recovery under the “beta-min“ condition, providing rigorous theoretical assurance of its effectiveness. To the best of our knowledge, this is perhaps the first result for support recovery guarantees of elastic-net penalized SVM.

Numerous methods have been proposed in the distributed learning literature, broadly categorized into two main frameworks. A central node coordinates the learning process, as explored in Hector andSong (2020, 2021); Tanget al. (2020); Zhouet al. (2023); Chen andZhu (2023). However, these methods face limitations, including bandwidth constraints at the central node and vulnerability to system-wide failure in the event of node disruption. When a central node is unavailable or impractical, decentralized learning offers a robust alternative. For instance, Yadav andSalapaka (2007) employed an averaging consensus protocol leveraging the spectral properties of the Laplacian matrix, although it often produced undesired dense estimates. Changet al. (2014) introduced inexact consensus ADMM with linear convergence guarantees for smooth, strongly convex objectives, but the method is unsuitable for high-dimensional settings. Further work by Shiet al. (2015) and Liet al. (2019) developed decentralized (proximal) gradient descent algorithms that eschew the use of Lagrangian duals. Subgradient methods have also been applied to quantile regression (QR) in Wang andLi (2018); Wanget al. (2019); Zhanget al. (2019), though they generally yield dense estimates and prioritize optimization convergence over statistical guarantees.

human: The pursuit of a solution to the decentralized penalized SVM problem () faces two significant challenges. First, the hinge loss function is nonsmooth, which complicates the application of gradient-based or Newton-based optimization algorithms. Second, the inclusion of the elastic-net penalty renders problem () devoid of closed-form solutions in general.To address these challenges concurrently, we propose a decentralized convoluted SVM, detailed in the following sections. We begin by constructing a convolution-based smoothing procedure for the hinge loss function, resulting in a new loss function that is both convex and smooth. Subsequently, we introduce a generalized ADMM algorithm to solve the decentralized elastic-net penalized convoluted SVM efficiently. This generalized ADMM leverages a local majorization approximation, enabling each local update to have a closed-form solution, thereby significantly reducing computational costs.This efficiency is particularly critical in scenarios such as wireless sensing networks, where local nodes are often inexpensive, battery-powered, and computationally constrained.As demonstrated in , the convexity and smoothness of the smoothed loss ensure that the approximation does not impair convergence. In particular, we will show that the proposed optimization algorithm converges .
ai: The effort to tackle the decentralized penalized SVM problem, commonly referred to as problem (), encounters two primary hurdles. The first obstacle is the hinge loss function’s nonsmooth nature, which presents difficulties for the implementation of optimization methods reliant on gradients or Newton’s method. Secondly, the problem becomes even more complex with the elastic-net penalty, as this typically precludes the availability of a straightforward solution or closed-form in many cases. To effectively overcome these joint challenges, we introduce what we term a decentralized convoluted SVM, described extensively in subsequent sections. We commence by developing a novel convolution-based smoothing technique specifically for the hinge loss function, which transforms it into a novel loss function characterized by both convexity and smoothness. Following this, we present a generalized ADMM (Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers) strategy designed to efficiently address the decentralized elastic-net penalized convoluted SVM. This strategy employs a local majorization approximation approach, facilitating each local update to possess a closed-form solution and consequently substantially reducing computational expenses. This increase in computational efficiency is particularly crucial in environments like wireless sensing networks, where local computational units are typically low-cost, reliant on battery power, and have limited processing capabilities. As illustrated in , the features of convexity and smoothness intrinsic to the smoothed loss function ensure that the approximation process does not compromise the convergence of the algorithm. Specifically, it will be demonstrated that the proposed optimization algorithm reaches convergence.

human: We propose decentralized convoluted support vector machines for efficiently learning sparse classification rules over networks. By applying convolution to the non-smooth hinge loss, we transform it into a smooth and convex loss function. This modification facilitates the development of a linearly convergent algorithm with straightforward implementation, even when communication is constrained to local neighborhoods. Our work can be extended in three key directions. First, while the current approach focuses on the l 1 and elastic-net penalties, its inherent flexibility allows for the incorporation of general nonconvex penalties via a straightforward linear approximation (Zou andLi, 2008). Second, in many practical applications, a substantial amount of unlabeled auxiliary data is available. Leveraging these data has the potential to significantly improve classification accuracy. Third, an important direction for future research is the development of methods for conducting statistical inference on the learned classification rules.
ai: We introduce a novel approach utilizing decentralized convoluted support vector machines designed to effectively derive sparse classification rules across networked systems. By integrating convolution into the otherwise non-smooth hinge loss, we convert it into a loss function that is both smooth and convex. This transformation paves the way for devising an algorithm that achieves linear convergence and can be implemented with ease, even when communication is limited to interactions within local neighborhoods. Our research has room for expansion in three significant avenues. Firstly, although our current methodology is concentrated on the l 1 and elastic-net penalties, the model’s inherent adaptability allows for the integration of a wide range of general nonconvex penalties using a simple linear approximation, as demonstrated by Zou and Li in 2008. Secondly, in real-world scenarios, there is often a large pool of unlabeled auxiliary data available. Proper utilization of this data has the potential to markedly enhance the accuracy of our classification models. Lastly, a critical area for forthcoming research is the formulation of approaches for performing statistical inference on the classification rules that our methods develop.

human: Fairness of machine learning algorithms is receiving increasing attention, as such algorithms permeate the day-to-day aspects of our lives. One way in which bias can manifest in a dataset is through missing values. If data are missing, these data are often assumed to be missing completely randomly; in reality the propensity of data being missing is often tied to the demographic characteristics of individuals. There is limited research into how missing values and the handling thereof can impact the fairness of an algorithm. Most researchers either apply listwise deletion or tend to use the simpler methods of imputation (e.g. mean or mode) compared to the more advanced ones (e.g. multiple imputation); we therefore study the impact of the simpler methods on the fairness of algorithms. The starting point of the study is the mechanism of missingness, leading into how the missing data are processed and finally how this impacts fairness. Three popular datasets in the field of fairness are amputed in a simulation study. The results show that under certain scenarios the impact on fairness can be pronounced when the missingness mechanism is missing at random. Furthermore, elementary missing data handling techniques like listwise deletion and mode imputation can lead to higher fairness compared to more complex imputation methods like k-nearest neighbour imputation, albeit often at the cost of lower accuracy.
ai: The issue of fairness within machine learning algorithms is garnering increased scrutiny, as these algorithms are becoming integral to numerous facets of everyday life. A notable source of bias within datasets arises from missing values. Often, such absent data are presumed to be randomly missing; however, in truth, the likelihood of data omissions often correlates strongly with individuals’ demographic attributes. There remains a scarcity of research exploring the ways in which missing data and their subsequent treatment affect an algorithm’s fairness. Many researchers opt either for listwise deletion or simpler imputation methods, such as mean or mode imputation, over more sophisticated strategies like multiple imputation. Consequently, our investigation focuses on the effects that these more straightforward imputation methods have on algorithmic fairness. The investigation commences with an examination of the mechanisms of data absence and progresses through the process of handling missing data, culminating in an assessment of their impact on fairness. In a simulation study, three widely utilized datasets pertinent to fairness are artificially subjected to missingness. Our findings highlight that, in particular instances, the effect on fairness is distinctly noticeable when the missing data mechanism follows a “missing at random“ pattern. Additionally, basic handling techniques for missing data, like listwise deletion and mode imputation, may enhance fairness when contrasted with more intricate methods such as k-nearest neighbor imputation. Nevertheless, these simpler methods often achieve this increased fairness at the expense of reduced accuracy.

human: The pervasiveness of machine learning (ML) algorithms in our everyday lives is undeniable. The breadth of examples is substantial and includes algorithms used to award or deny bank loans, manage admission into educational institutions, considerably speed up the process of hiring and even aid law enforcement to decide the severity of sentencing of criminals joy, zlio, book. Some of the more seemingly innocuous examples include algorithms making movie recommendations, dating websites recommending a suitable partner choice for users and retail websites with shopping recommendations mehrabi, hardt, 2020bias.There are many worthwhile reasons for transferring some decisions from humans to computers: they are faster, they can deal with much larger amounts of information more efficiently and accurately, they do not get lazy or bored and overall, they reduce human error book, 2020bias, mehrabi. Despite these advantages, there are many instances where these algorithms have acted far from justly, with respect to certain sensitive or protected attributes such as race, sex or age. An example is the Correctional Offender Management Profiling for Alternative Sanctions (COMPAS) system, which is used by courts in the United States to assess the risk of re-offence, which gave higher risk values for black offenders and lower risk values for white offenders than their actual risk. Further examples include facial recognition software which has the lowest accuracy on females who are darker skinned, and the online advertisement platform Google Ads which showed considerably fewer advertisements for high-paying jobs to women than to men joy, 2020bias, mehrabi.One of the main reasons for the biased behaviour of algorithms is the quality of data they are trained on. Historic human biases for or against certain groups are inherent in many datasets. ML algorithms, which are designed to detect and learn patterns in data, exploit and can even amplify these patterns in making decisions.An important way in which bias manifests in a dataset is through the absence of certain fields or inputs. Missing data refers to those instances of data which contain fields which have not been captured or have been lost or deleted enders. If data are missing, these data are often assumed to be missing completely randomly, but usually this is not the case, and the propensity of data being missing is often tied to socio-economic status or demographic characteristics of individuals ugduck. For convenience sake but detrimentally, the way that data are missing is usually not taken into account before proceeding with the treatment of missing data missingmethodsprop.In practice, missing data is often dealt with in one of two ways before any statistical analysis can be performed. The first of these is listwise deletion (LD), which refers to complete removal of that instance of data which contains the missing fields. The second way is imputation, where at least one value is presented as a placeholder for the field where there is a missing value. Surprisingly, there is limited research on fairness of algorithms in the context of the above missing data considerations ugduck, zhanglong, wangsingh, caton, when it is plausible that missing data and bias of an algorithm are related ugduck. For example, if LD is implemented and there are many more observations with missing fields for one group over another, the algorithm might give more accurate predictions for the group with more remaining observations and perform comparatively worse for the other group. When applied in a real world context, these biased decisions could have a tangible impact on an individual joy, wmd, airbnb.The research field at the intersection of ML fairness and missing values is an important but relatively new one. In this work we address some foundational aspects of this research to complement existing work: we investigate the impact of missing data and missing data handling procedures on the fairness and accuracy of ML algorithms. We approach the problem starting from the issue of how the data are missing, i.e. the missing data mechanism (MDM), how the missing data are typically dealt with (i.e. LD and imputation) and how this impacts the fairness and accuracy. The simpler missing data handling methods (i.e. LD and single imputation methods such as mode imputation and regression imputation) are considered despite the existence of superior approaches like multiple imputation (MI), because the former continue to be used widely by researchers vim, missingmethodsprop. Our results show that simple methods like LD and mode imputation can lead to higher fairness in comparison to more complex methods like k-nearest neighbour () imputation, and the influence of the missing at random (MAR) MDM can be striking in certain situations.To this end, the remaining sections are organised as follows: In Section 2 we cover the relevant background material for fairness in ML and missing values. In Section 3 we present a literature review of the limited work which combines the two fields of fairness and missing values. In Section 4 the details of our experimental process are covered, while in Section 5 the results of the experiments are presented. We end with Section 6 which covers our conclusions and recommendations.
ai: The omnipresence of machine learning ML algorithms in our daily routines is indisputable. A wide array of instances exists, showcasing the applications of these algorithms in determining access to bank loans, orchestrating admissions to educational institutions, streamlining the hiring process, and even assisting law enforcement agencies in deciding on sentencing duration based on criminal actions. More benign examples include algorithms suggesting movies to watch, facilitating dating websites in matching users with potential partners, and recommending shopping items on retail platforms. There are numerous compelling reasons to transition some decision-making responsibilities from humans to computers: they operate at faster speeds, handle greater quantities of data with impressive efficiency, and make fewer mistakes, as they do not tire or lose focus. However, notwithstanding these benefits, there are numerous cases where these algorithms have acted unfairly, especially concerning sensitive attributes like race, gender, or age. A case in point is the Correctional Offender Management Profiling for Alternative Sanctions COMPAS utilized in U.S. courts for evaluating repeat-offender risks, which has been known to produce biased risk scores-showing higher risks for black individuals and lower for white individuals than their true risk levels. Moreover, automated facial recognition technologies often lack accuracy, especially for darker-skinned females, while Google’s advertising platform has reportedly displayed fewer high-paying job ads to women compared to men.One fundamental reason for the biased actions of algorithms lies in the data quality they are trained on. Many datasets inherently contain historical human biases for or against particular groups. ML algorithms, which are crafted to recognize and learn from data patterns, might leverage these biases, sometimes amplifying them in decision-making processes. Bias in datasets notably surfaces through the absence of specific inputs or fields-referred to as missing data, which could be randomly absent or, as is often the case, correlatively absent due to socioeconomic or demographic attributes. This problematic oversight is frequently ignored during the initiation of data treatment processes.In practical scenarios, handling missing data is approached primarily in two ways before statistical analysis occurs. The first method, listwise deletion LD, involves entirely discarding data instances with missing fields. The second, imputation, introduces at least one placeholder value for missing data fields. Surprisingly, there’s a scarcity of research concerning algorithmic fairness amidst such missing data considerations, despite the plausible linkage between lacking data and algorithm bias. For instance, if LD is employed and a disproportionate number of missing entries occur more in one group than another, it could erroneously elevate prediction accuracy for the group with more intact data, while yielding poorer outcomes for the group with increased omissions. When implemented in real-world scenarios, such biased decision-making processes can significantly affect individuals.The field of study united around the fairness of ML systems and the intricacies of missing data is crucial, albeit still relatively nascent. In this work, we delve into foundational elements of this research to augment existing knowledge: examining the influence of missing data and its handling on the fairness and accuracy of ML algorithms. Our exploration begins by investigating the missing data mechanism MDM and the common methods employed to manage it, such as LD and imputation, evaluating their implications for fairness and accuracy. While more sophisticated techniques such as multiple imputation MI exist, we also examine simpler methods given their prevalent usage. Our analysis reveals that basic approaches, like LD and mode imputation, can sometimes enhance fairness relative to more complex strategies like k-nearest neighbor (k-NN) imputation, particularly under the influence of the missing at random MAR MDM in some contexts. Hence, the paper is structured as follows: Section 2 discusses relevant background terms related to fairness in ML and missing data. Section 3 reviews existing literature that combines the concepts of fairness and missing data. Section 4 outlines the experimental methodology, and the findings are detailed in Section 5. Conclusions and recommendations are offered in Section 6.

human: Fairness (or bias) of algorithms in ML is quantified by statistical definitions of so called , which are based on subsetting the outcomes of an algorithm in various ways to allow the difference in treatment of one group over another to be measured.Broadly, there are two main categories of fairness metrics ven, zlio, verma, mehrabi, book, hardt:Group fairness metrics: They aim to ensure non-discrimination across groups based on sensitive variables.Individual fairness metrics: They aim to give similar classification to similar individuals, where similarity is quantified by a distance metric.The dominant research approach in fairness in ML involves group metrics, and so in this work we will only consider the group metrics and how they are influenced by missing values. Details of individual fairness approaches can be found in [Dwork et al. et al.(2012)Dwork, Hardt, Pitassi, Reingold Zemel].Before providing the definitions of the group metrics which we consider in this study, some notation is introduced. Without loss of generality we assume a binary classification situation. Let Y be the binary classification label taking values in {0, 1} where 1 is the positive outcome and 0 is the negative outcome. Considering the case of paying back a loan, an outcome of 1 would mean the loan was paid back in full. S is the binary sensitive or protected attribute where 1 is the privileged group and 0 is the unprivileged group. If S is the variable race, 1 could be assumed to correspond to white, and 0 to non-white, for example. Y ^ are the predicted outcomes from a classifier, which are class predictions in {0, 1}. We assume that S is fully observed, i.e. it contains no missing values.The group metrics can be divided into two broad categories: those based on predicted outcome only and those based on both predicted and actual outcomes.A measure that is based on the predicted outcome only is , which we denote as . This measure requires the probability for an individual to be assigned the favourable outcome to be equal across the privileged and unprivileged groups: Two instances of measures which are based on both predicted and actual outcomes are:, denoted , which requires equality of the true positive rate for both groups: , denoted , which requires equality of the false positive rate for both groups: We chose to focus on these three metrics as they are commonly studied in the fairness literature hardt, verma, mehrabi. Note that in practice, for the above metrics, the difference of the two terms in the equations is taken to give a value for the discrimination. Henceforth for ease of notation when we say , or in this article, we will be referring to this difference. For example, when we say we mean The smaller the value of the metric, the smaller the discrimination and hence the higher the fairness. We also note that a negative metric value means that we have ’positive discrimination’ in favour of the disadvantaged group. Other than the above mentioned three there also exist a variety of other group metrics book, zlio, which is beyond the scope of this study.

Consider the following example to aid in the understanding of the MDMs. Suppose our dataset contains the variables and , and we are interested in the probability of missingness in (we assume that there is no missingness in the variable).There are three MDMs: (MCAR): The probability of being missing is unrelated to the data. In the given example, the observed values of can be seen as a simple random sample of the complete variable. The missingness in does not depend on either or . (MAR): The missingness probability only depends on the observed information. In the given example, suppose that the variable has two categories: white and non-white. The probability of missingness in depends only on the respondent’s , for example non-whites are less likely to give their . human: : This method simply removes the entire observation that contains missing values for some predictors. It is one of the most frequently employed techniques to deal with missing data, used as the default method by many statistical software packages. The advantage of LD is that it is a straightforward convenient technique to use. Disadvantages are a reduction in sample size, and if data are not MCAR then it produces biased parameter estimates enders, kang.:The meaning of the term ’single’ here is that this imputation method generates a single replacement value per missing value. An advantage of imputation is the retention of those rows of data which contained missing values. Disadvantages are that most single imputation techniques produce biased parameter estimates and underestimate sampling error enders. Some popular single imputation techniques are::The mode of a variable is calculated on the available cases of the variable and used to impute its missing values.:In regression imputation a set of regression equations is estimated to predict the incomplete variables from the complete variables.: In imputation, we take the k most similar observations to the missing observation (where similarity is measured by a distance metric); then for a continuous variable you replace the missing value by the mean of the k nearest neighbours and the mode for a categorical variable knn.

Although there is limited literature that combines the research of fairness of ML algorithms and missing data, relevant aspects of these studies provide the basis of the research presented in this article.[Fernando et al. et al.(2021)Fernando, Cèsar, David José] aimed to shed light on how missing data and fairness are related, whether the subsamples with missing data are more unfair or less unfair, and whether LD or imputation is the more appropriate procedure to handle these values. Six benchmark datasets from the field of fairness in ML were used which contain missing values. Demographic parity is the only fairness metric used. The experiments consistently show that the smallest absolute value of the metric is found on the subsets of instances containing only the missing value rows. The authors conclude that this result implies that the rows with missing values are fairer than the rest. This interpretation could be misleading; the rows with missing data could potentially contain a higher proportion of individuals from both groups for whom the rate of favourable outcome is lower, as compared to in the full set or the set without the missing rows. This could have resulted in a smaller metric value on the missing data rows. Furthermore, the trade-off between fairness and accuracy is explored. Overall, lower fairness (and higher accuracy) was found for imputation compared to LD. The impact of the MDM on fairness was not explicitly investigated.The study in [Zhang Long(2021)] investigates the impact of missing data imputation methods on fairness metrics. Seven imputation methods are investigated: MICE, missForest, , two matrix completion methods (Soft-Impute and OptSpace), and two deep learning methods (Gain and Misgan). Most of these methods are state of the art and not widely known or used by practitioners. Their results are based on only one of the fairness benchmark datasets. They propose a novel notion for measuring the fairness of imputations, based on the imputation accuracy (which refers to the success of an imputation algorithm and is different from accuracy in the usual sense as a performance metric). The usefulness of this measure in regard to measuring fairness is unclear, as higher imputation accuracy does not necessarily mean higher fairness, especially if the dataset contains historic biases. The authors conclude that severe imputation unfairness exists among all the imputation methods, but the threshold of ’severe’ has not been defined, and is usually context dependent. It is also observed that imputation unfairness tends to grow as the missingness proportion increases and imbalance in the size of sensitive classes leads to imputation unfairness. Importantly, they observe that prediction fairness is linked to the MDM, and there is a trade-off between accuracy and fairness in prediction.A reweighting method for missing values in categorical predictors is considered by [Wang Singh(2021)]. The algorithm that is used as a starting point learns a probabilistic transformation to change feature value labels in the data to reduce discrimination, which is adapted with a reweighting scheme to account for missing values. Missingness is created according to the three MDMs in one of the categorical variables, but the specifications of the MDMs and variable selection are not provided. The empirical work is undertaken on two of the fairness benchmark datasets and one synthetic dataset. The authors analyse the impact of their reweighting scheme, different proportions of missingness and the three MDMs on accuracy and fairness. They conclude that the reweighting algorithm has very little impact on fairness for MCAR, whereas the biggest improvement in fairness is seen for MNAR. For MAR and MNAR the reweighting algorithm is able to mitigate the negative effects of the missing values on fairness with a small impact on accuracy.Finally, the work in [Caton et al. et al.(2022)Caton, Malisetty Haas] considers fairness and performance metrics on three benchmark datasets, after performing a variety of imputation methods. The variables as well as the number of variables where missing data is introduced are both randomly determined; only MCAR missingness is created. The distributions of the metrics are explored and it is concluded that the choice of imputation strategy and classification algorithm significantly affects both performance and fairness. However, the authors combine the results from all three datasets before presenting them, which could have masked the effects of the different combinations of classification algorithm and imputation method when these differ across the datasets. The authors also perform a 3-way ANOVA to determine if there is any effect of three categorical factors on fairness and performance: imputation strategy, classification algorithm and percentage of missing values. They find that the interaction effects between the imputation strategy and the classification algorithm are consistently significant. Hence they conclude that different imputation strategies affect the performance and fairness metrics differently depending on which classification algorithm is used.
ai: Despite the limited body of literature intersecting the realms of fairness in machine learning ML algorithms and handling missing data, certain essential aspects of existing studies ground the research discussed in this paper. Fernando et al. 2021 aimed to elucidate the relationship between missing data and fairness, specifically exploring whether datasets with missing information exhibit higher or lower levels of fairness and which method-listwise deletion LD or imputation-more suitably addresses these absent values. The study made use of six benchmark datasets from the ML fairness domain, all featuring missing values, with demographic parity employed as the sole fairness metric. Consistently across experiments, it was observed that subsets consisting solely of instances with missing data exhibited the smallest absolute metric value. The authors infer from this finding that datasets comprising missing values appear to be fairer. However, this conclusion might be misleading; missing data subsets could disproportionately represent individuals with lower favorable outcome rates from various groups, potentially explaining the diminished metric values observed. Moreover, the study delves into the balance between fairness and accuracy, revealing that imputation tends to yield less fairness (but greater accuracy) when compared to LD. Notably, the influence of the missing data mechanism MDM on fairness remains unexplored in this context.In contrast, the study conducted by Zhang Long 2021 takes a closer look at how different missing data imputation techniques impact fairness metrics. It evaluates seven approaches: Multiple Imputation by Chained Equations MICE, missForest, two matrix completion techniques (Soft-Impute and OptSpace), and two deep learning solutions (Gain and Misgan). While these methods represent cutting-edge advances, they have yet to gain widespread application among practitioners. Their conclusions are derived from only a single fairness benchmark dataset. A novel measure of imputation fairness is proposed, based on imputation accuracy, which differs from the traditional sense of accuracy as a performance metric. The utility of this measurement for assessing fairness remains questionable since higher imputation accuracy might not translate to increased fairness, especially in datasets plagued by historical biases. The authors observe significant unfairness across all imputation methods, though the definition of ’severe’ remains vague and tends to depend on context. Furthermore, they note that imputation unfairness escalates with higher proportions of missing data, and imbalances in sensitive class sizes can exacerbate this unfairness. Crucially, they find that prediction fairness correlates with MDM and highlight an intrinsic trade-off between prediction accuracy and fairness.Wang Singh 2021 introduces a reweighting approach for addressing missing values in categorical predictors. The initial algorithm employs a probabilistic transformation to modify feature labels, thus minimizing discrimination. This algorithm is then adapted with a reweighting mechanism to manage missing values. The researchers induce missingness based on three MDMs within a categorical variable, though specifics on the MDMs and variable selection remain unspecified. Empirical evaluations are conducted on two fairness benchmark datasets and a synthetic dataset. These evaluations assess the impact of their reweighting strategy, varying missingness proportions, and the three MDMs on accuracy and fairness. The findings suggest minimal effect on fairness for Missing Completely at Random MCAR, but notable improvements for Missing Not at Random MNAR. For both MAR (Missing at Random) and MNAR, the reweighting strategy effectively mitigates the adverse effects of missing data on fairness, exerting a minor impact on accuracy.Lastly, Caton et al. 2022 investigate fairness alongside performance metrics across three benchmark datasets following various imputation techniques. Both the variables and the instances with introduced missing data are randomly selected, exclusively creating MCAR missingness. Their exploration of metric distributions leads to the conclusion that the selection of imputation strategy and classification algorithm significantly affects both fairness and performance. However, their aggregation of results across all datasets before making conclusions may obscure the distinct effects of different combinations of imputation methods and classification algorithms. Crucially, a 3-way ANOVA is performed to test the effects of three categorical factors-imputation strategy, classification algorithm, and missing data percentage-on fairness and performance. Interaction effects between imputation strategies and classification algorithms consistently prove significant, leading the researchers to conclude that different imputation methods impact performance and fairness differently, contingent on the classification algorithm applied.

human: The aim of our study is to investigate the effects of both the MDM (MCAR, MAR or MNAR) and the simpler missing data handling methods (LD and single imputation methods) on fairness, and to understand the relationship between fairness and accuracy in this context. We first describe some ways in which our research departs from existing studies, followed by the experiments for this study.We investigate LD and the single imputation methods: mode imputation, regression imputation and imputation, and their effect on fairness and accuracy. The investigation in [Eekhout et al. et al.(2012)Eekhout, de Boer, Twisk, de Vet Heymans] shows that most studies (81%) used LD, 14% of studies used a single imputation technique and MI was used in 8% of the studies. Also, the study in [Kowarik Templ(2016)] reminds us that in a usual statistical analysis, it is often sufficient to generate a single complete dataset which is then used in subsequent analyses. Hence LD and single imputation still have importance in the missing data field. Similar to [Fernando et al. et al.(2021)Fernando, Cèsar, David José], the effect of LD and mode imputation on the fairness of ML models is studied, however, the context of the MDM is a core characteristic of our study.Missingness is created in variables which are strongly related to the sensitive variable, strongly related to the outcome variable or strongly related to both. When we refer to variable(s) being ’strongly related’ to another variable, this means strong in a relative sense to the other predictor variables in the dataset. We use random forest variable importance to choose variables in which missingness is created, by seeing how important they are for the outcome variable, the sensitive variable or both. Hence the variables in which missingness is created are chosen in a meaningful manner, which allows us to take the relationships between variables into account. This strategy is in contrast to previous studies zhanglong, caton, where the variables in which missingness was created were chosen at random or without any context. Missing data might not be evenly distributed between the privileged and unprivileged groups ugduck since disadvantaged individuals may intentionally omit information if they believe that a complete answer might lead to a discriminatory or unfair action. This could then lead to unfairness in the models fitted. In this study, the MAR missingness in a variable is created by dependence of missingness on the sensitive attribute; in particular we implement the assumption that observations from disadvantaged groups are more likely to contain missing values.In the research in [Zhang Long(2021)], missingness was generated in numerical variables only. We generate missingness in both numerical and categorical variables, up to two variables at a time, which is a more realistic scenario, especially for datasets in the field of fairness in ML. In such datasets there are often many categorical variables with missing values (as these are used to capture personal data) and this situation has not been studied in detail before ugduck, wangsingh.We now summarise our experimental process. We employ three of the most widely used datasets in the field of fairness in ML; these three datasets cover some pertinent real world fairness contexts: credit risk, the justice system and income level. We limit ourselves to three datasets because we create missingness in a meaningful manner, rather than at random or without any context, in order to incorporate the relationships between the variables into our analysis. This means understanding the datasets themselves in some detail. All experiments are done in R. We create missingness (’amputation’) in our datasets artificially according to the three MDMs. Following this, missing data are dealt with either by LD or by single imputation (mode, regression or ). Four types of ML models are trained on this data: logistic regression, random forests, boosting and support vector machine (), and the parameters of these models are tuned by cross-validation. Fairness metrics (, and ) and accuracy are calculated from the predictions on the test sets. Repeating these steps for a reasonable number of iterations gives us a distribution of fairness and accuracy values.Relevant details of the experiments are provided in the following sections.
ai: The primary goal of our research is to examine how different missing data mechanisms MDM-which include MCAR, MAR, or MNAR-alongside simpler techniques for handling missing data such as listwise deletion LD and single imputation methods, influence fairness. We also aim to understand how these aspects are intertwined with accuracy within this framework. To begin, we will delineate the ways in which our research diverges from previous studies, followed by a detailed account of our experimental procedures. Our investigation includes an analysis of LD as well as single imputation methods like mode imputation, regression imputation, and simple imputation, to assess their impact on both fairness and accuracy. The study conducted by Eekhout et al. 2012 reveals that LD is employed in a majority (81%) of cases, with a mere 14% utilizing single imputation techniques, and even fewer (8%) opting for Multiple Imputation MI. Similarly, the work by Kowarik and Templ 2016 underscores the practicality of generating just one complete dataset for standard statistical analysis, which underscores the continued relevance of LD and single imputation in the realm of missing data. Drawing a parallel with the study by Fernando et al. 2021, our focus on the effect of LD and mode imputation incorporates the specific context provided by various MDMs.In our exploration, missingness is deliberately introduced in variables that have a strong correlation, either with the sensitive variable, the outcome variable, or both. Here, the term ’strongly related’ is used in a relative context compared to other predictor variables within the dataset. We harness the random forest variable importance measure to discern which variables should have missing data introduced, thereby considering their importance to the outcome and sensitive variables. This method distinguishes our approach from prior studies like those by Zhang Long and Caton, where missingness was assigned to variables randomly, without strategic context. Missing data is often not homogeneously distributed between privileged and less privileged groups, as disadvantaged individuals might intentionally leave questions unanswered to avoid potentially discriminatory consequences. This behavior could contribute to unfairness in the resulting predictive models. In our study, a MAR missingness pattern is established where the likelihood of missing data is influenced by sensitive attributes, particularly with the presumption that individuals from disadvantaged groups exhibit a higher propensity for incomplete responses.Unlike Zhang Long 2021, who confined missingness generation to numerical variables exclusively, our study expands to include both numerical and categorical variables, selecting up to two at once. This approach mirrors a more realistic scenario, especially prevalent in datasets concerned with fairness in machine learning, where it is common to encounter numerous categorical variables with missing entries due to their role in capturing personal data-a scenario not extensively examined previously.The summary of our experimental approach is as follows: we utilize three predominantly regarded datasets pertinent to fairness in machine learning, encompassing critical real-world contexts like credit risk evaluation, justice systems, and income classifications. The deliberate, context-driven introduction of missingness necessitates a robust understanding of these datasets, hence our limitation to three. All analyses are conducted using R. By purposefully introducing missingness-or ’amputation’-based on the three MDM configurations, we subsequently address this through LD or single imputation (using mode, regression, or another method). Four machine learning models are trained on this modified data: logistic regression, random forests, boosting, and support vector machines, with all models fine-tuned through cross-validation. We evaluate the models using specific metrics for fairness and accuracy, gauged from predictions on test datasets. Reiterating this experiment across multiple iterations offers a comprehensive distribution of fairness and accuracy measurements. The subsequent sections will provide more in-depth information about the experimental methodologies.

All three datasets contain both numerical and categorical variables.The dataset gc classifies individuals described by a set of features as good or bad credit risks. The sensitive variables are (male, female) and (young, old). The outcome variable is (positive outcome: good, negative outcome: bad). It is a relatively small dataset containing no missing values, with 1000 observations and 20 predictor variables.The dataset adult contains information about individuals from the 1994 U.S. census. This publicly available dataset is published as a separated training and test set, which is combined into one dataset to allow for a new assignment of the subsets. The sensitive variables are (male, female) and (white, non-white). The outcome variable is whether an individual makes more or less than 50,000). It is a relatively large dataset with 13 predictors and 45222 observations remaining after the removal of 3620 missing value rows.The dataset compas refers to data collected about the use of the COMPAS risk assessment tool in Broward County, Florida. The outcome variable is indicating whether offenders were rearrested within two years after the first arrest. The positive outcome is not being rearrested.

human: In this section we try to determine whether the type of variable which contains missing values has an effect on fairness. Here we remind the reader that in this study missingness is created in variables which are strongly related to the outcome variable, strongly related to the sensitive variable or strongly related to both. The details are given in Section of this article.Note that for the COMPAS dataset, we only create missingness in variables that are strongly related to the sensitive attribute and outcome variable, as the variable importance analysis highlighted most of the same variables for either relationship separately. Hence in this section we only refer to the German and Adult dataset.In order to aid interpretation, for both datasets we firstly only focus on the boosting model results as there is not much difference in results between the classification models, and it is easier to see the overall fairness distribution trends for boosting as the variance is smaller and the distributions are more symmetric as compared to the other classification models. In this study, we aimed to understand the effects of missing data and missing data imputation techniques on the fairness of ML models. From the results obtained from our experiments, we can summarise the main findings of the study into the following points:The type of variable where missingness is present can influence the fairness distributions. In particular, when missingness is present in a variable strongly related to the outcome variable, the fairness distribution for MAR often stands out as compared to MCAR or MNAR, resulting in an average effect of the highest or lowest fairness.For LD, we often observe on average higher fairness and lower accuracy as compared to other combinations.For MAR missingness and mode imputation, we often observe that the fairness is higher on average as compared to other combinations.More complex imputation methods like often have the lowest fairness on average.A general recommendation to the reader is that care should be taken when choosing an imputation technique because it can influence fairness. We also note that even a simple imputation technique like mode imputation can be beneficial from the point of view of fairness, often without compromising the accuracy. Hence if fairness is a concern, such a technique may be employed without use of significant time or computational power, as compared to more advanced imputation techniques like , to avoid discarding valuable instances of data. The effect of LD on fairness does not appear to be seriously deleterious although this often comes at the cost of reduced accuracy. Given that LD leads to loss of data and can reduce statistical power enders, in accordance with fairness we would recommend that this technique be employed when the proportion of missing values is small.We also observe that the fairness distribution is particularly impacted when missingness is present in a variable strongly related to the outcome variable, whereas the effect is more subdued if the missingness is present in a variable strongly related to the sensitive attribute. This suggests that we should keep in mind the relationships between the variables in a dataset when it comes to handling the missing values. More care should perhaps be taken in the handling of the missing values when the variable with missingness is strongly related to the outcome variable.The missing data handling techniques (LD and single imputation) which were reviewed in this study require the MCAR MDM to produce unbiased parameter estimates but this restrictive constraint is unlikely to hold in practice enders. Interestingly, some of our main findings are highlighted in the context of MAR. While in a real world missingness situation it is not possible to ascertain that the MDM is MAR enders, our results highlight those scenarios where fairness is impacted in this context. Apart from the emphasis on MAR for certain situations, most of the results of the study were observed irrespective of the MDM underlying the missingness.As a direction of future research, we propose to conduct an analogous study to understand the impact of more advanced imputation methods such as MI on the fairness of ML algorithms, in order to establish whether there are improvements in fairness when applying MI over the simple approaches in the current study. Careful attention should be paid to the combination of the fairness metric estimates in the analysis and pooling phases of MI.

human: To construct a test which has level control at α , we rely on two bootstrap methods (permutations and wild bootstrap) introduced below, which are used to simulate values of the statistic under the null (either non-asymptotically or asymptotically).Using either of these methods, we can compute many bootstrapped statistics.The test can then be constructed either via the quantile point of view, or via the p-value point of view, which are equivalent (Kim and Schrab, 2023, Lemma 17).For the quantile case, the test threshold is set to be the -quantile of all the statistics (original and bootstrapped) which simulate the null, the test is then defined as rejecting the null if the test statistic is strictly larger than the test threshold.Equivalently, the p-value can be computed as the proportion of statistics (original and bootstrapped) which are smaller of equal to the original statistic (see Kim and Schrab, 2023, Equation 3 for a formal definition), the test is then defined as rejecting the null if the p-value is smaller or equal to α .These procedures result in a test with type I error exactly equal to α under mild conditions (Kim and Schrab, 2023, Lemma 15).
ai: To design a statistical test with control over its level at α, we employ two bootstrap methodologies-permutations and wild bootstrap-outlined below. These techniques help us replicate the distribution of the test statistic under the null hypothesis, either in a non-asymptotic or asymptotic manner. By utilizing either method, a multitude of bootstrapped statistics can be generated. The test itself can be formulated through two perspectives: the quantile approach or the p-value approach, both of which are equivalent as demonstrated by Kim and Schrab (2023, Lemma 17). In the quantile scenario, we determine the test threshold as the -quantile of the collective statistics, both original and bootstrapped, that simulate the null hypothesis. Consequently, the test leads to rejecting the null hypothesis if the actual test statistic exceeds this threshold. In parallel, the p-value can be determined as the fraction of statistics, both original and bootstrapped, that are less than or equal to the original statistic (refer to Kim and Schrab, 2023, Equation 3 for detailed formulation). The test then discards the null hypothesis if this p-value is less than or equal to α. human: A sample is said to be exchangeable if, for any permutation, the joint distribution over the permuted samples is equal to the joint distribution over the original samples.Some hypothesis testing problems can be framed as testing whether exchangeability holds (Lehmann and Romano, 2005, Chapter 15.2).Hence, the null hypothesis can be simulated by permuting samples, and the permutation test can then be constructed by following the above construction with randomly sampled permutations.The resulting test can then be guaranteed to control the type I error non-asymptotically at the desired level α (Romano and Wolf, 2005a, Lemma 1, see also Kim and Schrab, 2023, Lemma 15).As explained in , and , the two-sample and independence problems can be framed as testing for exchangeability, but the goodness-of-fit one cannot.
ai: A given sample is considered exchangeable if the joint probability distribution of the samples remains unchanged under any rearrangement or permutation of the sample order. The challenge in some hypothesis testing scenarios is to determine if this property of exchangeability is valid (as discussed by Lehmann and Romano in 2005, Chapter 15.2). Consequently, one can test the null hypothesis by rearranging the samples, whereupon constructing a permutation test is achieved through this method by randomly selecting permutations. Such a test ensures control over the type I error rate, adhering to the specified level α, and does so without relying on asymptotic properties (see Romano and Wolf, 2005a, Lemma 1, along with Kim and Schrab, 2023, Lemma 15, for more details). As outlined in various discussions and explanations, problems such as the two-sample and independence problems can be approached by testing for exchangeability; however, this methodology does not apply to the goodness-of-fit problem, which cannot be reframed in this manner.

human: The computational complexities of the tests based on either permutations or wild bootstrap are of the order of the cost of computing the statistic times the number of bootstrapped statistics.It is common to use a large number of bootstrapped statistics ( e.g. e.g., 500, 1000, 2000) but this is not necessary: our results ( e.g. e.g., Kim and Schrab, 2023, Theorem 7) require only 192 of them (for ), and Domingo-Enrich et al. Our findings, for instance, as demonstrated by Kim and Schrab (2023, Theorem 7), indicate that only 192 bootstrapped statistics are needed. Furthermore, Domingo-Enrich et al. For further elaboration on this methodological requirement, refer to Biggs et al., 2023, Section 3. In situations where the parameter k is aligned with selecting a kernel, a typical strategy involves utilizing a collection of kernels, as outlined by Schrab (2025b, Equation 81). This collection often comprises Gaussian and Laplace kernels, with ten distinct bandwidths engineered to cover the spectrum of inter-sample distances. Notably, this selection is conducted in a permutation-invariant fashion, ensuring that it remains unbiased by the data. Consequently, employing multiple testing procedures enables the test to adapt flexibly to various kernel choices.

In scenarios involving multiple tests, we declare the null hypothesis rejected if any one of those tests indicates a rejection. The likelihood of this occurrence, assuming the null hypothesis, can be managed by implementing a union bound. ai: The Bonferroni correction represents an extremely conservative approach, applicable even when all rejection events are distinct and separate, making the union bound exact. However, this is not the situation here, as the rejection events are expected to have significant overlap, such as applying the same test with varying kernels. Consequently, the stringent nature of the Bonferroni correction can be refined to retain type I error control at the α level. This refinement is achievable through the use of an aggregation method (Romano and Wolf, 2005a, b; Schrab et al., 2023), which estimates the most extensive adjusted level α P between the existing level and α itself for the defined data distribution. This ensures that the multiple testing procedure adequately controls the level at α. This control applies where a permuted variant of P is positioned within P 0, indicative of testing for exchangeability under the null hypothesis. In this situation, given certain regularity conditions in the null space P 0, it can be suggested that this holds true for all involved, implying that we have the potential for complete reliability. The probability P within this framework can be effectively calculated using a Monte Carlo approach by permuting samples (or alternatively, through a wild bootstrap), and the maximum in this instance can be identified through a bisection method. According to Schrab et al. (2023, Proposition 8), the aggregation level control remains intact, even when these estimated values are used, in a non-asymptotic context. As a result, this aggregation procedure generates the most powerful multiple testing approach while still managing type I error at the α level. This procedure consistently surpasses those utilizing the Bonferroni correction since α P is always at least equal to α. Furthermore, it allows for the assignment of unique weights w k (summing to a value no greater than one) to each kernel within the level correction u. For extensive details on implementation, refer to Schrab et al. (2023, Algorithm 1 and Section 3.5). From the perspective of p-values, the aggregation method can be connected to the approach of Shah and Bühlmann 2018; however, more expansive exploration of these relationships is reserved for further research.

(2023).The collection of kernels can be taken to be the same as the aforementioned one used for aggregation ( e.g. e.g., Schrab, 2025b, Equation 81).To conclude, adaptive tests can be constructed either via aggregation or via kernel pooling.

The kernel set can mirror the previously mentioned aggregate set, as indicated, for instance, in Schrab, 2025b, Equation 81. In summary, adaptive tests can be formulated either through aggregation techniques or through the process of kernel pooling.

human: The kernel tests with complete estimators run in quadratic time, which can be prohibitive for very large datasets.As such, it can be interesting to construct tests with lower computational complexity.Typical approaches to reduce runtimes include relying on Nyström approximation (Zhang et al., 2018; Cherfaoui et al., 2022) or on random Fourier features (Zhang et al., 2018; Zhao and Meng, 2015; Chwialkowski et al., 2015).Domingo-Enrich et al. (2023) propose another interesting approach to constructing an efficient MMD test by relying on kernel thinning (Dwivedi and Mackey, 2021) which still achieves the minimax separation in the kernel metric for alternatives with a certain decay.We choose to focus instead on incomplete statistics, introduced in details in Schrab (2025b, Section 3), and to study the trade-off between computational efficiency and test power via uniform separation rates.
ai: Kernel tests that utilize complete estimators typically operate with quadratic time complexity, which can become a substantial barrier when dealing with very large datasets. Because of this, exploring methods that offer reduced computational demands becomes an attractive avenue of research. Some of the conventional strategies employed to curtail execution times involve the use of Nyström approximation (as discussed by Zhang et al. in 2018 and Cherfaoui et al. in 2022) or the application of random Fourier features (as described by Zhang et al. in 2018, Zhao and Meng in 2015, and Chwialkowski et al. in 2015). An alternative and intriguing technique is presented by Domingo-Enrich et al. 2023, who suggest formulating an efficient Maximum Mean Discrepancy MMD test through the use of kernel thinning, a concept explored in depth by Dwivedi and Mackey in 2021. This method retains the ability to achieve minimax separation within the kernel metric for alternatives that exhibit a certain decay pattern. Instead, our research is directed towards investigating incomplete statistics, which are elaborated comprehensively in Schrab’s 2025b work, specifically in Section 3. Our aim is to explore the balance or trade-off between computational efficiency and the power of the test by examining uniform separation rates.

human: In practice, hypothesis tests are often used on sensitive data such as medical records, personally identifiable information, facial recognition, etc etc. (Apple, 2017; Erlingsson et al., 2014; Ding et al., 2017; see Kim and Schrab, 2023, Section 1 for further relevant discussions and references).This can cause privacy issues, to address this we design differentially private tests which guarantee user privacy.A randomised test ( e.g. e.g., using some random noise) is said to be -differentially private (Dwork et al., 2014) if for any two datasets X n and X n differing only in one entry, for and , and where the probability is taken with respect to the randomness of the test ( i.e. i.e., not with respect to the data).See Kim and Schrab (2023, Definition 1) for a more general definition.Intuitively, differential privacy guarantees that the probability of a given test output remains roughly the same when the data of a single user is modified, hence guaranteeing user privacy.We propose a procedure in Kim and Schrab (2023, Algorithm 1) to privatise any permutation test by relying on the Laplace mechanism (see Kim and Schrab, 2023, Definition 3) to inject noise in every permuted statistic.A naive application of the Laplace mechanism would see the Laplacian noise scale linearly with the number of permutations and would render the test obsolete.Instead, we prove in Kim and Schrab (2023, Theorem 2) that differential privacy can still be guaranteed when the noise is scaled only by a small factor of 2 (independent of the number of permutations).By deriving tight upper bounds on the global sensitivity of the MMD and HSIC V-statistics (Kim and Schrab, 2023, Lemmas 5 and 6), we can leverage our privatisation procedure to construct -differentially private dpMMD and dpHSIC tests (Kim and Schrab, 2023, Sections 4.1 and 4.2).
ai: In real-world scenarios, hypothesis testing is frequently applied to sensitive data, including medical records, personally identifiable information, and facial recognition data, among others (see Apple, 2017; Erlingsson et al., 2014; Ding et al., 2017 for examples; for more detailed discussions and additional references, refer to Kim and Schrab, 2023, Section 1). This practice raises significant privacy concerns. To mitigate these issues, we have developed differentially private tests that are designed to ensure user privacy. A randomized test (such as one incorporating random noise) achieves the status of ε-differentially private (Dwork et al., 2014) if the conditions hold for any two datasets X n and (X n’) differing by just a single entry, and where the probability measure considers the randomness inherent in the test (hence disregarding randomness in the data itself). For a broader definition, consult Kim and Schrab (2023, Definition 1). The essence of differential privacy is that the likelihood of a particular test outcome should remain essentially unchanged even when a single user’s data is altered, thereby ensuring privacy protection. In our work (Kim and Schrab, 2023, Algorithm 1), we introduce a method to privatize any permutation test by employing the Laplace mechanism (outlined in Kim and Schrab, 2023, Definition 3) to infuse noise into each permuted statistic. A straightforward application of the Laplace mechanism would involve scaling the Laplacian noise proportionate to the number of permutations, which would render the test ineffective. Nevertheless, in Kim and Schrab (2023, Theorem 2), we demonstrate that it is possible to maintain differential privacy by scaling the noise with a modest factor of 2, regardless of the number of permutations. By calculating precise upper bounds on the global sensitivity for MMD and HSIC V-statistics (as discussed in Kim and Schrab, 2023, Lemmas 5 and 6), we can apply our privacy procedure to devise ε-differentially private dpMMD and dpHSIC tests (explored in Kim and Schrab, 2023, Sections 4.1 and 4.2).

human: Another practical problem is the one of corrupted data, in real-world applications it is often the case that a portion of the data does not actually follow the distributions we would like to test ( e.g. e.g., fake data, adversarially corrupted data, etc etc.).In some cases, these outliers are actually important and we want the tests to able to detect them.In other cases, these are just noise that we wish to be robust against in order to test the real problem.The aim of robust testing is then to test the null hypothesis when at most r samples have been corrupted, possibly in an adversarial manner (this setting is more general than Huber’s contamination model).That is, the new ’robust null hypothesis’ is that the condition H 0 holds for at least of the N samples, where the robustness parameter r is specified by the user in advance depending on the testing setting and the amount of robustness required.See Schrab and Kim (2025, Section 2.1) for details on the robust testing framework.While we show that differentially private tests with adjusted level can be robust (Schrab and Kim, 2025, Algoritm 2), our main contribution is to propose a new procedure to robustify any permutation test (Schrab and Kim, 2025, Algoritm 1) by adding a factor of to the rejection threshold ( i.e. i.e., quantile obtained using permutations), where Δ is the global sensitivity of the test statistic (Kim and Schrab, 2023, Definition 2).Using these procedures,robust two-sample and independence tests, dcMMD and dcHSIC, can be constructed, which are robust up to r corruption.
ai: One of the significant challenges encountered in practical applications relates to the issue of corrupted data. In many real-world scenarios, we find that a segment of the data deviates from the distributions we intend to examine. This could be due to the presence of fake data, adversarially manipulated data, among other distortions. In certain instances, these anomalies are crucial, and our tests should be capable of identifying them. Conversely, there are situations where these anomalies are merely noise, and it is preferable for the tests to maintain robustness against them, allowing us to focus on the actual problem at hand.The primary goal of robust testing, therefore, is to evaluate the null hypothesis under circumstances where up to r data samples might have been altered, possibly through adversarial means. This framework is broader than the traditional Huber’s contamination model. Essentially, the ’robust null hypothesis’ asserts that the null condition, denoted as H0, holds true for a minimum of the N samples. Here, the robustness parameter r is predetermined by the user, tailored to the specific testing scenario and the level of robustness desired. For an in-depth exploration of this robust testing framework, refer to Schrab and Kim (2025, Section 2.1).While it is demonstrated that differentially private tests with an appropriate adjustment to their level can achieve robustness (as shown in Schrab and Kim, 2025, Algorithm 2), our principal innovation is the introduction of a novel procedure designed to enhance any permutation test’s robustness (Schrab and Kim, 2025, Algorithm 1). This is achieved by incorporating a factor into the rejection threshold, which is essentially the quantile derived from permutations. The factor Δ represents the global sensitivity of the test statistic as defined in Kim and Schrab (2023, Definition 2). Using these methodologies, it is feasible to construct robust two-sample and independence tests, specifically, dcMMD and dcHSIC, which exhibit robustness in the face of up to r corrupted data points.

human: Two-sample testing can be framed as testing for exchangeability ( ).Permuted two samples are constructed by, first, combining the two original samples, permuting all the elements, and then splitting them again into two separate samples (of the original sample sizes).Samples which come from the same distribution ( i.e. i.e., null hypothesis) are exactly the ones which are exchangeable.Indeed, it is clear that null samples, which are i.i.d., are exchangeable.Under the alternative, both permuted samples can be seen as drawn i.i.d. from a mixture of the two distinct distributions, this shows that the original and permuted samples do not have the same distribution ( i.e. i.e., samples are not exchangeable).Hence, two-sample testing corresponds to testing for exchangeability, and the two-sample null hypothesis can be simulated using permutations.
ai: Two-sample testing can be conceptualized as examining the principle of exchangeability. This process begins by first amalgamating the two original datasets, randomly rearranging all the entries, and subsequently redistributing them into two new samples, each retaining the original sample sizes. When samples derive from an identical distribution-embodying the null hypothesis-they exhibit exchangeability. Clearly, under conditions where samples are identically and independently distributed (i.i.d.), said samples are interchangeable in nature. Conversely, when considering the alternative hypothesis, both permuted samples emerge as independently and identically distributed from a composite of the two distinct original distributions. This scenario highlights a disparity in the distribution between the initial and permuted samples, signaling that they are, in fact, not exchangeable. Thus, two-sample testing essentially equates to assessing the criterion of exchangeability, wherein the null hypothesis of two independent samples can be effectively modeled through the use of permutations.

2503.07084.section: Solving the independence problem with a two-sample test.
human: Consider the independence testing problem where we are given paired samples drawn i.i.d. from a joint distribution P .Note that the samples and naturally come from the marginals P X and P Y , by pairing them randomly we can obtain samples from the product of the marginals .Since we are interested in testing for independence, i.e. i.e., whether the joint is equal to the product of marginals, it is possible to tackle this with a two-sample test with the first sample being sampled from the joint, and the second being sampled from the product of marginals.However, to run a two-sample test, it is crucial that the two samples are independent from each other.For this reason, we must split the paired samples into two separate paired samples (most likely of the same size), one which is left as is ( i.e. i.e., sampled from the joint), and the other which is randomly shuffled ( i.e. i.e., sampled from the product of marginals).Running a two-sample test on these two samples then solves the independence problem.Solving the independence problem in such a way using a two-sample test is, however, far from optimal due to the signal loss incurred as the potential dependence in the data is being ignored for half of it.This justifies the need for metrics and tests specifically designed for the independence problem, such as the HSIC.While the HSIC metric is equal to the MMD metric between the joint and the product of marginals (see paragraph ’HSIC as an MMD’ in Schrab, 2025b, Section 2.2), its estimator as a fourth-order statistic is more complex than using an MMD estimator on paired data as described above, and exploits all the data and signal available (Schrab, 2025b, Equation 21).

2503.07084.section: Solving the goodness-of-fit problem with a two-sample test.
human: Consider the goodness-of-fit problem where we are given i.i.d. samples from Q and a model distribution P from which we can draw samples ( i.e. i.e., via a simulator).Then, a two-sample test can be performed to solve this goodness-of-fit problem.If an MMD estimator is computed with a Stein kernel (Schrab, 2025b, Equation 43), as the model sample size grows to infinity, the MMD estimator converges to the KSD estimator.Indeed, the terms involving the model samples in the MMD estimator approximate kernel expectations under the model, which are zero by Stein’s identity, the term involving only the samples from Q is the KSD estimator itself.However, this only works when one is able to sample from the model, which is not the setting we consider here ( i.e. i.e., access only to the model score function).
ai: Let’s delve into the goodness-of-fit problem where we have independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) samples drawn from a distribution Q and are also provided with a model distribution P that allows us to generate samples, typically through a simulator. In this context, one way to tackle the goodness-of-fit dilemma is by implementing a two-sample test. When using a Maximum Mean Discrepancy MMD estimator with a Stein kernel, as detailed in Schrab’s 2025 study, specifically in Equation 43, an interesting phenomenon occurs: as the number of model samples approaches infinity, the MMD estimator begins to align with the Kernelized Stein Discrepancy KSD estimator. This convergence is rooted in the fact that the segments of the MMD estimator pertaining to the model samples serve to estimate kernel expectations under the model. According to Stein’s identity, these expectations equate to zero, which leaves the estimator based solely on Q’s samples to align perfectly with the KSD estimator.It is crucial to note, however, that this method assumes the feasibility of drawing samples directly from the model itself. The current context deviates from this assumption since our setup restricts access merely to the model’s score function, lacking the ability to sample directly from P.

2503.07084.section: Solving the two-sample problem with a goodness-of-fit test.

human: In the two-sample and independence cases, the validity of the tests using kernel pooling with a wild bootstrap is guaranteed due to the correspondence of the wild bootstrap to a subgroup of permutations (Schrab et al., 2023, Appendix B and Schrab et al., 2022b, Appendix F.1).Hence, the permutation validity guarantees (holding for any statistic) can be leveraged using a pooled statistic, even for the wild bootstrap.However, in the goodness-of-fit setting this correspondence is broken and permutations cannot be used.In order to prove that the KSD test using kernel pooling controls the level as desired, we need to show that the asymptotic distributions of the pooled KSD estimator and pooled wild bootstrap estimator are matching.By linearity of the wild bootstrap statistic with respect to the kernel, and the fact that the original and wild bootstrap KSD estimators with the mean kernel have the same asymptotic distributions (Chwialkowski et al., 2014, Theorem 1), Cramér-Wold Theorem guarantees that the joint distribution of the wild bootstrap KSD statistics for all kernels in the collection is asymptotically the same as the joint distribution of the KSD statistics for all the kernels.Then, the continuous mapping theorem (with continuous mean/max/fuse functions) guarantees that the pooled KSD wild bootstrap and original estimators have the same asympotitic distribution, and, hence,asymptotic type I error control is guaranteed for KSD tests using a kernel pooling method.

Thereafter, the continuous mapping theorem, incorporating continuous mean, maximum, and fusion functions, ensures that both the pooled KSD wild bootstrap and the original estimators exhibit equivalent asymptotic distributions.
