human: Collecting labeled data for machine learning models is often expensive and time-consuming. Active learning addresses this challenge by selectively labeling the most informative observations, but when initial labeled data is limited, it becomes difficult to distinguish genuinely informative points from those appearing uncertain primarily due to noise. Ensemble methods like random forests are a powerful approach to quantifying this uncertainty but do so by aggregating all models indiscriminately. This includes poor performing models and redundant models, a problem that worsens in the presence of noisy data. We introduce UNique Rashomon Ensembled Active Learning (), which selectively ensembles only distinct models from the Rashomon set, which is the set of nearly optimal models. Restricting ensemble membership to high-performing models with different explanations helps distinguish genuine uncertainty from noise-induced variation. We show that achieves faster theoretical convergence rates than traditional active learning approaches and demonstrates empirical improvements of up to 20% in predictive accuracy across five benchmark datasets, while simultaneously enhancing model interpretability.
ai: Acquiring labeled data necessary for training machine learning algorithms is frequently a costly and time-intensive endeavor. Active learning seeks to tackle this issue by concentrating on labeling the observations that provide the most insight. However, when the amount of initially labeled data is scant, it becomes a formidable task to separate truly informative data points from those that merely seem uncertain due to noise. Ensemble techniques, such as random forests, offer a robust way to assess this uncertainty, but they do so by combining outputs from all models indiscriminately, including those that underperform or are redundant. This issue is exacerbated in datasets laden with noise. To address these challenges, we propose the UNique Rashomon Ensembled Active Learning UNREAL, a method that intelligently selects models by choosing only the distinct ones from the Rashomon set-a collection of nearly optimal models. By confining the ensemble to high-quality models that offer diverse explanations, we enhance the ability to differentiate between true uncertainty and noise-induced discrepancies. Our findings reveal that UNREAL attains quicker theoretical convergence than conventional active learning methods and achieves empirical enhancements in predictive accuracy of up to 20% when tested on five prominent benchmark datasets. Additionally, UNREAL notably contributes to improving the interpretability of models.

human: Collecting labeled data to train data-hungry modern artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) models can be expensive or time-consuming. This challenge arises in a wide range of applications: image labeling (Zhu & Bento, 2017; Huijser & van Gemert, 2017), sentence classification (Schumann & Rehbein, 2019), and verbal autopsy (Setel et al., 2007; McCormick et al., 2016; Jha et al., 2019; Fan et al., 2024). In such scenarios, strategically determining which observations are most informative for model training will greatly reduce data redundancy and improve the model’s ability to generalize from limited data.

In these contexts, making strategic choices about which observations to prioritize can substantially minimize data overlap, thereby enhancing the model’s capacity to deduce insights from a more concise data set.

human: To address time and budget constraints, active learning provides a framework where observations are adaptively and strategically selected for labeling based on their potential informativity. The key task in active learning is choosing the most informative observations that will enhance the predictive quality of the model when labeled. However, this selection process faces a fundamental challenge: with limited labeled data initially available, how can we confidently identify truly informative observations rather than noise?

This selection hinges on the potential informativeness of the observations. At the heart of active learning lies the critical task: determining which observations, when labeled, will most significantly boost the model’s predictive accuracy. Yet, this task encounters a principal difficulty: given the initial scarcity of labeled data, how can we reliably pinpoint observations that are genuinely informative as opposed to merely being background noise?

human: Amongst the many metrics of informativity, Lewis & Gale (1994); Freund et al. (1997); Roy & McCallum (2001), uncertainty is the most commonly employed (Liu et al., 2022). One particularly effective approach to quantifying uncertainty is through query-by-committee (QBC), where multiple models form a committee whose disagreement in predictions indicates which observations are most uncertain and therefore informative to label. Ensemble methods such as random forests are especially well-suited for active learning with QBC techniques (Freund et al., 1997; Melville & Mooney, 2004) as their weak learners naturally form a diverse committee. This diversity is crucial as it incorporates different explanations of the data into the committee, with disagreement among ensemble members then serving as a direct measure of uncertainty and informativity (Dagan & Engelson, 1995; Kee et al., 2018).
ai: In the realm of informativity metrics, uncertainty is recognized as the most frequently utilized, as showcased in numerous studies such as those by Lewis & Gale 1994, Freund et al. 1997, and Roy & McCallum 2001 (Liu et al., 2022). A notably effective strategy for assessing uncertainty involves the query-by-committee QBC framework. This method operates by assembling multiple models into a committee, and the degree to which these models’ predictions differ reveals the observations that are most uncertain and thus most valuable to label for further analysis. Ensemble methodologies, specifically random forests, are particularly adept when employing QBC in active learning scenarios (Freund et al., 1997; Melville & Mooney, 2004) because they inherently comprise weak learners that contribute to a diverse committee composition. Such diversity is essential as it introduces a variety of data interpretations within the committee, with the resultant disagreements among the ensemble’s constituents providing a tangible measure of uncertainty and informativity (Dagan & Engelson, 1995; Kee et al., 2018).

human: While ensemble methods offer a natural way to quantify uncertainty through the diversity of multiple learners (models), ensemble methods tend to aggregate over the space of models, even if some of the models may have relatively poor accuracy. While some approaches such as Bayesian model averaging account for this by weighting the models by how likely they are given the data (Hoeting et al., 1999b), having a large number of mediocre models can make such weighting approaches difficult, especially in cases of limited, high-dimensional, or noisy data (Graefe et al., 2015).
ai: Ensemble methods inherently provide a structured approach for assessing uncertainty as they leverage the diversity present across several models or learners. However, these techniques often perform aggregation across the entirety of the model space, including models that may not demonstrate high accuracy. Although Bayesian model averaging techniques address this issue by assigning weights to models based on their posterior probabilities derived from the data (Hoeting et al., 1999b), employing such weighting strategies becomes particularly challenging. This is especially true when dealing with a substantial number of subpar models, or in scenarios characterized by sparse, high-dimensional, or noisy datasets (Graefe et al., 2015).

human: This challenge is further exacerbated in the presence of label noise, which although common in realistic settings, is well-known to be detrimental to active learning strategies (Willett et al., 2005). Active learning strategies, designed to prioritize querying points where models are most uncertain, may overfit to noisy labels instead of focusing on true areas of uncertainty. This challenge makes incorporating a diverse set of explanations among committee members even more crucial.

Such noise, although frequently encountered in real-world environments, is recognized for its detrimental impact on active learning methodologies (as noted by Willett et al., 2005). However, when confronted with noisy labels, there is a tendency for models to fit these inaccuracies too closely instead of concentrating on genuine areas of ambiguity. This predicament underscores the vital importance of integrating a broad array of explanatory perspectives among the members of the committee.

human: To address these limitations, we propose an algorithm that enhances active learning by restricting aggregation to a subset of well-performing and high-evidence models known as the Rashomon set. Importantly, in the presence of label noise, the Rashomon set naturally expands to encompass a more diverse set of valid explanations, providing a principled way to capture and utilize the inherent ambiguity in noisy data. By ensembling the models within the Rashomon set, which is the set of nearly optimal models, our approach ensures that the active learning process is driven by models with high evidence while accounting for noise through multiple diverse yet equally valid explanations of the data.

By creating an ensemble of models from this Rashomon set, which comprises nearly optimal models, our methodology guarantees that the active learning mechanism is propelled by models backed by substantial evidence. Additionally, it accommodates data noise by integrating multiple varied yet equally plausible data interpretations.

human: Throughout the paper, we rely on tree-based models. These models partition the feature space into groups with similar outcomes. Tree-based models are widely used in practice and have been extensively explored, particularly in combination with a sparsity requirement, in the context of Rashomon sets. However, a common and widely known issue with tree-based models is that multiple trees can represent the same partition.

Extensively studied in practical applications, tree-based models are often explored alongside a sparsity condition, especially when considering Rashomon sets. A notable and well-documented limitation of these models, however, is the fact that various different trees can ultimately depict identical partitions.

human: The multiplicity of trees creates two distinct challenges. First, it means that more complex partitions are more likely to appear in the Rashomon set simply by chance (because as the complexity of the partition increases, there are more possible trees that represent the same partition). A similar issue occurs in discrete Bayesian model averaging with uniform priors over models-there are more medium sized models, so the “flat“ prior actually strongly favors models of a particular size. Second, the multiplicity of trees means that approaches that sample from the space of trees expend additional, unnecessary, computational cycles evaluating redundant trees. This issue arises because trees enforce an ordering, or hierarchy among variables that have no natural order. Venkateswaran et al. (2024) address this issue by using a Hasse diagram, which, unlike trees, is a geometric object compatible with partially ordered sets.

Secondly, due to the multitude of trees, methodologies that involve sampling from the vast space of trees end up needlessly engaging in extra computational efforts to assess redundant trees. This problem is rooted in the nature of trees, which impose an order or hierarchy on variables that fundamentally lack any inherent sequence. Addressing this dilemma, Venkateswaran and colleagues in their 2024 study propose the use of a Hasse diagram. Unlike trees, a Hasse diagram serves as a geometric structure that aligns well with partially ordered sets, providing a more fitting framework.

This Rashomon-based method, titled UNique Rashomon Ensembled Active Learning (), ensures that the ensemble incorporates the interpretability of weak learners by only including the set of unique and diverse explanations. Simulations on five benchmark datasets demonstrate improvements in prediction accuracy compared to standard approaches.

human: When constructing machine learning models, researchers face two distinct types of uncertainty. The first originates from the variability in the predicted outcomes generated by a given model, often referred to as a model’s . The second originates from selecting the right model from a vast and diverse hypothesis space, a phenomenon known as . This distinction, originally articulated by economist Kenneth Arrow in 1951, separates the uncertainty of prediction from a given model from the uncertainty of choosing among many plausible models (Arrow, 1951).
ai: In the realm of building machine learning models, researchers encounter two separate forms of uncertainty. The first type arises from the fluctuations in the predictions that a particular model can produce, commonly known as the model’s inherent uncertainty. The second type stems from the challenge of picking the most appropriate model from a wide-ranging and varied set of possible hypotheses. This aspect is usually referred to as model selection uncertainty. The distinction between these two forms of uncertainty was first delineated by economist Kenneth Arrow back in 1951. He clearly distinguished between the unpredictability associated with forecasts made by a specific model and the uncertainty involved in selecting from among multiple potential models (Arrow, 1951).

human: Many modern machine learning approaches have become extremely good at reducing intrinsic risk within a model, but often fail to fully account for model ambiguity. Methods such as LASSO search for a single optimal model and conclusions tend by drawn based on the sole optimal model. This ignores any potential for model ambiguity, as there may in fact exist many models with similar predictive power for a given dataset (Rudin et al., 2024). On the other hand, ensemble methods such as Bayesian Model Averaging (Hoeting et al., 1999b) aggregate models across the full space of models, but this involves soliciting input from many models that are implausible given the observed data (Hoeting et al., 1999a). To choose either of these approaches, an analyst would need to have extreme preferences. Choosing a single model indicates absolutely no aversion to ambiguity in the model, whereas averaging over all models (even those that look exceedingly unlikely given the data at hand) would indicate an extreme aversion to the possibility of selecting the wrong model.
ai: A wide array of contemporary machine learning techniques excel at minimizing intrinsic risk within models, yet they often fall short when it comes to thoroughly addressing model uncertainty. Approaches like LASSO strive to pinpoint a singular, optimal model, leading analysts to draw conclusions reliant on this one optimal representation. This process neglects the existence of any ambiguity in modeling, despite the real possibility that numerous models could yield comparable predictive efficacy for the same dataset (Rudin et al., 2024). Similarly, ensemble methods, such as Bayesian Model Averaging as discussed by Hoeting et al. 1999b, combine predictions from an entire spectrum of models. However, this method invites input from numerous models that might not even make sense given the actual data (Hoeting et al., 1999a). Hence, adopting either method demands polarized preferences from analysts. Opting for a single model suggests a complete disregard for potential model ambiguity, while embracing all models indiscriminately-even those that seem implausible with the available data-implies an overwhelming concern for making an erroneous model choice.

human: The Rashomon Effect posits the existence of near-optimal models that have similarly high predictive performance, but arrive at predictions in different and diverse ways. This phenomenon exposes a core issue in the current machine learning paradigm: reliance on a single predictive model is overly sensitive to specific data patterns and conceals the potential existence of alternative equally valid explanations (Semenova et al., 2022; Rudin et al., 2024).

This effect highlights a fundamental problem within today’s machine learning landscape: depending on a singular predictive framework makes the model overly contingent on particular data configurations and hides the possibility of other equally plausible interpretations (Semenova et al., 2022; Rudin et al., 2024).

human: To quantify the impact of Rashomon Effect, we introduce the Rashomon set.

human: Intuitively, the Rashomon set is the set of all plausible models that come within an ε distance of the empirical risk minimizer. By enumerating the Rashomon set, researchers can explore the full range of plausible explanations supported by the data. This range of diverse explanations is particularly valuable in noisy settings, in which the uncertainty across different models of the Rashomon set can highlight regions of the data where different reasonable models are giving ambiguous results.

By cataloging the models included in the Rashomon set, scholars have the opportunity to examine the entire spectrum of possible interpretations backed by the data. This variety of interpretations holds particular significance in environments characterized by noise, where the variability among the models within the Rashomon set can underscore areas in the data where multiple valid models provide unclear or conflicting outcomes.

human: Importantly, near-optimal does not mean identical. Models that share similar loss do not necessarily share the same classification pattern. Even if all the models in the Rashomon set have similar performance, they can (and often do) differ in how they partition the covariate space. If the models are trees, this will mean that trees with similar losses still partition the feature space differently. Multiple distinct trees in the Rashomon set may be similar in accuracy but disagree in specific regions of the feature space (see Figure of the Appendix). That disagreement is particularly meaningful in active learning, where many algorithms rely on querying candidate observations from regions where near-optimal models diverge..
ai: Crucially, when referring to near-optimal models, it’s essential to recognize that they are not necessarily identical. Models that exhibit comparable loss values do not, by default, categorize data in the same way. Even when considering models within the Rashomon set that show comparable levels of effectiveness, there remains the possibility-and indeed, it often happens-that these models differ in their approach to dividing the covariate space. In cases where the models are structured as decision trees, for instance, this implies that trees with equivalent loss metrics might still decompose the feature space in diverse manners. Multiple distinct trees existing within the Rashomon set can display similar accuracy rates yet still yield conflicting classifications in particular areas of the feature space (refer to Figure in the Appendix). Such differences are particularly significant within the realm of active learning, where a majority of algorithms depend on identifying candidate observations precisely from areas where near-optimal models disagree.

human: Despite this potential to identify meaningful disagreement regions among near-optimal models, implementing this insight presents practical challenges. Traditional ensemble methods such as random forests rely on randomization through the sampling of features and observations to form and aggregate base learners. While this randomization creates less-correlated trees, this often incorporates implausible base models that perform relatively poorly, introducing spurious disagreements that can cause the active learner to chase noise rather than true uncertainty. In contrast, Rashomon sets allow for the targeted aggregation of only high-performing models, reducing the risk of incorporating poor models in the query-selection process. This means that disagreements across the Rashomon ensemble are more likely to reflect more genuine and meaningful uncertainty in the data rather than random instability or overfitting to noise.

Although such randomness helps generate trees that are less correlated with one another, it often results in the inclusion of base models that are not plausible and underperform, thereby generating unjustified disagreements. This can mislead the active learner into focusing on noise rather than genuine uncertainty. On the other hand, Rashomon sets enable the aggregation of solely top-performing models, thereby minimizing the chance of including subpar models in the process of query selection. As a consequence, the disagreements observed within the Rashomon ensemble are more inclined to represent authentic and significant uncertainty in the data, as opposed to random volatility or overfitting that captures mere noise.

Their algorithm, , provides an exhaustive yet computationally feasible method to generate, store, and view the entire Rashomon set of decision trees. However, due to the inherent structure and geometry of the decision trees, many trees in this set offer redundant expressions of the same partition of the covariate space, which becomes increasingly problematic in active learning, as it has the potential to further skew our metric of uncertainty in the committee by artificially inflating agreement (Melville & Mooney, 2004). This can be seen in Figure and more deeply in Figure of the Appendix. To address this limitation, Section 4 will outline our method of grouping trees based on their unique classification patterns.

Despite these advancements, the intrinsic architecture and geometric properties of decision trees often result in multiple trees that redundantly express identical divisions of the covariate space. This redundancy is particularly problematic in active learning contexts as it risks distorting our measures of uncertainty within the committee. The model is learned from a training dataset and tested by an independent dataset . The goal is to train to predict the labels of the out-of-sample test set with a budget-constrained number of labeled observations.

human: Active learning seeks to adaptively and strategically choose which unlabeled observations should be queried for oracle labeling and then be used in the supervised learning model. Let the query iteration in the active learning framework be denoted by n . Denote the reservoir of unlabeled candidate observations as with y k initially unknown. A selector is the strategy used to select samples from D to be Oracle labeled. At each iteration, will sample one observation, denoted B , from the candidate dataset D without replacement to query for oracle labeling. B is then added to the training set and removed from the candidate set: and . The model is then retrained on the new training set as . As such, the B is chosen to find the observations that are most informative to improving predictive performance.

Within the active learning framework, each round of sample selection is represented by n. Imagine a collection of unlabeled potential samples, with each having an unknown outcome denoted as y k. The selection of samples is guided by a strategy known as the selector, which determines which samples from this assortment, labeled D, should be sent for oracle labeling. During each cycle of the process, a single observation, referred to as B, is extracted from the candidate dataset D, ensuring no repetition occurs, before submitting it for oracle labeling. Post-labeling, observation B is incorporated into the training dataset while being eliminated from the candidate pool. Consequently, the model undergoes retraining using this updated training data collection, now expanded to include B. The intention is to select B such that it contributes the most significant insights or data toward enhancing the model’s predictive accuracy.

human: Picking a selector metric is a key topic in the active learning literature. Common methods are uncertainty (Lewis & Gale, 1994), query-by-committee metrics (Freund et al., 1997; Settles, 2012), or expected error (Roy & McCallum, 2001). Due to the ensembling nature of our methods, we choose to measure informativity by query-by-committee (QBC) metrics, particularly Argamomn-Engelson and Dagan’s vote entropy (Dagan & Engelson, 1995): where is the number of “votes“ that label receives for x amongst the members c of committee C .
ai: Selecting an appropriate selector metric is a fundamental issue frequently explored in the active learning literature. Among the popular techniques are uncertainty metrics (as discussed by Lewis & Gale in 1994), query-by-committee QBC methodologies (highlighted by Freund et al., 1997, and Settles, 2012), and anticipated error estimations (explored by Roy & McCallum in 2001). Our approach, which involves ensemble methods, leads us to prioritize informativity assessment through query-by-committee metrics. Specifically, we focus on the concept of vote entropy as put forth by Argamon-Engelson and Dagan (Dagan & Engelson, 1995). This method evaluates the number of “votes“ a particular label garners for a given instance x from the individual members c who comprise the committee C.

2503.06770.section: From Noise to Signal: The Rashomon Advantage
human: Active learning strategies suffer greatly in the presence of label noise (Willett et al., 2005; Burbidge et al., 2007; Mots’oehli & Baek, 2023; Khosla et al., 2023; Nuggehalli et al., 2024). Specifically, label noise decreases the accuracy of each supervised learning model in the committee and thus increases the possibility of suboptimal models. This leads to a less optimal active learning strategy in general. While one option is to expand to the committee to include noise-resistant models, we employ a different strategy based on Rashomon theory which does not require finding and implementing such noise-resistant models.

Specifically, the presence of label noise significantly diminishes the performance of each supervised learning algorithm within the ensemble, thereby elevating the likelihood of developing subpar models. Consequently, this degradation in model reliability results in an overall decline in the optimality of the active learning strategy. Although one potential remedy involves broadening the ensemble to incorporate models that are robust against noise, we are opting for an alternative approach anchored in Rashomon theory, which circumvents the necessity of discovering and integrating such noise-resilient models.

2503.06770.section: From Noise to Signal: The Rashomon Advantage

(2024) discovered that increasing the label noise while keeping the sample size fixed increases the number of models that exhibit similar performance, i.e. the size of the Rashomon set. Specifically, they argue that label noise leads to increased pattern diversity - the average difference in predictions between distinct classification patterns in the Rashomon set. The increase in pattern diversity manifests as predictive multiplicity (Marx et al., 2020), indicating that there are more differences in model predictions and thus more diverse models in the Rashomon set. Thus, in the presence of noise, the distinction of being the “best-fitting“ model becomes increasingly arbitrary, as multiple models capture different, yet equally valid patterns in the data.

This highlights a notable average variation in predictions across the different classification configurations within the Rashomon set. Such an escalation in pattern variety is what Marx et al. 2020 termed predictive multiplicity, underlining that there is a wider range of variability in model predictions, resulting in a richer diversity of models in the Rashomon set. Consequently, amid such noise, the notion of a “best-fitting“ model becomes less definitive and more subjective, as several models encapsulate distinct yet equally plausible patterns present within the data.

Rashomon sets offer a natural defense against noise in active learning: instead of relying on a single model that may overfit to noise points, we can leverage the entire set of plausible explanations to capture a comprehensive view of uncertainty in the dataset. That is, incorporating multiple valid explanations from the Rashomon set can help distinguish between genuine uncertainty and noise-induced variability in the sampling strategy.

Secondly, the Rashomon set provides a natural defense against one of active learning’s main weakness: noise. By ensembling across a set of plausible models, the selector committee has a more robust view of uncertainty than if it had incorporated potentially suboptimal models. Finally, as the committee ensembles these near-optimal yet diverse models, the algorithm prioritizes querying points with true uncertainty.

2503.06770.section: 5.1 How to Choose the Rashomon Threshold
human: The Rashomon threshold ε provides a principled way to navigate the exploration-exploitation tradeoff inherent in active learning. A larger ε includes more diverse models in the committee, promoting exploration of alternative explanations, while a smaller ε restricts the committee to models closest to the empirical risk minimizer, favoring exploitation of established patterns. This choice significantly impacts how the algorithm handles uncertainty, particularly in the presence of noise.

Opting for a larger ε broadens the committee of models, thereby encouraging exploration by considering a wider array of possible explanations. Conversely, selecting a smaller ε narrows the focus to models that align closely with the empirical risk minimizer, thus emphasizing the exploitation of well-established patterns. This selection is crucial as it plays a pivotal role in determining how the algorithm contends with uncertainty, especially when noise is present in the data.

2503.06770.section: 5.1 How to Choose the Rashomon Threshold

2503.06770.section: 5.1 How to Choose the Rashomon Threshold
human: The threshold effectively serves as a lever balancing between current accuracy and robustness. When ε is too small, the committee may consist of nearly identical models, oversampling regions that initially appear uncertain but may reflect only the limitations of the current best model. Conversely, when ε is too large, the committee may include relatively poor-performing models, potentially drowning genuine signals in a sea of noise.

On the other hand, setting ε too high could result in the committee incorporating models that don’t perform very well, which might overwhelm genuine data signals with a vast array of irrelevant noise.

In particular, we study a loop obtained by traversing a one-sided closed geodesic and the m -th power of another one-sided closed geodesic for odd m . 2503.05932.section: Abstract
human: In this paper, we introduce a streamlined procedure for constructing small symplectic 4 -manifolds via contact gluing, based on a technique invented by David Gay around 2000 [20]. We also give a few applications, ranging from embeddings of singular Lagrangian s to realizing an infinite family of lens spaces as hypersurfaces of contact type in a symplectic Hirzebruch surface. Furthermore, our investigation on S 1 -invariant contact structures also suggests there should be a universal upper bound for the self-intersection of a rational unicuspidal curve with one Puiseux pairin any algebraic surface (the bound depends only on the singularity).
ai: In this article, we present an efficient technique for constructing compact symplectic 4-manifolds through the method of contact gluing, which is based on an approach pioneered by David Gay around the year 2000 [20]. Additionally, we explore several applications of this method. These applications include embedding singular Lagrangians and representing an infinite series of lens spaces as hypersurfaces of contact nature within a symplectic Hirzebruch surface. Moreover, our study of S1-invariant contact structures hints at the possibility of a universal upper boundary for the self-intersection number of a rational unicuspidal curve with one Puiseux pair on any algebraic surface. This proposed bound is contingent solely upon the specifics of the singularity.

human: This section is devoted to a study of relative handlebodies of symplectic 2 -handles built on a(generalized) Seifert manifold equipped with a certain S 1 -invariant contact structure. The construction of such relative handlebodies is based on a technique introduced by Gay in [20];in particular, the two boundary components of the relative handlebody are both concave contact boundaries. It turns out that the other boundary component is also a (generalized) Seifert manifold equipped with a certain S 1 -invariant contact structure. Among the results of this section, we give a recipe to determine what are the possible values of the Seifert invariants and the possible S 1 -invariant contact structures on the other boundary component which can be realized by a Gay’s construction. We also give a recipe to compute the framings of the symplectic 2 -handles using the relevant Seifert invariants from the two boundary components.

human: The quantum calculus (or q -calculus) emerged as a link between mathematics and physics. It turns out to be even more significant than classical computation. It depends on a parameter . It encompasses classical computation: when , the various results obtained reduce to classical operations. The q -calculus can thus be considered as an extension of the classical calculus. A another example can be found in classical analysis, where the definition of the derivative relies on the existence of a limit, in contrast, in q -calculus, the notion of q -derivatives can exist without requiring the definition of a limit. It has many applications in different areas of mathematics such as number theory, combinatorics, orthogonal polynomials, basic hypergeometric functions, quantum theory and electronics, and in different areas of applied mathematics such as probability and statistics in which it abounds [2, 4, 10, 16]. In the specific case of probability and statistics, two types of functions are the focus of a great deal of research due to their importance: density and regression functions. Their significance arises from their applications in many areas of probability, statistics, and even beyond [7, 17, 18]. It is therefore clear that estimating the density and regression function using various methods is a crucial task in the field of statistics and probability. However, despite the abundance of statistical results related to q -calculus, there is very few which address to nonparametric statistics using kernel methods in the estimation of density functions and regression functions. Nonparametric estimation by kernel method using q -calculus is performed in [1]. The authors, with q -calculus methods and in the case where , obtain the q -asymptotic normality of kernel density estimator.In this paper, we adopt a similar approach to the study of the asymptotic normality of the density in [1] and extend this work. More precisely, under relaxed assumptions, we investigate the strong convergence of this estimator and determine its rate of convergence. Furthermore, we apply the same q -calculus operations to investigate the asymptotic normality and almost sure convergence of the regression function estimation using the kernel method, referred to as the q -kernel method.
ai: Quantum calculus, commonly referred to as q-calculus, serves as a fascinating bridge between the realms of mathematics and physics. Its emergence has revealed a depth that surpasses even the significance traditionally attributed to classical computation. The framework of q-calculus revolves around a specific parameter. Notably, it integrates classical computation within its scope, such that when this parameter equals one, the outcomes seamlessly transition into those of conventional operations. Hence, q-calculus can be perceived as a comprehensive extension of classical calculus principles. A notable distinction is apparent when examining classical analysis, where the concept of a derivative is fundamentally dependent on the existence of a limit. In contrast, q-calculus introduces q-derivatives that can be defined independently, without adhering to the traditional requirement of defining a limit. This flexibility results in numerous applications across a wide spectrum of mathematical disciplines, including areas like number theory, combinatorics, orthogonal polynomials, basic hypergeometric functions, quantum theory, and electronics. Moreover, q-calculus finds significant relevance in various domains of applied mathematics, such as probability and statistics, where its impact is profound and widespread [2, 4, 10, 16].Particularly in the fields of probability and statistics, special attention is dedicated to two types of functions due to their pivotal role: density functions and regression functions. Their importance is underscored by their wide-ranging applications within probability, statistics, and beyond [7, 17, 18]. Consequently, the task of estimating density and regression functions by employing diverse techniques becomes indispensable in statistics and probability. Despite the extensive body of statistical research pertaining to q-calculus, there remains a scarcity of studies focusing on nonparametric statistics using kernel methods specifically for estimating density and regression functions.Nonparametric estimation utilizing kernel methods within the framework of q-calculus is explored in [1]. By leveraging q-calculus when the parameter equals one, the authors succeed in demonstrating the q-asymptotic normality of the kernel density estimator. Our paper adopts a parallel approach to that of [1], delving into the investigation of asymptotic normality of density estimation and aiming to expand on this prior work. More specifically, we scrutinize the strong convergence of this estimator under less stringent assumptions and elucidate its convergence rate. Additionally, we implement q-calculus operations to explore both the asymptotic normality and almost sure convergence in the estimation of the regression function through the application of the q-kernel method.

human: Community detection, which focuses on recovering the group structure within networks, is a crucial and fundamental task in network analysis. However, the detection process can be quite challenging and unstable when community signals are weak. Motivated by a newly collected large-scale academic network dataset from the , which includes multi-layer network information, we propose a Bipartite Assisted Spectral-clustering approach for Identifying Communities (BASIC), which incorporates the bipartite network information into the community structure learning of the primary network. The accuracy and stability enhancement of BASIC is validated theoretically on the basis of the degree-corrected stochastic block model framework, as well as numerically through extensive simulation studies. We rigorously study the convergence rate of BASIC even under weak signal scenarios and prove that BASIC yields a tighter upper error bound than that based on the primary network information alone. We utilize the proposed BASIC method to analyze the newly collected large-scale academic network dataset from statistical papers. ai: Identifying clusters within networks, commonly known as community detection, is a critical endeavor in the field of network analysis. This task becomes particularly difficult and unpredictable when the signals indicating community boundaries are faint. Inspired by a recently gathered extensive academic network dataset that offers multi-layer network details, we have introduced a novel method called Bipartite Assisted Spectral-Clustering for Community Identification, abbreviated as BASIC. This approach cleverly integrates information from bipartite networks to enrich the process of deciphering the community structure within the primary network.The improvements in accuracy and stability offered by BASIC are supported both theoretically, within the framework of the degree-corrected stochastic block model, and through comprehensive numerical simulations. We undertake a detailed investigation of how quickly BASIC converges even when signals are weak and demonstrate that BASIC achieves a narrower upper error limit than what could be achieved using just the primary network’s data.By employing the BASIC method, we embark on an analysis of the substantial academic network dataset compiled from statistical scholarly works. In the endeavor to learn the structure of the author collaboration network, we apply the bipartite network data stemming from relationships such as author-paper, author-institution, and author-region connections. Examined from both statistical and interpretational viewpoints, these bipartite networks significantly enhance the ability to detect communities within the key collaboration network.

human: In recent years, network analysis, which focuses primarily on depicting intricate relationships and interactions between entities in complex systems, has attracted substantial interest in various disciplines, such as physics (Newman, 2008), biology (Dong et al., 2023), sociology (Newman, 2001; Ji et al., 2022), transportation science (Tian et al., 2016), among many other fields (Wu et al., 2023; Miething et al., 2016). An extensively used modeling strategy for network analysis is the stochastic block model (SBM) where the edge probabilities depend only on the communities to which the correponding nodes belong (Holland et al., 1983) and its variants, such as degree-corrected block model (DCBM) (Karrer and Newman, 2011), mixed membership stochastic block model (MMSB) (Airoldi et al., 2008; Zhang et al., 2020), degree-corrected mixed membership model (DCMM) (Jin et al., 2017), bipartite stochastic block model (BiSBM) (Larremore et al., 2014; Yen and Larremore, 2020), superimposed stochastic block model (SupSBM) (Huang et al., 2020; Paul et al., 2023), motif tensor block model (MoTBM) (Yu and Zhu, 2024), and so forth.

human: During network analysis, community detection is a crucial tool that focuses on identifying closely connected groups within networks (Girvan and Newman, 2002; Newman, 2012; Jin, 2015). Jin (2015) proposed a spectral clustering method on ratios-of-eigenvectors (SCORE) for DCBM that utilizes eigenvectors to correct for degree heterogeneity in community detection via spectral clustering. Ji and Jin (2016) and Ji et al. (2022) further extended SCORE to directed-DCBM and DCMM. Recently, Xu et al. (2023) introduced an additional layer of nodal covariates to the adjacency matrix, in order to improve accuracy of clustering. Paul et al. (2023) defined motif adjacency matrices and proposed a higher-order spectral clustering method for SupSBM.

More recently, research by Xu et al. in 2023 added another dimension by incorporating nodal covariates into the adjacency matrix, thereby refining clustering precision. In 2023, Paul and collaborators introduced the concept of motif adjacency matrices and proposed an advanced spectral clustering method tailored for Supervised Stochastic Block Models SupSBM, marking another step forward in the field.

human: However, community detection can be quite challenging when the signal-to-noise ratio of the network structure is weak, where the probability that the edges within certain communities are close to that between communities; thus, community structures might be masked by noises. Many practical networks, including the collaboration network studied in this work, are typical weak-signal networks. To address weak signals, Jin et al. (2021) proposed a SCORE+ method that applies pre-PCA normalization and Laplacian transformation to the adjacency matrix and considered an additional eigenvector for clustering. Furthermore, Jin et al. (2023) suggested estimating the number of communities using a stepwise goodness-of-fit test for the adjacency matrix. These methods mainly focus on extracting key information from the network itself to address the challenges posed by weak signals.
ai: Detecting communities within networks becomes particularly difficult when the signal-to-noise ratio is low. In such cases, the probabilities that edges exist within communities nearly match those between different communities, which can obscure the underlying community structures with noise. Many real-world networks, such as the collaboration network explored in this analysis, exemplify these weak-signal characteristics. To tackle this issue of faint signals, Jin et al. 2021 introduced the SCORE+ method. This approach involves normalizing the data using pre-PCA techniques and transforming the adjacency matrix with the Laplacian, in addition to incorporating an extra eigenvector to aid in clustering. Building on this, Jin et al. 2023 proposed determining the number of communities through an incremental goodness-of-fit test applied to the adjacency matrix. These techniques are primarily dedicated to isolating essential insights from the network data itself, thereby effectively addressing the obstacles posed by weak signals.

human: The contributions of this paper are threefold.First, to the best of our knowledge, this is the first study to leverage bipartite network information to improve community detection performance. In contrast, existing research focuses primarily on extracting additional insights from the primary network itself, such as nodal covariates or higher-order structures. It is important to note that the proposed BASIC can readily be integrated with existing methods to further tackle weak network signals. It can also be extended to other network models and community detection approaches.Second, we rigorously establish the theoretical guarantee of BASIC by deriving its convergence rate even under extremely weak signals of the primary network. More importantly, we prove that BASIC has a tighter upper bound of the number of error nodes compared to merely using the primary network for community detection, and hence indeed enhances detection power. Third, we collect a large-scale academic network dataset, including collaboration network, author-paper, author-institution, and author-region networks. These datasets serve as valuable resources for investigating community structures in collaborative networks, leading to numerous intriguing and meaningful findings via the proposed BASIC method.

A noteworthy feature of the proposed BASIC method is its compatibility with existing techniques, allowing it to address challenges related to weak network signals further, and it can also be adapted to other network models and community detection methodologies. Secondly, the paper provides a thorough theoretical validation of BASIC, establishing its convergence rate even when faced with very faint signals from the primary network. Crucially, our research demonstrates that BASIC achieves a tighter upper bound on the number of error nodes compared to conventional methods that rely solely on the primary network for community detection, thereby enhancing the efficacy of detection. Lastly, we’ve assembled a comprehensive academic network dataset, encompassing collaboration, author-paper, author-institution, and author-region networks. These datasets offer rich resources for the exploration of community structures within collaborative networks, enabling the discovery of numerous compelling and valuable insights through the utilization of the BASIC method.

human: In this paper, we propose a Bipartite Assisted Spectral-clustering approach for Identifying Communities (BASIC). It incorporates bipartite network information to community structure learning in social network analysis. By introducing an aggregated squared adjacency matrix, BASIC effectively takes into account the bipartite information without distorting the primary network structure. We systematically study the theoretical properties of BASIC, and demonstrate its privilege across various scenarios of simulation studies. Furthermore, we collect a large-scale academic network dataset from the statistics field, with author collaboration network being our primary interest. We also construct three bipartite networks - author-paper, author-institution, and author-region, from the collected data. Then we explore the community structure of the collaboration network using BASIC, leading to numerous intriguing findings.
ai: In this study, we introduce a novel method called the Bipartite Assisted Spectral-Clustering for Community Identification, abbreviated as BASIC. This technique integrates data from bipartite networks into the process of learning community structures, particularly within the realm of social network analysis. Utilizing an aggregated squared adjacency matrix, BASIC adeptly incorporates bipartite network data while preserving the inherent structure of the primary network. Our research delves deeply into the theoretical aspects of BASIC, showcasing its advantages across a multitude of simulation scenarios. Additionally, we gather an extensive dataset from the academic sphere, specifically targeting networks formed through collaborations among authors in the field of statistics. From this data, we delineate three distinct bipartite network types: author-paper, author-institution, and author-region. Subsequently, we apply BASIC to analyze the community structure within the collaboration network, which yields a series of intriguing and enlightening discoveries.

human: It is a folklore belief that metastable wells in low-temperature statistical mechanics models exhibit high-temperature behavior.We prove a rigorous version of this phenomenon in the setting of the exponential random graph model (ERGM) through the lens ofconcentration of measure.To do this, we first present a new general result deriving concentration inequalities in a metastable well from the metastable mixing of aMarkov chain with the appropriate stationary distribution, extending a result ofChatterjee [Cha05] which is suited for more traditional forms of global mixing.We then apply this result to the supercritical (low-temperature) ERGM which was recently proven toexhibit metastable mixing by Bresler, Nagaraj, and Nichani [BNN24],and obtain a novel concentration inequality for Lipschitz observables of the supercritical ERGM conditioned on alarge metastable well, answering a question posed by [BNN24].This extends a result of Ganguly and Nam [GN24] from the subcritical (high-temperature)regime to a metastable well in the supercritical regime, and we are also able to extend the applicationsof their concentration inequality to these metastable wells.Namely, we obtain an upper bound on the Wasserstein distance between the ERGM conditioned on a metastable welland an appropriate Erdős-Rényi model, as well as derive a central limit theoremfor the count of edges in certain small subcollections of possible edges.Finally, to supplement the mathematical content of the article, we also discuss the results of what appears to be the firstsimulation study of a metastable well in the supercritical ERGM.
ai: There is a widespread belief in folklore that metastable wells within models of statistical mechanics at low temperatures demonstrate behaviors typically associated with high-temperature conditions. We substantiate a precise version of this intriguing phenomenon by analyzing the exponential random graph model ERGM through the perspective of measure concentration. Our approach begins with presenting a novel general result that derives concentration inequalities within a metastable well from the metastable mixing of a Markov chain possessing the appropriate stationary distribution. This enhances a finding by Chatterjee [Cha05], which applies to more conventional forms of global mixing dynamics. Subsequently, we apply our result to the supercritical, or low-temperature, ERGM-recently shown by Bresler, Nagaraj, and Nichani [BNN24] to demonstrate metastable mixing-and derive a new concentration inequality for Lipschitz observables of the supercritical ERGM, conditioned upon a substantial metastable well, effectively addressing a question raised in [BNN24].This development expands upon the work by Ganguly and Nam [GN24], which initially addressed the subcritical, or high-temperature, regime, by extending their concentration inequality applications to include these metastable wells. Specifically, we attain an upper limit on the Wasserstein distance between an ERGM conditioned on a metastable well and a corresponding Erdős-Rényi model. Moreover, we establish a central limit theorem concerning the count of edges within particular small subsets of potential edges. In conclusion, to enrich the mathematical discussion presented in the article, we highlight the outcomes of what is seemingly the inaugural simulation study concerning a metastable well in the supercritical ERGM context.

ai: The Exponential Random Graph Model ERGM serves as a framework for analyzing intricate networks characterized by a range of clustering properties. It has been employed in disciplines such as sociology and biology [FS86, HL81, WF94]. In its early development, statistical physicists made significant nonrigorous contributions to analyzing the ERGM [BJK04, PN04, PN05]. From a mathematical angle, ERGM emerges as one of the most straightforward natural models that incorporate higher-order interactions-beyond mere pairwise relationships. This is because the existence of a subgraph that isomorphic to the network relies on multiple different edges. Consequently, the ERGM has captivated the interests of probabilists, statisticians, and computer scientists who have explored the model through various lenses, including large deviations and phase transitions [CD13, RS13, RY13, EG18], distributional limit theorems [MX23, FLS24], sampling methodologies [BBS08, RR19, BNN24], and the concentration of measure phenomena [SS20, GN24]. Furthermore, the ERGM remains a pivotal tool for examining random graphs that are required to have an unusual number of triangles or other specific subgraphs [RRS14, LZ15]. Our characterization of the ERGM typically pertains to dense graph structures; however, recent research has also delved into adaptations that result in sparse graphs [YZ17, CD24]. The citations provided herein showcase the extensive range of the subject and are not exhaustive; numerous critical studies have been excluded.

human: We present two limit theorems, a mean ergodic and a central limit theorem, for a specific class of one-dimensional diffusion processes that depend on a small-scale parameter ε and converge weakly to a homogenized diffusion process in the limit . In these results, we allow for the time horizon to blow up such that as . The novelty of the results arises from the circumstance that many quantities are unbounded for , so that formerly established theory is not directly applicable here and a careful investigation of all relevant ε -dependent terms is required. As a mathematical application, we then use these limit theorems to prove asymptotic properties of a minimum distance estimator for parameters in a homogenized diffusion equation.
ai: In this work, we develop two distinct limit theorems: one a mean ergodic theorem and the other a central limit theorem. These are tailored for a particular category of one-dimensional diffusion processes, which are characterized by their dependence on a minuscule parameter, denoted as ε, and which, over time, gradually converge in a weak sense to a homogenized diffusion process as the parameter approaches its limit. Our findings are notable because they accommodate scenarios where the temporal scope becomes indefinitely large, corresponding to the situation as ε approaches zero. The distinctive contribution of our results lies in addressing the complexities introduced by the fact that numerous associated quantities become unbounded as ε nears zero, rendering pre-existing theories inapplicable without modifications. Consequently, a meticulous examination of the terms that depend on ε is indispensable. As a practical mathematical application, these limit theorems provide the foundational basis to demonstrate the asymptotic behaviors of a minimum distance estimator, which is instrumental in estimating parameters within a homogenized diffusion equation.

The proposed minimum distance estimator, based on the characteristic function of the limit invariant density, turned out to be consistent and asymptotically normal under observations of the process X ε in the simultaneous long-time and small-scale limiting regime, that is as .

Furthermore, we utilized these theoretical advancements to tackle a straightforward issue of statistical parameter estimation under the framework of model misspecification in a continuous-time environment. The proposed estimator, which minimizes distance based on the characteristic function of the limit invariant density, was found to be both consistent and asymptotically normal when observing the process X^ε. This holds true in the concurrent regime of long-time observations and a reduction in scale, effectively as ε becomes infinitesimal.

human: We see two immediate chances for future research. The first one is the extension of the limit theorems to unbounded test functions that are integrable with respect to the limit invariant measure. This is certainly more useful for statistical estimation purposes where moments of processes are an ubiquitous occurrence. We suspect that, in this case, one must shift away the attention from the mean ergodic theorem and pursue an almost sure ergodic theorem. After all, if the ultimate aim is the consistency or asymptotic normality of estimators, then it is irrelevant if one has the mean ergodic or the almost sure ergodic theorem - even a stochastic ergodic theorem would suffice.

Another difficulty is the question about the convergence of the asymptotic variances in the central limit theorem, which remains unclear in more general settings. Despite these preliminary problems, the stochastic convergence results in subsection would be easier to establish since they heavily rely on interior Schauder estimates, which can be proved analogously in several dimensions. human: The behavior of extreme observations is well-understood for time series or spatial data, but little is known if the data generating process is a structural causal model (SCM).We study the behavior of extremes in this model class, both for the observational distribution and under extremal interventions. We show that under suitable regularity conditions on the structure functions, the extremal behavior is described by a multivariate Pareto distribution, which can be represented as a new SCM on an extremal graph. Importantly, the latter is a sub-graph of the graph in the original SCM, which means that causal links can disappear in the tails.We further introduce a directed version of extremal graphical models and show that an extremal SCM satisfies the corresponding Markov properties.Based on a new test of extremal conditional independence, we proposetwo algorithms for learning the extremal causal structure from data. The first is an extremal version of the PC-algorithm, and the second is a pruning algorithm that removes edges from the original graph to consistently recover the extremal graph. The methods are illustrated on river data with known causal ground truth. Keywords: Keywords: causality, extreme value theory, graphical model, structure learning.

In this study, we delve into the behavior of extreme events within this specific class of models, considering both the distributive properties of observations and the effects of extreme interventions. Our results reveal that, given appropriate regularity conditions on the structure functions, the extreme occurrences align with a multivariate Pareto distribution. This distribution can be conceptualized as a novel SCM situated on an extremal graph. Notably, this extremal graph is a subset of the original SCM’s graph, implying that some causal connections may vanish in the tails.We further propose a directed variant of extremal graphical models, demonstrating how an extremal SCM adheres to related Markov properties. Leveraging a newly developed test for extremal conditional independence, we introduce two algorithms aimed at deriving the extremal causal architecture from the data. Our first algorithm is an extremal adaptation of the well-known PC-algorithm, and the second is a pruning mechanism that methodically trims edges from the initial graph to accurately reconstruct the extremal graph. These methodologies are exemplified through an analysis of river data, where the causal ground truth is established. Keywords: causality, extreme value theory, graphical model, structure learning.

Interestingly, the extremal graph G e can be shown to be a subgraph of G in the sense that . That means that causal links that are present in the overall system can disappear in extreme observations.Conversely, any set of additive extremal structure functions of the form with homogeneous functions yields a valid extremal SCM. It turns out that many of the standard extreme value models in the literature have such an additive structure. In the primary findings of this study, we establish the behavior of limits for general Structural Causal Models SCMs under the observational distribution of X when one variable grows exceedingly large. This property is well-documented by Resnick in 2008 and is crucial as it assures the existence of a limiting vector that effectively describes tail dependence. This resultant limit manifests as a multivariate Pareto distribution, which can also be interpreted as a novel SCM on the extremal Directed Acyclic Graph DAG, utilizing what we term as extremal structure functions that adhere to homogeneity for all inputs and outputs. human: The study of graphical models and causal inference in the context of extreme observations has attracted increasing attention in recent years.A particular focus has been on sparse extremal dependence modeling on undirected graphs. Segers (2020) and Asenova andSegers (2023) study extremes of probabilistic graphical models on trees and block graphs, respectively, and Engelke andHitz (2020) introduce the concept of general, undirected extremal graphical models. There has been ample of work on the estimation (Asenovaet al., 2021; Röttgeret al., 2023; Lederer andOesting, 2024) and structure learning (Engelke andVolgushev, 2022; Huet al., 2024; Engelkeet al., 2024; Wan andZhou, 2025; Engelke andTaeb, 2024) of these models, but the directed case has only been considered for very particular model classes so far (Gissibl andKlüppelberg, 2018; Gnecco et al., 2021); for a recent review see Engelkeet al. (2024).

A major area of concentration within this field is the modeling of sparse extremal dependencies on undirected graphs. Distinguished studies by Segers 2020 and Asenova and Segers 2023 have delved into the extremes of probabilistic graphical models within the confines of trees and block graphs, respectively. Meanwhile, Engelke and Hitz 2020 have pioneered the notion of generalized, undirected extremal graphical models. Considerable research has been dedicated to the estimation of these models, as seen in the works of Asenova et al. 2021, Röttger et al. 2023, and Lederer and Oesting 2024. Furthermore, significant advances have been made in understanding the structure learning of these models, with contributions from Engelke and Volgushev 2022, Hu et al. 2024, Engelke et al. 2024, Wan and Zhou 2025, and Engelke and Taeb 2024 prominently defining the field. However, the exploration of directed extremal graphical models has thus far been confined to a few specialized model classes. Notable works in this niche include Gissibl and Klüppelberg 2018 and Gnecco et al. 2021. For those seeking a comprehensive overview of recent advancements in this domain, the review by Engelke et al. 2024 offers valuable insights.

human: Most of the work on causality related to extremes considers treatment effects in the tails of the distributions. Closely related to extreme quantile estimation (Chernozhukov, 2005; Youngman, 2019; Velthoen et al., 2019), this line of work studies the difference in the extremal quantiles of the response variable under different potential outcomes (Zhanget al., 2018; Deuberet al., 2024). The treatment is binary in these cases, which fundamentally differs from our work where we consider continuous variables that can be extreme simultaneously.Interestingly, Wang andMiao (2024)observe that for light-tailed responses, confounding may become negligible in the extremes, and that average treatment effects can be estimated from the tails only. While in a different setting, this parallels the phenomenon in our theory that causal links can disappear in the extremal DAG G e .Extremal causal discovery in multivariate systems with continuous data has mostly been studied using bivariate summary statistics (Mhallaet al., 2020, 2024; Deiddaet al., 2023), but a theoretical justification in terms of interventions is often difficult.For reviews on causality and extremes see Engelke andIvanovs (2021) and Chavez-Demoulinand Mhalla (2024).
ai: In the realm of causality research involving extremes, much focus has been placed on evaluating treatment impacts at the outer edges of statistical distributions. This approach, intimately connected with the estimation of extreme quantiles (as discussed by Chernozhukov, 2005; Youngman, 2019; Velthoen et al., 2019), delves into analyzing the disparities between the extremal quantiles of a response variable given different hypothetical scenarios (explored by Zhang et al., 2018; Deuber et al., 2024). Typically, this research involves binary treatments, setting it apart from our investigation where we scrutinize continuous variables which have the potential to achieve extreme values concurrently. Notably, Wang and Miao 2024 highlight that for responses with light-tailed distributions, confounding effects may diminish at the extremes, allowing for the estimation of average treatment effects based solely on tail data. Although their findings are in a different context, they mirror our theoretical observations regarding the disappearance of causal relationships in the extremal Directed Acyclic Graph G e. In multivariate systems with continuous data, the pursuit of discovering extremal causal pathways has largely relied on bivariate summary statistics (cited in the works of Mhalla et al., 2020, 2024; Deidda et al., 2023), yet substantiating these with theoretical robustness through interventions frequently poses a challenge. For further readings on the intersection of causality and extremes, consult the reviews by Engelke and Ivanovs 2021 and Chavez-Demoulin and Mhalla 2024.

human: In this section we provide some background on directed graphical models and their connection to structural causal models.A directed graph is a pair consisting of a node (or vertex) set and an edge set containing ordered pairs of distinct nodes.An undirected graph is a graph where there is an edge if and only if ; the two edges are then graphically represented by a single undirected connection.In this paper, we always consider the sub-class of directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) defined as a directed graph that does not contain any directed cycles.For a DAG G , the set of parents of node is defined as all nodes such that . The set of non-descendants of node i contains all nodes j forwhich there is no directed path from i to j in G , and the set of ancestors is the collection of all nodes j for which there is a directed path from j to i in G ; we sometimes drop the subscript when there is no ambiguity about the corresponding graph.For details and more graph notions we refer to Lauritzen (1996, Chapter 2).
ai: In this section, we delve into the foundational aspects of directed graphical models and their links to structural causal models. A directed graph is characterized by two primary components: a set of nodes, also known as vertices, and a set of edges, which are ordered pairs of distinct nodes. In contrast, an undirected graph is characterized by the presence of an edge only if there exists a bi-directional connection between two nodes, depicted by a single line without an arrow. Throughout this study, our focus is confined to a specific subset of directed graphs called directed acyclic graphs DAGs, which are defined by the absence of any directed cycles.For a given DAG G, the parent set of a node encompasses all nodes that have direct arrows pointing towards it. Conversely, the non-descendants of a node i include all nodes j that lack any directed path originating from i and terminating at j within the graph G. The ancestor set consists of all nodes j for which there exists a directed path from j leading to i in G. In instances where the pertinent graph is clear from context, the subscript indication may be omitted for simplicity. For an expansive exploration of these concepts and other related graph-theoretical notions, one is encouraged to consult Lauritzen’s work from 1996, specifically Chapter 2.

human: Sequential change point detection, also known as online or quickest change point detection, is a classic topic in statistics with roots in ordnance testing and quality control (Shewhart,, 1931; Wald,, 1945; Anscombe,, 1946). The primary goal is to monitor a (random) process and issue an alert when the distribution of this process deviates significantly from its historical pattern. Applications range widely, including social network monitoring (Chen,, 2019), quality control in industrial processes (Amiri and Allahyari,, 2012), cybersecurity (Tartakovsky et al.,, 2012), and seismic tremor detection (Li et al.,, 2018), among others.
ai: Sequential change point detection, often referred to as both online change point detection and the quickest change point detection method, is a foundational topic within the field of statistics. Its historical context draws connections to earlier applications in ordnance testing and quality control as documented by pioneers like Shewhart in 1931, Wald in 1945, and Anscombe in 1946. The central objective of this technique is to scrutinize a stochastic process with the intention of generating a timely signal once there’s a notable shift in the distribution pattern from its established norm.This methodology finds diverse applications across a variety of domains. For instance, it is used extensively in tracking activities on social networks, as explored by Chen in 2019. In the domain of industrial processes, it ensures effective quality control, a topic elaborated upon by Amiri and Allahyari in 2012. The scope of its application further extends into the realm of cybersecurity, with significant contributions from Tartakovsky and colleagues in 2012, aimed at identifying anomalies rapidly to preempt potential threats. Additionally, it serves a crucial role in detecting seismic tremors, a particular interest of Li and team in 2018. These examples highlight the technique’s broad relevance and utility across different fields of study and industry practices.

human: In early work, Page, (1954) introduced the celebrated CUSUM statistic based on the the log-likelihood ratio between two known distributions (representing the control and the anomaly). Lorden, (1971) later established the asymptotic minimax optimality of CUSUM regarding detection delay under constraints on average run lengths. From a Bayesian perspective, the Shiryaev-Roberts procedure (Shiryaev,, 1961, 1963; Roberts,, 1966) is similar to CUSUM and has several optimality properties (including the aforementioned minimax optimality as well as Bayesian optimality; see e.g. Pollak,, 1985; Polunchenko and Tartakovsky,, 2010). Subsequent developments have expanded this scope to address unknown anomaly distributions and various models (see e.g. Siegmund,, 1985, Lai,, 2001, Tartakovsky,, 2020 and Wang and Xie,, 2024 for an overview).

These distributions typically characterize the normal state and the anomaly. Building on this groundwork, Lorden 1971 further substantiated the CUSUM’s reputation by demonstrating its asymptotic minimax optimality in terms of minimizing detection delay, all while adhering to limitations on average run lengths. From a Bayesian perspective, the procedure developed by Shiryaev and later refined by Roberts-often called the Shiryaev-Roberts procedure (Shiryaev, 1961, 1963; Roberts, 1966)-shares similarities with the CUSUM approach. This method boasts a multitude of optimal properties, encompassing the previously mentioned minimax optimality as well as Bayesian optimality, as documented by scholars such as Pollak 1985 and Polunchenko and Tartakovsky 2010. Further advancements in this field have broadened the application to encompass scenarios with unknown anomaly distributions and diverse models. Comprehensive discussions of these expansions can be found in research by figures such as Siegmund 1985, Lai 2001, Tartakovsky 2020, and Wang and Xie 2024.

2503.05270.section: FLOC: Statistical theory and computational complexity
human: In this section, we introduce the Fast Limited-memory Optimal Change (FLOC) detector, on the basis of two test statistics, one of which is used to detect a jump and the other to detect a kink. We then derive upper bounds on the quadratic risk of FLOC as well as its computational cost.
ai: In this part of our study, we present the Fast Limited-memory Optimal Change FLOC detector, which is constructed around two distinct test statistics. One of these statistics serves to identify a sudden change or “jump,“ while the other is designed to pinpoint a “kink“ in data patterns. Following this introduction, we proceed to establish upper limits on both the quadratic risk associated with FLOC and its computational expenses.

human: The idea of the online detection algorithm is to estimate the pre-change signal f - at the beginning of the data sequence and subsequently to verify over the most recent time interval whether the data continues to adhere to the same underlying function. The detector is built upon certain test statistics, which report a change if the test statistics exceed pre-specified thresholds. For a jump we use the mean of the data on the most recent time interval as the test statistic, and for a kink we employ a weighted mean, tuned to estimate the slope of a linear function, with higher weights on more recent observations.
ai: The concept behind the online detection algorithm involves the initial estimation of the pre-change signal, denoted as f, right at the start of the data sequence. This foundational signal serves as the benchmark to later determine if the incoming data across the most recent time period consistently aligns with this original underlying function. To accomplish this, the algorithm relies on specific test statistics, which act as indicators of change; these statistics will flag a change when they surpass certain predefined thresholds. In the event of detecting a sudden shift, we utilize the average of the data gathered over the latest time interval as our test statistic. Conversely, for discerning a gradual change in the rate or direction-a kink-we apply a weighted mean. This weighted mean is expertly calibrated to gauge the slope of a linear function, with greater importance assigned to the most current observations.

human: A pseudocode implementation of FLOC is provided in . The algorithm maintains sums and weighted sums in bins of fixed size to calculate the test statistics. When the third bin is full, the first bin is discarded, and a new bin is initiated. The benefits of varying window sizes over a fixed window size become evident in the implementation of FLOC. While a constant window size achieves the same asymptotic properties, it would require storing individual observations to allow for gradual updates as the window moves. As the window size depends on n , the storage cost for a fixed window size would grow with the rate of observations. In contrast, achieves computational and memory costs of , independent of the window size or the number of observation until the current time. This property is particularly advantageous for online detectors, as minimal computational and memory requirements are often considered essential design criteria (cf. Introduction).

These rates closely align with the offline setup, differing only in log factors (see in the Introduction). Notably, FLOC attains the minimax optimality in detection of both jumps and kinks. For the detection of a jump, the optimal rate for the segmented linear regression model coincides with the optimal rate for the submodel with piecewise constant signal and a single jump (see e.g. Chapter 6 in Korostelev and Korosteleva,, 2011). Further, for the submodel with piecewise constant signal, Yu et al., (2023) showed a rate of order on the detection delay under the condition , which ensures that under the null hypothesis the false alarm probability of online detector is at most α . In contrast, our FLOC detector, designed for a more general model, attains the same detection delay rate in this specific submodel, and requires a computational and memory costs independent of time t , see also .

human: To evaluate the empirical performance of FLOC on real-world data, we analyze excess mortality data from the CDC website https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/nvss/vsrr/covid19/excess deaths.htm. This data set consists of estimates of excess deaths in the United States from the beginning of 2017 through September of 2023 by states (see and ), which were calculated based on weekly counts of deaths using Farrington surveillancee algorithms (Noufaily et al.,, 2013, see the CDC website for further details). For our analysis, we treat the data through the end of June 2019 as historical data, and standardize the entire data set with the mean and the standard deviation of the historical period. The primary objective of this analysis is to study the impact of Covid-19. This data set was also used by Chen et al., (2024) to demonstrate the effectiveness of their online algorithm , which detects changes in high-dimensional means. We thus include as a baseline for comparison with FLOC.
