2503.06138.section: 4.2 Two Types of Memory and Thickness of the Present
human: Bergson’s theory of time explains natural phenomena through the combined effect of two types of “memory.“ This distinction is often referred to as a precursor to modern procedural and episodic memory ([146], [106]); however, it has a broader scope. One type is “motor memory,“ which refers to a series of motor modules learned through repetition, such as skills and habits in humans. The other is “pure memory,“ which preserves original experiences before they are organized into such patterns. For example, through instances of bicycle riding trials (r1, r2, r3), a motor memory for riding a bicycle (R) is acquired. However, one can also recall r1 as a specific event in life on a particular date. Pure memory is what retains these instances.
ai: Henri Bergson’s conceptualization of time delves into the intricacies of natural phenomena by analyzing the interplay of two distinct types of memory he identifies. This differentiation is commonly viewed as a forerunner to what we now define as procedural and episodic memory, as noted in works such as [146] and [106]. Nonetheless, Bergson’s classification expands beyond these modern understandings. The first category is what Bergson calls “motor memory,“ which encompasses sequences of actions learned and refined through continuous repetition, similar to the development of skills and habits observed in humans. The second category, termed “pure memory,“ is responsible for preserving original experiences before they are synthesized into structured patterns of behavior. To illustrate, through repeated experiences of riding a bicycle-let’s say events labeled as r1, r2, and r3-an individual develops a motor memory that encapsulates the skill of cycling, denoted as R. Despite this, the specific occasion r1 remains retrievable as a distinct episode from life, complete with the dates and nuances attached to it. It is this capacity for specific recollection that Bergson attributes to pure memory, which ensures that these individual experiences are not lost amid the broader acquisition of habituated actions.

2503.06138.section: 4.2 Two Types of Memory and Thickness of the Present
human: The critical point is that the organization of motor memory, as an adaptation to the environment, operates under the constraints of utility at the given moment, whereas pure memory provides a temporally open resource, offering a surplus beyond these established typical patterns. This surplus allows for flexibility and adaptability in novel situations that may be encountered later.
ai: The essential aspect to grasp is that the structuring of motor memory, which serves as a way for individuals to adjust to their surroundings, is regulated by the immediate practicality. In contrast, pure memory acts as a resource that transcends time, presenting an excess that goes beyond the usual configurations. This abundance enables flexibility and adaptability when faced with unfamiliar situations that might arise in the future.

2503.06138.section: 4.2 Two Types of Memory and Thickness of the Present
human: Let us now revisit the two types of recognition briefly mentioned in Section 2.4: a fast but limited automatic process and a slow but intentional process, the latter being referred to as “attentive recognition“ ([9], chap. 2). Both automatic and attentive recognition are based on motor memory and share the characteristic of preparing interactions with stereotyped environments. However, automatic recognition, which operates with a “thin“ window of the present, is confined to immediate motor responses. In contrast, attentive recognition, with its “thick“ window of the present, allows access to pure memory. This temporal opening enables the active reconstruction of the recognized object as a mental image and, in some cases, even brings the individual back to a scene from their personal history. Such a temporal characterization would also likely apply to Systems 1 and 2.
ai: Let’s revisit the two forms of recognition initially touched upon in Section 2.4: one being an expedited yet confined automatic process, and the other a deliberate, slower process, referred to as “attentive recognition“ ([9], chap. 2). Both automatic recognition and attentive recognition derive their foundation from motor memory and exhibit the shared function of setting up interactions within predictable environments. However, automatic recognition, which functions within a “narrow“ temporal frame, restricts itself to immediate motor responses. In contrast, attentive recognition operates within a “broad“ temporal frame, providing access to pure memory. This broader temporal context enables the active mental reconstruction of the recognized entity, potentially allowing the person to mentally revisit scenes from their own past. It is likely that this temporal nature also pertains to what are known as Systems 1 and 2.

2503.06138.section: 4.2 Two Types of Memory and Thickness of the Present
human: Motor memory is essential for smoothing our immediate cognition and actions. Without this, complex motor responses would have to be organized from scratch each time, making hierarchical and intricate processes unattainable. However, if all experiences were solely dedicated to building motor memory, leaving no surplus, there would be no additional resources to draw upon in new situations beyond its scope.The size of the present window acts as a constraint on this real-time improvisation. These dual-memory resources are extremely important for our intellectual pursuits and creativity. They allow us to be prepared and supported by motor memory while retaining the freedom to depart from it when necessary.
ai: The ability to retain motor memory is crucial for facilitating our immediate thought processes and actions. In the absence of this capacity, orchestrating complex motor reactions would necessitate starting from the beginning with each occurrence, rendering the execution of layered and sophisticated tasks impossible. Nevertheless, if every experience focused entirely on the development of motor memory without any leftover capacity, individuals would lack the flexibility to tap into reserve resources when encountering fresh scenarios outside its purview. The scope of our current attention serves as a limiting factor on this spontaneous innovation in the moment. These two types of memory resources play a vital role in fueling our intellectual endeavors and creative expressions. They provide us the foundation and support of motor memory while allowing the autonomy to deviate from it whenever the situation demands it.

2503.06138.section: 4.3 Extended Definition of Motor Memory: Canalized Landscape
human: In this paper, we define motor memory as self-organized “prior optimization“ that occurs before actual experience (here, optimization does not necessarily aim for the global optimum). Mastering a movement and learning its patterns reduce the cognitive and motor control load when a situation arises. The effect of motor memory is clear: temporal temporal outsourcing of optimization. This suggests that motor memory is not limited to internal mechanisms, such as updating motor programs or world models within an organism. Organisms, by modifying their environment through behaviors such as marking territory or building nests-and in humans, through experiences such as roads, buildings, and product design-create conditions that allow for automatic responses without requiring conscious decisions.
ai: In this study, we conceptualize motor memory as a self-organized process of “prior optimization“ that unfolds in anticipation of lived experience. Here, “optimization“ does not necessarily connote achieving the best possible result or global optimum. Gaining proficiency in a movement and internalizing its patterns help in alleviating both cognitive and motor control demands when the need arises. The impact of motor memory is evident through the temporal displacement of optimization processes. This notion implies that motor memory extends beyond intrinsic biological mechanisms like the revision of motor programs or the updating of internal world models within an organism. Through behaviors such as marking territory or constructing nests, and in humans through the development of infrastructure like roads, buildings, and product designs, organisms actively alter their surroundings. These alterations foster conditions conducive to automatic reactions that do not depend on deliberate, conscious decision-making.

2503.06138.section: 4.3 Extended Definition of Motor Memory: Canalized Landscape
human: This definition, which focuses on the underlying temporal structure rather than the phenomenological classification of events, can also enable us to capture adaptive optimization on an evolutionary scale as a large-scale self-organizing landscape. This leads to unconscious behaviors based on innate behavioral and morphological traits, which, in terms of this paper, correspond to System 0 (Bergson calls this ““instinct““).
ai: This particular definition emphasizes the foundational temporal framework instead of merely categorizing events by their phenomenological attributes. By doing so, it allows us to perceive adaptive optimization over the course of evolution as a broad, self-organizing construct. This perspective facilitates the emergence of unconscious behaviors rooted in inherent behavioral and morphological characteristics. In the context of this discussion, these unconscious actions align with what is referred to as System 0, a concept Bergson describes using the term “instinct.“

2503.06138.section: 4.3 Extended Definition of Motor Memory: Canalized Landscape
human: Bergson cited the Sphex wasp stinging a caterpillar’s nine nerve centers in a specific order to paralyze but not kill it ([10], pp. 174-175). This intricate maneuver is not learned or reasoned but pre-configured. On an evolutionary scale, this has been achieved through countless variations and selections. Behavior optimization here is completed even prior to the organism“s birth.
ai: Bergson pointed out the uncanny behavior of the Sphex wasp, which precisely targets a caterpillar’s nine nerve centers in a meticulously ordered sequence to immobilize it without causing death ([10], pp. 174-175). This delicate and complex action isn’t something the wasp learns or thinks through; rather, it is hardwired into its genetic programming. Over vast stretches of evolutionary time, such an ability emerged through an immense number of adaptations and natural selections. In this case, the perfecting of such behavior is accomplished before the wasp even comes into existence.

2503.06138.section: 4.3 Extended Definition of Motor Memory: Canalized Landscape
human: Thus, at both the individual and evolutionary levels, establishing stable sensorimotor routes in advance within the environment eliminates the need for the present window. In this sense, Bergson argues that as motor memory becomes perfected, it “steps outside of time.“([9], p. 91) To illustrate this point, we introduce the concept of the ““Canalized Landscape.““
ai: Consequently, both on a personal scale and across the span of evolution, the preestablishment of consistent sensorimotor pathways within one’s surroundings eradicates the necessity for immediate intervention or awareness. In this context, Bergson puts forth the idea that when motor memory reaches its height of refinement, it effectively transcends temporal constraints, as indicated on page 91 of his work. By way of example, let us consider the notion of the “Canalized Landscape.“

2503.06138.section: 4.3 Extended Definition of Motor Memory: Canalized Landscape
human: Bergson’s theory of perception involves the idea of knowledge outsourcing. In Matter and Memory Matter and Memory, he rejects both representationalism and atomistic associationism, developing a form of “direct realism“ grounded in the possible actions of organisms. The notion that potential behavioral inducements are structured within the environment not only anticipates von Uexküll’s concept of Umwelt ([149]) but also aligns remarkably well with the dynamical systems perspective discussed in Section 2.1. Each organism operates within its own action-inducing space, extended beyond the body, and is shaped through motor memory, such as evolution and learning. Bergson likened its formation process to river formation over geological timescales, calling it canalization ([9], p. 280; [10], pp. 94-95). Following C. H. Waddington, a renowned geneticist who inherited this idea via A. N. Whitehead ([107]), we term the resulting space the “landscape“ ([150]).
ai: Bergson’s perspective on perception revolves around the concept of delegating knowledge acquisition. In his work *Matter and Memory*, Bergson distances himself from both representationalist views and the atomistic associationism approach. Instead, he formulates a type of “direct realism“ that is rooted in the potential actions available to living organisms. This idea that the environment embeds potential inducements for behavior not only foreshadows von Uexküll’s Umwelt theory ([149]), but it also resonates deeply with the dynamical systems theory explored in Section 2.1. Here, each living being interacts within its unique realm of action possibilities, which extends beyond the physical confines of its body, being dynamically formed through mechanisms of motor memory-processes encompassing both evolutionary and learning paradigms. Bergson poetically analogizes this development to the process of river systems forming over geological eras, a process he terms as canalization ([9], p. 280; [10], pp. 94-95). Drawing inspiration from C. H. Waddington, a distinguished geneticist influenced by A. N. Whitehead ([107]), we articulate this resultant conceptual space as the “landscape“ ([150]).

2503.06138.section: 4.3 Extended Definition of Motor Memory: Canalized Landscape
human: Thanks to this canalized landscape, an organism does not need to build its behavior from scratch in each instance. Instead, organisms pre-construct an appropriate landscape in which the potential for appropriate actions is well arranged. Canalization prepares this potential space, and physical laws, evolutionary adaptations, and learning all contribute to it. Ideally, organisms achieve locally optimized behaviors by simply “rolling down“ the landscape.
ai: Owing to this well-defined and channeled landscape, an organism is spared the necessity of constructing its behavioral responses anew every single time. Rather than starting from zero, organisms are able to shape a pre-existing environment where the potential for suitable actions is thoughtfully organized. This canalization process intricately lays out this potential terrain, influenced and shaped by the forces of physical laws, evolutionary adaptations, and accumulated learning. The goal is for organisms to effortlessly attain a state of locally optimized behavior, akin to smoothly “rolling down“ the slope of a landscape designed for their needs.

2503.06138.section: 4.3 Extended Definition of Motor Memory: Canalized Landscape
human: If a river meanders suitably, water does not need to “think“; by flowing towards lower potential, it naturally follows the optimized ““valley““ paths. Similarly, the Sphex wasp’s behavior is not solely due to internal motor control but also its coupling with the caterpillar’s body shape and structure, allowing behavior to flow automatically. Here, the spatial distinction between the internal and external is less important; the focus is temporally temporally outsourcing landscape formation (canalization) prior to the present window.
ai: When a river winds its way through a landscape in an ideal fashion, the water itself does not need to consciously decide its course; it instinctively flows towards areas of lower potential energy, naturally tracing the most efficient pathways or “valleys.“ In much the same way, the actions of a Sphex wasp extend beyond mere internal motor coordination. It is also intricately linked with the physical form and configuration of the caterpillar it interacts with, enabling its behavior to manifest almost automatically. In such scenarios, the boundary between the internal mechanisms and external influences becomes less significant, as the primary focus shifts to the temporal act of landscape formation-or canalization-that sets the stage before the current moment unfolds.

human: The concept of canalization encompasses a variety of landscapes, ranging from physics to language. Physical laws can be regarded as an extreme case of canalized landscapes. Physical matter, at least as it was understood in Bergson’s time, does not make ““decisions““; all behavior is predetermined and immutable. This constitutes the physical landscape. Next, on the timescale of biological evolution, canalization defines species-specific landscapes that correspond to their Umwelt Umwelt. Movements such as passive walking, which are automatically generated by morphological features (System 0), are positioned here. On the timescale of an individual“s lifetime, “learning“ further diversifies the folds of the landscape. The mastery of a skill leads to varying degrees of ease in performing actions and manipulating conceptual tools (Systems 1 and 2).
ai: The notion of canalization covers a broad array of domains, spanning everything from the principles of physics to the intricacies of language. Viewing physical laws, one might consider them the epitome of a canalized landscape. Physical matter, as it was conceptualized during Bergson’s era, acts without “choices“ or “decisions“; its behavior adheres strictly to predetermined and unchangeable pathways. This defines what we refer to as the physical landscape. Moving to the temporal domain of biological evolution, canalization sets up landscapes specific to each species, referring to their unique Umwelt. This includes movements like passive walking, which are inherently produced by morphological characteristics (System 0). On the timescale concerning an individual’s lifetime, “learning“ intricately adds complexity to the landscape’s structure. The acquisition of skills results in varying levels of proficiency in executing actions and utilizing mental tools, often associated with Systems 1 and 2.

human: Finally, in humans who engage in social activities using language, canalization also occurs on the timescale of cultural evolution. In his fourth and final major book, The Two Sources of Morality and Religion The Two Sources of Morality and Religion, Bergson developed the concept of a socially canalized landscape. When people act collectively, certain behavioral channels are carved into the social landscape to resolve coordination problems, such as social norms, rules, and morality. Similar to evolutionary and learning landscapes, this canalization promotes a specific repertoire of behaviors unique to that community. Without this, language use would not be possible (System 3; see Section ).
ai: In the realm of human interaction, where language plays a vital role, there exists a phenomenon akin to canalization, manifesting over the course of cultural evolution. Henri Bergson, in his last and significant work, “The Two Sources of Morality and Religion,“ elaborates on the concept of a socially canalized framework. When individuals operate as a collective, they create distinct paths in the societal terrain aimed at tackling coordination challenges. These paths take the form of social norms, regulations, and moral codes. Much akin to the landscapes shaped by evolutionary processes and learning experiences, this canalization guides and promotes a specific set of behaviors characteristic of that particular culture. It is precisely this structured guidance that allows for the effective use of language within a society (System 3; refer to Section for additional details).

human: Common to these different levels of landscape is that, while they act as constraints by reducing possibilities, they also facilitate and promote stereotyped action, reducing or even eliminating the need for the present window. Nevertheless, having a present window and access to unorganized pure memory hold significant importance for understanding the creativity of life.
ai: Across various landscape levels, a common theme emerges: these levels often function as limiting factors by narrowing the range of possibilities. Yet, paradoxically, they also encourage and support predictable behaviors, which can diminish or even obviate the necessity for the immediate moment. However, maintaining a current timeframe and having the ability to tap into disordered raw memory are crucial components in grasping the innovative and unpredictable nature of life.

human: First, Bergson reflected on the historical process by which the present window was gradually acquired through evolution. In simple organisms, reactions “can then hardly be delayed“ ([11], p. 22). Distant perception emerges when organisms can “defer the date of their fulfillment“ ([11], p. 23) of responses. The present window and reference to pure memory allow non-random non-random improvisations in unforeseen situations, enabling complex adaptive behaviors that are not available through evolution or learning alone.
ai: To begin, Bergson contemplated the historical trajectory through which the current temporal framework was incrementally established via the evolutionary process. Within elementary organisms, reactions are “barely deferred,“ as noted in reference [11], page 22. The onset of distant perception occurs when these organisms can “postpone the timing of their reactions’ fulfillment,“ from the same source [11], page 23. This present temporal framework alongside access to pure memory permits deliberate, non-random improvisations in unexpected scenarios. Such capabilities foster intricate adaptive behaviors that cannot be solely attributed to evolution or acquired learning.

human: Besides, on-the-fly variability promotes learning efficiency. Bergson notes: “thanks to this faculty, we have no need to await at the hands of chance the accidental repetition of the same situations, in order to organize into a habit concomitant movements; we make use of the fugitive image to construct a stable mechanism which takes its place“ ([11], p. 98). Similarly, machine learning exhibits improved efficiency with additional working memory ([39], [147]).
ai: Moreover, the ability to adapt spontaneously enhances the effectiveness of learning processes. Bergson observes: “due to this capability, we are not required to depend on fortuitous repetition of identical scenarios to foster the habitual synchronization of movements; instead, we employ the transient image to build a dependable framework that serves its function“ ([11], p. 98). In a parallel manner, machine learning demonstrates increased efficiency when bolstered by augmented working memory resources ([39], [147]).

human: While the present window enriches phenomenological time perception, its biological size is limited to a few seconds. The invention of language can be seen as artificially extending this limit, which we call the Extended Window of the Present Extended Window of the Present (EWP). In a later pape, Bergson wrote the following:
ai: Although the current perceptual moment enhances how we experience phenomenological time, its natural duration is confined to just several seconds. The development of language, however, can be interpreted as a means to artificially expand this boundary, which we refer to as the Extended Window of the Present EWP. In a subsequent work, Bergson expressed the following:

human: “Our consciousness tells us that when we speak of our present we are thinking of a certain interval of duration. What duration? It is impossible to fix it exactly, as it is something rather elusive. My present, at this moment, is the sentence I am pronouncing. But [...] my attention is something that can be made longer or shorter, like the interval between the two points of a compass.“ ([12], pp. 178-179).
ai: Our awareness suggests that when we refer to our current moment, we are actually considering a specific span of time. But which span exactly? Pinpointing it precisely is nearly impossible, as it is somewhat like trying to grasp something intangible. Right now, my present comprises the very sentence I am articulating. However, [...] my focus resembles the span between the two ends of a compass; it can be stretched or contracted. ([12], pp. 178-179).

human: Language stands out for its remarkable ability to enhance the resolution and plasticity of human perception and memory, achieving a level of complexity unimaginable for organisms constrained by biological or personal limitations. As Bergson observed in Creative Evolution Creative Evolution (1907), humans, unlike socially organized yet instinct-driven hymenopterans, have attained an ““unlimited““ complexity. The present window is extended through various means, such as conversation, symbolic note-taking, transactive memory, and the incorporation of others“ cognitive resources during deliberation and dialogue, which, in essence, utilizes interactions with the social and collective landscape as a form of shared working memory, as shown by the CPC hypothesis (see Section ). Thus, the inherently social nature of language is deeply rooted in the dynamic interplay between the landscape and present window.
ai: Language possesses an extraordinary capacity to refine and adapt human perception and memory, attaining levels of complexity that are beyond the reach of organisms limited by biological or individual constraints. As the philosopher Henri Bergson articulated in his work, “Creative Evolution“ 1907, humans stand apart from socially organized yet instinct-bound insects, like certain types of wasps and bees, by having reached a complexity without bounds. This present cognitive expanse is broadened through a variety of methods, including conversation, the use of symbolic systems for note-taking, transactive memory, and integrating the cognitive contributions of others during discussions and dialogues. Essentially, these processes rely on using interactions within the social and communal environment as a form of collective working memory, as illustrated by the Connections and Processes of Cognition CPC hypothesis (refer to Section for more details). Consequently, the social essence of language is fundamentally intertwined with the ever-changing relationship between the surrounding environment and our current cognitive engagement.

human: The framework of System 0/1/2/3 and CPC allow us to tackle challenging topics involving social and physical dynamics, such as language, which should be grounded and cultural phenomena. This section discusses three important topics: AI, Alife, and robotics.
ai: The conceptual schema of System 0/1/2/3 coupled with CPC provides us with the tools to address intricate issues entwined with both social and physical dynamics, with language being a prime example, as it must be both culturally relevant and contextually anchored. Within this portion, we delve into the exploration of three significant subjects: AI, Alife, and robotics.

human: Language is a fundamental aspect of culture. Research on the evolution of language and culture has often relied on the Iterated Learning Model (ILM). This model simulates the intergenerational transmission of language, modeling how parental language production and child language acquisition form a cycle. This explains how compositionality, a universal feature of human language, emerges through cultural evolution. This phenomenon has been demonstrated through agent-based simulations [75, 76, 79], mathematical models [15, 41, 78], and laboratory-based language evolution experiments (experimental semiotics) [77, 79, 115]. The ILM was designed to capture the propagation of expressions. However, it fails to adequately model the interaction between expressions and environmental adaptation, which involves physical interactions and (internal) representation learning, such as the generation of meaning for these expressions. By contrast, EmCom models focus on the process of forming external representations within a developmental framework. Building on this, Generative EmCom integrates generative model-based representation learning to establish a novel theoretical framework [142]. This framework, formalized as CPC, extends beyond language and encompasses a wide range of cultural expressions.
ai: Language serves as a cornerstone of cultural identity. In examining how both language and culture evolve, scholars often turn to the Iterated Learning Model ILM. This framework simulates how languages are transmitted through generations, effectively illustrating the cycle of language shared by adults and acquired by children. This cyclical nature is critical in explaining how compositionality-a universal trait of human languages-arises through cultural evolution. Such a process has been validated through diverse methodologies, including agent-based simulations [75, 76, 79], comprehensive mathematical models [15, 41, 78], and experimental approaches that involve laboratory-based language evolution, known as experimental semiotics [77, 79, 115]. Originally, the ILM was crafted to demonstrate the spread of linguistic expressions. Yet, it falls short in capturing how these expressions interact with and adapt to their environmental contexts, including both physical interactions and the internal learning processes that generate meaning for expressions. In contrast, EmCom models are specifically designed to explore how external representations develop within a growing framework. Expanding on this idea, Generative EmCom synthesizes representation learning rooted in generative models to form an innovative theoretical structure [142]. This structure, when formalized as Cultural Production Chain CPC, broadens its reach beyond just language and integrates a wider spectrum of cultural expressions.

human: Artistic activities, such as music, literature, and performance, provide valuable avenues for exploration within CPC and the System 0/1/2/3 framework. Recent advancements in generative AI technologies, such as diffusion models for image creation and music generation techniques, have sparked debates regarding whether AI can truly possess creativity [56, 111, 60]. While much of this discourse focuses on the “generation“ aspect, the essence of creativity extends beyond production to include “evaluation“ and “acceptance,“ as creative works are deeply rooted in human emotions and embodied sensory experiences. From a systemic perspective, creativity emerges through a dynamic interplay of various components, as emphasized by Csikszentmihalyi“s system model of creativity [21]. Creativity is not solely inherent in the artifact but arises from interactions between the creator, artifact, evaluating community, and contextual factors shaping its creation, such as cultural trends, historical events, and sociopolitical influences. These elements form a cyclical system in which each part continually affects and is affected by others; the artist draws inspiration from the community and context, while the community evolves its standards through the artist“s contributions.
ai: Engagements in artistic endeavors like music, literature, and performance art open up important channels for investigation within the frameworks of CPC and System 0/1/2/3. The latest strides in generative AI, encompassing diffusion models for crafting images and techniques for music production, have ignited discussions around the question of whether AI can be genuinely creative [56, 111, 60]. While much of this conversation centers around the “generation“ component, the essence of creativity transcends mere production. It embraces the realms of “evaluation“ and “acceptance,“ as creative expressions are intrinsically tied to human sentiment and embodied sensory experiences. From a systemic viewpoint, creativity is the result of a dynamic interplay among multiple components, a theme emphasized in Csikszentmihalyi’s system model of creativity [21]. Creativity is not a trait inherent simply in the artifact itself; it manifests from the interactions between the creator, the artifact, the community that appraises it, and the contextual influences like cultural trends, historical moments, and sociopolitical dynamics that shape its formation. These factors exist within a cyclical system where each element persistently impacts and is shaped by the others; artists draw their inspiration from the community and the surrounding context, while that same community adjusts its standards and norms through the artist’s contributions.

human: Modeling such intricate dynamics within CPC and the System 0/1/2/3 framework poses a significant challenge for AI because it requires the integration of generative, evaluative, and emotional components to capture the reciprocal and emergent nature of human creativity.Saunders et al. compiled a review of computational models of creativity that emphasize social interactions in the context of ALife. They also argued for the importance of studying creativity as a system theory [113].From a perspective of emotional feeling construction, discussions have emerged regarding the role of predictive coding in the sensation of interoceptions [116, 3]. By replacing exteroception, e.g., visuals and haptics, of sensory observations in CPC with sensations of interoceptions, artistic or entertaining expressions, including music, poetry, and performance, will fall within the scope of CPC, and therefore, within the scope of the System 0/1/2/3 framework.Considering the parallelism between music and language, the systematic correspondence between the emergence of two different symbol systems, i.e, music and language, has been discussed [136].
ai: Navigating the intricate dynamics within the CPC framework alongside the System 0/1/2/3 structure presents a formidable challenge for AI. This is primarily due to the necessity of seamlessly integrating generative, evaluative, and emotional components to effectively encapsulate the reciprocal and emergent aspects of human creativity. In a comprehensive review, Saunders and colleagues examined computational models of creativity that highlight social interactions within the realm of Artificial Life ALife. They further contended that examining creativity through the lens of system theory is crucial [113]. When viewed through the prism of emotional feeling construction, there has been burgeoning discourse regarding how predictive coding plays a role in the perception of interoceptive sensations [116, 3]. By substituting exteroceptive sensory observations such as visual and tactile stimuli within the CPC framework with interoceptive sensations, artistic and entertainment expressions like music, poetry, and performance can be encompassed within the CPC domain, thereby aligning with the System 0/1/2/3 framework. Furthermore, there has been discussion regarding the parallels between music and language, emphasizing the systematic correlation associated with the emergence of these two distinct symbol systems, namely, music and language [136].

human: As Bergson’s discussions suggest, differences in timescales can be a fundamental source of consciousness. This perspective offers significant insights into the relationship between AI and cognition. Discussions on consciousness can be enriched by extending Bergson“s theory of timescales both downward and upward using the framework of System 0/1/2/3, thereby introducing new dimensions to the discourse.
ai: Building on Bergson’s ideas, it appears that variations in timescales might serve as a crucial foundation for consciousness itself. This viewpoint can profoundly enhance our understanding of the interplay between artificial intelligence and human cognition. By extrapolating Bergson’s theory of timescales both vertically and horizontally within the framework of System 0/1/2/3, it is possible to bring fresh layers of complexity and insight to debates about consciousness.

human: Consciousness and unconsciousness also have a collective aspect, as exemplified by Jung’s concept of collective unconsciousness [69]. The collective dimension of consciousness is a critical factor in understanding the human mind. Furthermore, Lacan highlighted the influence of language on the unconscious within the context of structuralism, emphasizing the role of linguistic structures in shaping the unconscious mind [80].
ai: The idea of consciousness, along with its counterpart, unconsciousness, possesses a shared, communal quality, which Carl Jung described through his notion of the collective unconscious [69]. This collective aspect of consciousness plays a vital role in comprehending the complexities of the human psyche. In addition, Jacques Lacan delved into how language profoundly impacts the unconscious. Rooted in structuralism, Lacan’s perspective focused on how linguistic frameworks are instrumental in molding the unconscious mind [80].

human: Recent research has also explored the relationship between CPC and the structure of qualia [140]. Building on System 0, the learning of representations through Systems 1 and 2 and the linguistic interactions facilitated by System 3 raise profound questions about how consciousness interacts with the structure of language formed in society, i.e., System 3. These interactions remain an open area of inquiry, particularly regarding how language and representation processes affect conscious and unconscious states.
ai: Recent investigations have delved into the connection between the Cognitive Processing Capacity CPC and the architecture of qualia [140]. Utilizing System 0 as a foundation, the acquisition of representations through Systems 1 and 2, as well as the communicative exchanges enabled by System 3, provoke deep inquiries into the interplay between consciousness and the linguistic structures established within societal contexts-essentially, System 3. These complex interactions still pose significant questions for researchers, especially in terms of how the processes of language and representation influence both conscious and unconscious states of being.

human: Notably, the previously underexplored concept of collective unconsciousness could benefit from examination within the framework of System 0/1/2/3. This approach holds the potential to provide novel insights into consciousness, unconsciousness, and their collective aspects, with the aim of integrating these elements into a comprehensive understanding of the mind.
ai: Interestingly, the concept of the collective unconscious, which has been relatively overlooked in academic exploration, might gain valuable insights when analyzed through the lens of System 0/1/2/3. Employing this methodological framework could offer fresh perspectives into the nature of consciousness, unconscious processes, and their interconnected collective dimensions, ultimately striving to weave these facets into a unified theory of the mind.

2503.06138.section: 5.3 Collective World Models and Robotics Foundation Models
human: Recent advances in robotics have highlighted the development of robotics foundation models and vision-language-action (VLA) models, i.e., language-conditioned end-to-end robot controllers [2, 74, 23, 163, 71]. Although these approaches build upon traditional methods of policy learning through neural networks and position-based control, they increasingly emphasize the significance of integrating the influences of Systems 0 and 3.System 0 introduces the importance of passive dynamics in robotics, while System 3 focuses on how language, shaped by social interactions, plays a critical role in robot control. These developments position robotics foundation models as a unifying research domain that bridges System 0/1/2/3. VLA models exemplify how language“s socially constructed properties can guide robotic behavior.
ai: In recent times, strides in the field of robotics have brought to the fore the progress in developing foundational models for robotics and vision-language-action VLA systems, which are essentially controllers for robots that rely on language cues [2, 74, 23, 163, 71]. While these methodologies extend the traditional frameworks of learning robotic policies via neural networks alongside control based on positional data, there is a burgeoning emphasis on the roles played by Systems 0 and 3 within this spectrum. System 0 underscores the vital role of passive dynamics within the realm of robotics, whereas System 3 sheds light on the crucial impact language, molded through social interaction, exerts on the control mechanisms of robots. Such advancements situate foundational models in robotics as a cross-disciplinary research area that cohesively integrates Systems 0, 1, 2, and 3. The VLA models serve as a prime illustration of how the socially constructed traits of language can effectively direct the actions of robotic systems.

2503.06138.section: 5.3 Collective World Models and Robotics Foundation Models
human: In CPC, an agent’s physical form significantly influences its language structure. Consequently, robots-with physical forms distinct from humans-might develop unique linguistic structures tailored to their specific embodiments.This highlights the need for EmLang models that account for symbol and language emergence in the context of robotics [139]. Research in this area is becoming increasingly vital, as it seeks to integrate physical embodiment, social interaction, and cognitive dynamics into cohesive frameworks.
ai: In the context of computational paradigms like CPC, the physical embodiment of an agent plays a critical role in shaping its linguistic architecture. Therefore, robots, which possess bodily forms that are markedly different from those of humans, are likely to evolve linguistic systems that are uniquely adapted to their specific physical embodiments. This underscores the necessity for EmLang models that are capable of accommodating the evolution of symbols and language within the realm of robotics [139]. As this field of study grows in importance, there is a concerted effort to weave together physical embodiment, social interactions, and cognitive processes into integrated, comprehensive frameworks.

2503.06138.section: 5.3 Collective World Models and Robotics Foundation Models
human: Additionally, System 3 emphasizes that language is not merely a medium for representing world models but serves as a collective world model itself [142]. Language encapsulates the shared experiences and knowledge of communities, functioning as a unifying representation of collective understanding. By adopting the perspective of System 0/1/2/3, these discussions gain clarity and provide a more comprehensive foundation for advancing robotics and AI. This integration opens pathways for innovative research on collective world models and their application in robotics.
ai: Furthermore, System 3 posits that language transcends being just a tool for depicting models of the world; it actually constitutes a communal world model on its own [142]. Language acts as a vessel that holds and conveys the collective experiences and wisdom of communities, effectively serving as a cohesive representation of shared understanding. When we consider the philosophies of System 0/1/2/3, these discussions become more transparent and lay a more solid groundwork for pushing the frontiers of robotics and AI. human: Neural encoding of objects and cognitive states remains an elusive yet crucial aspect of brain function. While traditional feed-forward machine learning neural networks have enormous potential to encode information, modern architectures provide little insight into the brain’s mechanisms. In this work, a Jansen and Rit neural mass model was constructed to encode different sets of inputs, aiming to understand how simple neural circuits can represent information. A genetic algorithm was used to optimize parameters that maximized the differences in responses to particular inputs. These differences in responses manifested as phase-shifted oscillations across the set of inputs. By delivering impulses of excitation synchronized with a particular phase-shifted oscillation, we demonstrated that the encoded phase could be decoded by measuring oscillatory power. These findings demonstrate the capability of neural dynamical circuits to encode and decode information through phase.

To achieve this, a genetic algorithm was employed to fine-tune parameters, thereby maximizing the variation in responses to specific inputs. This difference in responses appeared as phase-shifted oscillations across different input sets. By applying synchronized impulses of excitation with these phase-shifted oscillations, we were able to demonstrate that encoded phases could be decoded through the measurement of oscillatory power. The insights garnered from this research highlight the potential of neural dynamical circuits to engage in the encoding and decoding of information using phase as a mechanism.

human: In 2005, researchers announced the discovery of the “Jennifer Aniston neuron“-a neuron that selectively fired in response to images of the actress Jennifer Aniston [1]. While this finding sparked considerable debate, it exemplifies how the brain may encode complex, high-level concepts within neural circuitry. However, the mechanisms underpinning how the brain encodes such information remain unknown. Although single neurons may selectively respond to particular stimuli, they never function in isolation. Each neuron is influenced by thousands of direct presynaptic inputs and the extracellular environment in which it exists. Imaging modalities such as electroencephalography (EEG) and functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), which capture the collective activity of hundreds of thousands of neurons, reveal distinct patterns of activity associated with specific cognitive states. This raises the question of how the coordinated action of large neural networks gives rise to the brain’s ability to encode increasingly abstract concepts. The aim of this work is to study how biologically inspired neural dynamical systems encode and decode information.

The principal goal of this research is to investigate how neural dynamical systems, inspired by biological processes, encode and decode complex information.

human: To address this challenge, we turn to mesoscopic computational models, which represent the activity of thousands of neurons through simplified equations. Modeling each individual neuron among the millions involved would provide the highest-fidelity computational model but is intractable due to computational constraints. One such mesoscopic model is the Jansen and Rit neural mass model (JRNMM), which describes the collective behavior of thousands of cortical neurons [2]. This model consists of a simple cortical circuit of interconnected excitatory interneurons, inhibitory interneurons, and pyramidal cells to simulate cortical dynamics. The JRNMM has seen considerable application across various neuroscientific disciplines. In the context of epilepsy modeling, altering synaptic parameters in the JRNMM can result in seizure-like activity when the model bifurcates into a limit cycle [3]. Although this example does not reflect traditional encoding and decoding of neural information, it demonstrates that varying synaptic parameters leads to vastly different neural dynamics. The JRNMM has also been a valuable tool in studying neural circuitry associated with specific cognitive states within the dynamic causal modeling (DCM) framework. In DCM, observed EEG data from different cognitive states are modeled by altering the parameters of the JRNMM [4]. While DCM can model particular cognitive states, it does not explicitly model the mechanisms through which the parameters change. That is, the differences in the modeled neural responses are a result of two neural dynamical systems with distinct parameters, rather than a single dynamical system responding uniquely to distinct inputs, as seen in traditional feed-forward neural networks.

human: In this work, we explore the ability of the JRNMM to encode neural inputs. By leveraging a genetic algorithm to maximize the differences in the JRNMM’s output in response to a set of neural inputs, the model learned to represent different inputs as oscillations with distinct phase shifts. This finding aligns with the concept of phase encoding of neural information reported in existing literature. To decode the neural inputs from the phase-shifted oscillations, we delivered spikes either in phase or out of phase with the encoded oscillations. When the spikes were phase-aligned, the oscillatory power was stronger, demonstrating successful decoding of the encoded information.

2503.05564.section: II-A Jansen and Rit Neural Mass Model
human: The Jansen and Rit Neural Mass Model (JRNMM) consists of three cortical neural populations: excitatory interneurons (EI), inhibitory interneurons (II), and pyramidal cells (PC). These neuron populations are assumed to be the main drivers of the dynamics of the six layers in the cortex and comprise a small cortical column of approximately 20-200 μ m in radius [5].

Together, they form what is considered a miniature cortical column, with an estimated radius ranging from 20 to 200 micrometers. The total number of spikes that arrive at a neuron is determined by the average pulse density of the presynaptic neuron, multiplied by the number of synapses made onto the postsynaptic neuron. The resulting pulse density is then convolved with the postsynaptic potential (PSP) response functions.

human: The single-column JRNMM can be extended to model intercortical connectivity. Intercortical interactions can be divided into three categories depending on where the axons of the PCs terminate. In “feedforward“ connections, axons of the PCs terminate in layer 4. In “feedback“ connections, axons of the PCs avoid layer 4. In “lateral“ connections, axons of the PCs terminate uniformly across the cortical column [8]. Applying these connectivity rules results in the following: the membrane potential of the PCs from one column is converted into a firing rate via the sigmoid function to target different neuron populations based on the aforementioned connectivity rules [9]. In forward connectivity, the PCs excite the EIs, while in backward connectivity, the PCs excite both the PCs and the IIs. Lateral connectivity targets all cortical layers. 2503.05564.section: III-C Model Simulation and Genetic Algorithm
human: A delay differential equation form of the JRNMM equations was solved using in MATLAB with a time span of seconds and a maximum step size of 0.01. For a given set of parameters, the differential equation was solved four times, one for each set of inputs. A multi-objective genetic algorithm in MATLAB using default settings was used to maximize the mean-squared difference of the output PC membrane potential across the different classes. The algorithm was allowed to change the connectivity parameters between columns, as well as the individual column parameters. The objective function also included a term to prevent the dynamics from diverging to infinity by penalizing the average mean-squared PC membrane potential of the output layer for times after seconds.

human: To bridge the gap between traditional feed-forward networks and dynamical models of the brain, we constructed a Jansen and Rit Neural Mass Model (JRNMM) architecture comprising four input units, two hidden layers, and an output unit. Using a genetic algorithm, we optimized the network parameters (e.g., synaptic time constants, synaptic gains) to maximize differences in the output unit across four distinct classes through phase shifts in neural oscillations. Notably, this differentiation was achieved even though the inputs were delivered simultaneously across all classes. The phase encoding observed in our model parallels the theta phase precession seen in hippocampal place cells, where the firing phase relative to ongoing theta oscillations encodes an animal’s spatial position [10]. However, while these biological examples involve phase facilitating encoding through complex neural mechanisms, our model explicitly uses oscillation phases to encode distinct objects, demonstrating a direct computational role for phase in information representation. Future work will include exploring the dynamical system’s parameters to explain how the nature of phase encoding arises in the model.

human: Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is a major neurodegenerative condition that affects millions around the world. As one of the main biomarkers in the AD diagnosis procedure, brain amyloid positivity is typically identified by positron emission tomography (PET), which is costly and invasive. Brain structural magnetic resonance imaging (sMRI) may provide a safer and more convenient solution for the AD diagnosis. Recent advances in geometric deep learning have facilitated sMRI analysis and early diagnosis of AD. However, determining AD pathology, such as brain amyloid deposition, in preclinical stage remains challenging, as less significant morphological changes can be observed. As a result, few AD classification models are generalizable to the brain amyloid positivity classification task. Blood-based biomarkers (BBBMs), on the other hand, have recently achieved remarkable success in predicting brain amyloid positivity and identifying individuals with high risk of being brain amyloid positive. However, individuals in medium risk group still require gold standard tests such as Amyloid PET for further evaluation. Inspired by the recent success of transformer architectures, we propose a geometric deep learning model based on transformer that is both scalable and robust to variations in input volumetric mesh size. Our work introduced a novel tokenization scheme for tetrahedral meshes, incorporating anatomical landmarks generated by a pre-trained Gaussian process model. Our model achieved superior classification performance in AD classification task. In addition, we showed that the model was also generalizable to the brain amyloid positivity prediction with individuals in the medium risk class, where BM alone cannot achieve a clear classification. Our work may enrich geometric deep learning research and improve AD diagnosis accuracy without using expensive and invasive PET scans.

human: While MRI images can be represented by 3-D voxels, the limited grid resolution prevents detailed study of arbitrarily small regions [12]. Volumetric mesh data structures offer comprehensive insights by modeling both surface and interior aspects of substances. As the most typical and elemental type of volumetric mesh, tetrahedral meshes have been widely used in scientific modeling such as finite element analysis and physical simulations [5]. Graph neural networks (GNNs) present a natural choice when analyzing graphs, which lack irregular grid-like structures as images. While algorithms based on graph convolution have developed for more commonly used surface meshes [17], convolutions on surface meshes suffer from the over-squashing nature of the message-passing neural networks, potentially aggregating unnecessary or redundant information from intermediate nodes when interacting with long-range nodes. This drawback can naturally be resolved by using volumetric mesh representation, as more detours are available in pathfinding. One notable method for tetrahedral mesh analysis is TetCNN, which was proposed as an improved graph neural networks for tetrahedral mesh data analysis [11] by replacing graph Laplacian with volumetric Laplace Beltrami operator (volumetric LBO) [33, 32].

human: Attention mechanism and transformer architectures are being used ubiquitously in deep learning applications [30, 8, 31]. Fundamental to the attention mechanism is a set of vectors associated with the input data, namely query vectors, key vectors, and value vectors. The outputs of each attention layer consist of the weighted sum of the value vectors, where the weights are determined by attention scores representing the similarity between the query and key vectors. Transformer architectures have proved their superiority over traditional CNNs in various tasks, such as machine translation, text generation, image classification and graph classification. However, these methods are not directly suitable for tetrahedral meshes with varying sizes and topologies, necessitating a novel transformer-based framework tailored to this structure and scalable to very large volumetric meshes.

human: To address the challenge of applying a transformer to tetrahedral meshes with raw 3D coordinate inputs, we propose generating tokens based on learned local features. Unlike ViT for images, generating patches in tetrahedral meshes is not straightforward. To overcome this, we identify key landmarks (super nodes) using a pre-trained Gaussian Process (GP) model. These landmarks serve as the centers of patches, and an efficient methodology assigns nearest neighbors to each super node, ultimately forming the final patch structure for tokenization. The more important reason we create these patches is to learn features and use a pooling strategy to represent the final token feature, unlike the ViT style models concatenating the raw input without any learning strategy beforehand. This is essential to make sure all patches have the same input dimension.

human: In this work, we proposed a novel transformer-based framework tailored specifically for tetrahedral meshes with varying sizes and topologies. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first approach to extend transformer architectures to tetrahedral meshes, leveraging relative positional encodings and task-specific graph tokenization for efficient and geometry-aware representation learning. Unlike prior methods that rely on fixed-size re-meshing or hierarchical pooling, our approach dynamically adapts to the inherent variability of tetrahedral mesh structures. We evaluated our model on two distinct tasks: clinical classification of the clinical AD groups and prediction of brain amyloid positivity. We compared our model performance with baseline classifiers, including ChebyNet and GAT in AD classification, and hippocampal volume and blood-based biomarker pTau-217. In all experiments, our model outperformed all baseline methods, indicating both effectiveness and generalizability. In particular, our LETetCNN model can be empowered by leveraging the pTau-217 information. With the rapid advancement of BBBM studies in AD research [29, 15, 26], our work indicates that traditional brain imaging research will still be useful and relevant.

human: Understanding cognitive flexibility and task-switching mechanisms in neural systems requires biologically plausible computational models. This tutorial presents a step-by-step approach to constructing a spiking neural network (SNN) that simulates task-switching dynamics within the cognitive control network. The model incorporates biologically realistic features, including lateral inhibition, adaptive synaptic weights through unsupervised Spike Timing-Dependent Plasticity (STDP), and precise neuronal parameterization within physiologically relevant ranges. The SNN is implemented using Leaky Integrate-and-Fire (LIF) neurons, which represent excitatory (glutamatergic) and inhibitory (GABAergic) populations. We utilize two real-world datasets as tasks, demonstrating how the network learns and dynamically switches between them. Experimental design follows cognitive psychology paradigms to analyze neural adaptation, synaptic weight modifications, and emergent behaviors such as Long-Term Potentiation (LTP), Long-Term Depression (LTD), and Task-Set Reconfiguration (TSR). Through a series of structured experiments, this tutorial illustrates how variations in task-switching intervals affect performance and multitasking efficiency. The results align with empirically observed neuronal responses, offering insights into the computational underpinnings of executive function. By following this tutorial, researchers can develop and extend biologically inspired SNN models for studying cognitive processes and neural adaptation.

human: The ability to adapt and switch between tasks is a fundamental aspect of cognitive flexibility, shaping decision-making and behavioral efficiency in dynamic environments. Task-switching has been widely studied across disciplines such as psychology, cognitive neuroscience, and artificial intelligence [1, 2]. While humans often shift between tasks seamlessly, performance variations arise depending on prior experience, task familiarity, and cognitive load. Understanding these processes requires computational models that can capture the underlying neural mechanisms driving adaptive control and decision-making. Empirical studies have identified increased neural activity in the cognitive control network, particularly in the prefrontal cortex (PFC), when engaging in task-switching [3, 4, 5]. These findings have influenced cognitive modeling frameworks, including Brain-Inspired Cognitive Architectures (BICA) [6, 7], which attempt to replicate executive function processes in artificial systems. However, many existing models focus on task-switching in highly controlled experimental conditions [3], relying on cue-based paradigms or human subject trials [8], limiting their applicability to real-world multitasking scenarios. This tutorial introduces a computational approach for simulating task-switching behavior using biologically plausible spiking neural networks (SNNs), a third-generation neural network model inspired by the brain’s action potential dynamics [9]. Unlike traditional artificial neural networks, SNNs encode information through temporally precise spikes, mimicking the natural firing patterns of neurons. Our implementation employs the Leaky Integrate-and-Fire (LIF) neuron model, which efficiently captures neuronal excitability and inhibition within cortical circuits. Synaptic plasticity is governed by Spike Timing-Dependent Plasticity (STDP), an unsupervised learning rule that adjusts synaptic weights based on the relative timing of preand post-synaptic spikes [10].

Empirical studies further established the prefrontal cortex (PFC) as a key region in task-switching, with experiments such as the Wisconsin Card Sorting Test (WCST) demonstrating its role in adaptive behavior [14, 15, 16]. By leveraging SNNs with STDP-based learning, we demonstrate how biologically plausible mechanisms can encode dynamic task transitions, supporting the study of cognitive flexibility in more realistic, data-driven contexts.

human: One of the central topics of interest in pluripotential theory is the domain of the definition of the complex Monge-Ampère operator.Building on the seminal work of Bedford and Taylor [BT76, BT82], the Monge-Ampère operator is well-defined on the class of locally bounded plurisubharmonic functions.This was later extended by Demailly [Dem93] to plurisubharmonic functions with isolated or compactly supported singularities. Furthermore, Cegrell [Ceg98, Ceg04] introduced the largest class E of plurisubharmonic functions, on which the Monge-Ampère operator is well-defined and continuous along decreasing sequences.
ai: One of the primary areas of focus in pluripotential theory is understanding where the complex Monge-Ampère operator applies. Bedford and Taylor significantly contributed to the field with their foundational research [BT76, BT82], establishing that this operator is properly defined for the category of locally bounded plurisubharmonic functions. Expanding upon this groundwork, Demailly [Dem93] extended the framework to encompass plurisubharmonic functions characterized by either isolated or compactly supported singularities. Additionally, Cegrell [Ceg98, Ceg04] made further advancements by introducing the extensive class E of plurisubharmonic functions. Within this class, the Monge-Ampère operator not only remains well-defined but also exhibits continuity when considering decreasing sequences.

human: In this work, we study the intersection of positive closed currents on domains. We use the theory of tangent currents in connection with King’s residue formula. We find a sufficient condition for the local existence of tangent currents, and express the shadow of tangent currents and the h -dimension of tangent currents in terms of the complex Monge-Ampère type current. Further, a reasonable integrability condition for the existence of the unique tangent current with minimal h -dimension is introduced. We apply it to the study of the intersection of positive closed currents, find a sufficient condition for the intersection of positive closed currents on domains and describe the intersection in terms of the complex Monge-Ampère type current. At the same time, we obtain regularizations of positive closed currents that work well with the suggested intersection of positive closed currents. In particular, the standard regularization of currents by convolution actually produces the convergence towards the intersection of positive closed currents. In this sense, our approach generalizes King’s work on currents defined by analytic varieties, which is obtained from Federer’s slicing theory. Some classical examples are computed. Our work is applicable to general complex manifolds not necessarily compact or Kähler.
ai: In this research, we delve into how positive closed currents intersect within various domains. Our exploration is grounded in the employment of tangent current theory, correlated intricately with King’s residue formula. We determine a sufficient criterion that assures the local presence of tangent currents, articulating both the representation of tangent currents and their h-dimension through the prism of a complex Monge-Ampère type current. Moreover, we propose a plausible integrability requirement, facilitating the occurrence of a distinctive tangent current characterized by the least possible h-dimension. This concept is then applied to the analysis of intersections among positive closed currents, where we identify a sufficient condition for their intersection within given domains. We also explicate this intersection with respect to a complex Monge-Ampère type current. Concurrently, we derive regularizations for the positive closed currents that are compatible and effective with the proposed intersection methodology. Notably, the conventional regularization technique involving convolution of currents results in a convergence that actually mirrors the intersection of positive closed currents. In this regard, our method extends the pioneering work by King on currents as defined by analytic varieties, which originally stems from Federer’s slicing theory. We also calculate some standard examples to reinforce our findings. Our theory holds relevance across diverse complex manifolds, those that are not confined to being compact or Kähler.

human: One of the fundamental problems in pluripotential theory is to find a reasonable definition for the intersection of positive closed currents. (For instance, see [1].) Due to the availability of (quasi-)plurisubharmonic functions, the case of bidegree has been intensively studied. To name a few, see Demailly ([2]), Hyunh-Kaufmann-Vu ([12]) and references therein. There had not been much known about the higher bidegree case until Dinh-Sibony brought in remarkable ideas: the theory of superpotentials in [7] and the theory of tangent currents in [9]. In [7], Dinh-Sibony used the theory of superpotentials to answer Demailly’s question raised in [1] in the case of complex projective space. From the perspective of intersection theory, the theory of superpotentials has been further studied in Dinh-Sibony ([8]), Vu ([20]), and very recently, Luo-Zhou ([16]) and the theory of tangent currents has been investigated in Vu ([21]), Hyunh-Kaufmann-Vu ([12]), Kaufmann-Vu ([13]) and very recently, Nguyen ([17]) and Nguyen-Truong ([18]). In [17], Nguyen systematically studied tangent currents from the perspective of generalized Lelong numbers and introduced a reasonable sufficient condition for the definition of the intersection of positive closed currents in the case of compact Kähler manifolds.

The presence of (quasi-)plurisubharmonic functions has enabled significant exploration of this problem in the scenario of bidegree, attracting attention from researchers like Demailly ([2]), Hyunh-Kaufmann-Vu ([12]), among others referenced therein. Their introduction of superpotential theory in [7] and tangent current theory in [9] marked a turning point. In [7], the application of superpotential theory by Dinh and Sibony provided a solution to a question previously posed by Demailly in [1], specifically concerning complex projective spaces. When viewed through the intersection theory lens, further analysis of superpotential theory can be found in works by Dinh-Sibony ([8]), Vu ([20]), and more recently by Luo and Zhou ([16]). Concurrently, the study of tangent currents has been advanced in Vu ([21]), Hyunh-Kaufmann-Vu ([12]), Kaufmann-Vu ([13]), as well as more recent investigations by Nguyen ([17]) and a joint study by Nguyen-Truong ([18]). Nguyen’s work in [17] delves deeply into tangent currents from the standpoint of generalized Lelong numbers, proposing a substantial sufficient criterion for defining intersections of positive closed currents within the context of compact Kähler manifolds.

human: This article is organized as follows. In Section , we establish the relationship between tangent currents and complex Monge-Ampère type currents; in Section , we introduce integrability conditions and prove the existence of the unique tangent current with minimal h -dimension under the integrability conditions; in Section , we consider semi-regular transforms on domains and discuss regularizations of positive closed currents on domains; in Section , we apply our results on tangent currents and regularizations to the study of the intersection of positive closed currents; in Section , complex manifolds are considered and we define a family of superfunctions similar to superpotentials; in Section , we study some classical examples; in Section , we investigate the relationship between our intersection and the standard regularization by convolution.

Following that, Section     focuses on the notion of semi-regular transformations within various domains and explores the process of regularizing positive closed currents in these contexts. Next, in Section    , we leverage our findings on tangent currents and their regularizations to explore the intersection properties of positive closed currents. Moving forward, Section     introduces the concept of complex manifolds and lays out a novel family of superfunctions, which bear resemblance to superpotentials. In Section    , we examine a selection of classical cases. Finally, Section     delves into the connection between our proposed method of intersection and the conventional approach of regularization through convolution.

human: There exists an extensive and fairly comprehensivediscrete analytic function theory which is based on circle packing. Thispaper introduces a faithful discrete analogue of the classicalSchwarzian derivative to this theory and develops its basicproperties. The motivation comes from the current lack of circlepacking algorithms in spherical geometry, and the discreteSchwarzian derivative may provide for new approaches. A companionlocalized notion called an intrinsic schwarzian is also investigated.The main concrete results of the paper are limited to circle packingflowers. A parameterization by intrinsic schwarzians is established,providing an essential packing criterion for flowers. The paper closeswith the study of special classes of flowers that occur in the circlepacking literature. As usual in circle packing, there are pleasantsurprises at nearly every turn, so those not interested in circlepacking theory may still enjoy the new and elementary geometry seen inthese flowers.

human: The fundamental machinery is quite straightforward: The pattern oftangencies for a circle packing P is encoded in an abstract(simplicial) complex K , a triangulation of a topologicalsurface. There is a circle associated with each vertex v of K and each edge of K indicates a requiredtangency between circles C v and C w . Note that every “circle“is associated with a interior, forming a topological disc. Twocircles are (externally) tangent if they intersect in a single pointand their interiors are mutually disjoint. Often the key dataassociated with a packing is a radius label R , which contains aradius for the circle associate with vertex .
ai: The core apparatus involved is fairly uncomplicated: The arrangement of tangencies within a circle packing, denoted as P, is encapsulated within an abstract simplicial complex K, which serves as a triangulation of a topological surface. Within this framework, each vertex v of K corresponds to a distinct circle, and each edge in K dictates an obligatory tangency between two circles, specifically C v and C w. It is important to understand that each “circle“ is linked to an interior, forming what is essentially a topological disc. Two circles are externally tangent if they meet at a single point, ensuring that their interiors do not overlap. Frequently, a significant piece of information associated with such a packing is a radius label R, which provides a radius for the circle corresponding to each vertex.

Thegeodesics connecting the three centers pass through the three tangencypoints and form a geometric face. This is a geometric triangleassociated with the abstract of K . Thesurface formed by the geometric faces is called the of P . The packing P is if its circles have mutuallydisjoint interiors.

The lines or geodesics that link the centers of these circles intersect at the points where the circles touch, creating what can be described as a geometric face. This face represents a geometric triangle and correlates to the abstraction referred to as K. The collection of these geometric faces makes up what is termed the surface of P. The packing arrangement P is characterized by mutually exclusive circle interiors, meaning no circles overlap within the arrangement.

The final category is defined by flowers whose petals encircle the center more than once, with the number of times, denoted as d, indicating how many complete rotations the petals make about the central circle.

human: The surprising richness of the topic is seen in the foundationalexistence and uniqueness result; namely, the Koebe-Andreev-Thurston(KAT) Theorem, which states that for any triangulation K of atopological sphere, there exists an associated univalent circlepacking P K of the Riemann sphere P , and that P K isunique up to Möbius transformations (and inversions) of P . Thurston also proposed in [24] a clever algorithm foractually computing such packings, allowing us today to treat circlepacking as a verb: to “circle pack“ a complex K is to create andmanipulate associated circle packings.

Remarkably, this circle packing is unique, except for possible variations due to Möbius transformations and inversions applied to P. Further advancing the field, Thurston offered an ingenious method in [24] to practically compute these packings. Thanks to this methodology, we can now use “circle pack“ as an active verb; to “circle pack“ a complex K involves constructing and manipulating its corresponding circle packings.

human: It is the conjecture Thurston made about such discrete conformalmappings that kicked off the nearly 40 years of development efforts incircle packing. He suggested that if one were to refine thisconstruction - used circle packings P with ever more and smallercircles - that the resulting circle packing maps f would convergeuniformly on compact subset of D to the classical Riemann Mappingfrom D onto Ω . Shortly thereafter, this was proven byB. Rodin and D. Sullivan [18] in the case of hexagonal circlepackings. This result has subsequently be expanded to nearly fullgenerality by many authors; see [23] for the story.
ai: The nearly four-decade evolution of circle packing in mathematics was notably sparked by Thurston’s hypothesis regarding discrete conformal mappings. He postulated that by progressively enhancing this method with circle packings P comprising an increasing number of increasingly smaller circles, the subsequent circle packing maps f would show consistent convergence on compact subsets of D, aligning with the classical Riemann Mapping from D to Ω. Not long after, B. Rodin and D. Sullivan [18] substantiated this conjecture for hexagonal circle packings. Following this breakthrough, numerous scholars have broadened the findings to encompass virtually every general instance, as detailed in reference [23].

human: In the vicinity of the liquid-vapor critical point, supercritical fluids behave strongly compressibly and, in parallel, thermophysical properties have strong state dependence. These lead to various peculiar phenomena, one of which being the piston effect where a sudden heating induces a mechanical pulse. The coupling between thermal and mechanical processes, in the linear approximation, yields a non-trivially rich thermoacoustics. The numerous applications of supercritical fluids raise the need for reliable yet fast and efficient numerical solution for thermoacoustic time and space dependence in this sensitive domain. Here, we present a second-order accurate, fully explicit staggered space-time grid finite difference method for such coupled linear thermoacoustic problems. Time integration is based on the splitting of the state space vector field representing the interactions that affect the dynamics into reversible and irreversible parts, which splitting procedure leads to decoupled wave and heat equations. The former is a hyperbolic partial differential equation, while the latter is a parabolic one, therefore, different time integration algorithms must be amalgamated to obtain a reliable, dispersion error-free, and dissipation error-free numerical solution. Finally, the thermoacoustic approximation of the supercritical piston effect is investigated via the developed method.

When thermal and mechanical processes are coupled, even within a linear framework, a complex and rich field of thermoacoustics emerges. The broad range of uses for supercritical fluids necessitates the development of numerical solutions that are both fast and efficient, ensuring reliable predictions of thermoacoustic behavior in terms of both time and space within this delicate domain. In response, we have developed a second-order accurate, fully explicit finite difference method utilizing a staggered space-time grid to tackle these coupled linear thermoacoustic issues. The time integration is achieved by dividing the state space vector field, which encapsulates the dynamics-affecting interactions, into reversible and irreversible elements. This division allows the separation into wave and heat equations-the wave equation being a hyperbolic partial differential equation, and the heat equation being a parabolic one-necessitating the fusion of different algorithms for time integration to ensure a numerical solution that is devoid of both dispersion and dissipation errors. In conclusion, our innovative method is employed to examine the thermoacoustic approximation of the supercritical piston effect.
