Regarding heat conduction, thermal equilibration near the critical point is expected to be very slow since thermal diffusivity tends to zero in the vicinity of the critical point (see Figure ). This effect is usually called the ’critical slowing down’. In contrast, a fast temperature equilibration is observed in experiments, which under normal gravity circumstances is explained by the mixing of the fluid induced by buoyancy convection. However, measurements performed under microgravity circumstances presented the same fast equilibration of temperature Straub et al. et al. (1995), but density homogenization was still very slow. The fast temperature equilibration is called ’critical speeding up’ phenomenon, which is explained by Onuki with an isentropic - wave-like - propagation of temperature Onuki et al. et al. (1990).

2503.07449.section: III.2 Time integration via reversible-irreversible splitting
human: A similar approach has already proved to be successful Shang and Öttinger (2020). The main advantage of reversible-irreversible splitting is that different numerical methods can be used for integrating the different vector fields: a symplectic or quasi-symplectic one for the reversible part and a different, generic, one for the irreversible part. This allows for preserving some structure present in the original physical equations, while using an identical numerical method for the different types of processes would destroy that structure, resulting in qualitatively and quantitatively worse results. Identifying reversible and irreversible parts of a vector field is relatively straightforward, while other types of splittings are usually less generalizable (as explored in McLachlan and Quispel (2002)). Additionally, the above-identified hyperbolic and parabolic nature of the corresponding PDE-s makes this splitting a natural choice: the splitting also preserves this distinction.

human: The increasing spread of technologies operating with supercritical fluids requires a deeper understanding and more accurate calculations of the appearing coupled thermomechanical phenomena. In supercritical fluids, due to the relative large thermal expansion, mechanical and thermal processes can be intensively coupled, causing both diffusive and dispersive wave propagation in the medium. To develop and test novel numerical methods supported by physics, the piston effect proves to be a well-suited benchmark problem. Althoughseveral built-in time integration algorithms exist in commercial simulation tools, reliable numerical treatment of multiple time scale problems is a serious challenge for them, raising the need for novel self-developed numerical schemes.

In environments where supercritical fluids are present, the notable thermal expansion results in a strong interconnection between mechanical and thermal activities. This linkage initiates the propagation of both diffusive and dispersive waves throughout the medium. The piston effect emerges as particularly valuable for the innovation and validation of new numerical methods grounded in physical principles. Although numerous built-in time integration algorithms are available in commercial simulation tools, effectively handling problems that involve multiple time scales remains a formidable challenge. This complexity underscores the necessity for the development of specialized numerical schemes designed specifically to address these intricate scenarios.

human: During preparing the numerical procedure introduced here, we have reviewed the governing equations of linearized thermoacoustics, addressing thermodynamical questions such as entropy-preserving and entropy-increasing contributions. We have then developed a second-order accurate, fully explicit numerical time integration scheme for the linearized equations of thermoacoustics. The method is based on the splitting of the generating vector field of the spatially semi-discretized equations into reversible and irreversible - entropy-preserving and entropy-increasing - contributions. The method is applicable for nonlinear equations, too. Within the framework of linear partial differential equations, this procedure leads to the numerical splitting of the governing equations into wave and heat equations, therefore, these separated parts can be numerically integrated according to their own individual mathematical properties. Since the presented method is fully explicit, treating material nonlinearities does not cause any particular complications, material properties should be considered as functions of the state variables and should be evaluated at the appropriate time instant, when values of the state variables are already known. Nonlinear treatment of thermofluid dynamical problems leads to the emergence of the convective terms, however, we do not expect any extra complications at this time, an accurate scheme developed to solve the advection equation can be implemented into the sequence of splitting steps. The generalization of the method to 3 spatial dimensions can be done directly along the lines of Pozsár et al. et al. (2020). A further advantage of the developed scheme is that the discrete problem can be formulated by finite difference equations, which methods are successfully implemented on GPUs and offer an attractive tool for fluid dynamical simulations Pekkilä et al. et al. (2017). Implementing finite difference methods on GPU can offer about 5 times speed-up compared to implementing finite element methods on the same GPU Arduino et al. et al. (2021).
ai: In the course of crafting the numerical method detailed here, we thoroughly examined the fundamental equations governing linearized thermoacoustics, particularly focusing on thermodynamic aspects like components that conserve or increase entropy. We subsequently devised a time integration scheme for the linearized thermoacoustic equations that is second-order accurate and completely explicit. Our approach involves decomposing the generating vector field of the spatially semi-discretized equations into contributions that either preserve or augment entropy-these are reversible and irreversible components. This approach is not limited to linear problems; it can also be applied to nonlinear equations. Specifically, for linear partial differential equations, this technique results in the numerical division of the governing equations into wave and heat equations, thereby allowing these distinct sections to be integrated numerically based on their unique mathematical characteristics. The method we propose boasts complete explicitness, which means handling material nonlinearities poses no unique challenges. Here, material properties are treated as functions of the state variables and should be evaluated at the necessary time point, provided the state variables’ values are already determined. When addressing thermofluid dynamics in a nonlinear context, convective terms typically emerge; nonetheless, we currently foresee no significant obstacles. It is feasible to integrate an accurate advection equation-solving scheme into our splitting sequence. Furthermore, the method extends naturally to three spatial dimensions, directly following the methodology outlined in Pozsár et al. 2020. One notable advantage of our scheme is the ability to establish the discrete problem using finite difference equations. Such methods have been effectively implemented on GPUs, providing a robust tool for fluid dynamics simulations, as noted by Pekkilä et al. 2017. Employing finite difference techniques on GPUs can yield a performance enhancement of roughly fivefold compared to utilizing finite element methods on the same hardware, as reported by Arduino et al. 2021.

human: The approach presented here may be generalized to other dynamic problems where a coupled process takes place at significantly different time scales. In such cases, dispersion and dissipation error-free numerical solutions are required to reliably predict the time evolution of some physical quantities. One such problem is condensation induced water hammer phenomenon, which causes significant thermohydraulic transients (high-amplitude pressure waves) in the primary loop of nuclear power reactors, which can lead to deformations or even to the breakage of pipelines. The study presented by Barna (see also Imre et al. et al. (2010)) reports unphysical pressure peaks - dispersion error - obtained by numerical calculations and inapplicability of the commercial thermohydraulic tools RELAP5 and CATHARE. Figures presented in Datta et al. et al. (2016) reveal similar dispersion errors. Condensation induced water hammer phenomenon is modeled via two-phase flow equations, therefore, the corresponding generalization of our presented method is required to treat this problem via our scheme. Another seminal area where the approach presented here is expected to be beneficial is sonochemistry (see, ).
ai: The method outlined in this research holds the potential for broad application to other dynamic issues characterized by coupled processes occurring on markedly distinct time scales. In situations where this is the case, it is imperative to achieve numerical solutions that are free from dispersion and dissipation errors to accurately forecast the temporal progression of certain physical properties. One particular challenge in this realm is the condensation-induced water hammer phenomenon. This issue results in considerable thermo-hydraulic transients, manifesting as high-amplitude pressure waves, within the primary loop of nuclear power plants. Such waves pose the risk of causing deformations, or in extreme scenarios, the rupture of pipelines. Barna’s study (refer also to Imre et al. 2010) highlights how numerical calculations have led to unphysical pressure peaks due to dispersion errors, while also noting the limitations of commercial thermohydraulic software like RELAP5 and CATHARE. Similarly, findings illustrated in Datta et al. 2016 expose comparable dispersion errors. Since the phenomenon of the condensation-induced water hammer is modeled using two-phase flow equations, it necessitates an adaptation of our proposed method to address this issue effectively through our approach. Additionally, another pioneering field where this method is anticipated to have significant success is sonochemistry (as indicated by related studies).

human: Many problems arising in science and engineering often contain dimensionless parameters that appear when suitable non-dimensionalisation is employed. For barotropic/full Euler systems, the Mach number appears as a parameter (denoted by ε ), which dictates whether the flow is compressible ( ) or incompressible ( ). The appearance of such a small parameter in the denominator also leads to stiffness in the system, reflected in wide disparity of propagating wave speeds. It has been rigorously proved in [25, 26, 35] that the solutions of such hyperbolic systems converge to those of mixed hyperbolic-elliptic incompressible system when ε approaches zero. Explicit numerical methods for these systems require restrictive dependent stability condition on time step, and hence they become computationally very expensive when ε becomes small. Further, Godunov-type compressible flow solvers suffer from loss of accuracy as numerical dissipation is inversely proportional to ε [14]. Fully implicit numerical methods, on the other hand, are complicated to implement due to non-linearity of the Euler systems. Hence, attempts were made to efficiently extend the compressible flow solvers to incompressible/low Mach number limit consisting of divergence-free constraint on velocity field. In particular, semi-implicit time stepping techniques allow for the compressible solver to transform into an incompressible solver as ε becomes small, and its stability requirements are independent of ε . Such schemes are called asymptotic preserving (AP) schemes, first introduced by Jin [23] for kinetic equations and later extended to hyperbolic systems (see [24] for review). Semi-implicit time stepping is often achieved by implicit-explicit (IMEX) approach involving implicit treatment of stiff terms and explicit treatment of non-stiff terms. Several IMEX-AP schemes have been formulated by using different strategies to split the flux into stiff and non-stiff parts, and we refer the interested reader to [13, 39, 11, 21, 4, 27, 5, 15, 7, 16, 42, 6, 43, 2, 34]. In addition to asymptotic preserving properties, another crucially required property for a numerical method is its stability. For the Euler equations, this also means non-linear stability dictated by the second law of thermodynamics, the entropy inequality. Consequently, entropy stability has emerged as a non-linear stability criterion for numerical schemes since the seminal work of Tadmor [36, 37, 38]. Several entropy stable numerical methods for different hyperbolic systems have been developed. These include developments specific to shallow water equations [18, 40, 28, 1], the Euler equations [3, 22, 29, 30, 8, 31, 32, 19, 12, 10, 41],and magnetohydrodynamics equations [9]. However, these entropy stable schemes were proposed for fixed Mach number ( ε being order one). On the other hand, the governing system is associated with an entropy inequality for all non-zero values of ε . Hence, our aim in this paper is to develop a numerical scheme that is entropy stable for different values of ε , and also AP as ε approaches zero. As fas as we are aware, this question has not yet been studied in literature. The present paper makes the first step in this research direction, discusses possible discretisation strategies, and validates them by a series of numerical experiments. The paper is organised as follows: Section presents the barotropic Euler system, its entropy stability property for different values of Mach number ε , and its asymptotic limit as ε approaches zero. Section presents the numerical method that employs an IMEX-AP time discretisation in the spirit of [15, 6], and three different space discretisation strategies. The asymptotic preserving property of fully discrete scheme is also presented. Section presents the numerical validation of our scheme by depicting the AP and entropy stability properties. Section concludes the paper.

human: In this paper, we have derived and analysed entropy stable methods in the low Mach number regime. First, an entropy inequality corresponding to convex entropy function depending on Mach number ε is derived for the baratropic Euler system. Then, in order to accurately and efficiently approximate low Mach number regimes in the barotropic Euler system, the IMEX-type discretisation in time is combined with a suitable entropy stable discretisation in space yielding asymptotic preserving methods. We have proposed three strategies for dicretisation in space and analysed them with respect to accuracy and entropy stability. Numerical experiments confirm entropy stable approximation in the low Mach number regime.
ai: In this research endeavor, we meticulously explored and developed methods that maintain entropy stability within the context of low Mach number conditions. Initially, we established an entropy inequality linked to a convex entropy function that varies with the Mach number ε, specifically tailored for the barotropic Euler system. To adeptly and effectively approximate these low Mach number scenarios within the barotropic Euler framework, we employed an IMEX-type temporal discretization, ingeniously combined with a carefully chosen, entropy-stable spatial discretization. This synthesis results in methods that preserve asymptotic characteristics. We put forward three distinct strategies for spatial discretization, thoroughly analyzing each concerning their precision and capacity to maintain entropy stability. Our numerical experiments validate that the methods provide reliable entropy-stable approximations when tackling scenarios at low Mach numbers.

human: A characteristic Galerkin-type semi-Lagrangian discontinuous finite element scheme (CSLDG) is investigated,which directly discretizes an integral invariant model derived from the coupling of a transport equation and its dual equation.Despite extensive research on the numerical implementation of this method,no studies have yet explored the well-posedness of the integral invariant model itself.To address this gap, a weak solution theory for CSLDG is developed:A precise definition of the weak solution for the integral invariant model is formulated.Utilizing the “slice method,“ which is frequently employed in existence proofs for parabolic equations,the existence of the weak solution is established through the application of the Riesz Representation Theorem and mollifier techniques.The stability of the integral invariant weak solution is subsequently demonstrated by the strategic selection of the test function Ψ ,leading to the proof of its uniqueness.
ai: A characteristic type of Galerkin semi-Lagrangian discontinuous finite element method, known as the CSLDG scheme, is analyzed in this study. It directly discretizes an integral invariant model that results from the combination of a transport equation and its corresponding dual equation. Although there has been significant investigation into the numerical execution of this approach, there remains an absence of research regarding the well-posedness of the integral invariant model itself. In an effort to fill this void, a theory surrounding the weak solution for the CSLDG is developed. This involves crafting an exact definition of what constitutes a weak solution for the integral invariant model. By employing the “slice method,“ a technique often utilized in proving the existence of solutions to parabolic equations, the existence of this weak solution is confirmed through the application of the Riesz Representation Theorem alongside mollifier techniques. Following this, the stability of the weak solution pertaining to the integral invariant is demonstrated. This is accomplished through the careful selection of the test function Ψ, which ultimately establishes the uniqueness of the solution.

human: Over the course of the upcoming High-Luminosity LHC (HL-LHC) era, the integrated luminosity is expected to rise by an order of magnitude when compared to the end of Run-3 (Schmidt 2016, ). The measurements made at the LHC need to be statistically compared with Monte-Carlo (MC) generated simulated events, and the predicted precision of HL-LHC experiments necessitate not only an order of magnitude increase in the number of generated events, but also of their precision (HSFPhysicsEventGeneratorWG:2020gxw, ). In perturbative quantum field theory (QFT), this entails moving from predictions made at leading order (LO) to ones at next-to-leading order (NLO).

The anticipated sharp enhancement in precision for HL-LHC experiments calls for not only a substantial increment in the quantity of events generated but also a marked improvement in their exactitude, as outlined by the HSF Physics Event Generator Working Group in 2020. Within the domain of perturbative quantum field theory QFT, this requirement propels us to transition from making projections at the leading order LO to advancing towards next-to-leading order NLO predictions.

human: Spatial distributions are defined via a Fourier transform of the matrix elements evaluated in some particular frame. Three-dimensional EMT distributions in the Breit frame (BF) have been introduced in Polyakov (2003). BF distributions are known to be plagued by relativistic recoil corrections which spoil their interpretation as genuine densities. Alternatively, the light-front (LF) formalism allows one to define genuine two-dimensional relativistic densities in the Drell-Yan frame (DYF) Burkardt (2000, 2003); Miller (2007, 2010). The LF EMT distributions for an unpolarized nucleon with vanishing transverse momentum have been introduced in Lorcé et al. (2019) and shown to coincide with the EMT distributions in the infinite-momentum frame (IMF). These LF distributions have then been generalized to arbitrary values of the nucleon transverse momentum Freese and Miller (2021). As a result of the Galilean symmetry of the LF formalism in the transverse plane, the intrinsic LF distributions simply coincide with those defined at vanishing transverse momentum. An annoying feature of this formalism is that transverse nucleon polarization induces distortions in e.g. the LF charge Carlson and Vanderhaeghen (2008) and LF momentum Abidin and Carlson (2008) distributions.

The frame dependence of these distributions has then been studied in detail and illustrated using a simple multipole model for the EMT form factors.

We utilized the quantum phase-space formalism to explore these distributions specifically for nucleons, incorporating for the first time the impact of the transverse polarization of nucleons into our analysis. Our primary focus has been on the “longitudinal“ components of the EMT. In this context, we have articulated and elaborated the scaled distributions pertaining to energy, longitudinal momentum, longitudinal energy flux, and longitudinal thrust. Importantly, these elements have been dissected into their respective quark and gluon contributions. We have thoroughly examined the frame dependence inherent in these distributions and employed a straightforward multipole model for the EMT form factors to effectively illustrate our findings.

human: More specifically, we have demonstrated that the spin structure of the EMT matrix elements is the simplest in the Breit frame, which can be thought of as the average rest frame of the system. The latter is therefore the natural frame for defining the intrinsic EMT distributions. We have also explicitly shown that the structure of the relativistic distributions for arbitrary values of the nucleon longitudinal momentum results from a combination of both the familiar mixing of the rank-two tensor components under a longitudinal boost and the Wigner spin rotation. In the infinite-momentum frame, all the “longitudinal“ distributions become equal. The mixing of components under a longitudinal boost can be avoided by switching to the light-front components. In this form, we have shown that not only the “good“ T but also the “bad“ distributions coincide in the infinite-momentum frame with those defined within the light-front formalism.

human: The interaction of solitary waves with external wave fields has been extensively studied in the literature using various equations, including the Korteweg-de Vries (KdV) equation [1, 39, 38, 40, 33, 14, 15, 16, 3, 6], the Benjamin-Ono equation [11, 12, 31, 32], the modified KdV (mKdV) equation [9], the Gardner equation [20, 8], and non-integrable models [7, 4, 10]. Understanding the response of wave fields to external forces is important, as these forces can represent a direct pressure distribution on the wave field, variable topography, or even random noise [1, 2]. From a physical perspective, forced equations are utilized as models to investigate a variety of nonlinear wave phenomena. These include ship wakes, fluid flows around obstacles, waves on the surface of a conductive fluid under the influence of an electric field [36], quantum-dimensional film waves, and elastic waves in solids [34]. Additionally, they describe trapped waves [30, 19, 17, 29, 21, 28], as well as wave turbulence in free-surface magnetohydrodynamic and electro-hydrodynamic systems [22, 23, 24, 25, 26, 27].

[18], who demonstrated strong agreement between theoretical predictions and numerical results and established conditions for wave trapping. Most studies have concentrated on localized external forces, with only a few exploring the effects of periodic external forces [30, 8]. The introduction of a periodic force poses a substantial mathematical challenge, as it produces radiation throughout the domain as the force moves. This pervasive radiation complicates the task of distinguishing between radiation arising from the interaction of the solitary wave with the external force and that originating solely from the periodic force. The pioneering work on solitary wave interactions with a periodic external force was conducted by Malomed et al. [30], who introduced a change of variables to filter out the linear wave interactions generated by the periodic force. Building on this approach, Flamarion and Pelinovsky [8] later applied the method to the Gardner equation, establishing conditions under which waves could be trapped by the external force.

human: This work aims to investigate, both numerically and asymptotically, the interaction between solitons and an external force with variable speed, using the forced modified Korteweg-de Vries (mKdV) equation with positive cubic nonlinearity. The mKdV equation supports breathers-traveling oscillatory wave packets-as well as solitons of both polarities [35, 5]. In this work, we qualitatively and quantitatively compare asymptotic and numerical results and discuss conditions for soliton trapping. Specifically, we demonstrate that while the asymptotic theory predicts the existence of perfect resonance between the soliton and the external term, with closed orbits in the soliton-amplitude vs. soliton-phase space, this behavior is not observed in direct numerical simulations. Instead, numerical simulations reveal that the soliton behaves as an unstable spiral, spiraling outward more rapidly as the external force wavelength increases. Notably, when the wavelength of the periodic force is short, the soliton nearly exhibits perfectly closed trajectories. Besides, when the external force oscillates with time, a resonant frequency is derived.
ai: This study seeks to explore the dynamics, both through computational methods and asymptotic analysis, of how solitons interact with an external force whose velocity changes over time, employing the forced modified Korteweg-de Vries mKdV equation characterized by a positive cubic nonlinearity. The mKdV equation is known for accommodating breathers, which are oscillatory wave packets that exhibit traveling behavior, along with solitons that can possess either positive or negative polarity [35, 5]. The investigation involves a qualitative and quantitative juxtaposition of asymptotic theory against numerical outcomes, alongside an examination of the conditions conducive to soliton capture. Particularly, we illustrate that although the asymptotic framework suggests a scenario where there is flawless resonance between the soliton and the external force-resulting in closed loops within the soliton-amplitude versus soliton-phase plane-this specific behavior fails to manifest in the numerical simulations conducted. Contrarily, the simulations depict the soliton as engaging in an unstable spiral, with its outward trajectory accelerating in response to an increase in the external force’s wavelength. Interestingly, in instances where the force exhibits a shorter wavelength period, the soliton traces paths that are almost entirely closed. Moreover, when the external force undergoes temporal oscillation, a resonant frequency emerges and can be precisely determined.

human: In this work, we have investigated the interactions of solitons with a periodic external field within the modified Korteweg-de Vries (mKdV) framework, employing both asymptotic analysis and direct numerical simulations. Interestingly, we found that the asymptotic results qualitatively diverge from the behavior observed in the numerical simulations. Specifically, while the asymptotic approach predicts an equilibrium center and closed orbits in the soliton-crest vs. soliton-amplitude phase space, the numerical simulations reveal unstable spiral trajectories under the same conditions. Notably, however, the soliton remains near its initial position during early times, consistent with both approaches.
